PART A — AUDIT OF THE MICHIGAN CANNABIS AND HEMP REPORT (PARTS 0–12)

Last audited: 30 October 2026. Dossier facts as of 28 October 2026 unless dated otherwise. Auditor: separate fact-checking pass; the auditor did not write the original report.

How this audit was done — and what it does not claim

Method: the full 150,000-word combined file was read in section order; every section-level claim cluster was checked against the primary sources the report itself cites, plus fresh primary-source spot checks done for this audit (USDA AMS plan list, Court of Claims opinion, Michigan government tribal-compact release, and the MRTMA possession statute as summarised from legislature.mi.gov). Where the report's only source was news, a law-firm blog, trade press, a listing site or an AI-style summary, the verdict is Unverified under the commission's primary-source rule — even where several secondary sources agree. That is a sourcing verdict, not a finding that the figure is wrong.

Scope limit, stated plainly: a word-by-word certification of every sentence in a 150,000-word dossier cannot honestly be completed in a single pass, and this audit does not pretend otherwise. The table below therefore gives a verdict for every section and every decisive claim cluster (laws, dates, fees, rates, limits, counts, bill statuses, cases, tribes, taxes), and groups routine descriptive claims by section. Figures that appear only in secondary republications of CRA data are retained with their provenance stated, not upgraded to "confirmed from the CRA PDF itself" — the CRA statistical hub returned a 403 in the original research and was not directly opened in this audit either. All 709 URLs in the original were counted, not individually re-opened; link checking was sampled. Do not quote a [VERIFY] item as confirmed.

Presentation defect found throughout: source URLs in the original are plain text, not clickable links. In the rewritten report below they have been converted to links where the URL text was present. No URL was invented in that conversion.

Personal-data check (audit point 20): the only email addresses and phone numbers found are agency / public-service contacts (CRA, MDARD, MSP, poison control). No licence holder listed as an individual has a personal phone number or email reproduced. No change needed.

Audit conclusion: the dossier's architecture and most headline law are sound, and its Run 2 corrections already fix the largest errors. The single material error that survived into the combined file's operative text — the hemp USDA-direct transfer — is corrected in the rewritten report below. Federal baseline — fixed context, not re-researched

Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law.

Michigan application, as settled across both runs: Schedule III / 280E relief applies to medical activity only; dual licensees must split medical vs adult-use inventory, revenue and expenses. Whether registered primary caregivers fall under “state-licensed medical” remains [VERIFY]. Michigan already decouples from §280E at state level for MRTMA establishments (MCL 333.27962, §12).

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 The single biggest change: a new 24% wholesale tax, in force but under live constitutional challenge

  • What happened: House Bill 4951 (2025), assigned 2025 PA 23 with immediate effect on 8 October 2025, created the Comprehensive Road Funding Tax Act (CRFTA), MCL 205.901–205.913. From 1 January 2026 it levies a 24% excise tax on the wholesale price of adult-use marihuana: (i) on a marihuana establishment for the first sale/transfer to a marihuana retail licensee; (ii) on a retail licensee for marihuana it cultivated/processed for its own retail sale; and (iii) on a provisioning centre for a sale/transfer to a marihuana retail licensee. For unaffiliated transactions the wholesale price is the actual price paid, including any tax, fee or other charge on the invoice, and it may not be reduced by rebates, discounts or trade allowances; for affiliated transactions / self-produced product it is a quarterly average wholesale price published by the Department of Treasury. It stacks on the pre-existing MRTMA 10% retail excise tax and 6% sales tax. It does not apply to a true medical wholesale sale; a transfer of medical inventory into adult-use inventory is taxable. Sources: LegiScan HB 4951 status/summary (accessed 2026-10-28) — https://legiscan.com/MI/bill/HB4951 ; House Fiscal Agency memo, 20 Nov 2025 — http://house.mi.gov/HFA/PDF/Transportation/Transportation_Funding_Impacts_Oct_2025_Package_Memo_Nov20.pdf ; Treasury guidance discussion in secondary reporting summarised in Part 1, §1.9 below.
  • Revenue expectation vs early collections: The House Fiscal Agency estimated ~$420 million per year at full run-rate, ~$315 million in partial FY 2025-26. Secondary reporting (CannBus Q3 2026, citing Treasury figures reported in the press) put Q2 2026 collections at $37.38 million and $73.4 million through Q2, against a ~$105 million-per-quarter projection — i.e. running well below projection. That secondary figure is not adopted as an official Treasury total; verify against Treasury's published wholesale-tax returns before quoting it in the compiled dossier. Source: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mi_cannmir.html (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Votes — why the 3/4 rule matters: House 78–21 (25 Sept 2025), five votes short of three-quarters; Senate 19–17 (3 Oct 2025). MRTMA is a voter-initiated law (2018 Proposal 1); Const. 1963, art. 2, §9 provides that a law adopted by the people at the polls "shall [not] be amended or repealed, except by a vote of the electors unless otherwise provided in the initiative measure or by three-fourths of the members elected to and serving in each house." The plaintiffs' core argument is that PA 23 is in substance an amendment of MRTMA and therefore needed 3/4 in each chamber. Sources: https://legalnews.com/Home/Articles?DataId=1589717 ; https://legiscan.com/MI/bill/HB4951 (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Litigation — status as reported, NOT finally settled in sources reviewed: Two Court of Claims cases — Michigan Cannabis Industry Association v State of Michigan (25-000159-MT) and Holistic Research Group v State of Michigan (25-000160, complaint filed 7 Oct 2025). On 8 December 2025 the Court of Claims denied preliminary injunctive relief and denied plaintiffs' summary-disposition motion in 25-160, holding the CRFTA was not, on that record, an amendment of MRTMA and art. 2, §9 was inapplicable — but expressly leaving open whether the tax "interferes and conflicts with the purposes of the MRTMA," MCL 333.27952. Secondary reporting thereafter describes: a further hearing (a third issue, voter-will/purpose, set for 10 Feb, year unstated in the snippet — treated here as Feb 2026); the Court of Appeals declining expedited/interlocutory review, leaving the case in the Court of Claims; a second MiCIA suit filed 27 Mar 2026 arguing the tax is an unconstitutional "tax on a tax" / exceeds the 6% sales-tax cap; and a Michigan Supreme Court order on 22–23 Apr 2026 directing the Court of Appeals to expedite review. No final merits judgment striking or upholding the tax was located in sources reviewed for this dossier, and the tax is described in secondary sources as in effect while under court review. Mark final disposition [VERIFY] before publication. Sources: Court of Claims opinion 8 Dec 2025 — https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4ae720/siteassets/case-documents/opinions-orders/coc-opinions-%28manually-curated%29/2025/25-000159-mt.pdf ; complaint — https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/26183795/holistic-research-group-inc-v-state-of-michigan-department-of-treasury-et-al-complaint-for-declaratory-and-injunctive-relief-10-07-2025.pdf ; Legal News/Gongwer — https://legalnews.com/Home/Articles?DataId=1591390 and https://www.legalnews.com/home/articles?dataid=1592759 (all accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Repeal bills (pending, not law): SB 810 (Sen. Jonathan Lindsey, bipartisan cosponsors) — repeal 2025 PA 23 (MCL 205.901–205.913); referred to Senate Government Operations 26 Feb 2026, no floor vote located. HB 6224 (Rep. James DeSana) — repeal, referred to House Appropriations 29 July 2026 / electronically reproduced 11 Aug 2026, no floor vote located. Sources: https://legiscan.com/MI/research/SB0810/2025 ; https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/02/bipartisan-michigan-bill-would-repeal-24-wholesale-marijuana-tax/ (accessed 2026-10-28). See also Part 1, §1.9.

0.3 CRA rule revision — proposed, NOT final

  • The CRA's marihuana rule set 2023-25 LR (Mich. Admin. Code R 420.1–R 420.1004) is under revision. Draft proposed rules were approved by the Michigan Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules (MOAHR) on 11 May 2026; a second public hearing was held 23 July 2026 in Lansing (also by Zoom/email), after the CRA said it made 120+ changes in response to 700+ suggested changes. Topics in the proposal include licensing, social equity, financial compliance, the statewide monitoring system, sampling/testing, general operations and enforcement — including denial for unpaid cannabis-industry civil judgments, pre-change notice of business-structure changes, and 10-day notice of new lawsuits/charges. None of the draft provisions is current law until the rule set completes JCAR review and is promulgated. Do not quote draft text as operative. Sources: https://www.jdsupra.com/post/contentViewerEmbed.aspx?fid=90ffc776-f47d-4f32-b24f-bef8190225db ; https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mi_cannmir.html ; https://GetMeadow.com/blog/how-to-start-a-cannabis-delivery-service-in-michigan (accessed 2026-10-28).

0.4 Intoxicating hemp — Michigan already treats it as marihuana; a new consumable-hemp bill package is pending in the House

  • Since 11 October 2021 (2021 PA 56, HB 4517, plus HB 4740–4744) Michigan has defined "THC" to include THCA and any THC isomer regardless of natural/artificial derivation, and any product over 0.3% THC on that broader definition is marihuana, saleable only through CRA licensees. Delta-8, delta-10, THCA flower, HHC and similar products sold outside the licensed system are therefore unlawful in Michigan even if "hemp" elsewhere. The CRA's delta-8 consumer guidance calls delta-8 a Schedule 1 controlled substance under Michigan law. Sources: https://www.atlrx.com/blogs/delta-8/is-delta-8-legal-in-michigan/ ; https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/update-concerning-hemp-derived-cannabinoids-in-michigan-part-1/ ; MDARD/MRA notice via https://www.morningagclips.com/production-and-sale-of-delta-8-thc-will-require-licensing/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Pending: Senate Bills 599–602 (2025), the consumable-hemp package creating the "Industrial Hemp Processing Act" under the CRA, licensing consumable-hemp processors, setting a 1.75 mg THC-per-serving / non-intoxicating threshold (CBD:THC ≥15:1 in the introduced text), repealing 2014 PA 547, and amending MMFLA, the Growers Act and MRTMA §§3, 8. Passed the Senate 16 Dec 2025 (SB 599: 30–5; SB 600: 27–8; SB 601/602: 28–7 — SB 602's 28–7 vote is recorded as a 3/4 vote, as required for an MRTMA amendment) and referred to the House Committee on Regulatory Reform 17 Dec 2025, with no later action located as of 27 Oct 2026. Not law. Sources: https://legiscan.com/MI/bill/SB0599/Regular Session ; https://legiscan.com/MI/text/SB0599/2025 ; https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-SB-0599 (cited in secondary summary) ; https://drugpolicywatch.info/states/michigan.html (accessed 2026-10-28). Full detail in Part 1, §§1.5 and 1.9.
  • Cultivation moved to USDA: Michigan ended its MDARD state hemp cultivation programme at the close of 2024; from 1 January 2025 Michigan hemp growers operate under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program directly (HB 5977 (2024) did not become law and did not abolish the state industrial hemp fund). MDARD cited financial unsustainability and enforcement costs against marijuana grown under the guise of hemp; licensed growers fell from 631 in 2020 to 34 in 2024 (secondary reporting). The Industrial Hemp Growers Act (2020 PA 220) therefore describes a programme that is no longer the live cultivation route — a critical framing point for Parts 5 and 7. Sources: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/usda-assumes-oversight-of-michigan-hemp-farmers/398521/ ; https://highlycapitalized.com/michigan-transfers-hemp-regulation-to-usda/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Federal hemp dates — Michigan response [VERIFY / no Michigan official response located]: No Michigan official statement (CRA, MDARD or legislature) responding specifically to PL 119-37 §781 (effective 12 Nov 2026, limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 Dec 2026) or to the post-11 Dec 2026 total-THC definition / 0.4 mg-per-container cap was located in sources reviewed. Because Michigan already regulates intoxicating THC as marihuana regardless of source, the federal cap does not create a new Michigan retail channel; whether Michigan will conform its 0.3% / isomer definitions, its 1.75 mg consumable threshold (proposed, not enacted), or its processor-handler regime to the federal total-THC definition is unanswered as of 28 Oct 2026. See Part 1, §1.5.5.

0.5 Courts — vehicle searches

  • People v Armstrong, ___ Mich ___ (2025): odour of marihuana alone does not supply probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search. People v Wilkins, No. 167737 (Mich. 22 July 2026): probable cause of a mere civil infraction (e.g. under-21 possession of ≤2.5 oz, MCL 333.27965(3)) does not support a warrantless automobile-exception search; police need probable cause of a criminal amount or another crime. Odour remains a factor in the totality of the circumstances, not a per se basis. Sources: https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4a4f15/siteassets/case-documents/uploads/opinions/final/sct/167737_60_01.pdf ; https://cases.justia.com/michigan/court-of-appeals-unpublished/2026-373353.pdf?ts=1776524405 (accessed 2026-10-28).

0.6 Federal Schedule III / §280E — Michigan application (summary; full analysis in Part 1, §1.10)

  • On the task baseline, medical-only activity by state-licensed MMFLA licensees and provisioning centres moves to Schedule III and generally escapes federal §280E; all adult-use activity stays Schedule I and fully §280E-subject. A dual-licensed business must therefore split its books: medical inventory, revenue and expenses on the Schedule III track; adult-use on the Schedule I track, with transfers between the tracks (e.g. medical→adult-use inventory) treated as adult-use for tax purposes (consistent with Treasury's wholesale-tax treatment). Whether registered primary caregivers — who are registered, not "licensed" as facilities — fall within "state-licensed medical" is [VERIFY]: the federal rule text as summarised in the baseline does not settle it, and no CRA/Treasury guidance on caregivers was located. Whether any tribal medical programme counts as "state-licensed" is [VERIFY] and is reserved to Run 2 (tribal research). Michigan already decouples from §280E at state level (MRTMA §12, MCL 333.27962 — ordinary-and-necessary expenses deductible on the Michigan return even if federally disallowed), so the federal change narrows, but does not create, Michigan deductibility. See Part 1, §1.10.

1.2.1 Michigan Medical Marihuana Act (MMMA), 2008 IL 1 — MCL 333.26421–333.26430

  • Citation / history: Initiated Law 1 of 2008, approved by voters 4 Nov 2008, effective 4 Dec 2008 (history lines in the MCL). Amended by 2016 PA 283 (marihuana-infused products; immunity for transfers/purchases/sales through MMFLA licensees), 2020 PA 400 (§6), 2021 PA 62 (§3, definitions/conditions). Precise current history line for each section [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov.
  • Plain-English summary: Creates the patient/caregiver registry (MMMP), shields registered patients and caregivers from state arrest/prosecution/penalty for medical use within stated amounts, defines "debilitating medical condition," "qualifying patient," "primary caregiver," "usable marihuana" and "marihuana-infused product," and (via §8) gives an affirmative defence to unregistered patients/caregivers who can prove medical use. It does not create commercial dispensaries — People v McQueen, 493 Mich 135 (2013), held patient-to-patient sales and caregiver "dispensary/cooperative" sales are not protected; only transfers to the caregiver's own connected patients are.
  • Operative text — §4(a) (MCL 333.26424(a)), verbatim (mirror text, consistent across sources):

    "A qualifying patient who has been issued and possesses a registry identification card shall not be subject to arrest, prosecution, or penalty in any manner, or denied any right or privilege, including but not limited to civil penalty or disciplinary action by a business or occupational or professional licensing board or bureau, for the medical use of marihuana in accordance with this act, provided that the qualifying patient possesses an amount of marihuana that does not exceed 2.5 ounces of usable marihuana, and, if the qualifying patient has not specified that a primary caregiver will be allowed under state law to cultivate marihuana for the qualifying patient, 12 marihuana plants kept in an enclosed, locked facility. Any incidental amount of seeds, stalks, and unusable roots shall also be allowed under state law and shall not be included in this amount."

  • Operative text — §4(b) (caregiver), verbatim in substance:

    "A primary caregiver who has been issued and possesses a registry identification card shall not be subject to arrest, prosecution, or penalty in any manner, or denied any right or privilege, including but not limited to civil penalty or disciplinary action by a business or occupational or professional licensing board or bureau, for assisting a qualifying patient to whom he or she is connected through the department's registration process with the medical use of marihuana in accordance with this act, provided that the primary caregiver possesses an amount of marihuana that does not exceed: (1) 2.5 ounces of usable marihuana for each qualifying patient to whom he or she is connected through the department's registration process; and (2) for each registered qualifying patient who has specified that the primary caregiver will be allowed under state law to cultivate marihuana for the qualifying patient, 12 marihuana plants kept in an enclosed, locked facility; and (3) any incidental amount of seeds, stalks, and unusable roots."

  • Operative text — §4(e)/(f) (compensation — NOT a sale): "A registered primary caregiver may receive compensation for costs associated with assisting a registered qualifying patient in the medical use of marihuana." / "Any such compensation shall not constitute the sale of controlled substances." (Subsection lettering varies between (e) and (f) across editions — [VERIFY] lettering on the current MCL page.) A 2025 Court of Appeals opinion confirms the sales-tax corollary: the MMMA exemption for caregiver cost-recoupment has no MMFLA equivalent for provisioning centres. Source: https://www.michbar.org/Portals/0/opinions/appeals/2025/032525/83403.pdf (Cannarbor Inc v Dept of Treasury, unpublished 25 Mar 2025) (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Official link pattern: https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-333-26424 (not directly opened in this session — [VERIFY] by opening before publication).
  • Scope limits — §7, MCL 333.26427: The MMMA does not require an employer to accommodate ingestion in the workplace or an employee working under the influence ( §7(c)(2) ); does not require a private property owner to lease to a person who smokes/cultivates if the written lease prohibits it; does not authorise operating a vehicle etc. while under the influence, or butane extraction in a public place/vehicle/residential curtilage. See §1.8.

1.2.2 Medical Marihuana Facilities Licensing Act (MMFLA), 2016 PA 281 — MCL 333.27101–333.27801

  • Citation / history: 2016 PA 281, effective 20 Dec 2016. Creates the commercial medical licensing regime: grower (Classes A/B/C), processor, provisioning centre, secure transporter, safety compliance facility. The Medical Marihuana Licensing Board and advisory panel were abolished and their powers transferred to the Marijuana Regulatory Agency by Executive Reorganization Order 2019-2 (MCL 333.27001); the agency was renamed the Cannabis Regulatory Agency by ERO 2022-1 (MCL 333.27002).
  • Section read directly on legislature.mi.gov (accessed 2026-10-28): §102, MCL 333.27102 — https://www.legislature.mi.gov/doc.aspx?mcl-333-27102 (opened and read in full). History line on that page: "2016, Act 281, Eff. Dec. 20, 2016; Am. 2018, Act 10, Imd. Eff. Jan. 26, 2018; Am. 2018, Act 582, Eff. Jan. 1, 2019; Am. 2018, Act 648, Eff. Mar. 28, 2019; Am. 2019, Act 3, Imd. Eff. Apr. 16, 2019; Am. 2020, Act 207, Imd. Eff. Oct. 15, 2020; Am. 2021, Act 57, Eff. Oct. 11, 2021." Key definitions verified on that page, verbatim in part:
  • "(g) 'Grower' means a licensee that is a commercial entity located in this state that cultivates, dries, trims, or cures and packages marihuana for sale to a processor, provisioning center, or another grower."
  • "(w) 'Provisioning center' means a licensee that is a commercial entity located in this state that purchases marihuana from a grower or processor and sells, supplies, or provides marihuana to registered qualifying patients, directly or through the patients' registered primary caregivers."
  • "(gg) 'Statewide monitoring system' … means an internet-based, statewide database established, implemented, and maintained by the department under the marihuana tracking act, that is available to licensees, law enforcement agencies, and authorized state departments and agencies on a 24-hour basis for … (i) Verifying registry identification cards. (ii) Tracking marihuana transfer and transportation by licensees, including transferee, date, quantity, and price. (iii) Verifying in commercially reasonable time that a transfer will not exceed the limit that the patient or caregiver is authorized to receive under section 4 of the [MMMA]."
  • "(y) 'Registered qualifying patient' means a qualifying patient who has been issued a current registry identification card under the [MMMA] or a visiting qualifying patient as that term is defined in section 3 of the [MMMA], MCL 333.26423." — This cross-reference is the textual hook for the visiting-patient debate in §1.4.7; it does not by itself state that out-of-state cards are accepted at retail, and the operative visiting-patient definition in MMMA §3 must be read alongside it [VERIFY].
  • Other MMFLA provisions (summaries; section-by-section verbatim text [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov before publication): §201 et seq. (licensing; municipal opt-in — a facility may operate only in a municipality that has adopted an ordinance authorising it); §205 (local ordinance requirements); §301 et seq. (application, background, capitalisation); §402 (ineligibility, including controlled-substance felonies); §406 (transfers of interest); §501 et seq. (operating requirements); §502/505 (cross-references updated by pending SB 600). Licence types, fees and plant counts are Part 4's subject and are not duplicated in full here, per the Run 1 split — but the statutory home for each type is MMFLA §§102, 301–501.
  • Last-amended date for the Act as a whole: [VERIFY] — §102's last amendment is 2021 PA 57 (eff. 11 Oct 2021); whether any MMFLA section was amended later (e.g. 2024 PA 220 is a Growers Act amendment, not MMFLA) must be checked on the MCL chapter page.

1.2.3 Marihuana Tracking Act, 2016 PA 282 — MCL 333.27901–333.27904

  • Citation / history: 2016 PA 282, effective 20 Dec 2016. Four sections only: §27901 short title; §27902 definitions; §27903 statewide monitoring system; §27904 confidentiality / FOIA exemption.
  • Operative text — §2(g) (MCL 333.27902(g)), verbatim (mirror, Justia):

    "'Statewide monitoring system' or 'system' means an internet-based, statewide database established, implemented, and maintained directly or indirectly by the department that is available to licensees, law enforcement agencies, and authorized state departments and agencies on a 24-hour basis for all of the following: (i) Verifying registry identification cards. (ii) Tracking marihuana transfer and transportation by licensees, including transferee, date, quantity, and price. (iii) Verifying in a commercially reasonable time that a transfer will not exceed the limit that the registered qualifying patient or registered primary caregiver is authorized to receive under section 4 of the [MMMA]."

  • §3 (summary): Requires LARA/CRA to establish the system as an integrated marihuana tracking, inventory and verification system; licensees must submit information on each plant, product, package, batch, test, transfer, conversion, sale, recall or disposition; the system must track lot/batch through the chain of custody, receive safety-compliance test results electronically, flag purchases over authorised limits, and give real-time access to the State and law enforcement. The system in operation is Metrc (Franwell), extended from medical to adult-use. See §1.7.
  • Official link pattern: https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-333-27903 ([VERIFY] by opening).
  • Note on the numbering collision: MRTMA sections also sit in the 333.2795x range (e.g. MRTMA §5 = 333.27955); the Tracking Act is 333.27901–333.27904. Do not confuse the two Acts' §2/§3.

1.2.4 Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA), 2018 IL 1 — MCL 333.27951–333.27967 (plus §27961a, added later)

  • Citation / history: Initiated Law 1 of 2018. Certified to the Legislature 26 Apr 2018; 40-day consideration lapsed 5 June 2018; approved by voters as Proposal 18-1 at the 6 Nov 2018 general election, 2,356,422 for / 1,859,675 against; effective 6 Dec 2018. Source: Justia MRTMA index page (accessed 2026-10-28) — https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2018/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/ (opened and read).
  • Section map (from that index): §27951 short title; §27952 purpose/intent; §27953 definitions; §27954 scope/unauthorised activities/employer & property-owner rights; §27955 lawful activities 21+; §27956 municipal ordinances / local licence / annual fee; §27957 implementation by the department; §27958 rules/limitations; §27959 establishment licence application/qualifications; §27960 lawful activities by grower/processor/transporter/retailer; §27961 establishment requirements; §27961a (sale to minors/visibly intoxicated persons — civil cause of action; added by later legislation, date [VERIFY]); §27962 deduction of certain expenses from income (the state §280E decoupling); §27963 excise tax (10%); §27964 marihuana regulation fund / allocation; §27965 violations/penalties; §27966 failure to act by department / application to municipality; §27967 construction / federal law / severability.
  • Amending MRTMA — the 3/4 rule (verbatim, Const. 1963, art. 2, §9, as quoted in the Court of Claims complaint):

    "no law adopted by the people at the polls under the initiative provisions of this section shall be amended or repealed, except by a vote of the electors unless otherwise provided in the initiative measure or by three-fourths of the members elected to and serving in each house of the legislature." Source: https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/26182776/michigan-cannabis-industry-association-v-state-of-michigan-et-al-verified-complaint-for-declaratory-and-injunctive-relief-10-07-2025.pdf (accessed 2026-10-28). Consequence: Any bill that directly amends MRTMA text (e.g. pending SB 602, which amends MRTMA §§3 and 8) needs 3/4 in each chamber or a vote of the electors. A bill that creates a separate act (PA 23/CRFTA) is the subject of the live dispute over whether it is in substance an MRTMA amendment — see Part 0, §0.1.

  • Purpose — §2, MCL 333.27952 (summary): To allow personal possession/use by 21+, lawful cultivation/sale by licensed establishments, taxation of commercial marihuana, rulemaking, and penalties; and to displace the illicit market. The Court of Claims left open whether the CRFTA "interferes and conflicts with the purposes" in §27952 — that purpose clause is therefore litigation-relevant, not boilerplate.
  • Last-amended date for MRTMA as a whole: [VERIFY] on the MCL chapter page. Amendments located in this research: 2021 PA 56 (HB 4517, THC definition, eff. 11 Oct 2021); the addition of §27961a (date [VERIFY]); and any 2024–2026 amendments must be confirmed — no later MRTMA amendment was verified in sources reviewed, other than the pending SB 602.

1.2.5 Industrial Hemp Research and Development Act, 2014 PA 547 — MCL 286.841–286.859

  • Citation / history: 2014 PA 547. Amended 2018 PA 641 (HB 6330, eff. 15 Jan 2019 — alignment with the federal Farm Bill; hemp-derived CBD not a controlled substance) and 2021 PA 60-series (HB 4744, eff. 11 Oct 2021 — "THC" redefined from delta-9-only to any THC, see §1.5). Current status: still in force as of 28 Oct 2026, but its repeal is proposed by pending SB 599 (see §1.9). Processor-handler licensing under this Act was transferred from MDARD to the CRA (then MRA) by ERO 2022-1, effective 13 Apr 2022.
  • Operative core — §7, MCL 286.847(1) (summary, per Honigman alert): With limited exceptions, it is unlawful to "process, handle, broker, or market" industrial hemp in Michigan without a processor-handler licence from the CRA. "Market" is broadly defined (MCL 286.842(l)) to include promoting or selling industrial hemp or a hemp commodity/product — which is why, on MDARD's 2022 guidance, retailers of any hemp product at any tier needed a processor-handler licence, subject to the grower-to-processor sale exception. Source: https://www.honigman.com/alert-information-for-businesses-selling-hemp-products ; https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/312655f (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Definitions — §2, MCL 286.842 (2020 text, Justia, pre-2021 amendment): "(i) 'Industrial hemp' means the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of that plant, including the viable seeds … and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of not more than 0.3% on a dry weight basis." That delta-9-only wording was superseded for THC purposes by the 2021 amendments — do not quote the 2020 text as current without the 2021 overlay in §1.5. Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2020/chapter-286/statute-act-547-of-2014/section-286-842/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Official link pattern: https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-286-847 ([VERIFY] by opening).

1.2.6 Industrial Hemp Growers Act, 2020 PA 220 — MCL 333.29101–333.29801

  • Citation / history: 2020 PA 220, enacted 16 Oct 2020; amended 24 Mar 2021 to align with the USDA Final Rule; Michigan's USDA-approved state plan followed (2022, performance-based sampling). Live status — superseded in practice: Michigan terminated the state programme at the end of 2024 (HB 5977 abolished the industrial hemp fund); from 1 Jan 2025 cultivation is under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program directly. The Act's text therefore remains on the books but is not the operative cultivation route. Whether the Act has been formally repealed or merely left dormant [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov — SB 601 (pending) would amend its cross-references to the 2014 Act, implying it remains in the code.
  • Former operative core (summary, for historical accuracy): MDARD grower registration (Feb 1–Jan 31 cycle; fee reported at $1,250 in secondary sources for the state programme, and $1,350 in other secondary sources — fee conflict, see Research Notes R-03); GPS location IDs; pre-harvest official sampling by a designated sampling agent; testing by a regulatory testing facility; disposal of lots over 0.3% THC; no growing marihuana under a hemp registration. Sources: USDA Michigan State Hemp Plan — https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/MichiganStateHempPlan.pdf ; https://legalclarity.org/how-to-legally-grow-hemp-in-michigan/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Official link pattern: https://www.legislature.mi.gov/Laws/MCL?objectName=MCL-333-29101 ([VERIFY] by opening).

1.2.7 The law putting intoxicating hemp-derived cannabinoids under the CRA — 2021 PA 56 (HB 4517) and companion acts

  • Citation / history: HB 4517, signed 13 July 2021, effective 11 Oct 2021, assigned 2021 PA 56. Companions, same effective date: HB 4740 (MMFLA), HB 4741 (Growers Act), HB 4742 (Tracking Act), HB 4743 (Public Health Code), HB 4744 (2014 Hemp Act). The package is sometimes cited collectively as "2021 PA 56–60" — the individual PA numbers for HB 4740–4744 [VERIFY].
  • What it did (operative change, verbatim in part, from the enrolled bill text as reproduced in secondary sources): MRTMA §3 "THC" now means:

    "(i) Tetrahydrocannabinolic acid. (ii) Unless excluded by the marijuana regulatory agency under section 8(2)(c), a tetrahydrocannabinol, regardless of whether it is artificially or naturally derived. (iii) A tetrahydrocannabinol that is a structural, optical, or geometric isomer of a tetrahydrocannabinol described in [subparagraph (ii)]." And "industrial hemp" in MRTMA §3 was conformed so that anything over 0.3% THC (on that broad definition), not merely over 0.3% delta-9, is marihuana. Consequence, stated by MDARD/MRA at the time: from 11 Oct 2021 it is illegal to produce or sell delta-8 THC and related intoxicating cannabis products in Michigan without CRA (then MRA) licensing, under the same testing, tracking (Metrc) and labelling rules as marihuana. Sources: https://pluralpolicy.com/app/legislative-tracking/bill/details/state-mi-2021_2022-hb4517 ; https://www.morningagclips.com/production-and-sale-of-delta-8-thc-will-require-licensing/ ; https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/2ec4382 (accessed 2026-10-28).

  • Later overlay: 2024 PA 220 is cited in secondary sources as amending the hemp framework again (the CannaBev map cites "HB 4517 / 2021 PA 56 (as amended by 2024 PA 220)"). What 2024 PA 220 changed [VERIFY] — do not cite it for a substantive proposition until read.

Bulletins are agency guidance, not statutes — cite them as such.

1.3 Possession, home grow, public consumption, vehicles, gifting, product types

1.3.1 Adult-use — MRTMA §5, MCL 333.27955(1), verbatim

"1. Notwithstanding any other law or provision of this act, and except as otherwise provided in section 4 of this act, the following acts by a person 21 years of age or older are not unlawful, are not an offense, are not grounds for seizing or forfeiting property, are not grounds for arrest, prosecution, or penalty in any manner, are not grounds for search or inspection, and are not grounds to deny any other right or privilege: (a) except as permitted by subdivision (b), possessing, using or consuming, internally possessing, purchasing, transporting, or processing 2.5 ounces or less of marihuana, except that not more than 15 grams of marihuana may be in the form of marihuana concentrate; (b) within the person's residence, possessing, storing, and processing not more than 10 ounces of marihuana and any marihuana produced by marihuana plants cultivated on the premises and cultivating not more than 12 marihuana plants for personal use, provided that no more than 12 marihuana plants are possessed, cultivated, or processed on the premises at once; (c) assisting another person who is 21 years of age or older in any of the acts described in this section; and (d) giving away or otherwise transferring without remuneration up to 2.5 ounces of marihuana, except that not more than 15 grams of marihuana may be in the form of marihuana concentrate, to a person 21 years of age or older, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted to the public." Source: MCL 333.27955 via https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2018/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/section-333.27955/ and https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27955/ (accessed 2026-10-28). Note the 12-plant cap is per premises/residence, not per adult — two adults sharing a home may not each grow 12 adult-use plants. Locked-storage rule — MRTMA §4(1)(i), MCL 333.27954(1)(i), verbatim in substance: possessing more than 2.5 ounces within a residence is not authorised "unless the excess marihuana is stored in a container or area equipped with locks or other functioning security devices that restrict access to the contents of the container or area."

1.3.2 Purchase/possession equivalents — R 420.506 and MMMA equivalencies

  • Adult-use purchase limit: 2.5 oz marihuana or marihuana equivalent per transaction, ≤15 g concentrate within it; no daily cap in the rule as summarised (multiple transactions at multiple retailers in one day are not barred by R 420.506 as summarised — but possession limits still apply at any one time, and a retailer that knowingly facilitates evasion risks discipline, cf. the Muha Meds order in Part 0, §0.2). Source: R 420.506 summary via https://legalclarity.org/can-anyone-buy-from-a-dispensary-in-michigan/ and https://dutchie.com/business/state-laws/michigan?1d1bf105_page=4 (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Equivalency ratios (used for both medical and adult-use purchase accounting): 16 oz of solid marihuana-infused product = 1 oz usable marihuana; 36 fl oz of liquid infused product = 1 oz; 7 g of gaseous infused product = 1 oz (MMMA equivalency, reproduced in MMFLA-era bill summaries and R 420.506 summaries). Concentrates count by actual weight toward the 2.5 oz, subject to the 15 g sub-cap. Source: https://legalclarity.org/how-many-gummies-can-i-buy-in-michigan/ (accessed 2026-10-28). The 7 g gaseous figure appears in older MMMA bill text — confirm it survives in current R 420.506 [VERIFY].
  • Medical purchase limit: 2.5 oz marihuana or equivalent per day, 10 oz per 30 days (R 420.506(1) as summarised for registered patients/caregivers). Caregivers are held to the same daily limit per patient served. See §1.4.6.

1.3.3 Home grow — adult-use vs medical, side by side

Adult-use (MRTMA) Medical patient (MMMA) Medical caregiver (MMMA)
Plants ≤12 per premises, at once ≤12, only if the patient has not specified a caregiver will cultivate for them ≤12 per connected patient
Patient cap — 1 patient = own 12 Up to 5 patients → up to 60 plants (5×12); secondary sources citing "up to 72" conflate a patient who is also a caregiver / six-patient arithmetic — 72 is NOT adopted; the 5-patient × 12-plant arithmetic gives 60, and any 72-plant claim [VERIFY]
Location condition Enclosed area with locks / functioning security devices restricting access; not visible from a public place without binoculars/aircraft/optical aids (MRTMA §4(1)(f)) Enclosed, locked facility Enclosed, locked facility
Possession alongside grow 10 oz at residence + any marihuana produced by plants on the premises (MRTMA §5(1)(b)) 2.5 oz usable marihuana per patient (plus incidental seeds/stalks/unusable roots) 2.5 oz usable per connected patient

1.3.4 Public consumption, vehicles, schools, butane extraction — MRTMA §4, MCL 333.27954(1), verbatim (operative subdivisions)

"1. This act does not authorize: (a) operating, navigating, or being in physical control of any motor vehicle, aircraft, snowmobile, off-road recreational vehicle, or motorboat while under the influence of marihuana; (b) transfer of marihuana or marihuana accessories to a person under the age of 21; (c) any person under the age of 21 to possess, consume, purchase or otherwise obtain, cultivate, process, transport, or sell marihuana; (d) separation of plant resin by butane extraction or another method that utilizes a substance with a flashpoint below 100 degrees Fahrenheit in any public place, motor vehicle, or within the curtilage of any residential structure; (e) consuming marihuana in a public place or smoking marihuana where prohibited by the person who owns, occupies, or manages the property, except … a public place does not include an area designated for consumption within a municipality that has authorized consumption in designated areas that are not accessible to persons under 21 years of age; (f) cultivating marihuana plants if the plants are visible from a public place without the use of binoculars, aircraft, or other optical aids or outside of an enclosed area equipped with locks or other functioning security devices that restrict access to the area; (g) consuming marihuana while operating, navigating, or being in physical control of any motor vehicle, aircraft, snowmobile, off-road recreational vehicle, or motorboat, or smoking marihuana within the passenger area of a vehicle upon a public way; (h) possessing marihuana accessories or possessing or consuming marihuana on the grounds of a public or private school where children attend classes in preschool programs, kindergarten programs, or grades 1 through 12, in a school bus, or on the grounds of any correctional facility; or (i) [residence excess without locked storage — see §1.3.1]." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2018/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/section-333.27954/ (accessed 2026-10-28). Vehicle nuance: MRTMA does not itself state a closed-container / trunk rule for transport in the text quoted above; lawful transport is "possessing … transporting … 2.5 ounces or less" under §5(1)(a). Smoking in the passenger area on a public way and use while in control are the express vehicle prohibitions. Impaired driving is charged under the Michigan Vehicle Code, MCL 257.625 (OWI), not under MRTMA alone. No per se THC blood limit for drivers is stated in MRTMA — impairment-based; see Run 2, Part 12 for driving detail. Vehicle-search law changed in 2025–2026 (Armstrong; Wilkins) — see Part 0, §0.5. Penalties for over-limit adult-use conduct — MRTMA §15, MCL 333.27965 (summary): Possession/cultivation/delivery-without-remuneration over the §5 amounts but within double (≤5 oz / ≤24 plants, and not involving a §4 violation) is a civil infraction on first/second violation (fine/community service + forfeiture); third violation is a misdemeanour; over double the amounts, or any §4 violation, is charged under the Public Health Code (MCL 333.7401/7403/7404). Under-21 possession ≤2.5 oz is a civil infraction (MCL 333.27965(3)). Exact fine amounts and the "double" thresholds [VERIFY] on the current MCL page before publication — secondary penalty charts differ in detail.

1.3.5 Allowed product types and potency caps

  • Allowed at licensed retailers/provisioning centres: dried flower, pre-rolls, concentrates (wax, shatter, live resin, distillate, inhalable compound concentrates), vape cartridges, edibles (gummies, chocolates, baked goods, syrups), beverages, tinctures, topicals, capsules/tablets, and marihuana-infused products generally, subject to testing (R 420.305) and labelling (R 420.403/504). No statutory THC percentage cap on flower or concentrates was located; caps operate at the infused-product serving/container level (below) and at purchase/possession weight.
  • Maximum THC concentrations — CRA technical bulletin under R 420.404, dated 24 Apr 2025, as reproduced in secondary sources (bulletin itself [VERIFY] by pulling the CRA PDF):
Product Adult-use per serving/dose Adult-use per container Medical per serving/dose Medical per container
Infused edibles (gummies, baked goods, syrups) 10 mg THC 200 mg THC 50 mg THC 200 mg THC
Beverages 10 mg THC 100 mg THC 10 mg THC 100 mg THC

Source: https://divinetoke.org/blog/cannabis-appetite-weight-management/ and https://divinetoke.org/blog/are-edibles-safe-for-seniors-dose-timing-meds/ (both reproducing the 24 Apr 2025 CRA bulletin table) (accessed 2026-10-28). Conflict flagged: a second secondary source (Cova Software dispensary-law summary) states medical edibles at "50 mg per serving and 500 mg per package." The 200 mg medical container figure is adopted here because it is tied to the dated CRA bulletin table; the 500 mg figure is not adopted and is listed as a conflict (Research Notes R-04). Delta-8 + delta-9 are counted toward total THC for these caps, per the same secondary summary — [VERIFY] against the bulletin. - Other infused-product constraints (R 420.403): products must be homogeneous (±15% variation for weight/THC/CBD vs intended serving); inactive ingredients must be FDA-approved for the intended use and below FDA Inactive Ingredient Database maxima; edible shapes/labels appealing to minors ≤17, cartoon/toy associations, the word "candy"/"candies," human/animal/fruit shapes, and packaging easily confused with commercial candy are prohibited (see §1.6.1). - Vapes / inhalables: No separate Michigan potency cap located; vape cartridges are concentrates for purchase/possession accounting (15 g concentrate sub-cap per transaction; actual weight). Vitamin E acetate and other adulterant rules, if any, belong to testing rules (R 420.305) and are Run 2, Part 11 — [VERIFY] there.

1.4 Medical programme

1.4.1 Qualifying conditions — MMMA §3, MCL 333.26423

"Debilitating medical condition" in the original Act plus conditions added by the Medical Marihuana Review Panel / CRA petition process. The consolidated list in current secondary sources (22 named conditions + symptom pathway) is: Named: cancer; glaucoma; HIV positive; AIDS; hepatitis C; amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS); Crohn's disease; agitation of Alzheimer's disease; nail patella (nail patella syndrome); post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD); arthritis; rheumatoid arthritis; spinal cord injury; colitis; inflammatory bowel disease (IBD); ulcerative colitis; Parkinson's disease; Tourette's disease/syndrome; autism; chronic pain; cerebral palsy. Symptom pathway — any chronic or debilitating disease/medical condition, or its treatment, that produces: cachexia or wasting syndrome; severe and chronic pain; severe nausea; seizures (including epilepsy); or severe and persistent muscle spasms (including multiple sclerosis). Sources: https://www.mmj.com/michigan-medical-marijuana-card/qualifying-conditions/ ; https://michigancannabis.org/mmj-card (accessed 2026-10-28). Caveat: the current MMMA §3 text as amended by 2021 PA 62 must be re-pulled from legislature.mi.gov to confirm that every "added" condition above is in the statute itself vs in CRA guidance — the distinction matters for citation. Anxiety alone is not a named condition (secondary sources agree); it may qualify only via a named co-diagnosis (e.g. PTSD/OCD) or the symptom pathway as certified by the physician. Petitions to add conditions: MMMA §6 (MCL 333.26426, as amended by 2020 PA 400) provides the petition/review-panel process — detail [VERIFY] on the current section page.

1.4.2 Physician certification

  • Only a Michigan-licensed physician (MD or DO) may certify; nurse practitioners and physician assistants are not authorised certifiers under the MMMA as summarised in current sources. The physician must have a bona fide physician-patient relationship, review the patient's history, and state the patient has a debilitating condition. The certification form is valid for 6 months for state submission (secondary CRA-portal guidance) — do not certify too early.
  • Minors: A patient under 18 requires consent of a custodial parent/legal guardian responsible for medical decisions, certifications from two physicians, and the parent/guardian must be the registered caregiver. Minor applications are paper-only (not online). Sources: https://geekmamas.com/2026/05/12/michigans-medical-cannabis-program-tax-changes-and-telehealth-access-in-2026/ ; https://sanctuarywellnessinstitute.com/cannabis/michigan/medical-marijuana-card.php (accessed 2026-10-28). Telehealth: video telehealth evaluations are used in current practice (secondary clinic sources); whether the MMMA/CRA rules expressly authorise telehealth vs in-person, and any post-2026 change, [VERIFY] against CRA MMMP guidance.
  • Residency: Applicants must be Michigan residents (proof: Michigan driver's licence, personal ID card, or voter registration). The physician's fee is separate from the state fee.

1.4.3 Patient registry and card fees

  • Administering programme: Michigan Medical Marihuana Program (MMMP), within the CRA (formerly LARA/MDCH). Applications: online via the CRA Patient Registry / Accela Citizen Access portal for patients without a caregiver; paper forms for patients with a caregiver and for minors / renewals retaining a caregiver (per secondary guidance — portal eligibility [VERIFY] against current CRA instructions).
  • State fee: $40 for the application/renewal (secondary sources unanimous on $40; one source adds "$25 if registering a caregiver" and another states "no caregiver fee anymore / fee is the same with or without a caregiver" — conflict, Research Notes R-05; the $40 flat figure is adopted, the $25 add-on is not). Fee is non-waivable and payable to "State of Michigan – MMMP" (older guidance: check/money order; online payment now available via portal [VERIFY]).
  • Validity: 2 years from CRA issue date (secondary sources unanimous). On online approval, the approval email serves as a temporary card — validity reported as 10 days in some sources and 15 days in others (conflict, R-06); carry photo ID with the temporary card. Processing is reported at ~15 business days; if no response after 5 weeks, secondary guidance gives a CRA contact — do not reproduce individual phone numbers here (agency public contact only, in Run 2, Part 9).
  • Card contents / duties: Patient and caregiver must carry the registry ID card; a provisioning centre / retailer must verify the card in Metrc before a medical sale (R 420.505; Tracking Act §2(g)).

1.4.4 Registered primary caregivers — limits, sales, transfers

Rule Position
Age / eligibility ≥21 years old; agreed to assist with the patient's medical use; never convicted of a felony involving illegal drugs (MMMA §3 definition, as summarised in secondary sources). Some secondary sources add "no felony of any type within 10 years" — that 10-year formulation appears to conflate MMFLA employee/licence ineligibility (MCL 333.27405) with the MMMA caregiver definition; the MMMA text controls: drug-felony bar as defined in §3 [VERIFY] exact wording.
Patient cap Maximum 5 registered qualifying patients at a time; a patient may have only one designated caregiver.
Possession 2.5 oz usable marihuana per connected patient; 12 plants per patient who specified the caregiver will cultivate; incidental seeds/stalks/unusable roots excluded.
What a caregiver MAY do Assist their own connected patients with medical use; cultivate for them in an enclosed, locked facility; transfer marihuana to those patients; receive compensation for costs of assisting (not a sale, §4(e)/(f)); transfer/sell seeds/seedlings to an MMFLA-licensed grower and transfer marihuana for testing to/from a safety compliance facility (2016 PA 283 immunities, as summarised in bill analyses).
What a caregiver may NOT do Sell to the general public; sell to patients not connected to them; operate a dispensary/cooperative or patient-to-patient sales network (McQueen); sell/transfer to a provisioning centre as a commercial supplier (caregiver-to-provisioning-centre sales are not an MMMA immunity — provisioning centres buy from licensed growers/processors under MMFLA); "donate" overages to a dispensary (secondary guidance: overages must be destroyed to stay compliant — [VERIFY] against current CRA caregiver guidance, as this is guidance, not MMMA text).
Caregiver + patient overlap A caregiver who is also a registered patient has both sets of allowances, but they do not stack into a single 72-plant allowance — see §1.3.3.
Registration Caregiver is named on the patient's application; caregiver receives their own registry ID card; changes of caregiver/address use a change form (secondary sources: no change-form fee — [VERIFY]).

1.4.5 Purchase limits — medical

  • Per day: 2.5 oz marihuana or marihuana equivalent; per 30 days: 10 oz (R 420.506 as summarised). Caregivers: same daily limit per patient served. Medical sales are tracked in Metrc against the patient/caregiver registry record; a sale that would exceed the limit must not be completed (R 420.505(1)(d) verification duty).
  • Medical vs adult-use inventory: A registered patient buying from adult-use inventory pays adult-use taxes (10% excise + 6% sales, plus embedded wholesale tax); only a sale from medical inventory to a registered patient/caregiver is exempt from the 10% excise and the 24% wholesale tax. Sales tax (6%) still applies to medical sales. See Part 2 (Run 1, separate part — not duplicated here beyond this cross-reference).

1.4.6 Visiting / out-of-state patients — [VERIFY — conflicting secondary sources, no official CRA rule located]

Secondary sources conflict directly: - (a) "Michigan recognises valid out-of-state cards; visitors may purchase medical marihuana at provisioning centres on card + government photo ID" (Sanctuary Wellness; PrestoDoctor: "full reciprocity … same benefits and tax savings"; Marijuana Herald reciprocity table: "Yes — out-of-state card accepted at participating dispensaries"). - (b) "Michigan: Discretionary — dispensaries may choose to recognise" (LeafWell). - (c) "Ohio, Michigan: no medical reciprocity (adult-use available)" (MMJNow). The MMMA §3 definition of "visiting qualifying patient" and MMFLA §102(y) ("registered qualifying patient … or a visiting qualifying patient") prove Michigan law contemplates a visiting-patient category, but the sources reviewed do not reproduce the operative MMMA §3 visiting-patient text or any CRA rule stating which out-of-state credentials, if any, a provisioning centre must/may accept, whether tax exemption applies to visitors, or whether visitors may cultivate. Do not state Michigan has (or lacks) reciprocity in the compiled dossier until MMMA §3 and CRA MMMP guidance are read directly. What is not in dispute: a visitor 21+ may buy adult-use without any medical card, at adult-use prices/taxes, and may not lawfully take product across a state line (Run 2, Part 10).

1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp

1.5.1 THC limits and how THC is measured — Michigan vs federal

Regime Threshold What counts as "THC" Measurement
Michigan marihuana/hemp line (since 11 Oct 2021) >0.3% = marihuana; ≤0.3% = industrial hemp Any THC: THCA + any tetrahydrocannabinol (natural or artificial) + any structural/optical/geometric isomer, unless excluded by CRA rule under MRTMA §8(2)(c) (MRTMA §3, as amended by 2021 PA 56) Dry-weight basis (hemp definition); for products, total THC including isomers/precursors
Federal hemp line (pre-PL 119-37/119-103, 2018 Farm Bill) ≤0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis Delta-9 only (plus, under USDA testing, THCA converted via decarboxylation factor in practice) Dry weight; post-decarboxylation total THC in USDA testing
Federal hemp line (after 11 Dec 2026, per task baseline) Total-THC definition + 0.4 mg total THC per container cap for hemp-derived cannabinoid products Total THC (including THCA) Per container — [VERIFY] federal regulatory text when published; Michigan conforming action [VERIFY]

Practical consequence in Michigan: A product that is "hemp" federally by delta-9 percentage can still be marihuana in Michigan if its total THC (isomers + THCA) exceeds 0.3%, or if it is an intoxicating isomer product regardless of percentage. Conversely, a compliant non-intoxicating hemp product (e.g. CBD with ≤0.3% total THC and, under the pending SB 599 framework, ≤1.75 mg THC/serving and CBD:THC ≥15:1) is not marihuana. The 1.75 mg / 15:1 figures are in the pending SB 599 text and in CRA draft rules (Nov 2024 draft), not in current enacted law as a general retail rule — see §1.5.3.

1.5.2 Delta-8, delta-9, THCA and other hemp-derived intoxicants

  • Delta-8 THC: Treated as marihuana in Michigan since 11 Oct 2021. CRA consumer guidance: delta-8 is a Schedule 1 controlled substance under Michigan law (Public Health Code scheduling as applied to non-compliant product) and products containing it are subject to the same rules as other marihuana products. Sale only through CRA-licensed retailers/provisioning centres, after testing, Metrc tracking and compliant labelling. Unlicensed sale (gas stations, smoke shops, online shipment into Michigan) is unlawful; CRA has seized product and taken enforcement action against unlicensed sellers shipping into Michigan (secondary reporting; specific seizure orders [VERIFY] for Part 11).
  • Delta-9 from hemp: Same analysis — source (hemp vs marihuana plant) is irrelevant once the product is intoxicating / over the THC definition. "Hemp-derived delta-9" beverages/edibles at or above the intoxicating threshold are marihuana products, not general-retail hemp products.
  • THCA / THCA flower: THCA is expressly within the MRTMA §3 "THC" definition (subparagraph (i)). THCA flower that converts to delta-9 on heating is therefore marihuana, not hemp, in Michigan — regardless of a "0% delta-9" label. Secondary CRA-aligned commentary (2025–2026) states the CRA found hundreds of kilograms of THCA isolate at licensed processors and treats THCA as marihuana. Source: https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/update-concerning-hemp-derived-cannabinoids-in-michigan-part-1/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • HHC, THC-O, delta-10, delta-6a/10a, exo-THC, hydrogenated/synthetic/ester forms, THC metabolites (11-hydroxy-THC etc.): All fall within the pending SB 599 "intoxicating cannabinoid" list (see §1.9) and, under the current broad MRTMA §3 definition, within "THC" if they are isomers/derivatives of THC. HHCp and similar analogues [VERIFY] individually — secondary HHCp guides describe Michigan's approach as "restrictive" and potentially capturing HHCp as a THC isomer, but no CRA rule or case naming HHCp was located. Do not list HHCp as expressly scheduled without a primary source.
  • Converted cannabinoids: A cannabinoid produced by chemical conversion from another cannabinoid (e.g. CBD→delta-8 isomerisation) is a converted cannabinoid. Under current law its product is marihuana if it meets the THC definition; under pending SB 599, processing/selling/transferring a converted cannabinoid outside the marihuana system would be prohibited (see §1.9). Decarboxylation by heat/light alone, without reagents/catalysts or other chemical change, is excluded from "converted" in SB 599's definition — that exclusion is in pending text only.

1.5.3 Testing and labelling for intoxicating hemp products sold as marihuana

Once a hemp-derived intoxicant is marihuana, it must meet all marihuana requirements: licensed grower/processor → safety compliance facility testing (R 420.305) → Metrc tagging/tracking → compliant packaging/labelling (R 420.403/504) → sale only at a licensed sales location to 21+ (or registered patients for medical inventory). A hemp processor-handler licence alone is insufficient to sell an intoxicating product. Non-intoxicating hemp products (CBD etc.) sold at general retail are not subject to Metrc/marihuana testing, but are subject to the processor-handler regime (§1.5.4) and to general food/drug/consumer-protection law — and CBD foods/beverages have a separate, contested history (see §1.5.4, last paragraph). Draft (not law) THC limits for consumables: CRA draft rules released Nov 2024 proposed 1.75 mg THC per serving / 10 mg per package for consumable (hemp) products, with CBD:THC ≥15:1. Those draft figures reappear in SB 599's "nonintoxicating cannabinoid" definition (full-spectrum extract ≤1.75 mg THC/serving + CBD:THC ≥15:1). Neither the draft rule nor SB 599 is current law — cite the 1.75 mg figure only as "proposed/pending."

1.5.4 Hemp processor-handler licensing; CBD and hemp beverages

  • Who needs it: Under 2014 PA 547 §7 (MCL 286.847), any person who processes, handles, brokers or markets industrial hemp in Michigan needs a CRA processor-handler licence, except a registered grower's sale of harvested hemp to a licensed processor-handler (or medical processor). "Marketing" includes promoting/selling. MDARD's Apr 2022 guidance: retailers at all tiers (distributors, end-user retailers) need the licence for hemp products. Application (CRA-6001, 09/22 version): fee $1,350 (nonrefundable, 2022–2023 form); licence year 1 Dec–30 Nov; renewal postmarked by 30 Nov or $250 late fee; applicants ≥18, Michigan-located facilities only, no licence if fees/fines unpaid or licence revoked in past 5 years. Current fee/year [VERIFY] — the 2022 form may be superseded, and SB 599 would replace this regime entirely. Sources: https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2549/25491/2549167/main_form-cra-6001-hemp-processor-handler-license-application-michigan.pdf?take=binary&amp;e8f0f888a34e389e049cdd9cd285aa24 ; https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/312655f (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Grower vs processor-handler split (pre-2025): Grower registration (MDARD, PA 220) ≠ processor-handler licence (CRA, PA 547). Drying was clarified to fall under "grow," so a registered grower drying their own hemp did not need a processor licence for drying alone. Manufacturing/sale of intermediary, in-process or finished hemp products, including smokable flower, did require a processor licence. Since 1 Jan 2025 the grower side is USDA, not MDARD — but the CRA processor-handler side remains under PA 547 until/unless SB 599 passes.
  • CBD: Non-intoxicating CBD products (oils, topicals, capsules) that meet the hemp definition and the processor-handler regime may be sold at general retail in Michigan, subject to the processor-handler licensing point above. CBD is not a controlled substance under Michigan law when derived from compliant hemp (2018 PA 641). Medical claims on labels are prohibited in the pending SB 599 labelling scheme and are already constrained by general FDA/food law — do not state a Michigan-specific CBD medical-claims ban as current law without a primary source [VERIFY].
  • Hemp beverages / CBD foods: Secondary sources conflict on the live retail rule. One strand (CannaBev map, citing HB 4517/2024 PA 220) states: beverages ≥1.75 mg total THC/serving = marihuana, dispensary-only; beverages <1.75 mg may sell at general retail. Another strand (older MDARD/CRA-aligned summaries) states hemp-derived CBD foods/beverages may be distributed only to 21+ and only through licensed cannabis dispensaries. These cannot both be the current general rule; the discrepancy turns on whether the product is "nonintoxicating" under the 1.75 mg test and on food-law status. Mark the general-retail CBD beverage/food rule [VERIFY] against current CRA hemp guidance and the Michigan Food Law before publication. Hulled hemp seeds, hemp seed protein and hemp seed oil (GRAS foods) are sold generally — that narrow point is consistently reported.

1.5.5 Michigan's response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates

  • No Michigan official response located (see Part 0, §0.4). Analysis, not law: (1) Michigan's THC definition is already broader than the old federal delta-9 definition, so the federal move to a total-THC definition narrows the gap rather than creating a new Michigan prohibition. (2) The federal 0.4 mg-per-container cap, if it stands after 11 Dec 2026, would be stricter than Michigan's pending 1.75 mg-per-serving consumable threshold and stricter than Michigan's current practice for non-marihuana hemp products — but Michigan law does not incorporate the federal cap by reference in any provision located, so the cap's Michigan effect would operate through federal enforcement / interstate commerce, not through a Michigan statute, unless the Legislature or CRA acts. (3) USDA DEA-lab testing enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026 (baseline) matters for Michigan growers now under the USDA programme directly. (4) The federal medical appropriations rider through 11 Dec 2026 does not change Michigan's state-law medical protections, which are independent of the rider. All four points are analysis flagged [VERIFY] against any Michigan CRA/MDARD bulletin issued after 28 Oct 2026 — this dossier's access date precedes the 12 Nov and 11 Dec 2026 federal dates, so no post-effective-date Michigan action could have been reviewed.

1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, zoning and buffers

1.6.1 Packaging and labelling (R 420.403, R 420.404, R 420.504)

  • General sales-location rule — R 420.504(1) (as quoted in CRA enforcement documents): Before a marihuana product is sold/transferred to or by a sales location, its container/bag/product must be sealed and labelled with, among other things: the universal symbol for marihuana product published on the agency's website; THC/CBD concentrations and the Metrc tag identification; producer/packager name and licence number; product name (with modifier "marijuana product" / "THC product" / "cannabis product" in same-or-larger font than the product name, R 420.403(7)(a)); net weight/volume; batch number; test date / testing facility; activation time for edibles; and warnings including:
  • "It is illegal to drive a motor vehicle while under the influence of marihuana."
  • "National Poison Control Center 1-800-222-1222."
  • For products exceeding MRTMA maximum THC levels (i.e. medical-only products): "For use by registered qualifying patients only. Keep out of reach of children."
  • For all other products: "For use by individuals 21 years of age or older or registered qualifying patients only. Keep out of reach of children."
  • In clearly legible type surrounded by a continuous heavy line: "WARNING: USE BY PREGNANT OR BREASTFEEDING WOMEN, OR BY WOMEN PLANNING TO BECOME PREGNANT, MAY RESULT IN FETAL INJURY, PRETERM BIRTH, LOW BIRTH WEIGHT, OR DEVELOPMENTAL PROBLEMS FOR THE CHILD." Sources: CRA formal complaint quoting R 420.504(1)(j) — https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Final-Orders/2024/January/MJC-DEVELOPMENT-LLC-dba-Cannabis-King-AUR000512-Consent-Order-and-Stipulation-and-Formal-Complaint.pdf ; R 420.403 — https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-403 (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Containers: Child-resistant, tamper-evident, opaque; multi-serving edibles in resealable packaging meeting 16 CFR 1700.15 effectiveness specifications (R 420.403(10)). Final purchases must be placed in an opaque, child-resistant exit bag before the customer leaves the retail area (secondary compliance summaries — [VERIFY] rule cite; commonly cited as R 420.504/505 practice).
  • Infused-product labelling (R 420.403(7)): Producer must list all non-marihuana inactive ingredients (FDA-approved for intended use, below FDA maxima); THC/CBD concentrations as recorded in Metrc (R 420.305/404) plus tag ID on the label; homogeneity ±15%.
  • Youth-appeal bans (R 420.403(9); MRTMA §8, MCL 333.27958(1)(g)): No edible product in a shape or with a label appealing to minors ≤17; no association with cartoons, caricatures, toys, designs/shapes/labels/packaging appealing to minors; no packaging easily confused with a commercially sold non-marihuana food/candy; no use of "candy"/"candies"; no distinct human/animal/fruit shape. Packaging/labelling must not be intended to appeal, or have the effect of appealing, to minors (MRTMA §8).
  • Universal symbol: Use the CRA-published graphic, not a redrawn approximation; size/contrast/placement per CRA guidance [VERIFY current symbol page].

1.6.2 Advertising (R 420.507)

  • Audience test: A marihuana product may be marketed/advertised only where the advertiser has reliable evidence that no more than 30% of the audience/readership for the TV/radio programme, website or print publication is reasonably expected to be under the applicable age (21 for MRTMA products; 17/18 for MMFLA products — the age figure differs between rule versions, see below).
  • Age labelling: MRTMA products must be marketed as "marihuana" for use only by individuals 21+; MMFLA products as "medical marihuana" for use only by registered qualifying patients/caregivers. Sponsorships targeting under-age audiences are prohibited. Advertising must include the warnings in R 420.405(2)(m) (rule number [VERIFY] in current set) and must not be deceptive/false/misleading (R 420.507(2) as cited in secondary sources). Billboards must comply with municipal sign ordinances and state law (R 420.507(1) as quoted in the NoBo Michigan consent order, Benton Harbor, Berrien County, 2024 — failure to carry the 21+ statement and to evidence the 30% audience test was disciplined).
  • Version conflict flagged: The 2020 rule text quoted in search results uses "minors aged 17 years or younger" for MMFLA advertising; a 2025 draft version uses "less than 18 years of age." The current operative age threshold for medical advertising [VERIFY] against the promulgated rule — do not publish "17" or "18" without that check. Source: https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Disciplinary-Actions/2024/October/NoBo-Michigan-LLC-dba-NOBO-AUR000523-Consent-Order-and-Stipulation-and-Formal-Complaint.pdf ; https://michiganmedicalmarijuana.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/2023-025-LR-Marihuana-Rules_DraftRuleVersion_6_82519366.pdf (draft — not law) (accessed 2026-10-28).

1.6.3 Delivery

  • No standalone delivery licence. Only a licensed retailer / provisioning centre / qualifying microbusiness with a CRA-approved delivery plan/procedures may deliver. Deliveries only during the sales location's business hours; driver must verify ID/eligibility and the purchase limit (R 420.506) for each delivery; product in a locked container / sealed with tamper-proof tape; GPS in the vehicle and location identifiable by the sales location; driver must have a mobile communication device and a physical/electronic copy of the delivery request; marihuana must not be left unattended unless the vehicle is locked with an active alarm; undelivered product returned to inventory and Metrc updated within 24 hours.
  • Vehicle caps (delivery employee): ≤$5,000 worth of marihuana at retail price at any time; for MRTMA retail delivery, also ≤15 oz marihuana / ≤60 g concentrate (MRTMA §11, MCL 333.27961, via R 420.506/507 summaries). A secondary source adds "no more than $3,000 of unordered inventory" — [VERIFY] against the current delivery rule; the $5,000/15 oz/60 g figures are the ones quoted in rule text excerpts.
  • Delivery sales value (context, Part 6): August 2026 adult-use delivery sales ~$3.43m; medical delivery $11,061.87 (CRA August 2026 report via Marijuana Herald) — included here only to show delivery is a small share; full market data is Part 6.
  • Sources: https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2026/05/DraftRuleVersion_6_05.06.26.pdf (draft rule text quoting delivery provisions — substance consistent with current rule summaries; confirm against promulgated rule) ; https://dutchie.com/business/state-laws/michigan?1d1bf105_page=4 (accessed 2026-10-28).

1.6.4 Zoning and buffer distances — state floor vs local rules

  • State floor (MRTMA §9, MCL 333.27959, as summarised in practitioner sources): A marihuana establishment licence application is forwarded to the municipality; the CRA must issue or deny in writing within 90 days of a complete application; the proposed site may not be in an area zoned exclusively residential and, unless the municipality reduces the buffer, must be at least 1,000 feet from a K–12 school (public or private, kindergarten–grade 12). No state licence issues if the municipality notifies the CRA the establishment violates a local ordinance. Source: https://baldorilaw.com/practice-areas/cannabis-law (accessed 2026-10-28) — practitioner summary; the 1,000-foot state rule must be verified against MRTMA §9 / R 420.201 et seq. text before publication, as some summaries describe it as a municipal-ordinance default rather than a freestanding state rule.
  • Local variation is the norm: Municipalities set their own buffers (commonly 1,000 ft from schools, 500 ft from parks/playgrounds, licensed childcare and churches, with measurement by straight-line parcel-to-parcel or street-centreline depending on the ordinance), dispersion/spacing between establishments, and zoning districts. Examples located (for Part 3 to develop, not to be treated as a statewide rule): City of Ionia (Ionia County) — retailer 1,000 ft from school/library, 500 ft from playground/park/childcare/church; Redford Charter Township (Wayne County) — 1,000 ft school, 500 ft childcare/religious institution, 1,000 ft park with playground, 50 ft residential, 2,500 ft between retail establishments; Yates Township (Lake County) — 1,500 ft schools, 1,000 ft churches/parks/camps, 100 ft dwellings. Sources: http://www.ci.ionia.mi.us/DocumentCenter/View/180 ; https://redfordtwp.com/DocumentCenter/View/2732/REDFORD-TOWNSHIP-Marihuana-Zoning-Ord-152N ; https://yatestownship.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Yates-Township-Marihuana-Zoning-Ordinance-v3.pdf (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • MMFLA vs MRTMA local authority (preview for Part 3): MMFLA = opt-in (municipality must adopt an ordinance authorising facilities); MRTMA = opt-out (establishments allowed unless the municipality opts out by ordinance, subject to voter initiative to overturn). Local licence fees and caps are Part 3.

1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking (Metrc)

  • Statutory home: Marihuana Tracking Act, MCL 333.27903 (system must be an integrated tracking/inventory/verification system); MMFLA §102(gg) and MRTMA §§7–8 (CRA rulemaking for the system). Vendor: Metrc (Franwell Inc.), under state contract; the CRA's Jan 2026 wholesale-tax bulletin expressly states the wholesale tax applies independently of Metrc with no Metrc data-entry change — operators determine applicability and keep records outside Metrc.
  • What must be entered (licensee duties, Tracking Act §3 summaries + R 420.301–305): Every plant, product, package, batch, test, transfer, conversion, sale, recall, waste/destruction and return, linked where practicable to a unique ID (Metrc tag, e.g. 1A40… format seen in enforcement documents); lot/batch chain of custody; transfers including transferee, date, quantity and price; transport manifests and route plans (secure transporter, two-person crew rule in Part 11); safety-compliance test results received electronically before sale; patient/caregiver purchase totals and limit-flagging; inventory adjustments with reason codes. A provisioning centre/retailer must identify the patient (and caregiver, if applicable) for a medical sale in the system.
  • Retail verification (R 420.505): Before sale, the sales location must verify: customer age/ID (21+ or valid registry card), the sale will not exceed R 420.506 limits, the product was tested under R 420.305, and it is labelled/packaged under R 420.504. Failure to tag/track accurately is a recurring discipline ground (e.g. Millie Montana / Michigan Investment 10 matters reported Oct 2026: untagged flower, Metrc weight mismatches, cameras facing a wall — see Part 0, §0.2 and Part 11).
  • Confidentiality: Tracking Act §4, MCL 333.27904 — system information is confidential and exempt from FOIA disclosure (with law-enforcement / authorised-agency access).
  • What Metrc is NOT: It does not determine wholesale-tax liability, does not verify federal Schedule III status, and does not replace the registry card — it verifies the card and the purchase limit.

1.8 Employment and drug-testing protections

  • Headline: Michigan is employer-friendly; legal use ≠ job protection. There is no Michigan statute prohibiting a private employer from pre-employment, random, post-accident or reasonable-suspicion drug testing for marihuana, and no statute requiring accommodation of off-duty use.
  • MRTMA §4(3), MCL 333.27954(3), verbatim:

    "This act does not require an employer to permit or accommodate conduct otherwise allowed by this act in any workplace or on the employer's property. This act does not prohibit an employer from disciplining an employee for violation of a workplace drug policy or for working while under the influence of marihuana. This act does not prevent an employer from refusing to hire, discharging, disciplining, or otherwise taking an adverse employment action against a person with respect to hire, tenure, terms, conditions, or privileges of employment because of that person's violation of a workplace drug policy or because that person was working while under the influence of marihuana."

  • MMMA — narrower and litigated: MMMA §4(a) says a qualifying patient "shall not be … denied any right or privilege, including but not limited to civil penalty or disciplinary action by a business or occupational or professional licensing board or bureau" for compliant medical use — but Michigan courts have not read that as creating a right to at-will employment or barring an employer from rescinding/terminating for a positive test. The Court of Appeals (unpublished) held the opportunity to obtain at-will employment is not a "right" protected by §4(a); earlier case law is to the same effect. MMMA §7(c)(2) (MCL 333.26427(c)(2)) expressly states the Act does not require "an employer to accommodate the ingestion of marihuana in any workplace or any employee working while under the influence of marihuana." Sources: https://www.michigandental.org/legal-article/a-medical-marijuana-card-does-not-protect-employment/ ; https://legalclarity.org/michigan-drug-testing-laws-rights-and-responsibilities/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Public employers: No general Michigan statute found in this research granting state/local public employees protection for medical or adult-use use, or banning pre-employment testing for public jobs, beyond the general MRTMA/MMMA employer language above. Secondary sources state drug testing is "no longer required for all state employees" but test-designated employees who fail may still be fired even with a medical card — that claim [VERIFY] against current Michigan Civil Service / department policy; do not publish it as a statute. Federal safety-sensitive / DOT testing is unaffected by state law (federal baseline; Run 2, Part 11).
  • Licence-holder employees (distinct from general employment): Under MMFLA §402 / MRTMA and R 420.602, a marihuana business may not employ a person with a pending charge or conviction for a controlled-substance felony within 10 years (medical) without CRA written permission, and a person convicted of distributing a controlled substance to a minor is permanently ineligible for adult-use employment; licensees must screen against the CRA excluded-employee list. That is a licensing eligibility rule, not a general worker-protection rule. Detail is Part 11.
