1.10 Federal Schedule III / §280E — Michigan application in full

  1. Medical only, and only state-licensed medical. On the baseline, the Schedule III move covers "state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products." In Michigan that maps to: (a) marihuana grown/processed/sold by MMFLA licensees (growers, processors, provisioning centres, and, for testing/transport, safety compliance facilities / secure transporters acting for medical inventory) for registered qualifying patients/caregivers; and (b) FDA-approved products (e.g. Epidiolex-type drugs — not a Michigan licence category). It does not map to MRTMA adult-use inventory, even if the same plant, same licence-holder, or same storefront is involved.
  2. Dual-licence splitting — the operative compliance point. Most Michigan operators hold both medical (MMFLA) and adult-use (MRTMA) licences, often at the same premises with shared staff/systems. For federal purposes they must be able to trace each unit, each dollar of revenue, and each deductible expense to the medical or adult-use track: separate Metrc inventory pools (medical vs adult-use), separate sales records, and a reasonable allocation method for shared overhead. A transfer from medical inventory to adult-use inventory converts the product to the adult-use track at transfer: it becomes subject to the 24% wholesale tax (Treasury treatment, Part 0, §0.1) and, on the baseline, to Schedule I / §280E treatment from that point. The reverse transfer (adult-use → medical) does not retroactively create Schedule III status for the period it was adult-use, and whether a provisioning centre may re-designate adult-use inventory as medical inventory at all is a CRA inventory rule question [VERIFY] — do not advise re-designation without a CRA rule cite.
  3. Registered primary caregivers — [VERIFY]. Caregivers are registered under the MMMA (registry ID card), not licensed as facilities under MMFLA. The baseline phrase "state-licensed medical" does not, on its face, clearly include or exclude a registration regime. Arguments for inclusion: the caregiver is state-registered, acts only for registered patients, and is part of the state medical programme. Arguments for exclusion: 91 FR 22714 (as described in the baseline) speaks of state-licensed activity, and caregivers are not licensees subject to CRA facility licensing, inspection, testing and Metrc as licensees are (caregiver product is not Metrc-tracked as commercial inventory). No IRS, DEA or Treasury guidance on caregivers was located in this research. Treat caregiver Schedule III / §280E status as unresolved; caregivers should not be advised they are Schedule III taxpayers on the basis of this dossier. Note also: caregiver "compensation for costs" is not a sale under MMMA §4(e)/(f) — its federal income-tax character is a separate question from scheduling and is [VERIFY] for tax advice.
  4. Tribal medical programmes — [VERIFY], reserved to Run 2. If any Michigan federally recognised tribe operates a medical programme (tribal licence, tribal registry, or tribal-state compact), whether that programme counts as "state-licensed" for 91 FR 22714 is unresolved on the baseline and on sources reviewed. Tribal operations are not researched in depth here per task; Run 2, Part 10 must answer: (i) does the programme exist; (ii) is it licensed by the tribe, the state, or both; (iii) is there a compact deeming tribal licensees equivalent to state licensees. Until then, do not describe any tribal product as Schedule III.
  5. Michigan §280E decoupling — already in place, unaffected in principle. MRTMA §12, MCL 333.27962 ("Deduction of certain expenses from income") permits a marihuana establishment to deduct ordinary-and-necessary business expenses on its Michigan return that are disallowed federally by §280E. Secondary summaries state Michigan decoupled in 2019 with no sunset date. Consequence of the federal change for Michigan filers: medical-track expenses become deductible federally as well (so the state decoupling is no longer needed for that track), while adult-use-track expenses remain federally disallowed but still Michigan-deductible. The exact text of MCL 333.27962 and whether it covers MMFLA medical licensees as well as MRTMA establishments [VERIFY] on the MCL page — the section sits in MRTMA, and its application to a purely medical licensee's Michigan return should be confirmed with Treasury guidance (RABs) before publication.
  6. What does NOT change federally on the baseline: No federal banking law (cannabis businesses remain subject to federal anti-money-laundering / FinCEN guidance, not a statute); no federal legalisation of adult-use; no change to federal firearms (18 USC §922(g)(3)) or immigration consequences on the baseline alone; the medical appropriations rider (through 11 Dec 2026) bars DOJ spending against state medical programmes but is not a permanent shield and does not cover adult-use. These are baseline statements, not Michigan-law findings.

2.2 The 10% adult-use excise tax — statute, verbatim, amendments

Law: Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA), 2018 Initiated Law 1, MCL 333.27963, §13. Effective 6 December 2018. Last amended: 2023 PA 166, immediate effect 19 October 2023 (the 2023 amendment rewrote §13(1) to reach "each marihuana establishment and … each person who sells marihuana" and added the tribal-business language in §13(4)(a); the pre-2023 text imposed the tax only on "each marihuana retailer and … each marihuana microbusiness").

Verbatim operative text (current, as reproduced — re-verify on legislature.mi.gov):

"(1) Except as otherwise provided in subsection (4), in addition to all other taxes, an excise tax is imposed on each marihuana establishment and on each person who sells marihuana at the rate of 10% of the sales price for marihuana sold or otherwise transferred to a person other than a marihuana establishment or tribal marihuana business."

"(2) Except as otherwise provided by a rule promulgated by the department of treasury, a product subject to the tax imposed under this section may not be bundled in a single transaction with a product or service that is not subject to the tax imposed by this section."

"(3) The department of treasury shall administer the taxes imposed under this act pursuant to 1941 PA 122, MCL 205.1 to 205.31. The department of treasury may promulgate rules pursuant to the administrative procedures act of 1969, 1969 PA 306, MCL 24.201 to MCL 24.328, that prescribe a method and manner for payment of the tax to ensure proper tax collection under this act."

"(4) The tax imposed under subsection (1) does not apply to any of the following: (a) Marihuana sold or otherwise transferred from a tribal marihuana business. (b) Marihuana sold or otherwise transferred under the Michigan Medical Marihuana Act, 2008 IL 1, MCL 333.26421 to 333.26430. (c) Marihuana sold or otherwise transferred under the medical marihuana facilities licensing act, 2016 PA 281, MCL 333.27101 to 333.27801."

Source: MCL 333.27963 via https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/chapter-333/statute-initiated-law-1-of-2018/section-333.27963/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — Justia reproduction; official text at legislature.mi.gov, MCL 333.27963].

Practical points, all [VERIFY] against Treasury RAB 2023-25 unless noted: - Retailers may include the excise in the sticker price or show it as a line item; if included, the excise portion is isolated by dividing gross marihuana sales by 11 (i.e. $110 inclusive ÷ 11 = $10). This is Treasury guidance, not statute text. - Bundling: a taxable marihuana product may not be bundled in one transaction with a non-taxable product/service except as a Treasury rule allows — MCL 333.27963(2) above. - Administration: Treasury, under the Revenue Act (1941 PA 122). Returns via Michigan Treasury Online (MTO), monthly — [VERIFY] filing frequency against Treasury's current marihuana tax page. - Amending MRTMA requires a three-quarters vote of each chamber (Mich. Const. 1963, art. 2, §9, voter-initiated law). This is central to the wholesale-tax litigation in §2.4: the wholesale tax was enacted as a separate act (2025 PA 23), not as an amendment to MRTMA, precisely to avoid that threshold — the plaintiffs argue that is a circumvention.

Former medical excise tax (history, not current law): The Medical Marihuana Facilities Licensing Act (MMFLA), 2016 PA 281, originally imposed a 3% excise tax on provisioning centres' gross retail receipts (former MCL 333.27601 et seq. — medical marihuana excise provisions). Secondary sources state it was eliminated effective 6 March 2019. Treasury's own excise series (as republished, see §2.9) shows medical marihuana excise collections falling to $2,000 in FY2022-23 and $0 in FY2024-25, consistent with a defunct tax, but the repeal act and exact effective date were not confirmed on legislature.mi.gov in this pass — [VERIFY] before stating a repeal date. Do not present the 3% tax as current.

2.3 The 6% sales tax (and use tax) — statute and the tax-on-tax rule

Law: General Sales Tax Act, 1933 PA 167, MCL 205.51–205.78, rate at MCL 205.52(1): 6% of gross proceeds of retail sales of tangible personal property. Use Tax Act, 1937 PA 94, MCL 205.91–205.111, also 6%.

Key rule — Mich. Admin. Code R 205.141 (Treasury rule, "Marihuana"):

"(1) All sales of marihuana, whether legal or illegal, are subject to the general sales tax act … based on the 'sales price' … The taxable 'sales price' of marihuana includes the 10% excise tax levied under section 13(1) of [MRTMA], MCL 333.27963(1). Example: ABC Inc. … sells marihuana to customer for $100.00. ABC is liable for $10.00 of marihuana excise tax. ABC is also liable for sales tax on this transaction. The amount of sales tax due is 6% of $110.00 or $6.60." "(3) For purposes of the general sales tax act and the use tax act, marihuana, in any form, does not constitute the exempt sale, use, storage, or consumption of food or prescription drugs under MCL 205.54g or 205.94d."

Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-205-141 — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — Cornell reproduction; confirm against the official Administrative Code]. Treasury RABs 2019-17, 2020-17 and 2023-25 are cited by practitioners for the same example — [VERIFY] those RAB numbers/dates on michigan.gov/treasury.

Consequences: - Medical sales are not exempt from sales tax: a registered patient's purchase at a provisioning centre pays 6% sales tax (on the price without the 10% excise, since the excise does not apply — see §2.5). A $100 medical sale = $106 out the door if tax is added on top. This is consistently reported; the statutory basis is that marihuana is tangible personal property and is expressly denied the food/prescription-drug exemptions by R 205.141(3). - There is no local-option sales tax on marihuana in Michigan law; the 6% is statewide only. - Sales tax revenue does NOT follow the MRTMA distribution formula in §2.6. It flows through the normal sales-tax channels (general fund / School Aid Fund under the sales-tax allocation statutes). Do not attribute sales-tax dollars to the 15/15/35/35 split.

2.4 The NEW 24% wholesale marijuana tax — 2025 PA 23 (HB 4951) — the dominant 2025–2026 tax story

2.4.1 Enactment, rate, effective dates, who pays

  • Bill: House Bill 4951 (2025–2026, 103rd Legislature), "Comprehensive Road Funding Tax Act."
  • Enacted as 2025 PA 23, signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer 7 October 2025 as part of the state's $81 billion budget / road-funding package. Act effective 7 October 2025; the tax itself applies from 1 January 2026.
  • Votes (as reported, [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov journal): House 78–21; Senate 19–17. Neither chamber reached three-quarters (House 78 of 110 = ~71%; Senate 19 of 38 = 50%). The three-quarters point is the plaintiffs' core argument (see §2.4.3). The House vote was five votes short of three-quarters, as reported.
  • Statutory home: MCL 205.901 et seq. (Comprehensive Road Funding Tax Act). The operative levy is cited as MCL 205.905: "In addition to all other taxes, beginning January 1, 2026," an excise tax is levied at 24% of the wholesale price.
  • Who pays / taxable events (enrolled summary, House Fiscal Agency, via LegiScan): 1. On a marihuana establishment, for the first sale or other transfer of marihuana to a marihuana retail licensee; 2. On a marihuana retail licensee, for the sale of marihuana it has cultivated or processed for retail sale by itself (based on the wholesale price of the aggregate amount/quantity so cultivated/processed); 3. On a provisioning centre (MMFLA medical licensee), for the sale or transfer of marihuana from the provisioning centre to a marihuana retail licensee — i.e. medical inventory moved into the adult-use channel is taxed at the transfer point.
  • Wholesale price definition:
  • Unaffiliated transactions: the actual price paid by the retail licensee, including any tax, fee or other charge on the invoice; no reduction for rebates, trade allowances, licensing/exclusivity agreements, volume or other discounts (enrolled summary).
  • Affiliated transactions (including vertically integrated self-supply): the Average Wholesale Price (AWP), "calculated and published by the department [of Treasury] each quarter based on the best available information" (2025 PA 23, §3). Treasury's published method, as reported, is to derive AWP by dividing average retail price by 1.5 (a 50% assumed markup). Example reported for Q4 2026: flower AWP $630.81/lb — [VERIFY] against Treasury's quarterly AWP publication; the ÷1.5 method is Treasury guidance, not in the act's text, and is itself criticised by practitioners (see Research Notes).
  • For a retail licensee cultivating/processing its own product, the tax is triggered at the point the product is packaged for retail sale (Treasury guidance as reported).
  • Companion-bill condition (as introduced — [VERIFY] whether it survived enrolment): The introduced summary stated the bill would not take effect unless three companion bills were also enacted (HB 4183 motor-fuel tax, HB 4961 income tax, HB 4968 insurance provider assessment). The enrolled act took effect 7 Oct 2025 with the tax from 1 Jan 2026, so any such condition was either satisfied or removed — do not repeat the condition as current law without checking the enrolled act.
  • Revenue destination: NOT the MRTMA 15/15/35/35 split. Revenue goes to the Comprehensive Road Funding Fund and the Neighborhood Road Fund for state and local road, bridge and transit infrastructure. Enrolled-summary detail (secondary, [VERIFY]): $500,000 annually to the Comprehensive Road Funding Fund from FY2026-27 (inflation-adjusted from FY2027-28), remaining balance to the Neighborhood Road Fund; in the first year the split description differed in introduced summaries. Do not publish a first-year split without checking the enrolled act, MCL 205.901 et seq.
  • Projected revenue: ~$420 million per year (Senate Fiscal Agency / administration estimate; also cited as $420.7 million). For FY2026 the nine-month expectation (Jan–Sep 2026) was ~$315 million.
  • Actual collections (secondary reporting of Treasury figures — [VERIFY] against Treasury monthly financial reports):
  • Jan–Apr 2026: ~$34.0 million (Treasury monthly financial report for April 2026, as reported: "$33,999 thousand").
  • Q2 2026: ~$37.38 million; cumulative through Q2 2026: ~$73.4 million (CannBus calculation from press-reported Treasury figures), against ~$210 million projected for two quarters (~35%).
  • The shortfall is a reported fact of collections vs projection, not a finding that the tax is repealed or enjoined. The tax remains in effect as of 28 Oct 2026 (see litigation below).
  • Administration: Treasury; Revenue Administrative Bulletin RAB 2026-3, approved 17 March 2026, updated 24 March 2026 (as reported) — [VERIFY] on michigan.gov/treasury. Treasury "Notice to Taxpayers Regarding the Wholesale Tax on Adult-Use Marihuana," 25 November 2025 (as reported via Wolters Kluwer summary). CRA Advisory Bulletin 14 January 2026 is cited for the point that Metrc is not determinative for tax purposes — [VERIFY].
  • Interaction with the federal baseline: The wholesale tax is a state tax on adult-use activity. It is unaffected by the federal Schedule III move for medical marijuana, because it does not apply to wholesale medical marijuana (see above). Adult-use activity remains Schedule I federally and fully §280E-subject (see §2.7); the wholesale tax is an additional state burden on top of that.

Sources for §2.4.1: 2025 PA 23 text via https://sa-datacore.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/bills/ingestion/mi/texts/MI_HB4951_3272771.pdf ; enrolled summary via https://legiscan.com/MI/supplement/HB4951/id/627885/Michigan-2025-HB4951-House_Revised_Summary_as_Enrolled-Enacted_Version.pdf ; Husch Blackwell summary https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/how-michigan-s-new-24-wholesale-3173259/ ; Treasury guidance summaries — all accessed 2026-10-28. The enrolled act itself should be opened on legislature.mi.gov (2025 PA 23) before publication — [VERIFY].

2.4.2 Earlier wholesale-tax proposals (context — do not confuse with PA 23)

Before PA 23, wholesale-tax proposals were debated for years (including a 2023–2024 CRA memo to the Governor's office, November 2023, on the repercussions of a wholesale tax, whose full text the administration declined to release — reported, [VERIFY]). No earlier wholesale tax was enacted. Any reference to a "proposed 24% tax" in pre-October 2025 sources is a proposal, not law. PA 23 is the first enacted wholesale tax.

2.4.3 Litigation — status as of 28 October 2026 [all litigation facts are secondary-reported; court dockets not opened in this pass — VERIFY on the Michigan Court of Claims / Court of Appeals dockets before publication]

Case 1 — the three-quarters / voter-initiative challenge: - Plaintiffs: Michigan Cannabis Industry Association (MiCIA / MCIA) and others, including Holistic Research Group (caption reported as Holistic Research Group v. State of Michigan and Michigan Cannabis Industry Association v. State of Michigan, Court of Claims, heard together). - Filed: same day as signing, October 2025 (as reported). - Argument: MRTMA is a voter-initiated law; Mich. Const. 1963, art. 2, §9 requires a three-quarters vote of each chamber to amend it; PA 23 (House 78–21, Senate 19–17) did not meet that threshold, so the wholesale tax is an unconstitutional amendment of MRTMA. Plaintiffs also argued the tax undermines MRTMA's purpose (competitive pricing to displace the illicit market) and, in later briefing, the Title-Object Clause. - State's argument: PA 23 is a separate tax act for road funding, not an amendment to MRTMA; MRTMA §13 itself says the 10% excise is "in addition to all other taxes," leaving the door open to additional taxes. - 8 December 2025: Court of Claims Judge Sima G. Patel DENIED a preliminary injunction. Reasoning as reported: the phrase "all other" is "broad and expansive" and does not prevent new marihuana-specific taxes; the tax is "consistent" with MRTMA. Crucially, Patel also found "questions of fact" about whether the tax undermines MRTMA's purpose and partially denied the state's request for summary disposition — so the core constitutional issue was NOT finally decided; it was set for trial / further proceedings (a 13 January 2026 conference was scheduled). - Appeal / expedition: As reported, the Michigan Supreme Court on 22 April 2026 ordered the Court of Appeals to speed up / take an expedited review of the challenge. The tax stays in effect while the case is pending. No final appellate ruling striking down the tax was located as of the latest secondary summaries (September 2026) — [VERIFY] current docket status; this is the single most important follow-up for Part 2. - A January 2026 report that the court "denied the state's request to toss the lawsuit" is consistent with Patel's partial denial of summary disposition above, not a separate ruling — do not double-count it.

Case 2 — the "tax pyramiding" / sales-tax-cap challenge: - Filed: 27 March 2026, Court of Claims, by MiCIA with a grower, a retailer and a consumer (as reported). - Argument: the wholesale tax, layered on the 10% excise and 6% sales tax (with the excise itself in the sales-tax base), is in substance a sales tax that pushes the effective sales-tax rate beyond Michigan's 6% constitutional limit — "tax on a tax" / pyramiding. A complaint excerpt cites MCL 205.909(1) (periodic returns) and MCL 205.905 (levy). - Status: pending as of the latest summaries checked; no ruling located — [VERIFY] docket. The $143.84-on-$116 illustration in that coverage is plaintiffs' arithmetic, not a court finding.

Legislative repeal attempts (proposals, NOT law): - Senate Bill 810 (2025–2026), sponsored by Sen. Jonathan Lindsey (R-Coldwater), introduced 26 February 2026, referred to Senate Government Operations; bipartisan, eight co-sponsors (five Republicans, three Democrats as reported). Would repeal the Comprehensive Road Funding Tax Act wholesale tax. No floor vote located as of 28 Oct 2026 — [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov; do not present as enacted. - House Bill 6224, Rep. James DeSana, introduced July 2026, referred to House Appropriations 29 July 2026, electronically reproduced 11 August 2026. Also a repeal bill. No floor vote located — [VERIFY].

Bottom line for the dossier: As of 28 Oct 2026, the 24% wholesale tax is in effect and being collected, its preliminary-injunction challenge failed on 8 Dec 2025, and its constitutionality remains undecided on the merits in pending litigation plus two pending repeal bills. Any statement that the tax "was struck down" or "was upheld finally" would be wrong.

2.5 Medical tax treatment

  • 10% MRTMA excise: EXEMPT. MCL 333.27963(4)(b)–(c) (quoted in §2.2): the tax does not apply to marihuana sold/transferred under the MMMA (2008 IL 1) or the MMFLA (2016 PA 281). Treasury RAB 2023-25 repeats the exemption for sales to a registered qualifying patient (as reported — [VERIFY]).
  • 24% wholesale tax: NOT applicable to wholesale medical marijuana (Treasury wholesale FAQ as reported). Exception: a dual-license operator that moves product from medical inventory into adult-use inventory triggers the 24% tax on that transfer (as reported — [VERIFY] against RAB 2026-3 / Treasury FAQ).
  • 6% sales tax: APPLIES to medical retail sales (see §2.3). There is no medical sales-tax exemption in Michigan law for marihuana. Older secondary summaries that say medical sales are "fully exempt from both excise and sales tax" are wrong on sales tax and must not be repeated; the correct statement is: exempt from the 10% excise (and from the 24% wholesale tax at the medical wholesale stage), but subject to 6% sales tax.
  • Caregiver transfers: The Court of Appeals decision in CannArbor Inc v. Department of Treasury, published 16 December 2025 (No. 370919), addressed whether a medical facility's sales fall under MRTMA's excise/deduction provisions and the MMMA's tax treatment of primary caregivers (who may only recoup costs, unlike provisioning centres which sell "at retail" under MCL 333.27102(w) and are subject to sales tax under MCL 205.52(1)). Full holding not summarised here — [VERIFY] the opinion at https://www.courts.michigan.gov/491196/siteassets/case-documents/uploads/opinions/final/coa/20251216_c370919_25_370919.opn.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Do not generalise CannArbor beyond its facts without reading it.
  • Federal interaction (per the fixed baseline, applied to Michigan): State-licensed medical activity (MMFLA licensees, provisioning centres) falls within the federal Schedule III / §280E-relief description for medical activity; registered primary caregivers' status under "state-licensed medical" is [VERIFY] — the federal rule text (91 FR 22714) was not re-examined in this sub-task and the commission itself flags this as Verify. Dual-licensed businesses must split medical vs adult-use income/expenses: Michigan's own decoupling (see §2.7) already required that discipline for state purposes, and the federal split now requires it federally as well. Adult-use activity remains Schedule I and fully §280E-subject at the federal level regardless of Michigan's state decoupling.

2.6 Distribution of the MRTMA excise revenue — the Marihuana Regulation Fund

Law: MRTMA §14, MCL 333.27964. The Marihuana Regulation Fund is created in the state treasury; Treasury deposits all money collected under §13 (the 10% excise) and all licence fees; the fund does not lapse to the general fund.

Verbatim allocation order (current text as reproduced — re-verify on legislature.mi.gov):

"The department shall expend money in the fund first for the implementation, administration, and enforcement of this act, and second, until 2022 or for at least two years, to provide $20 million annually to one or more clinical trials that are approved by the United States food and drug administration and sponsored by a nonprofit organization or researcher within an academic institution researching the efficacy of marihuana in treating the medical conditions of United States armed services veterans and preventing veteran suicide. Upon appropriation, the unexpended balances in the fund must be allocated as follows: (a) Subject to subsection (5), 15% to municipalities in which a marihuana retailer or marihuana microbusiness is located, allocated in proportion to the number of marihuana retailers and marihuana microbusinesses within each municipality. (b) Subject to subsection (5), 15% to counties in which a marihuana retailer or marihuana microbusiness is located, allocated in proportion to the number of marihuana retailers and marihuana microbusinesses within each county. (c) 35% to the school aid fund to be used for K-12 education. (d) 35% to the Michigan transportation fund to be used for the repair and maintenance of roads and bridges. (5) If a marihuana retailer or marihuana microbusiness is located in Indian lands, the portions … that would have otherwise been allocated to a municipality under subsection (4)(a) and a county under subsection (4)(b) must instead be allocated to the Indian tribe in whose Indian lands the marihuana retailer or marihuana microbusiness is located."

Source: MCL 333.27964 via https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/michigan/mi-laws/michigan_laws_333-27964 — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — LawServer reproduction; official text at legislature.mi.gov].

Critical reading notes (do not get these wrong): 1. The $20 million veterans-research tranche was by its terms "until 2022 or for at least two years" — it is a time-limited, front-loaded obligation, NOT a permanent $20M/year carve-out in the current distribution. Secondary summaries that present "$20M yearly for veterans" as a current, ongoing deduction from every year's fund misread §14(3). The Veteran Marijuana Research Grant Program (University of Michigan, Wayne State University, MAPS grants in 2021–2022) was funded under this provision. Whether any veterans-research appropriation continued after the two-year window is [VERIFY] against Treasury/CRA appropriations — do not assert a current $20M deduction. 2. The 15/15/35/35 percentages apply to unexpended balances after implementation/administration/enforcement costs (and, in the early years, the veterans tranche) — they are not percentages of gross excise collections. Press releases that say "15% to municipalities" without that qualifier are shorthand. 3. The local shares are allocated in proportion to the number of licensed retailers/microbusinesses in the municipality/county — NOT by population, NOT by sales volume, NOT by need. A municipality with one store gets the same per-store amount as a city with 60 stores gets per store (60× the amount). Tribes on Indian lands take the municipal + county shares attributable to stores on their lands (subsection (5), added by 2023 amendment — see below). 4. Tribal eligibility: The 2023 amendment (2023 PA 166, eff. 19 Oct 2023) is the change that recognised tribes in the distribution. FY2024 was the first year tribes received payments (over $931,000 among four federally recognised tribes — Treasury, 21 Feb 2025, opened directly, see §2.9). 5. Counties do not need to "opt in" to receive the county share; the county share follows the location of retailers/microbusinesses in the county regardless of county government action (counties are not "municipalities" under MRTMA — see §3.1). 6. Local recipients may spend the money however they deem fit — Treasury's releases state this expressly ("Local entities and tribes can spend these dollars however they deem fit for their needs"). There is no statutory earmark on the local 30%.

Former MMFLA medical distribution (history, not current): The MMFLA's former 3% provisioning-centre excise went into a Medical Marihuana Excise Fund distributed (as reproduced in secondary sources) 25% to municipalities by facility count, 30% to counties by facility count, 5% to counties for county sheriffs, 30% to the state, 5% to the Michigan Commission on Law Enforcement Standards, 5% to the Department of State Police. This fund is tied to the defunct 3% tax; do not present it as a current distribution — [VERIFY] its current statutory status.

2.7 IRS §280E and Michigan decoupling — state tax

Federal (fixed baseline, applied): §280E denies deductions/credits to a trade or business trafficking in Schedule I or II substances. For Schedule III state-licensed medical activity from 28 April 2026, that federal bar is generally lifted for that activity; adult-use remains fully §280E-subject federally. No new Michigan statute was needed for the federal change; Michigan's state rule below is independent of it.

Michigan state decoupling — MRTMA §12, MCL 333.27962 (voter-initiated, 2018 IL 1, eff. 6 Dec 2018; NOT a legislative decoupling act):

"In computing net income for marihuana establishments, deductions from state taxes are allowed for all the ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying out a trade or business."

Source: MCL 333.27962 via https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/michigan/mi-laws/michigan_laws_333-27962 — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — official text at legislature.mi.gov]. Note the statute as enacted does not mention §280E by number; the decoupling effect is by providing the deduction "in computing net income" for state purposes notwithstanding the federal disallowance. Secondary summaries that quote the section with an added "notwithstanding section 280E" clause are paraphrasing, not quoting — do not present that clause as statutory text.

Scope — the contested points (flag prominently): - Who is covered: "marihuana establishments" as defined in MRTMA §3, MCL 333.27953 — i.e. MRTMA (adult-use) licensees. Treasury's position, as reported (RAB 2022-26, cited by practitioners — [VERIFY] the RAB), is that the relief is §162-type "ordinary and necessary" expenses only; depreciation, amortisation and credits are NOT restored by §12 on Treasury's reading. - Practitioner divergence: Many cannabis CPAs restore all federally disallowed items (including depreciation/amortisation and credits such as the Small Business Alternative Credit) for Michigan purposes, arguing §12 does not import §280E's "no deduction, no credit" doctrine. This is a live compliance dispute, not settled law — present both readings and mark the broader reading [VERIFY / practitioner position only]. - Medical-only (MMFLA) licensees: Secondary analysis states MMFLA C-corps "remain fully 280E-bound" for Michigan purposes because §12 speaks to "marihuana establishments" (MRTMA), not MMFLA "marihuana facilities." The CannArbor litigation (Dec 2025, see §2.5) turns on exactly this boundary — whether a medical facility fits the MRTMA definitions. Therefore: Michigan decoupling for a medical-only business is [VERIFY] — do not state it as settled either way. The federal Schedule III change (medical only) and Michigan's MRTMA-only decoupling now point in opposite directions for dual licensees, which is why split books are essential. - Interaction with the new wholesale tax: Decoupling affects income tax computation; it does not reduce the 10% excise, 6% sales tax or 24% wholesale tax, which are transaction taxes. - No Michigan statute decoupling by reference to federal scheduling was located in this pass. If the legislature later ties state treatment to federal Schedule III status, that would be a new enactment — [VERIFY] no such 2026 act was found; SB 810 / HB 6224 (repeal bills) do not address §280E.

2.8 Hemp product tax

  • No Michigan hemp-specific excise tax was located. Hemp grown/processed under Michigan's hemp laws is not subject to the MRTMA 10% excise or the PA 23 24% wholesale tax, which by their terms apply to "marihuana" (as defined in MRTMA, excluding hemp as defined in state/federal law — [VERIFY] the definitional exclusion in MCL 333.27953).
  • Intoxicating hemp-derived cannabinoids (delta-8 etc.) brought under CRA/marihuana regulation by 2021 PA 56 (HB 4517) are regulated as marihuana for licensing/testing purposes; whether a product sold through a CRA licensee as marihuana then bears the 10% excise depends on whether it is sold as adult-use marihuana vs as a hemp product — the tax treatment of a specific intoxicating-hemp product is [VERIFY] against Treasury guidance and is a Part 7 / Part 1 cross-reference, not settled in this file.
  • Ordinary sales tax on hemp/CBD products sold at general retail (non-CRA channel): no Treasury ruling specific to hemp/CBD was opened in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE] in this pass; do not assume exemption or full taxation. CBD products are tangible personal property in principle, but food/drug/supplement characterisation questions (cf. R 205.141(3) for marihuana) were not resolved for hemp here.
  • Federal hemp dates in the baseline (12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026) create no Michigan tax in themselves; any Michigan conforming tax or fee change would require state action, none of which was located — [VERIFY] against 2026 Michigan hemp bills (SB 599–602 package, see §3.2 note) for any tax provision.

PART 3 — LOCAL RULES

3.1 Authority: who can do what — MMFLA opt-in vs MRTMA opt-out, and the county question

Definitions first (this resolves most confusion): - Under MRTMA, "municipality" means a city, village, or township (MCL 333.27953(v), cited in City of Farmington v. Farmington Survey Committee, Court of Appeals, 3 Sep 2024). Counties are NOT municipalities under MRTMA. A county therefore cannot opt out of, prohibit, or license marihuana establishments under MRTMA. A county's role is: (a) recipient of the 15% county distribution share (§2.6); (b) zoning authority only in the limited circumstances where state law gives counties zoning power (generally unincorporated areas are zoned by townships, not counties, in Michigan — [VERIFY] for any specific county zoning claim); (c) law-enforcement / sheriff functions. Any statement that a "county opted out" is wrong unless it means "the municipalities within the county opted out." - The same city/village/township-only scope applies in substance under MMFLA (municipality adopts an ordinance authorising a facility type — see below).

MMFLA (2016 PA 281) — OPT-IN: - Rule: No marihuana facility may be licensed by the state unless and until the municipality has adopted an ordinance that authorises that type of facility (MMFLA §205(1), MCL 333.27205 — cited in secondary summaries; [VERIFY] exact subsection on legislature.mi.gov). Inaction = no medical facilities. A municipality may authorise some types, all types, or none. - Local fee: MMFLA municipalities may charge an annual fee — secondary sources cite MCL 333.27205 as authorising up to $5,000 per facility per year, parallel to MRTMA (see §3.4). [VERIFY] the MMFLA fee cap text; the $5,000 figure is firmly sourced for MRTMA (§3.4) and only secondarily for MMFLA. - Consequence of the opt-in design: A medical facility cannot be sited in a municipality that never acted, even if the municipality never "banned" anything. This is why early CRA/MRA lists distinguished "opted-in with restrictions" municipalities from opt-out municipalities.

MRTMA (2018 IL 1) — OPT-OUT (with caps and local licensing): - MCL 333.27956, §6(1) (verbatim, as reproduced — re-verify on legislature.mi.gov):

"Except as provided in section 4, a municipality may completely prohibit or limit the number of marihuana establishments within its boundaries. Individuals may petition to initiate an ordinance to provide for the number of marihuana establishments allowed within a municipality or to completely prohibit marihuana establishments within a municipality, and such ordinance shall be submitted to the electors of the municipality at the next regular election when a petition is signed by qualified electors in the municipality in a number greater than 5% of the votes cast for governor by qualified electors in the municipality at the last gubernatorial election. A petition under this subsection is subject to section 488 of the Michigan election law, 1954 PA 116, MCL 168.488." - Default is ALLOW: Unlike MMFLA, a municipality that does nothing under MRTMA has not opted out; establishments may be licensed there subject to state law and any generally applicable zoning. Opt-out requires an affirmative prohibiting ordinance. This asymmetry (MMFLA: silence = no; MRTMA: silence = yes) is the single most common error in secondary coverage, including one secondary summary in this pass that called Michigan an "opt-in model" for adult-use — that summary is wrong for MRTMA and must not be repeated. (The "opt-in" label is sometimes used loosely because the CRA requires municipal attestation/confirmation before issuing a state licence — see below — but that is a verification step, not an opt-in statute.) - §6(2) — other ordinances allowed (verbatim summary): a municipality may adopt ordinances that are "not unreasonably impracticable" and do not conflict with MRTMA or CRA rules, that: (a) establish reasonable restrictions on public signs; (b) regulate time, place and manner of operation and of production/manufacture/sale/display of marihuana accessories; (c) authorise sale for consumption in designated areas not accessible to persons under 21, or at special events in limited areas/times; (d) designate a violation as a civil infraction with a civil fine of not more than $500. - §6(3)–(4) — local licence and fee: a municipality may require a marihuana establishment with a physical location in the municipality to obtain a municipal licence (but may not impose qualifications conflicting with MRTMA/rules); annual fee not more than $5,000 to defray application, administrative and enforcement costs (see §3.4). - §6(5) — prohibitions on local bans: a municipality may NOT adopt an ordinance that restricts transportation of marihuana through the municipality, or prohibits a grower, processor and retailer from operating within a single facility or at a location shared with an MMFLA facility. - §6 and §9 — competitive process: Where a municipality limits the number of establishments, MRTMA §9(4) (MCL 333.27959(4)) contemplates a competitive process; the Court of Appeals in Yellow Tail Ventures v. City of Berkley, 344 Mich App 689 (2022), upheld Berkley's scoring criteria (green infrastructure, sustainability, aesthetics, economic goals) as within "time, place, and manner" — see §3.2. MRTMA itself does not prescribe scoring or require award to the highest scorer (a point stressed in practitioner commentary — [VERIFY] §9(4) text). - State licence + local attestation: Under MRTMA §9(3) (MCL 333.27959(3)) and CRA rules, an applicant must show municipal compliance (the former "Attestation 2-C" / clerk attestation). Brightmoore Gardens (see §3.2) turned on clerk refusals to sign that attestation during opt-out windows. - State school buffer (baseline for §3.5): A marihuana establishment licence may not be issued for a location within 1,000 feet of a pre-existing public or private school providing K–12 education, BUT a municipality may by ordinance allow a location within less than 1,000 feet (MCL 333.27959(3)(c), as summarised in Royal Oak's official MRTMA summary — [VERIFY] exact text). Local buffers that are stricter than 1,000 feet, or that add parks/churches/child-care, are local choices, not state law. Ann Arbor's 2025 move to a 100-foot local minimum (see §3.5) is an exercise of local discretion within the state framework only if it complies with §9(3) — the interaction was not resolved in this pass and is flagged [VERIFY].

Local voter initiatives — both directions: - To prohibit or cap (MRTMA §6(1)): electors may petition (signatures >5% of votes cast for governor in the municipality at the last gubernatorial election) to put an ordinance providing for the number allowed, or complete prohibition, on the ballot at the next regular election. This is the mechanism used in Niles Charter Township (Berrien County) and Menominee (Menominee County) in November 2025 (see §3.5, cross-border). - To allow where officials opted out: the same §6(1) petition mechanism can initiate an ordinance providing for a number of establishments — i.e. voters can override a council opt-out by initiative. Niles Charter Township's November 2024 referendum allowing marihuana commerce, followed by its November 2025 reversal, is the clearest recent example of voters using the mechanism in both directions. A petition is subject to MCL 168.488 (Michigan Election Law §488). - MMFLA initiatives: MMFLA has no parallel voter-initiative override in the same terms; a medical opt-in requires a municipal ordinance adopted by the governing body. [VERIFY] whether any MMFLA municipality adopted medical authorisation by initiative — none was located.

Moratoriums: A municipality may impose a temporary moratorium while it drafts an ordinance (common in 2017–2019 for medical, and 2019 for adult-use). A moratorium is not an opt-out and does not permanently prohibit; its legal effect depends on its stated duration and whether it was extended. Several early "opt-out" lists conflated moratorium municipalities with opt-out municipalities — treat any pre-2020 list with that caution.

3.2 Local prohibitions, moratoriums, caps, competitive processes — and litigation over local awards

Scale (official-adjacent figures — read the dates): - September 2019: 839 cities, villages and townships had told the Marijuana Regulatory Agency they were opting out of adult-use facilities (MRA spokesperson David Harns, via Small Business Association of Michigan, Sep 2019). The state has 1,240 townships, 276 cities, 257 villages (1,773 municipalities total). Harns expressly noted locals are not required to tell the state, so the true opt-out count was higher. 13 of the 25 most populous municipalities were among the 839, including (in population order as reported) Sterling Heights (Macomb County), Clinton Township (Macomb County), Dearborn (Wayne County), Livonia (Wayne County), Canton Township (Wayne County), Macomb Township (Macomb County), Farmington Hills (Oakland County), Shelby Township (Macomb County), Wyoming (Kent County), Rochester Hills (Oakland County), Waterford Township (Oakland County), West Bloomfield Township (Oakland County) and Novi (Oakland County). Source: https://www.sbam.org/half-of-states-communities-opt-out-of-recreational-pot-businesses/ — accessed 2026-10-28. This is a 2019 snapshot, NOT a current count. Several of those municipalities have since opted in, in whole or in part (e.g. Sterling Heights — see §3.5; Dearborn's status must be re-checked, see §3.5). - 2023 secondary claim: "over 1,300 of 1,773 municipalities had opted out" (LegalClarity, citing 2023). Conflict / caution: That figure is inconsistent with the distribution data (313 entities receiving FY2025 payments implies at least 234 municipalities + 75 counties + tribes allowed retailers/microbusinesses, but a municipality can allow growers/processors without retailers and thus not appear in the distribution). The 1,300 figure counts any opt-out notification including partial opt-outs and is not an official CRA count — [VERIFY] against the current CRA municipality spreadsheet before publishing any statewide opt-out total. The dossier should NOT state a current statewide opt-out total on this pass. - Possession is NOT affected by opt-out: An opt-out ordinance prohibits establishments, not possession/use by adults 21+ or registered patients. Secondary lists that imply otherwise are wrong.

Competitive licensing and litigation — the cases that define the field: 1. Brightmoore Gardens, LLC v. Marijuana Regulatory Agency, 337 Mich App 149, 975 NW2d 52 (2021) — Consolidated appeals by applicants for Detroit (Wayne County) and Traverse City (Grand Traverse County) establishments. Detroit applicants applied 1–4 Nov 2019 without the city clerk's Attestation 2-C signature (clerk refused to sign); Detroit adopted a prohibiting ordinance 12 Nov 2019; MRA denied Jan 2020 under MCL 333.27959(3) and emergency rules. Traverse City's (Grand Traverse County) prohibiting ordinance had lapsed 6 Dec 2019; WL Green Ventures applied 8 Dec 2019, clerk refused to sign, city adopted a new opt-out ordinance 13 Dec 2019; denied Feb 2020. The Court of Appeals addressed whether the emergency rules requiring municipal attestation were contrary to MRTMA. Outcome detail beyond the facts above was not extracted in this pass — [VERIFY] the opinion before summarising its holding. Source: https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/mi-court-of-appeals/2126744.html — accessed 2026-10-28. 2. Yellow Tail Ventures, Inc v. City of Berkley, 344 Mich App 689 (2022) (Berkley is in Oakland County) — Ten companies sued Berkley over its competitive scoring process (three top scorers identified from 30 applicants; ten sued alleging undefined criteria and improper delegation). The Court of Appeals upheld Berkley's ordinance: scoring criteria including green infrastructure, sustainability, aesthetics and economic goals "fit neatly within a reasonable understanding of MRTMA's 'time, place, and manner' provision" and within §9(4); the city manager's scoring assistance was not a "public body" for Open Meetings Act purposes because final decisions remained with the council. Source: https://law.justia.com/cases/michigan/court-of-appeals-published/2022/357654.html — accessed 2026-10-28. 3. Detroit (Wayne County) adult-use ordinance litigation (2021–2022): Detroit's first adult-use ordinance (2020, 75 retailer licences, ≥50% Detroit Legacy) was challenged in federal court (Lowe v. City of Detroit, E.D. Mich. No. 2:21-cv-10709) and its application process was halted; a revised ordinance (Ordinance No. 2022-11) restructured caps (see §3.5, Detroit) and its August 2022 application period was itself subject to a Wayne County Circuit Court temporary restraining order (as noted in Detroit's own Planning Commission report). Current status of Detroit litigation after 2022 was not traced in this pass — [VERIFY] before stating Detroit's ordinance is litigation-free. 4. Warren (Macomb County) home-grow ordinance — preemption: The Court of Appeals held Warren's ordinance requiring home medical growers to register, pass safety inspections and install odour filtration was preempted by the MMMA (state law superior; MMMA requires only an enclosed, locked facility). Secondary summary at https://www.arborypsilaw.com/blog/court-rules-against-city-of-warren-ordinances/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — case name/citation not captured in this pass; do not cite without it]. Lesson for Part 3: local ordinances that add requirements in direct conflict with the MMMA fail, while MRTMA §6(2) time/place/manner ordinances survive if not unreasonably impracticable and not conflicting. 5. Menominee (Menominee County) and Niles Charter Township (Berrien County) ballot litigation risk (2025–2026): After the November 2025 votes (see §3.5), officials in both communities publicly anticipated lawsuits from excluded/left-out operators. A September 2026 circuit-court decision (Judge Mary Barglind, Menominee County Circuit Court, 21 Sep 2026, as reported) rejected a challenge to the format of the petition to raise Menominee's cap from 9 to 13 on the 3 Nov 2026 ballot — i.e. the vote could proceed; it did not decide the policy merits. The 3 Nov 2026 Menominee vote post-dates this dossier's 28 Oct 2026 date and must NOT be reported as decided. Source for the Barglind decision: https://www.fnaround.com/articles/four-licenses-in-one-license-out-michigans-cannabis-slippery-slope — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY — secondary, single-source].

General pattern (officially grounded, not estimated): Municipalities that cap licences and run competitive/scoring processes are the ones that generate litigation; municipalities that use zoning buffers and no cap (Grand Rapids, Kalamazoo city, Marquette — see §3.5) generate far less award litigation in the sources checked. That is an observation about the cases above, not a statistical claim.

3.4 Local licence fees and revenue shares

Statutory maximum — MRTMA: - MCL 333.27956(4): "A municipality may charge an annual fee of not more than $5,000 to defray application, administrative, and enforcement costs associated with the operation of the marihuana establishment in the municipality." (Quoted via Michigan Court of Appeals benchbook and Farmington opinion — re-verify on legislature.mi.gov.) - The $5,000 is per establishment licence (per establishment, as applied in local ordinances — e.g. Ionia's ordinance: "a nonrefundable fee … not to exceed $5,000 … for each license proposed for each establishment"). It is a cap, not a mandated fee — a municipality may charge less or nothing. Many ordinances charge the full $5,000 (e.g. Kalamazoo Charter Township, Kalamazoo County, application fee $5,000 per licence type, per its 2020 application instructions — that is an application fee in that document, distinguish from the annual fee). - MMFLA parallel: Secondary sources cite a $5,000 annual fee under MMFLA as well (MCL 333.27205) — [VERIFY] text; do not state the MMFLA cap as confirmed on the same footing as MRTMA's. - Detroit exception in practice (historical, not statutory): Detroit's 2021 adult-use programme charged $1,000 city licensing fees generally but $10 for Detroit Legacy applicants (press reporting of Mayor Duggan's announcement) — that is a city policy discount within the $5,000 cap, not a different cap. [VERIFY] current Detroit fee schedule; the 2022-11 ordinance may have changed it.

Revenue shares received (official Treasury distributions — see §2.9 for the full table): - The per-store amount IS the revenue share mechanism: FY2024 >$58,200 per retailer/microbusiness to EACH of the host municipality, host county and (where applicable) tribe — i.e. a municipality with n stores receives n × per-store amount, and its county receives the same n × amount for those stores (plus amounts for stores elsewhere in the county). - Examples from official/press reporting of Treasury releases (all [VERIFY] against the Treasury distribution tables at michigan.gov/RevenueSharing): - FY2024: Detroit (Wayne County) — largest municipal recipient (first year Detroit received, after adult-use sales began there in early 2023); Wayne County (Wayne County) — largest county recipient at ~$5M (secondary reporting of Feb 2025 release). - FY2024: Lansing (Ingham County) ~$1.4M (24 licences × ~$58,200) — third-most of any city/township (secondary reporting of Feb 2025 release); Mecosta County (Mecosta County) $698,743 (12 stores, as reported). - FY2025: Detroit (Wayne County) 61 active retailer licences → nearly $3.3M; Lansing (Ingham County) and other figures in the March 2026 release — see §2.9. - FY2021 (for trend): Kalamazoo (Kalamazoo County) ~$10.6M, Portage (Kalamazoo County) ~$5.3M, Kalamazoo Charter Township (Kalamazoo County) ~$4.2M, Kalamazoo County ~$1.07M — these figures are from a secondary county page citing Treasury and are internally inconsistent with the FY2021 per-store amounts in §2.9 (they appear to aggregate multiple years or include other revenue) — DO NOT PUBLISH without the Treasury FY2021 table; flagged as a conflict in Research Notes. - No county or municipality may levy its own cannabis tax to top up the distribution; the $5,000 fee + distribution + ordinary property/income taxes are the local fiscal channels.

State baseline to compare against: 1,000-foot buffer from a pre-existing K–12 school for state licensure, reducible by municipal ordinance (MCL 333.27959(3)(c) — [VERIFY]); no state buffer from parks, churches, child-care or other retailers (those are local additions); no state cap on number of licences (caps are local); zoning district eligibility is entirely local (CRA rules are silent on siting districts).

3.6 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say

What official sources actually publish (and what they do not): - The CRA publishes monthly sales reports and licence counts by type (Part 5/6 territory — not reproduced here) and Treasury publishes distribution tables by municipality/county (see §2.9). Neither publication, as retrieved in this pass, contains a ranking of "clusters" or a concentration analysis. - The distribution tables do show, arithmetically, that municipalities with more retailers/microbusinesses receive proportionally more money (formula, §2.6). That is not a concentration finding; it is the formula working as written. Examples that may be quoted as distribution facts, not as a ranking I created: Detroit (Wayne County) received the largest municipal payment in FY2024 and FY2025 because it had the most counted retailers (61 in FY2025); Wayne County (Wayne County) received the largest county payment in FY2024 (~$5M, secondary reporting). Those are Treasury-release facts as reported, not my ranking. - Border-county concentration: A November 2025 Indiana Lawyer report states that "on a per-capita basis, Michigan's border counties have two or three times the number of dispensaries as interior counties" and that Berrien County (Berrien County) had 27 shops. That is a secondary journalistic calculation, NOT an official source, and is therefore NOT adopted as an official concentration finding here. It is noted only so the parent does not mistake it for an official figure. If the dossier needs a border-concentration statement, it must be sourced to a CRA licence-count table by county (Part 5) and calculated transparently, or attributed to the Indiana Lawyer as secondary. - No official "top clusters" list is stated in this file. Any map or ranked list of clusters in the final dossier must come from a CRA/Treasury table cited by the parent, not from this section.

Parts 4–5 — Licence Types and Licence Data Sources (Run 1)

Dossier date / accessed date: 28 October 2026

Scope note. This file covers ONLY Part 4 (Licence Types) and Part 5 (Licence Data Sources) of the Michigan Run 1 commission. It does not build HTML; the parent agent compiles the dossier. No licence holder is listed individually in Part 5, per instructions.

Federal baseline (fixed context, not re-researched). State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. Nothing found in Parts 4–5 contradicts this baseline; licence-type and fee facts below are state law and do not change the federal schedule/280E split. Where a medical/adult-use licence pair exists, the medical licence is the one that falls on the Schedule III / 280E-relief side of the baseline and the adult-use licence stays on the Schedule I / full-280E side; a business holding both must split its activity — this Part does not re-litigate that split, it only identifies which licence is which.

Sourcing method and honesty rule used here. Official pages were opened directly where a verbatim URL was returned by search: the CRA Municipal Guide (revised March 2026, hosted by the Michigan Municipal League), Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.7 and R. 420.26 via Cornell LII, the CRA September 2025 Monthly Report (PDF), and USDA hemp-plan pages. Where the CRA's own current fee/assessment notice, social-equity community page, or statistical-report hub page could not be returned as a directly openable URL in this session, the figure is labelled [VERIFY] or attributed to the secondary source that cites the CRA, and is NOT upgraded to "confirmed from the CRA page itself." Search-result snippets alone were never treated as a direct opening. Every fact below carries a source link and the accessed date 2026-10-28.

Spelling note. Michigan statutes and rules spell the plant "marihuana." This report uses "marihuana" when quoting or naming a Michigan licence type and "marijuana/cannabis" in general prose. Licence prefixes seen in CRA documents: AU- = adult-use, GR-/PC-/PR- etc. for medical facility licences in older documents; current monthly reports use full type names rather than prefixes for counts.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

4.0 How Michigan licensing is organised — read this first

Michigan runs two overlapping commercial licensing systems under one regulator, the Cannabis Regulatory Agency (CRA) (within the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs, LARA):

  1. Medical — Medical Marihuana Facilities Licensing Act (MMFLA), 2016 PA 281, MCL 333.27101 et seq. Licence types are called "marihuana facilities" / state operating licences: Class A, B and C growers, processor, provisioning centre, secure transporter, safety compliance facility. There is no medical microbusiness, medical designated consumption establishment, medical event organiser, or medical excess grower.
  2. Adult-use — Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act (MRTMA), Initiated Law 1 of 2018, MCL 333.27951 et seq. Licence types are called "marihuana establishments": Class A, B and C growers, excess grower, processor, retailer, secure transporter, safety compliance facility, microbusiness, Class A microbusiness, designated consumption establishment, marihuana event organiser, temporary marihuana event, and marihuana educational research.

The CRA Municipal Guide (revised March 2026) states both lists verbatim in one place, which is why it is used as the anchor for the type inventory:

  • Medical (MMFLA): "Class A Grower (may grow up to 500 marijuana plants) • Class B Grower (may grow up to 1,000 marijuana plants) • Class C Grower (may grow up to 1,500 marijuana plants) • Processor • Provisioning Center • Safety Compliance Facility • Secure Transporter" — Source: CRA Municipal Guide, revised Mar-2026, hosted at https://mml.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/CRA-Municipal-Guide-updated-March-2026.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Adult-use (MRTMA): "Class A Marijuana Grower (may grow up to 100 plants) • Class B Marijuana Grower (may grow up to 500 plants) • Class C Marijuana Grower (may grow up to 2,000 plants) • Excess Marijuana Grower (may grow up to 2,000 plants, depending on the adult-use licensee's medical marijuana plant allowance) • Marijuana Microbusiness (may grow up to 150 plants, process, and retail) • Class A Marijuana Microbusiness (may grow up to 300 plants, process, and retail) • Marijuana Processor • Marijuana Retailer • Marijuana Safety Compliance Facility • Marijuana Secure Transporter • Designed [sic] Consumption Establishment • Marijuana Event Organizer • Temporary Marijuana Event • Marijuana Educational Research" — Source: same CRA Municipal Guide, revised Mar-2026 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Note the guide's own typo "Designed" for "Designated"; the rule text uses "Designated Consumption Establishment."

Critical plant-count trap — do not conflate the two systems. A summary table that lists "Class A ≤500, Class B ≤1,000, Class C ≤2,000" without saying which programme it means is wrong for both programmes in part: medical is 500 / 1,000 / 1,500; adult-use is 100 / 500 / 2,000. The CannBus Q3 2026 summary table that prints "A: ≤500, B: ≤1,000, C: ≤2,000" as a single row is therefore treated here as a conflated secondary summary, not as a source for plant limits. Source for the conflated table: https://www.cannbus.org/lsum/mi_lsum.html — Accessed 2026-10-28. The authoritative split above is from the CRA Municipal Guide.

Two-step application (both systems). Step 1 = prequalification (the entity and its owners/supplemental applicants: background checks, financial-source disclosure). Step 2 = establishment/facility licence (the specific premises: municipal authorisation, security plan, business plan, inspection). The CRA's own Step 1 instructions state: "The adult-use marijuana establishment licensing application process is divided into two steps. Step 1 is the prequalification application. During prequalification, background checks are completed on the main applicant and all supplemental applicants. There is a $3,000 application fee for the main applicant. The application fee is nonrefundable and does not apply to supplemental applicants." and "Prequalification status is valid for a period of two years after the CRA issues a notice of prequalification. If the applicant does not submit a Step 2 application within that timeframe, the prequalification status will expire." Step 2 should not be submitted more than 60 days before the establishment is ready to pass inspection; MRTMA requires a licence determination within 90 days. Source: CRA, "AU Step 1 – Supplemental Individual Prequalification Application Instructions" (PDF): https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Adult-Use-Establishment-Licensing/Adult-Use-Paper-Application-Forms-and-Resources/Paper-Application-Instructions/Step-1---Supplemental-Individual-Prequalification-Application-Instructions.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Licence term. Medical and adult-use licences are annual; the Municipal Guide states a renewed medical facility licence is "extended by one year" and a renewed adult-use establishment licence "will be renewed for a one-year period." Source: CRA Municipal Guide, revised Mar-2026 (same URL as above) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

No statewide cap on most types; local authorisation is the real gate. Michigan imposes no statewide numerical cap on most adult-use or medical licence types in statute or rule. What limits entry is (a) municipal authorisation — a medical facility needs a municipal ordinance authorising that facility type (MMFLA §205, MCL 333.27205), and an adult-use establishment may be completely prohibited or numerically limited by municipal ordinance (MRTMA §6, MCL 333.27956) — and (b) the stacking/eligibility rules below (excess grower, microbusiness, safety-compliance independence). This is covered in full in Part 3 of the full dossier; it is stated here only because "open or capped" cannot be answered without it. Sources: CRA Municipal Guide, revised Mar-2026, quoting MMFLA §205 and MRTMA §6 — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Official info pages. The CRA's home is https://www.michigan.gov/cra (cited in CRA documents as www.michigan.gov/cra). Individual CRA licence-type application/instruction pages are published as PDFs under that site; the two directly opened in this session are the Step 1 instructions above and the Municipal Guide. A single consolidated "licence types" HTML page on michigan.gov/cra was not returned as a directly openable URL in this session, so per-type "official info page" links below point to the CRA site root plus the specific rule (Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.x) and the Municipal Guide, and are marked [VERIFY] where a dedicated CRA type page could not be opened. Do not invent CRA sub-page URLs.

4.1 Adult-use fee schedule — the current rule (R. 420.7)

Verbatim operative text, Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.7, "Application; fees; assessment" (2020 AACS; 2022 MR 5, eff. 3/7/2022 — last amendment date shown on the Cornell LII copy; a later CRA rules rewrite, set 2023-25 LR, was in progress in 2026 with a second public hearing 23 July 2026, but no replacement fee table was confirmed as effective in this session — see Research Notes):

"(2) An applicant for a marihuana license shall submit an application that is accompanied by the nonrefundable application fee of $3,000." "(4) Additional fees for state licenses under MRTMA are listed in table 1"

Table 1 — Initial Licensure and Renewal Fees (same fee at initial licensure and at renewal, unless noted):

Adult-use licence type (R. 420.7 Table 1) Initial licensure AND renewal fee
Class A Marihuana Grower $1,200
Class B Marihuana Grower $6,000
Class C Marihuana Grower $24,000
Designated Consumption Establishment $1,000
Excess Marihuana Grower $24,000 *
Marihuana Event Organizer $1,000
Marihuana Microbusiness $8,300
Class A Marihuana Microbusiness $18,600
Marihuana Processor $24,000
Marihuana Retailer $15,000
Marihuana Safety Compliance Facility $15,000
Marihuana Secure Transporter $15,000
Temporary Marihuana Event See R. 420.26 (below)
Marihuana Educational Research N/A (no fee in Table 1)

* Excess-grower nuance — see §4.3: R. 420.23(8) provides the Class C fee "is assessed on the excess marihuana grower license at every 2,000 marihuana plant increment authorized," so a multi-increment excess licence costs multiples of $24,000. The $24,000 in Table 1 is therefore the per-increment figure, not a flat total for every excess licence. An older CRA rules-impact statement that listed Class A microbusiness at "$8,600" is superseded by the $18,600 in current R. 420.7; do not use $8,600.

Further verbatim R. 420.7 provisions:

"(1) At the beginning of each state fiscal year, the agency may increase the fees collected under the MRTMA by 10% in order to pay for implementation, administration, and enforcement of that act and these rules." "(3) If the costs of the investigation and processing the application exceed the application fee, the applicant shall pay the additional amount." "(5) The agency shall establish and publish annually the regulatory assessment for licensees under the MMFLA pursuant to section 603 of the MMFLA, MCL 333.27603." "(7) The agency shall not issue a marihuana license until a complete application is submitted, the fees required under these rules are paid, and the agency determines that the applicant is qualified to receive a marihuana license under the acts and these rules. An applicant under the MRTMA must pay initial licensure fees within 10 calendar days of approval of the marihuana license or within 90 calendar days of submitting a complete application, whichever date is first."

Source for all R. 420.7 text above: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-7 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Cross-check (same table): https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-licenses/section-r-420-7/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.

What the $3,000 does and does not cover. It is the Step 1 prequalification application fee for the main applicant only; supplemental applicants pay no separate application fee (CRA Step 1 instructions, above). It is nonrefundable and is separate from the initial licensure fee above, from any MMFLA regulatory assessment, and from any municipal fee (up to $5,000/year under MMFLA §205(2) and, for adult-use, under the municipality's own ordinance — see Part 3). Temporary marihuana event organiser applicants are the exception: R. 420.26(3) provides "A marihuana event organizer applicant is not required to pay an application fee" for a temporary event — see §4.8.

Sources: plant limits — CRA Municipal Guide, revised Mar-2026 (URL above) — Accessed 2026-10-28; adult-use rule text — Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.102(1): "a marihuana grower license authorizes the marihuana grower to cultivate not more than the following number of marihuana plants under the indicated license class for each marihuana grower license the marihuana grower holds in that class: Class C – 2,000 marihuana plants" (quoted in a CRA formal complaint, ENF-24-00816, and in the rules compilation at https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ — Accessed 2026-10-28). The "for each licence" wording is the stacking rule: each additional licence in the same class adds its own plant allowance at the same premises, subject to the co-location rules — see §4.9.

Stacking. Grower licences may be stacked (multiple licences of the same class held by the same person at one location), and the plant count is per licence. The CRA has enforced this as a combined cap: e.g. a respondent holding six co-located licences (five Class C + one excess) was held to a combined 12,000-plant maximum (2,000 per licence) — see CRA consent order discussed in Part 5, §5.5. Stacking does not allow plants authorised under one licence to be counted under another licence's inventory in Metrc without a proper internal transfer.

Eligibility / independence restriction [VERIFY for current rule text]. The rules compilation states: "To be eligible for a grower license, the applicant and each investor in the grower must not have an interest in a secure transporter or safety compliance facility" (R. 420.102(7) as reproduced at https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2026/05/Redline-March-2025-DraftRules-and-DraftRuleVersion_6_05.06.26.pdf — Accessed 2026-10-28). This is a draft-rules compilation, not the current official Administrative Code PDF opened directly, so it is marked [VERIFY] against the current R. 420.102 text before republication.

Applications open or capped? Open statewide (no statewide cap); subject to municipal authorisation and to the applicant meeting prequalification + Step 2. The former MRTMA restriction that Class B/C adult-use applicants first hold a medical licence was removed 1 March 2021 (secondary summary, https://www.mycannabis.com/what-are-the-cannabis-licensing-requirements-in-michigan/ — Accessed 2026-10-28) — marked [VERIFY] against the rule history, but consistent with the current open-application counts in CRA monthly reports.

4.3 Excess grower (adult-use only)

  • What it allows: Cultivate marihuana and sell/transfer it to marihuana establishments. R. 420.23(2): "An excess marihuana grower license authorizes sale of marihuana, other than seeds, seedlings, tissue cultures, immature plants, and cuttings, to a marihuana processor or marihuana retailer." Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-licenses/part-2/section-r-420-23/ — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Eligibility — the gate that makes it different from a fourth class: R. 420.23(3): "An excess marihuana grower license may be issued only to a person who holds 5 stacked class C marihuana grower licenses issued by the agency under the MRTMA and at least 2 grower class C licenses issued by the agency under the MMFLA." Same source — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Plant count: R. 420.23(7): "The agency shall set the total marihuana plant count for an excess marihuana grower license in increments of 2,000 marihuana plants not in excess of the total marihuana plants permitted under grower class C licenses held under the MMFLA." Worked example used consistently in CRA guidance and secondary summaries: five adult-use Class C licences = 10,000 plants; two medical Class C licences = 3,000 medical plants, so the excess licence may authorise 2,000 additional adult-use plants (one 2,000-plant increment, capped by the medical allowance); three medical Class C licences would support up to 4,000 excess plants (two increments), subject to CRA setting the count. The CRA Municipal Guide's shorthand — "may grow up to 2,000 plants, depending on the adult-use licensee's medical marijuana plant allowance" — describes the single-increment case, not a universal 2,000-plant ceiling. Sources: R. 420.23 via Justia (above); CRA Municipal Guide (above) — both Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Fee: $24,000 per 2,000-plant increment (R. 420.23(8): "the initial licensure fee of a class C marihuana grower license is assessed on the excess marihuana grower license at every 2,000 marihuana plant increment authorized by the state license"), plus the $3,000 prequalification application fee. R. 420.7 Table 1 lists "$24,000" for excess grower without the per-increment qualifier in the table itself — read Table 1 together with R. 420.23(8). Source: R. 420.23 via Justia — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Other rules: R. 420.23(9): "An excess marihuana grower licensee is subject to all requirements for a marihuana grower as provided for in the MRTMA and these rules, as applicable." Note in R. 420.7's older compilation: "The fee for an excess marihuana grower is a renewal fee only" — [VERIFY] whether that footnote survives in the current rule; the current Cornell R. 420.7 Table 1 heading says "Initial Licensure and Renewal Fees" for excess grower without that footnote.
  • Applications open or capped? Open only to operators who already meet the 5 + 2 stacking threshold; in that sense it is eligibility-capped, not numerically capped.

4.4 Processor (both programmes)

  • What it allows: Obtain marihuana from marihuana establishments/facilities; extract resin, manufacture marihuana-infused products, process and package marihuana; sell/transfer packaged product to marihuana establishments (adult-use) or to provisioning centres and other processors (medical). MRTMA definition (MCL 333.27953, "marihuana processor"): "a person licensed to obtain marihuana from marihuana establishments; process and package marihuana; and sell or otherwise transfer marihuana to marihuana establishments." Source: MRTMA §3 as reproduced at https://komornlaw.com/michigan-regulation-and-taxation-of-marihuana-act-section-3-2/ — Accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary reproduction; official text at legislature.mi.gov to be re-checked in Part 1].
  • Plant/canopy limit: None (processors do not cultivate).
  • Adult-use fee: $24,000 initial + $24,000 renewal, plus $3,000 prequalification application fee. Source: R. 420.7 Table 1 — Accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Medical fee: Annual regulatory assessment (§4.10). No plant limit applies.
  • Applications open or capped? Open statewide, subject to municipal authorisation.
  • Hemp interaction (cross-reference Part 7): A medical processor may purchase raw industrial hemp and hemp products under the hemp acts without a separate hemp processor-handler licence in the circumstances described in MDARD/CRA transition FAQs; an adult-use processor needs a hemp processor-handler licence to perform the same hemp activities. Source: MDARD bulletin via GovDelivery: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/2f69c1a — Accessed 2026-10-28. [VERIFY] against current CRA hemp FAQ before republication, as this is a transition-FAQ statement.

4.5 Retail: provisioning centre (medical) and retailer (adult-use)

Licence Programme Sells to Adult-use fee Medical fee
Provisioning Center MMFLA Registered qualifying patients and registered primary caregivers only — Annual regulatory assessment (§4.10)
Marihuana Retailer MRTMA Individuals 21+; also to other marihuana establishments under the MRTMA definition ("obtain marihuana from marihuana establishments and to sell or otherwise transfer marihuana to marihuana establishments and to individuals who are 21 years of age or older") $15,000 initial + $15,000 renewal, plus $3,000 prequalification —

Sources: MRTMA §3 definitions via https://komornlaw.com/michigan-regulation-and-taxation-of-marihuana-act-section-3-2/ — Accessed 2026-10-28; R. 420.7 Table 1 — Accessed 2026-10-28; CRA Municipal Guide MMFLA list (provisioning centre as a facility type) — Accessed 2026-10-28.

Co-location / "equivalent licences." The same person may hold a medical provisioning centre licence and an adult-use retailer licence at the same premises; Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.1 defines "equivalent licenses" to include a retailer + provisioning centre pair, a grower + grower pair across programmes, a processor + processor pair, a secure transporter + secure transporter pair, and a safety compliance facility + safety compliance facility pair. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-1 — Accessed 2026-10-28. Each licence is still separately fee'd and separately counted in CRA totals — a co-located retailer + provisioning centre is TWO licences, not one. This matters for every count in Part 5.

Delivery — no separate licence. Michigan issues no standalone delivery licence. Retailers, microbusinesses and provisioning centres may be approved for home delivery under the delivery rules; delivery employees must be 21+. This is stated here because a reader looking for a "delivery licence" in the fee table will not find one. Source: secondary summary citing CRA delivery checklist, https://legalclarity.org/michigan-cannabis-licensing-types-process-and-compliance/ — Accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against CRA delivery checklist]. CRA monthly reports separately count "Retailers Approved for Home Delivery" (adult-use: 350 as of 30 Sept 2025) and "Provisioning Centers Approved for Home Delivery" (medical: 58 as of 30 Sept 2025) — see Part 5, §5.2.

Applications open or capped? Open statewide; locally capped/prohibited by municipal ordinance in many municipalities (Part 3).
