Michigan Cannabis and Hemp — Run 2, Part 7: HEMP LICENCES ONLY

Dossier date / date accessed for every fact below: 28 October 2026. Scope: Part 7 ONLY. This file does not build HTML; the parent agent compiles the dossier. It covers every Michigan hemp licence/registration type, the state-plan vs USDA question, registries, intoxicating-hemp rules, and the effect of the new federal hemp dates on licences. Marihuana (MMFLA/MRTMA) licence types, fees and counts are Run 1 Part 4 and are not re-stated here except where a hemp rule expressly cross-references them. Spelling note: Michigan statutes spell the plant "marihuana." This report preserves "marihuana" in statute names, citations and verbatim quotations, and uses "marijuana" only in plain-English discussion or where a source uses it. Federal baseline — fixed by the commission, NOT re-researched, and used as given: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I; IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity and remains fully applicable to adult-use; hemp PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026 but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026, after which the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA enforcement of DEA-registered-lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026; the federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026; there is no federal cannabis banking law. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the Michigan hemp sources examined for this Part, except as flagged in §7.8 and Research Note R-09 (the Senate Fiscal Agency's Winter 2026 analysis of the federal bill's narrower hemp categories is analysis of the federal text, not a Michigan enactment, and is not adopted here as a restatement of the federal baseline). Sourcing method and honesty rule: Official pages were opened directly where a verbatim URL was returned: the USDA approved-plan list (updated 17 February 2026), the Michigan State Hemp Plan (v3, 3 June 2022), 7 CFR 990.21, MCL 286.847 (processor-handler) via FindLaw, MCL 333.29201 (grower registration) via FindLaw, and the engrossed texts of SB 599 and SB 609 via LegiScan. Where the CRA's own current hemp FAQ page or MDARD's current "Industrial Hemp Program Fees" sheet could not be returned as a directly openable URL in this session, the figure is labelled secondary-sourced and [VERIFY], and is NOT upgraded to "confirmed from the agency page itself." Search-result snippets alone were never treated as a direct opening. Every fact below carries a source link and the accessed date 2026-10-28. No personal phone number or email of an individual is reproduced; official public business contacts (agency programme pages) are cited only by URL, not by an individual's direct contact details. County is given for every Michigan place named (in this Part, only Lansing, Ingham County, is named as a place).

THE PLAIN ANSWER — WHICH PROGRAMME IS CURRENT ON 28 OCTOBER 2026 (read this first)

*On 28 October 2026 Michigan still runs its own USDA-approved state hemp plan for cultivation, administered by the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD). A Michigan hemp grower still registers with MDARD under the Industrial Hemp Growers Act, 2020 PA 220 — it does NOT yet hold a USDA-direct Hemp Producer License. The widely repeated Run 1 claim that Michigan "ended its MDARD state programme at the close of 2024" and that growers "moved to USDA direct from 1 January 2025" under HB 5977 is WRONG as a statement of enacted law: HB 5977 (2024) died in committee (Intro Sine Die, last action 15 October 2024, referred to the House Agriculture Committee, never passed), and the USDA's own plan-status page, updated 17 February 2026 and opened directly for this Part, still lists "Michigan — MI Approved Plan (pdf) " rather than "USDA Hemp Producer License." What DID happen in 2024 was a proposal and press reporting that treated the proposal as done: MDARD said the programme was no longer financially sustainable (631 growers in 2020 down to 34 in 2024) and asked for the programme to be abolished, and trade press reported the transfer as effective 1 January 2025. The actual legislative vehicle for that transfer is a NEW package introduced in October 2025 — Senate Bills 608 and 609 (with House companions HB 5094 and HB 5095) — which passed the Senate 32–0 on 4 June 2026 and were referred to the House Committee on Regulatory Reform the same day, with no House passage or Governor's signature located as of 28 October 2026. Until the House passes SB 608/609 (or a successor) and the Governor signs them, the MDARD state-plan registration at $1,250 remains the live cultivation route, the CRA processor-handler licence at $1,350 remains the live processing/handling/marketing route, and a USDA-direct licence for a Michigan grower is a FUTURE, contingent route — not the current one. Any dossier text, directory entry or advice page that tells a Michigan grower to "apply to USDA" today must be corrected. Remaining [VERIFY]: (i) whether MDARD has in practice stopped accepting new registrations for the 2026 cycle despite the plan remaining approved — the 2026-cycle fee sheet reported by secondary sources (see §7.1) suggests it has not, but the MDARD fee/application page itself could not be opened directly in this session, so a live MDARD-page check is the single most important follow-up; (ii) the engrossed effective date of SB 608 (see §7.6).

7.1 At a glance — every Michigan hemp authorisation, current vs pending vs future

# Authorisation Issuer (current, 28 Oct 2026) What it covers, in one line Fee (current) Term / cycle
H1 Industrial Hemp Grower Registration MDARD, under 2020 PA 220, USDA-approved state plan Grow (plant, propagate, cultivate, harvest, dry, store) industrial hemp; sell harvested hemp to a licensed processor-handler or a licensed MMFLA processor $1,250 registration fee, nonrefundable/nontransferable; $50 per growing-location modification; sampling/testing invoiced at reasonable cost (see §7.2) 1 February – 31 January; renewal after 31 January carries a $250 late fee (secondary-sourced — [VERIFY] against the MDARD fee sheet)
H2 Hemp Processor-Handler Licence CRA (since 13 April 2022, ERO 2022-1), under 2014 PA 547 Process, handle, broker or market industrial hemp — including retail sale of a hemp product — in Michigan $1,350 application fee, nonrefundable; $50 per site alteration; $250 late fee on renewals postmarked after 30 November 1 December – 30 November; initial licence expires 30 November of its issue year
H3 MMFLA processor licence used for hemp (NOT a hemp licence) CRA, under MMFLA 2016 PA 281 A licensed medical marihuana processor is EXEMPT from the processor-handler requirement for hemp it processes; it does not need H2 as well for the same hemp activity MMFLA regulatory assessment (Run 1 Part 4, §4.10 — not a hemp fee) Annual (MMFLA)
H4 USDA Hemp Producer License USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), under 7 CFR Part 990 Subpart C FUTURE/CONTINGENT ONLY for Michigan — would authorise hemp production in Michigan IF the state plan is withdrawn/repealed and Michigan becomes a USDA-direct state No licence fee is stated in 7 CFR 990.21 (see §7.3 — fee absence is [VERIFY] against the AMS application page, but no fee appears in the regulation text) Until 31 December of the year three years after the year of issue; renewal before expiry, not automatic
H5 Consumable Hemp Processor state licence (PENDING — NOT LAW) Would be CRA, under the proposed Industrial Hemp Processing Act (SB 599) Would license processing of CONSUMABLE hemp products only (edibles/beverages/infused liquids for human/animal consumption); non-consumable hemp processing would NOT need it (SB 599 §201(4)) Proposed $1,350 state licence fee + $50 site-location modification fee (SB 599 §405, engrossed text) Proposed 1 December – 30 November (SB 599 §203)
H6 Regulatory testing facility / compliance monitoring testing facility (NOT a grower/processor licence) No separate "hemp lab licence" is issued by MDARD or the CRA as a standalone authorisation in current law; a regulatory testing facility is a DEA-registered laboratory meeting Growers Act §403 Tests OFFICIAL hemp samples (regulatory testing facility) or UNOFFICIAL samples for compliance monitoring (compliance monitoring testing facility) No licence fee stated in the Growers Act definitions; testing/sampling costs are invoiced to the grower at reasonable cost N/A — laboratory status, not a term licence
— Hemp retail/store licence, hemp transporter licence, hemp seed licence None exists as a standalone type Retailing = H2 (processor-handler, because "market" includes selling); transporting/storing = H2 (or H1 for a grower's own harvested hemp to its buyer); seed supply = part of H5 if SB 599 passes, otherwise no standalone seed licence — —

How to use this table: A person who only grows hemp needs H1 only. A person who only processes, handles, brokers or sells hemp (including a shop that only retails CBD oil) needs H2 only — unless they are an MMFLA processor (H3) or a college/university (see §7.5). A person who both grows and processes needs BOTH H1 and H2 (drying one's own hemp is "grow," not processing — see §7.2.4 — but turning it into a marketable product, including smokable flower for sale, is processing). A person who grows hemp for research at a college/university is excepted from both H1 and H2 in the terms stated in §7.5. No hemp authorisation, current or pending, authorises handling marihuana: anything over the Michigan THC definition is marihuana and needs a CRA marihuana licence (Run 1 Part 4), not a hemp licence (§7.7).

7.2 H1 — MDARD Industrial Hemp Grower Registration (CURRENT — state plan)

7.2.1 Legal home and plan status

  • Statute: Industrial Hemp Growers Act, 2020 PA 220, MCL 333.29101–333.29801. Enacted 16 October 2020; amended 24 March 2021 (2021 PA 4) to align with the USDA Final Rule (7 CFR Part 990, effective 22 March 2021). The March 2021 amendments, as summarised in the Governor's signing release, changed the grower registration cycle from 1 December–30 November to 1 February–31 January and increased the harvest window from 15 to 30 days. Source: Governor's release via https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIEOG/bulletins/2c94b5f (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • USDA-approved state plan: Michigan's plan, v3 dated 3 June 2022 (performance-based pre-harvest sampling update), was submitted by MDARD and approved by USDA. The plan itself states MDARD "works closely with regulated businesses," that PA 220 "authorizes the Department to register persons engaged in the cultivation of industrial hemp," and that MDARD reports registered growers to USDA by the 1st of each month. Source: Michigan State Hemp Plan, opened directly — https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/MichiganStateHempPlan.pdf (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Plan-status evidence (the decisive current fact): USDA AMS, "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans," updated 17 February 2026, opened directly, lists in its States table: "Michigan | MI Approved Plan (pdf) " — where "" means "Plan approved under the final rule which took effect March 22, 2021" and the alternative entry for a USDA-direct state reads "USDA Hemp Producer License." Michigan is NOT in the USDA-direct column. The page's own rule is also stated on it: "Once a plan is approved by USDA, it remains in effect unless withdrawn by the State or Tribal government or revoked by USDA." No withdrawal or revocation of Michigan's plan is shown on that page. Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review (opened 2026-10-28).
  • Therefore: Run 1 Part 4, §4.13A and Part 5, §5.9 were CORRECT to describe Michigan as a state-plan state (USDA list, 17 February 2026), and Run 1 Part 0, §0.4 / Part 1, §1.2.6 / Part 6, §6.7 were WRONG to state the state programme "ended" / "was terminated" at the end of 2024 and cultivation "moved to USDA" from 1 January 2025 as enacted law. The correction is adopted in this Part: state plan = current; USDA-direct = pending/contingent (§7.3, §7.6). See Research Notes R-01 for the full conflict log.

7.2.2 What it allows — and what it does not

  • Operative prohibition — Growers Act §201(1), MCL 333.29201, verbatim (FindLaw reproduction, opened 2026-10-28):

    "A person shall not grow industrial hemp in this state unless the person is a grower." "Grower" means a person required to be registered under §201 (MCL 333.29103, via LawServer reproduction of §29307's definitions note, accessed 2026-10-28).

  • "Grow" / "growing" (MDARD 2024 guidance, summarising PA 220): "to plant, propagate, cultivate, or harvest live plants or viable seed; drying and storing harvested industrial hemp; possessing live industrial hemp plants or viable seed on a premises where the live industrial hemp plants or viable seed are grown; growing industrial hemp for the purposes of conducting research; and, selling harvested industrial hemp to a processor-handler licensed under [2014 PA 547], or [a] processor licensed under [MMFLA]." Source: MDARD GovDelivery bulletin, 11 January 2024 — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/384287a (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • What it does NOT allow: (a) Processing harvested hemp into a marketable form, brokering it, or marketing/selling a finished hemp product — that needs H2 (or H3), except for the grower's own sale of RAW harvested hemp to an H2/H3 buyer, which is inside "grow" (see above). (b) Growing marihuana under a hemp registration — MDARD's 31 May 2024 reminder states expressly: "You cannot grow marijuana under a hemp registration. MDARD conducts regular hemp inspections, which can be announced or unannounced… MDARD has the authority to test any plants they deem necessary, as well as order disposal of any plants that test as marijuana." Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/39fe078 (accessed 2026-10-28). (c) Selling an intermediary, in-process or finished hemp product, or smokable hemp flower, unless the grower is ALSO licensed as a processor-handler (H2) or as an MMFLA processor (H3) — Growers Act §303/§307 as reproduced in the SB 601 engrossed text (which quotes the current Act before amending it), accessed 2026-10-28 via https://legiscan.com/MI/text/SB0601/id/3291321/Michigan-2025-SB0601-Engrossed.html.
  • No acreage or grower-number cap: MSU Extension's hemp FAQ, summarising MDARD's position, states: "Is there a limit on the number of licenses for hemp issued from MDARD? No, there is no limit on the number of licenses issued or the number of acres grown in Michigan." Source: https://msu-prod.dotcmscloud.com/hemp/index (accessed 2026-10-28). That FAQ is old (it still quotes the $100 pilot grower fee — see §7.2.3), so the no-cap principle is carried forward only as a programme principle, [VERIFY] against the current MDARD programme page; no cap appears in PA 220's text as reproduced.

7.2.3 Fees — statute vs fee sheet (resolve the $100 / $1,250 / $1,350 confusion explicitly)

  • Statutory grower fee — Growers Act §511, MCL 333.29511, verbatim in substance (LawServer/US Lawyer Database reproductions, accessed 2026-10-28):

    "(1) A grower is subject to the following fees, as applicable: (a) A registration fee of $1,250.00. (b) A growing location modification fee of $50.00 for each growing location modification request form submitted under section 311. (2) A grower shall pay a fee required under this act at the time an application is submitted under section 201 or at the time the growing location modification request form is submitted under section 311. … (3) A fee required under this act is nonrefundable and nontransferable. (4) A grower shall pay a fee charged for total delta-9-THC testing under chapter IV within 15 days after receiving the invoice. A fee under this subsection is limited to the reasonable costs of conducting the testing. (5) A grower shall pay a fee charged for the collection of an official hemp sample within 15 days after receiving the invoice. A fee under this subsection is limited to the reasonable costs of collecting the official hemp sample." History line on that section: "2020, Act 220, Imd. Eff. Oct. 16, 2020; Am. 2021, Act 4, Imd. Eff. Mar. 24, 2021." Source: https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/michigan/mi-laws/michigan_laws_333-29511 (accessed 2026-10-28).

  • Where the other figures come from (do not conflate):
  • $100 = the OLD grower registration fee under the 2014 Act's §16, MCL 286.856(1)(a) ("A grower registration fee of $100.00"), added by 2018 PA 641. That was the 2019–2020 pilot-programme fee. It is superseded for cultivation by PA 220's $1,250. Any source still quoting $100 for a Michigan grower registration in 2026 is quoting the pilot Act, not current law. Source: https://law.uslawyerdatabase.com/section-286-856-fees/ (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • $1,350 = the PROCESSOR-HANDLER fee (§7.4), not a grower fee. Run 1 Part 1, Research Note R-03 correctly suspected conflation here: press reports that said growers "were paying $1,350" (MJBizDaily/Hemp Today, November 2024; Four20 Post, November 2024) conflated the grower and processor-handler fees, or quoted a combined grower-plus-processor cost. Adopted: grower = $1,250 (statute); processor-handler = $1,350 (statute/form). The $1,350-as-grower-fee figure is REJECTED.
  • $250 late fee / $150 sampling / $150 testing (2026 cycle): Secondary sources reporting MDARD's fee sheet state: "$1,250 nonrefundable grower registration application fee; $250 late fee on renewals after Jan 31; $50 per growing-location modification form; $150 per site visit for preharvest or remediation sampling; $150 per sample tested at MDARD's Geagley Lab, new from Jan 1, 2026" and "registration cycle runs Feb 1 to Jan 31 (2026 cycle: Feb 1, 2026 to Jan 31, 2027)." Sources: https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/michigan/ (checked 27 September 2026, per that page) and https://legalclarity.org/how-to-legally-grow-hemp-in-michigan/ (both accessed 2026-10-28). Status: secondary-sourced, [VERIFY] against MDARD's current fee sheet before publication. The $150 figures are consistent with §511(4)–(5)'s "reasonable costs, invoiced" mechanism (i.e. they are MDARD's invoiced reasonable-cost amounts, not a second statutory fee), but the fee sheet itself was not directly opened in this session, so $150 is not stated here as statute. The $250 late fee does NOT appear in §511's text as reproduced and is therefore also fee-sheet-only [VERIFY].
  • Payment/collection: §511(6) — MDARD "may refer a fee charged under subsection (4) or (5) that remains unpaid for more than 180 days to the department of treasury for collection." No sampling will be collected while fees/fines are outstanding (Growers Act §401(4), as reproduced in the State Hemp Plan attachment, accessed 2026-10-28).

7.2.4 Requirements — application, background, locations, sampling, testing, disposal

  • Application contents — §201(2), MCL 333.29201, verbatim in substance (FindLaw, opened 2026-10-28): full name, date of birth, mailing address, telephone number, email address; if not an individual, the EIN and, for each key participant, full name, date of birth, title and email address; total acreage and greenhouse/indoor square footage; address, legal description and GPS coordinates for each field, greenhouse, building or other location; maps depicting each location indicating entrances, field boundaries and specific locations corresponding to the GPS coordinates; a criminal history report for the applicant (or each key participant, if not an individual).
  • Background / disqualification: The application requires an FBI Identity History Summary for each key participant, dated within 60 days of submission (secondary summaries of the MDARD application, consistent across LegalClarity/Sativa, accessed 2026-10-28 — [VERIFY] the 60-day rule against the current MDARD application form; the 60-day rule IS in the USDA regulation at 7 CFR 990.21(a)(3)(ii) for USDA licences and is the same rule MDARD applies under the state plan). A person with a felony controlled-substance conviction in the past 10 years is disqualified under the federal plan requirements that PA 220 implements — the exact disqualification text in PA 220 §201/§203 is [VERIFY] against the current MCL text before publication; do not quote a 10-year rule as PA 220 verbatim on the basis of secondary summaries alone. MDARD's 2024 guidance adds the practical point: "Applying does not guarantee you are registered. If there are any deficiencies, you will receive an email requesting additional information. You will not be issued a certificate if you do not correct those deficiencies." Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/398a83d (accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Decision time: MDARD must approve or deny a completed application within 120 days (secondary summary citing the USDA state-plan summary — [VERIFY] against PA 220 §203; the 120-day figure is carried from Run 1 Part 4, §4.13A, also [VERIFY]).
  • Cycle and renewal: Registration cycle 1 February – 31 January (2021 PA 4 change, above). MDARD mailed 2024 renewal applications on 4 December 2023 and warned: "If any firms are still conducting any growing activities after January 31, 2024, hemp grower registration cannot lapse" and renewal applicants must not use the new-registrant online form (it "will be rejected"). Source: MDARD bulletin, 11 January 2024 — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/384287a (accessed 2026-10-28). The 2026 cycle (1 February 2026 – 31 January 2027) is reported by Sativa (above) — [VERIFY] against the MDARD renewal mailing for 2026.
  • Pre-harvest sampling — §401(1), MCL 333.29401, verbatim in substance (State Hemp Plan attachment, opened 2026-10-28): "A grower that intends to harvest an industrial hemp lot shall contact the department not more than 30 days or less than 20 days before the grower's anticipated harvest to collect an official hemp sample of each lot of industrial hemp grown. A designated sampling agent shall collect an official hemp sample before the grower's anticipated harvest, and the grower or the grower's authorized representative must be present." The grower must give the sampling agent "complete and unrestricted access" during normal business hours to all cannabis and all acreage/greenhouses/fields/buildings/locations where cannabis is growing or stored (§401(2)). A grower "may collect an unofficial hemp sample and submit [it] to a compliance monitoring testing facility for compliance monitoring at any time" (§401(5)). Performance-based sampling (reduced or no regulatory sampling for certified seed, consistently compliant varieties, academic-research lots, or growers with a compliant history) is permitted under §401(6) and is the subject of the plan's June 2022 v3 update.
  • Testing — what is tested, and by whom: Official samples go "to a regulatory testing facility for total delta-9-THC testing under section 403" (§401(3)). "Regulatory testing facility" is defined (MCL 333.29103) as a laboratory that (i) is registered with the DEA, (ii) is authorised to conduct chemical analysis of controlled substances under 21 CFR 1301.13, (iii) meets §403's requirements, and (iv) conducts testing of official hemp samples. "Total delta-9-THC" means delta-9-THC plus 87.7% of THCA (the post-decarboxylation calculation), per the §103 definitions reproduced in the SB 601 engrossed text. Note the terminology trap: Michigan's Growers Act testing is still described in the Act as "total delta-9-THC" (delta-9 + 0.877×THCA), while Michigan's marihuana/hemp LINE for classification purposes uses the broader MRTMA §3 "THC" definition (THCA + any THC isomer, natural or artificial — see §7.7). A lot can therefore pass Growers Act total-delta-9 testing and still be marihuana if its isomer content pushes total THC over 0.3% — [VERIFY] how MDARD/CRA reconcile the two tests in practice; no reconciling guidance was located in this session.
  • Disposal / remediation: Non-compliant lots must be disposed of or remediated under Growers Act Chapter IV (§§405–407 in the Act's numbering; remediation = "an activity that transitions noncompliant industrial hemp into industrial hemp that is in compliance" — §103 definition). Detail of disposal/remediation methods is [VERIFY] against the current Act text — this Part does not invent a disposal method.
  • Inspections, records, FSA reporting: MDARD conducts announced and unannounced inspections (31 May 2024 reminder, above). Growers must keep variety/seed documentation (invoices, Certificates of Analysis, seed labels) — without it, "sampling will likely occur" (same reminder). Growers must also report crop acreage to the USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) — MDARD's April 2024 cultivation-season reminder lists "USDA Farm Service Agency (FSA) Crop Acreage Reporting" as a grower requirement. Source: https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/398a83d (accessed 2026-10-28). MDARD must maintain registration applications for 5 years and report growers to USDA monthly (State Hemp Plan §1.1, above).
  • Info link (current): MDARD Industrial Hemp programme hub, as cited in MDARD bulletins: www.michigan.gov/industrialhemp (also cited as www.michigan.gov/mdard and www.Michigan.gov/HempGrowing for forms in older bulletins — the industrialhemp hub is the current citation in the 2024 bulletins). The hub page itself could not be text-opened as a fee/application page in this session — [VERIFY] the live hub URL and the current application form before publication; do not publish a guessed MDARD sub-page URL.

7.3 H4 (future/contingent) — USDA Hemp Producer License: what it WOULD be if Michigan becomes a USDA-direct state

Status warning (repeat, because this is the error to avoid): this licence is NOT the current route for a Michigan grower on 28 October 2026. It is described here only so the dossier can state accurately what would change if SB 608/609 (or a successor) are enacted and Michigan's plan is withdrawn, and so a reader who finds a USDA licence in another state is not misled into applying for one for Michigan today. If SB 608/609 are enacted with the engrossed dates (§7.6), the transition date to watch is 1 February 2027 (SB 609 engrossed effective date), with the industrial hemp fund abolished 1 October 2027 — both dates are engrossed-bill dates, not law, and the SB 608 engrossed effective date is [VERIFY].

  • Legal home: Domestic Hemp Production Program, 7 CFR Part 990, Subpart C (§§990.20–990.28). The licence is issued by USDA AMS, not by any Michigan agency.
  • Operative text — 7 CFR 990.21(a), verbatim in substance (Cornell LII, opened 2026-10-28): "Any person producing or intending to produce hemp must have a valid license prior to producing hemp. A valid license means the license is unexpired, unsuspended, and unrevoked." Applications "may [be submitted] at any time" (§990.21(a)(2)). Required information: contact information (full name, residential address, telephone, email; for a business entity, business name, principal business location, key participants' full names/titles, email if available, EIN) and "A current criminal history report for an individual, or if the applicant is a business entity, all key participants, dated within 60 days of the application submission date. A license application will not be considered complete without all required criminal history reports." (§990.21(a)(3)).
  • Term: "USDA-issued hemp producer licenses shall be valid until December 31 of the year three years after the year in which license was issued." (§990.21(a)(6)). Renewal "must be [sought] prior to license expiration. Licenses are not automatically renewed. Applications for renewal shall be subject to the same terms, information collection requirements, and approval criteria" as initial applications (§990.21(b)). A licence modification is required for any change to the application information, including sale of the business, production at a new location, or a change in key participants (§990.21(c)).
  • Fee: No licence fee is stated in §990.21. Secondary summaries of USDA-direct states state the same conclusion ("No USDA license fee"; "USDA hemp licenses at no cost" — Missouri transition notice, as summarised for Missouri, accessed 2026-10-28 via https://sativauniversity.com/cannabis-laws/missouri/). Status: [VERIFY] against the AMS HeMP application page — the absence of a fee in the regulation text is strong evidence, but the AMS page itself was not opened in this session, so "no fee" is not stated here as AMS-confirmed. What a USDA licensee DOES pay for, in every USDA-direct summary, is its own sampling and DEA-registered-lab testing (sampling agent + lab fees, at the licensee's expense) — those are service costs, not a licence fee.
  • Sampling/testing under USDA (for contrast with §7.2.4): A USDA licensee must, "No more than 30 days prior to the anticipated harvest," have a sampling agent collect samples for total delta-9-THC testing (§990.24(a), as reproduced in secondary summaries, accessed 2026-10-28); the sample is the flowering tops (top 5–8 inches of main stem/terminal bud/central cola); the licensee's authorised representative should be present if possible; the crop must not be harvested before sampling; testing must be by a DEA-registered laboratory, must use a post-decarboxylation (or similarly reliable) method, and must report a measurement of uncertainty — a lot is compliant if THC + measurement of uncertainty ≤ 0.3% on a dry-weight basis. The federal DEA-lab enforcement delay to 31 December 2026 (fixed baseline) is the only reason a USDA licensee's DEA-lab obligation is not already fully enforced on the dossier date; after that date the delay expires on the baseline as given.
  • Research: Producers producing hemp for research must still obtain a USDA licence, but hemp for research that does not enter the stream of commerce is not subject to §§990.24/990.26 sampling if the producer adopts a USDA-approved alternative sampling method with 95% confidence the crop will not exceed the acceptable hemp THC level (§990.21(d)(1)). Only DEA-registered research institutions may keep over-threshold hemp until the end of a study (§990.21(d)(2)).
  • Reporting: USDA licensees report land/acreage to FSA, report disposals, and retain sampling/testing documentation (3 years under the USDA rule summaries; Michigan's state plan requires 5-year retention of applications — the two retention periods are different obligations and must not be conflated).
  • What would NOT change on a USDA transition (on the baseline and current Michigan law): The CRA processor-handler licence (H2) is under a DIFFERENT Act (2014 PA 547) from the Growers Act. Repealing the Growers Act (SB 608) does not by itself repeal PA 547. A Michigan processor-handler would therefore still need H2 after a cultivation transition, unless SB 599 (which repeals PA 547) is also enacted. SB 608/609 are expressly NOT part of the SB 599 package (State Affairs correction note, June 2026, accessed 2026-10-28: "The bills that passed the Senate Thursday… are not part of the larger package"). Do not present the cultivation transition as ending processor-handler licensing.

7.4 H2 — CRA Hemp Processor-Handler Licence (CURRENT)

7.4.1 Legal home and issuer history

  • Statute: Industrial Hemp Research and Development Act, 2014 PA 547, MCL 286.841–286.859. History: enacted 2014 (research only, originally); amended by 2018 PA 641 (HB 6330, effective 15 January 2019 — commercial programme; hemp-derived CBD not a controlled substance); amended by the 2021 PA 56-series companions (HB 4744, effective 11 October 2021 — THC redefinition, see §7.7). Current status: still in force on 28 October 2026; its repeal is proposed by pending SB 599 only (§7.6).
  • Issuer transfer: Processor-handler licensing was transferred from MDARD to the CRA (then the Marijuana Regulatory Agency) by Executive Reorganization Order 2022-1, compiled at MCL 333.27002, effective 13 April 2022. Older MDARD forms and mailing addresses (including the P.O. Box 30776, Lansing, Ingham County, address that appears on both MDARD grower and CRA processor-handler forms in secondary reproductions) therefore do NOT prove MDARD is still the issuer. Current issuer is the CRA. Source for the transfer: ERO 2022-1 compiler's note on MCL 286.856, accessed 2026-10-28 via https://law.uslawyerdatabase.com/section-286-856-fees/.
  • Info link: CRA hemp processor-handler application form CRA-6001 (09/22 version cited in Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.4; a 2023 form is reproduced at https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2206/22065/2206596/main_hemp-processor-handler-license-application-michigan.pdf?f5640f45f775988f5f5b36cd4fd81f02 — accessed 2026-10-28). The CRA's own current hemp FAQ/processor-handler hub page could not be returned as a directly openable URL in this session — [VERIFY] the live CRA hemp page and the current CRA-6001 version before publication; the form version/date below is therefore the last form version evidenced, not a guarantee that CRA-6001 has not been reissued since.

7.4.2 What it allows — and who needs it (verbatim core)

  • Operative prohibition — PA 547 §7(1), MCL 286.847(1), verbatim (FindLaw, opened 2026-10-28):

    "Except as otherwise provided under this act for a college or university in this state, and except for a processor licensed under the medical marihuana facilities licensing act, 2016 PA 281, MCL 333.27101 to 333.27801, or a testing facility, a person shall not process, handle, broker, or market industrial hemp in this state unless the person is licensed as a processor-handler under this act."

  • "Market" is broad — PA 547 §2, MCL 286.842(l) (summary, per Run 1 Part 1, §1.2.5, carried forward): "market" includes promoting or selling industrial hemp or a hemp commodity/product. Consequence, stated in MDARD's April 2022 guidance (GovDelivery bulletin https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/312655f, accessed 2026-10-28): retailers of any hemp product at any tier (distributors and end-user retailers, in-state and out-of-state retailers marketing in Michigan) need a processor-handler licence. That is why there is no separate "hemp retail licence" — retailing IS processor-handler activity in Michigan.
  • Activities that require H2 (consolidated from §7(1), MDARD/CRA guidance, and CRA FAQ summaries, accessed 2026-10-28): processing raw hemp into marketable form; possessing, storing or transporting industrial hemp; brokering hemp (acting as intermediary between buyers and sellers); promoting or selling hemp, a hemp commodity or a hemp product (including finished CBD products at retail); cleaning hemp seeds or manufacturing a hemp product using another processor's product (secondary summary via https://michigancannabis.org/cannabis-business, accessed 2026-10-28 — [VERIFY] the seed-cleaning point against the CRA FAQ, as it is secondary-sourced).
  • Activities that do NOT require H2: (a) A registered grower's sale of RAW harvested hemp to a licensed processor-handler or a licensed MMFLA processor (inside "grow," §7.2.2). (b) A licensed MMFLA processor's hemp processing (express §7(1) exception — H3). (c) A testing facility's testing alone ("sampling and testing hemp alone does not require [a processor-handler licence]" — CRA FAQ summary via https://michigancannabis.org/cannabis-business, accessed 2026-10-28). (d) A college/university acting under the Act's college/university provisions (§7.5). (e) Manufacturing a food that contains ONLY FDA GRAS hemp ingredients (hulled hemp seed, hemp seed protein, hemp seed oil) with no other hemp or marihuana ingredients — the MRA transition FAQ stated such a manufacturer "will not require an MRA license to process," but must still comply with MDARD food rules (GovDelivery bulletin https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/312655f, accessed 2026-10-28). That GRAS-food exception is narrow and is [VERIFY] against the current CRA FAQ — do not generalise it to CBD foods, which are not GRAS (§7.7.4).
  • Individual products are NOT separately registered: "Individual hemp products are not separately registered" (CRA FAQ summary via https://michigancannabis.org/cannabis-business and via MyCannabis 2026 guide, both accessed 2026-10-28). The licence is on the PERSON/business and its sites, not on each SKU.
  • What H2 does NOT allow: Handling marihuana (see §7.7 — an intoxicating product needs a CRA marihuana licence, and H2 alone is insufficient); making a medical claim or a food/drug claim that general food/drug law forbids (§7.7.4); or selling a product that is unlawful for another reason (e.g. CBD in food) merely because the seller holds H2 — "Licensing does not waive restrictions on food ingredients or product claims" (MyCannabis 2026 guide, accessed 2026-10-28).

7.4.3 Fees, term, renewal, application contents

  • Fee — PA 547 §16, MCL 286.856, verbatim (LawServer/US Lawyer Database reproductions, accessed 2026-10-28):

    "(1) An applicant for a grower registration or processor-handler license, or a registered grower or licensed processor-handler, under this act is subject to the following fees, as applicable: (a) A grower registration fee of $100.00. (b) A processor-handler license application fee of $1,350.00. (c) A site modification fee of $50.00 for each alteration to a site listed in a grower registration after the registration has been issued. (2) All fees under this act shall be paid with a check or money order payable to the department within 15 days of invoice. (3) A fee required under this section is nonrefundable." Reading note: §16(a)'s $100 grower fee is the OLD pilot-act grower fee (see §7.2.3 — cultivation fees moved to PA 220's $1,250). §16(b)'s $1,350 processor-handler fee is the LIVE processor-handler fee and is corroborated independently by the CRA-6001 form itself ("Nonrefundable Application Fee: $1,350.00" — TemplateRoller reproduction of the form, accessed 2026-10-28 via https://data.templateroller.com/pdf_docs/2549/25491/2549167/main_form-cra-6001-hemp-processor-handler-license-application-michigan.pdf?take=binary&amp;e8f0f888a34e389e049cdd9cd285aa24) and by every current secondary summary (Sativa, MyCannabis, MichiganCannabis.org, all accessed 2026-10-28). Adopted: $1,350, initial and renewal, nonrefundable. No separate renewal fee is stated in §16 — the $1,350 is the application fee payable on initial and on renewal applications (CRA FAQ summary: "runs annually from December 1 to November 30, costs $1,350" — https://michigancannabis.org/cannabis-business, accessed 2026-10-28).

  • Term and renewal — §7(2)–(4), MCL 286.847, verbatim (FindLaw, opened 2026-10-28): "(2) An initial processor-handler license application may be submitted at any time. An initial processor-handler license issued by the department expires at midnight on November 30 in the year in which it is issued. (3) Other than an initial processor-handler license, a processor-handler license is valid for 1 year beginning on December 1 and expiring at midnight on the following November 30 each year. (4) An application to renew an existing processor-handler license shall be postmarked on or before November 30. An application submitted after November 30 is subject to a late fee of $250.00." (The statute still says "the department" in §7; after ERO 2022-1 "the department" for processor-handlers is the CRA — see §7.4.1.)
  • Application contents — §7(1)(a)–(c) (FindLaw, opened 2026-10-28): applicant's full name, date of birth, mailing address, telephone number, valid and monitored email address; if not an individual, full name of each officer/director and each partner/member/owner owning >10% of equity/stock, with birth date, title and email; street address, location ID and GPS coordinates for each building/site where hemp will be processed, handled, stored or brokered; maps depicting each building/site with entrances and specific locations corresponding to the GPS coordinates. CRA-6001 adds the acknowledgments that all physical addresses have been submitted, that the application constitutes consent to MDARD/CRA personnel access for inspection/sampling/testing (form text still says "MDARD personnel" in the reproduced form — form wording [VERIFY] against the current CRA-6001, as the issuer is now the CRA), and that finished products marketed/sold under the licence will comply with all applicable laws.
  • Eligibility bars (from Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.4, carried forward, [VERIFY] against current CRA-6001): applicants must be ≥18; facilities must be Michigan-located; no licence if fees/fines are unpaid or a licence was revoked in the past 5 years. The 5-year revocation bar and the Michigan-location requirement are form/FAQ points, not §7 text as reproduced — do not quote them as statute.
  • Disclosure: "An application and supporting documents submitted to the department under this section are exempt from disclosure under the freedom of information act" (§7(5), MCL 286.847) — this is the statutory basis for the "no public roster" finding in §7.9.
  • Applications open or capped? Open; no cap stated in PA 547 or in any CRA guidance located. No social-equity fee reduction applies to H2 (the CRA social-equity programme in Run 1 Part 4, §4.11 reduces CRA marihuana application/licensure fees; no hemp social-equity reduction was located — [VERIFY] against the CRA social-equity page, but do not assume one exists).

7.4.4 The marihuana-processor interaction (Run 1 Part 4, §4.4, confirmed and narrowed)

  • Run 1 Part 4, §4.4 stated: "A medical processor may purchase raw industrial hemp and hemp products under the hemp acts without a separate hemp processor-handler licence in the circumstances described in MDARD/CRA transition FAQs; an adult-use processor needs a hemp processor-handler licence to perform the same hemp activities." That statement is adopted with one narrowing: the statutory exception in §7(1) is expressly for "a processor licensed under the [MMFLA]" — i.e. a MEDICAL processor. An adult-use (MRTMA) processor is NOT within §7(1)'s exception as written, so an adult-use-only processor that processes hemp needs H2. A dual-licensed (medical + adult-use) processor is within the exception for its medical-processor capacity; whether its adult-use capacity can also process hemp without H2 is [VERIFY] against the current CRA hemp FAQ — the transition FAQ statement is secondary and was already flagged [VERIFY] in Run 1 Part 4, Research Note V7, and remains [VERIFY] here. Do not advise a dual licensee that H2 is unnecessary for all its hemp activity on the basis of §7(1) alone.

7.5 Other hemp authorisations — research, seed, testing, transport

  • College/university research (current, both Acts): PA 547 §7(1) excepts "a college or university in this state" from the processor-handler requirement ("Except as otherwise provided under this act for a college or university in this state…"). PA 547 §6 (MCL 286.846, Justia 2025 reproduction, accessed 2026-10-28) likewise excepts a college/university from the grower-registration requirement ("Except as otherwise provided under this act for a college or university in this state, a person shall not grow industrial hemp in this state unless the person is registered as a grower"). No separate "hemp research licence" is issued to a college/university under current Michigan law as a standalone type; the exception IS the authorisation, subject to whatever conditions the Acts impose on colleges/universities — those conditions are [VERIFY] against PA 547 §§6–7 and PA 220's research provisions before advising a university. Under the state plan, lots used for academic research by a college/university are also a performance-based-sampling category (§401(6), §7.2.4). If Michigan becomes USDA-direct, research production would instead need a USDA licence with a USDA-approved alternative sampling method (§990.21(d), §7.3).
  • Hemp seed: No standalone Michigan hemp seed licence exists in current law. Growing viable seed is inside H1 ("grow" includes growing for viable seed — §7.2.2); supplying seed to growers is not separately licensed today. Seed supply WOULD become a licensed activity under pending SB 599 (its title covers "supplying industrial hemp seed" — see §7.6). A seed cleaner, as noted in §7.4.2, is treated in secondary summaries as needing H2 — [VERIFY] against the CRA FAQ.
  • Testing facilities (current): No standalone MDARD/CRA "hemp testing licence" exists. The Growers Act recognises two laboratory ROLES, not licences: (i) a regulatory testing facility (DEA-registered, §403-compliant, tests official samples — §7.2.4); (ii) a compliance monitoring testing facility (receives unofficial samples a grower collects at any time — §401(5)). A marihuana safety compliance facility (CRA-licensed under MMFLA/MRTMA) is a different licence (Run 1 Part 4, §4.6) and does not by itself make a laboratory a Growers Act regulatory testing facility, though pending SB 599 would make safety compliance facilities one of the three permitted testers for consumable hemp products (§7.6). Do not list a "hemp lab licence" as a current Michigan licence type.
  • Transport: No standalone hemp transporter licence exists. Transporting hemp is inside H2 ("handle" includes possessing/storing/transporting — §7.4.2) and, for a grower's own harvested hemp to its H2/H3 buyer, inside H1. Federally, 7 CFR 990.63 (cited in an MDARD bulletin, accessed 2026-10-28 via https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/312655f) provides that "no state or tribe may prohibit transportation of hemp lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved by USDA" — i.e. lawfully produced Michigan hemp may be transported interstate, but the transporter still needs the Michigan licence (H2) for the Michigan handling leg. No Michigan hemp "handler sub-types" (e.g. broker-only, transporter-only, retailer-only licences) exist — H2 is a single licence covering process/handle/broker/market together.
  • Hemp-derived cannabinoid product licence (current): None as a standalone type. Non-intoxicating hemp products are covered by H2 (marketing) + general product law; intoxicating products are marihuana products covered by CRA marihuana licences (§7.7). The standalone consumable-hemp licence is pending only (H5, §7.6).

7.6 Pending and future legislation — what is NOT law (do not present any of this as current)

7.6.1 SB 599–602 (2025–2026) — the consumable-hemp package (PENDING in the House)

  • What it would do (engrossed SB 599 text, LegiScan, accessed 2026-10-28): Create the Industrial Hemp Processing Act (a new Act, administered by the CRA) licensing the processing of CONSUMABLE hemp products; repeal 2014 PA 547 (SB 599, Enacting section 1: "The industrial hemp research and development act, 2014 PA 547, MCL 286.841 to 286.859, is repealed."); and, via companions, amend MMFLA cross-references (SB 600), Growers Act cross-references (SB 601 — including repeal of Growers Act §801), and MRTMA §§3 and 8 (SB 602). The package is tie-barred: SB 599 "does not take effect unless" SB 600, SB 601 and SB 602 are all enacted (SB 599, Enacting section 2, engrossed text).
  • Status (confirmed, matching Run 1 Part 0, §0.4 and Part 1, §1.9 — no change): Passed the Senate 16 December 2025 — SB 599: 30–5 (Roll Call #339, Substitute S-3); SB 600: 27–8; SB 601: 28–7; SB 602: 28–7, recorded as a 3/4 vote (required because SB 602 directly amends MRTMA text). Referred to the House Committee on Regulatory Reform on 17 December 2025. No House passage, no Governor's signature, and no later action located as of 27 October 2026 (DrugPolicyWatch Michigan brief, accessed 2026-10-28 via https://drugpolicywatch.info/states/michigan.html, which states "with no later action recorded as of October 27, 2026"). NOT LAW. Run 1's status is adopted unchanged; the only update in this Part is the confirmation that the status had not changed by 27 October 2026.
  • Proposed licence (H5) — terms from the engrossed text, for planning only: §201(1): "A person shall not process a consumable hemp product unless the person is granted a state license under this act." §201(4): "A person does not need a state license under this section if the person is engaged in the processing of only industrial hemp products that are not intended for human consumption." §203(1): a state licence "is valid for 1 year beginning on December 1 and expiring at midnight on the following November 30," except an initial licence expires 30 November of its issue year. §203(2) (engrossed text via LegiScan, accessed 2026-10-28): renewal by 30 November, or within 60 days after 30 November with a $250 late fee. §405(1): "A state license fee of $1,350.00" + "$50.00 for each location modification request." Fees payable by check/money order to the agency, nonrefundable/nontransferable, deposited into the proposed Consumable Hemp Product Fund (§405(2)–(3)). Application contents (§201(2)): full name, date of birth, mailing address, telephone, Social Security number (individuals) / EIN + key participants (entities), address/legal description of each processing location. The agency must create the application form and retain applications ≥5 years (§403).
  • Proposed product rules (summary, engrossed text — NOT law): "Consumable hemp product" = an edible/beverage/infused liquid or similar product containing a nonintoxicating cannabinoid, for human/animal consumption/ingestion/inhalation, NOT a "food" under the Michigan Food Law, excluding hemp-seed ingredients. "Nonintoxicating cannabinoids" include full-spectrum extract ≤1.75 mg THC per serving with CBD:THC ≥15:1, broad-spectrum extract, CBD, THCV, CBC, CBT, CBL, CBG, CBDV, CBN, and any other CRA-designated nonintoxicating cannabinoid. "Intoxicating cannabinoids" include delta-9/8/7/10/6a/10a and isomers, exo-THC, THC metabolites (including 11-hydroxy-THC), hydrogenated forms (including HHC/HHCP), synthetic forms (including dronabinol), ester forms (including delta-8/9 THC-O-acetate), delta-8 THCV (excluding delta-9 THCV), analogues with alkyl chain ≥4 carbons (including THCP/THCO/THCH/THCB), combinations, and CRA-designated cannabinoids. "Converted cannabinoid" = a cannabinoid converted from a different cannabinoid by chemical reaction, EXCLUDING decarboxylation by heat/light alone without reagents/catalysts or other chemical change. Processing/selling/transferring an intoxicating, potentially intoxicating or converted cannabinoid outside the marihuana system would be prohibited; penalties in the engrossed text include misdemeanour fines of $10,000–$25,000 and up to 93 days (first violation) / up to 1 year (subsequent), higher where a minor is involved (§505), plus civil sanctions. All consumable hemp products would have to be tested before sale by (i) a licensed marihuana safety compliance facility, (ii) a Growers Act regulatory testing facility, or (iii) a substantially compliant out-of-state laboratory (§401(1)(a)). Labelling would require an FDA non-evaluation statement, "KEEP OUT OF REACH OF CHILDREN" in bold capitals, no medical claims, net weight, ingredients, % nonintoxicating cannabinoids by weight, and no appeal to minors (Run 1 Part 1, §1.9 summary, consistent with the engrossed text). None of this is current law. The 1.75 mg / 15:1 figures must be cited only as "proposed/pending" — exactly as Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.3 required.
  • House companions (separate vehicles, also pending — do not conflate with SB 599): HB 5040 (introduced 24 September 2025, House consumable-hemp framework mirroring SB 599 definitions, §§303/305 labelling/nonintoxicating/intoxicating lists, $1,350 licence, tie-barred to HB 4965–4967 companions in one summary and to the SB package in another — companion tie-bar detail [VERIFY]) and HB 4964–4967 (September 2025 House consumable package). Status for all House vehicles: introduced, no House passage located as of 28 October 2026 — [VERIFY] committee action on legislature.mi.gov before citing any House vehicle beyond "introduced/pending." Run 1 Part 1, §1.9's warning stands: "Do not treat HB 5040 and SB 599 as the same bill."

In that event, production of hemp in Michigan would be subject to a USDA plan." Source: http://senate.michigan.gov/sfa/publications/notes/notes_mostrecent.pdf (accessed 2026-10-28). 7.6.3 HB 5977 (2024) — the bill Run 1 mistook for law (CORRECTION)

  • What it was: "Agriculture: industrial hemp; administration of industrial hemp program; modify. Amends sec. 107 of 2020 PA 220 (MCL 333.29107) & repeals secs. 101, 103, 105, 201, [etc.]" — the same repeal-plus-fund-abolition design later reintroduced as SB 608/609. Sources: https://www.michiganvotes.org/legislation/2024/house/bill-5977 and LegiScan sponsor pages (both accessed 2026-10-28).

LegiScan status for the 2024 HB 5977 is "Intro Sine Die," last action "2024-10-15 To House Agriculture Committee" (accessed 2026-10-28). Every Run 1 statement that HB 5977 "abolished the state industrial hemp fund," "enacted" the transfer, or was "ENACTED (2024)" is therefore corrected by this Part: HB 5977 (2024) is a dead bill, and the 2024 press narrative that treated MDARD's proposal as enacted law must not be repeated. The 2024 press reports (MJBizDaily, Four20 Post, MITechNews, Highly Capitalized — all November 2024) are best read as reporting MDARD's ANNOUNCED INTENTION ("MDARD will be requesting the state's program be abolished"; "this is only a proposed change" — MDARD, via Hemp Gazette, accessed 2026-10-28) plus the bill's introduction, not an enacted transfer. Whether MDARD administratively wound down any part of the programme in late 2024 without legislation (e.g. by not recruiting new growers) is [VERIFY] — no MDARD wind-down order was located, and the USDA plan list (February 2026) and the 2026-cycle fee sheet both point the other way.

Do not cite "2024 PA 220" for any hemp proposition until it is read on legislature.mi.gov — [VERIFY].

7.7 Hemp-derived cannabinoid products — intoxicating hemp under the CRA (CURRENT law)

7.7.1 The Michigan line: over 0.3% THC (broad definition) = marihuana, since 11 October 2021

  • Law: 2021 PA 56 (HB 4517, signed 13 July 2021, effective 11 October 2021), with companions HB 4740 (MMFLA), HB 4741 (Growers Act), HB 4742 (Tracking Act), HB 4743 (Public Health Code), HB 4744 (2014 Hemp Act). Run 1 Part 1, §1.2.7 is adopted: MRTMA §3 "THC" now means "(i) Tetrahydrocannabinolic acid. (ii) Unless excluded by the [CRA] under section 8(2)(c), a tetrahydrocannabinol, regardless of whether it is artificially or naturally derived. (iii) A tetrahydrocannabinol that is a structural, optical, or geometric isomer of a tetrahydrocannabinol described in [subparagraph (ii)]." And "industrial hemp" in MRTMA §3 was conformed so anything over 0.3% THC on that BROAD definition, not merely over 0.3% delta-9, is marihuana. The Growers Act's "industrial hemp" definition (§103) in turn means "that term as defined in section 3 of [MRTMA]" — so the broad definition governs the hemp/marihuana line for growers as well.
  • Consequence (MDARD/MRA at the time, via Morning Ag Clips, accessed 2026-10-28): "from 11 Oct 2021 it is illegal to produce or sell delta-8 THC and related intoxicating cannabis products in Michigan without CRA (then MRA) licensing, under the same testing, tracking (Metrc) and labelling rules as marihuana." The CRA's delta-8 consumer guidance calls delta-8 a Schedule 1 controlled substance under Michigan law (Run 1 Part 0, §0.4, carried forward).
  • Products captured (current law, Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.2, adopted): Delta-8, delta-10, THCA flower (THCA is expressly in the THC definition, subparagraph (i) — a "0% delta-9" label does not make THCA flower hemp), HHC and similar hydrogenated/synthetic/ester forms, and any THC isomer, IF the product meets the THC definition / exceeds 0.3%. "Hemp-derived delta-9" beverages/edibles at or above the intoxicating threshold are marihuana products, not general-retail hemp products — source (hemp vs marihuana plant) is irrelevant once the product is intoxicating / over the definition. HHCp and similar analogues are [VERIFY] individually — no CRA rule or case naming HHCp was located in Run 1 or in this Part; do not list HHCp as expressly scheduled without a primary source.

7.7.2 Sale channel, testing, labelling, tracking (current law)

  • Sale channel: An intoxicating hemp-derived product, being marihuana, may be sold ONLY through a CRA-licensed marihuana establishment/facility (retailer/provisioning centre, as applicable), to a person 21+ (adult-use) or a registered patient/caregiver (medical), and may NOT be sold at general retail under H2 alone. A hemp processor-handler licence alone is insufficient to sell an intoxicating product. This is the single most important compliance point in this Part.
  • Testing/labelling/tracking once it is marihuana: Licensed grower/processor → safety compliance facility testing (Mich. Admin. Code R 420.305) → Metrc tagging/tracking → compliant packaging/labelling (R 420.403/504, including the universal symbol and warnings) → sale only at a licensed sales location with ID/age verification and purchase-limit checks (R 420.505/506). Non-intoxicating hemp products sold at general retail under H2 are NOT subject to Metrc/marihuana testing, but ARE subject to H2 and to general food/drug/consumer-protection law (see §7.7.4).
  • Maximum THC / serving limits for marihuana products: Governed by R 420.404 and the CRA's Maximum THC Concentrations technical bulletin (24 April 2025, cited in Run 1 Part 1, §1.2.8) — marihuana-product limits, not hemp-product limits. Do not apply the pending SB 599 1.75 mg figure to marihuana products, and do not apply marihuana-product limits to non-intoxicating hemp products.

7.7.3 What counts as "non-intoxicating" hemp product TODAY (current law — narrow)

  • Current law has NO general "non-intoxicating" product category with a mg-per-serving threshold. The only current-law product distinctions are: (a) the 0.3% THC (broad definition) hemp/marihuana line; (b) the GRAS food ingredients (hulled hemp seed, hemp seed protein, hemp seed oil — §7.7.4); and (c) the absence of a product-registration requirement (§7.4.2). The 1.75 mg/serving + CBD:THC ≥15:1 test is a PENDING SB 599 definition and a November 2024 CRA DRAFT rule proposal — neither is current law (Run 1 Part 1, §§1.5.3, 1.5.5, adopted). A product below 1.75 mg/serving is not thereby "lawful general-retail hemp" under current law unless it also meets the 0.3% broad-THC line, the H2 requirement, and applicable food/drug law. Conversely, a product above 1.75 mg/serving is not thereby automatically marihuana under current law unless it meets the THC definition / 0.3% line — the 1.75 mg figure is a proposed threshold, not the current classification rule. Secondary maps that state "beverages ≥1.75 mg = marihuana, dispensary-only; beverages <1.75 mg = general retail" as CURRENT Michigan law (e.g. CannaBev, accessed 2026-10-28) are stating the PENDING/DRAFT threshold as if it were law and must not be quoted as current law without that qualifier.

7.7.4 CBD, hemp foods/beverages, and the unresolved general-retail question (carried forward, unresolved)

  • CBD (non-food, non-drug): Non-intoxicating CBD products (oils, topicals, capsules) that meet the hemp definition and the H2 regime may be sold at general retail in Michigan, subject to H2 (the seller needs H2). CBD is not a controlled substance under Michigan law when derived from compliant hemp (2018 PA 641). No Michigan-specific CBD medical-claims ban is stated here as current law without a primary source [VERIFY] — medical claims are constrained by general FDA/food law, not by a Michigan CBD-claims statute located in this Part.
  • CBD foods/beverages/supplements: UNRESOLVED — [VERIFY] against current CRA hemp guidance and the Michigan Food Law before publication. The conflict identified in Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.4 / Research Note R-13 persists: (i) one strand (CannaBev map, citing HB 4517/2024 PA 220) states beverages <1.75 mg may sell at general retail; (ii) another strand (older MDARD/CRA-aligned summaries, and the MyCannabis 2026 guide, accessed 2026-10-28) states CBD cannot legally be added to food/beverages or marketed as a dietary supplement in Michigan, following the FDA's 26 January 2023 conclusion that existing food/supplement frameworks are not appropriate for CBD, and that only GRAS hemp ingredients (hulled hemp seed, hemp seed protein, hemp seed oil) are lawful in human food. The MyCannabis guide's position is the better-sourced current position (FDA GRAS list + MDARD food guidance), but the CRA's current hemp FAQ position on CBD foods was not directly opened in this session, so this Part does NOT resolve the conflict — it preserves it as [VERIFY]. What IS settled: hulled hemp seeds, hemp seed protein and hemp seed oil (GRAS foods) are sold generally; CBD itself is not on the GRAS list; a CBD food/pet-food ingredient cannot be made lawful merely by holding H2; and hemp-containing products under the Cottage Food Law must meet Cottage Food criteria and "can not contain CBD or ingredients containing THC" (MDARD food guidance via GovDelivery, accessed 2026-10-28).
  • Age for CBD retail: Secondary summaries state hemp-derived CBD products may be purchased by persons 18+ (with some retailers requiring 21+), while marihuana-sourced CBD requires 21+ (adult-use) or patient status (medical). The 18+ hemp-CBD age rule is secondary-sourced [VERIFY] against a Michigan statute/rule — no Michigan hemp-CBD minimum-age statute was located in this session, and H2 itself requires applicants to be ≥18, which is a different rule (seller age, not buyer age). Do not state an 18+ buyer age as statute without that check. The safest current statement is: no Michigan hemp-CBD buyer minimum age was confirmed in a primary source in this session; marihuana products are 21+ / patient-only.
  • Tax (cross-reference, not a licence fee): No Michigan hemp-specific excise tax exists (Run 1 Part 2, §2.8, adopted). Intoxicating products sold as marihuana through CRA licensees are taxed as marihuana (10% MRTMA excise where applicable + 6% sales tax + 24% wholesale tax at the adult-use wholesale stage — Run 1 Part 2); the tax treatment of a specific intoxicating-hemp product sold as marihuana vs as a hemp product remains [VERIFY] against Treasury guidance (Run 1 Part 2, §2.8). Hemp/CBD ordinary sales-tax treatment at general retail was [UNAVAILABLE] in Run 1 Part 2 and remains so here.

7.8 Michigan's response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates — as it affects LICENCES

This section does not contradict Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.5; it adds one official Michigan source Run 1 had not located (the Senate Fiscal Agency Winter 2026 note) and states the licence consequences plainly. The federal dates fall AFTER this dossier's access date (28 October 2026), so no post-effective-date Michigan action could have been reviewed; any Michigan action after 11 December 2026 is outside this dossier.

  • No CRA or MDARD bulletin responding specifically to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was located in this Part either (same finding as Run 1 Part 0, §0.4 / Part 1, §1.5.5). The CRA and MDARD hemp pages and bulletins opened or searched in this session contain no 12 November / 11 December 2026 conforming statement. That negative finding is preserved: as of 28 October 2026, Michigan has issued no CRA/MDARD bulletin conforming its hemp licences to the federal total-THC definition or the 0.4 mg-per-container cap.
  • What WAS located — Senate Fiscal Agency (SFA) Winter 2026 analysis (official Michigan legislative analysis, not a regulator bulletin): The SFA's "State Notes — Winter 2026 — Federal Hemp Program Changes, An Expanded View" (http://senate.michigan.gov/sfa/publications/notes/notes_mostrecent.pdf, accessed 2026-10-28) states, in substance: (a) Michigan's statutory framework for its hemp programme "is reliant on the old thresholds" and, under the new federal thresholds, "Michigan's hemp program will no longer meet Federal requirements. To continue maintaining its own hemp program, Michigan statute will need to be amended." (b) The number of hemp growers registered in Michigan "has dropped substantially. In May 2022, 80 growers were registered. As of December 2025, the number has dropped to 24" (citing MDARD communications 31 May 2022 and 2 December 2025). (c) "Some industry stakeholders have advocated shifting Michigan's program to a USDA-administered program. Legislation to do this has been introduced" (citing HB 5095 and SB 608). (d) If the Growers Act is repealed, "production of hemp in Michigan would be subject to a USDA plan" (citing 7 USC §1639q). This SFA analysis is the closest thing to an official Michigan response located, and it is ANALYSIS (a fiscal-agency note), not a CRA/MDARD licensing rule and not a statute. It does not change any licence requirement on 28 October 2026, and it must be cited as SFA analysis, not as MDARD/CRA policy.
  • Licence consequences, stated as analysis (not law) — each point [VERIFY] against any post-28-October-2026 CRA/MDARD bulletin: 1. Growers (H1): Because Michigan's hemp line already uses the broad MRTMA THC definition (THCA + isomers), the federal move to a total-THC definition NARROWS the gap between federal and Michigan classification rather than creating a new Michigan prohibition — a grower compliant under Michigan's broad definition is unlikely to become non-compliant under a total-THC definition on THC percentage alone. BUT the SFA's point (a) above warns the gap is not only about THC percentage: if the federal definition after 11 December 2026 also narrows WHAT COUNTS as hemp by end-use (stalk/fibre, grain/seed, edible leaf, research, viable seed — the categories summarised in the SFA note), a Michigan grower growing for cannabinoid extraction could fall outside the federal hemp definition even while remaining "industrial hemp" under Michigan's MRTMA-based definition. That end-use question is the largest unresolved licence risk for Michigan growers and is [VERIFY] against the federal regulatory text when published and any Michigan conforming amendment. 2. Processor-handlers (H2) and the pending consumable licence (H5): The federal 0.4 mg total THC per container cap, if it stands after 11 December 2026, would be STRICTER than SB 599's proposed 1.75 mg per serving threshold (a per-container cap vs a per-serving threshold are different units and must not be compared as if they were the same — a multi-serving container at 1.75 mg/serving would exceed 0.4 mg/container). Michigan law does not incorporate the federal cap by reference in any provision located, so the cap's Michigan effect on 28 October 2026 operates, if at all, through federal enforcement and interstate commerce, not through H2. If SB 599 were enacted AFTER 11 December 2026 without amendment, its 1.75 mg/serving framework would sit uneasily alongside a federal 0.4 mg/container cap — whether the Legislature amends SB 599 to conform is [VERIFY] and is a reason to re-check SB 599's House status after 11 December 2026. 3. Intoxicating products (§7.7): The federal cap does NOT create a new Michigan retail channel. A product over Michigan's THC definition remains marihuana in Michigan regardless of whether it meets the federal 0.4 mg cap, and a product under the federal cap but over Michigan's definition remains marihuana in Michigan. Conversely, a product that is lawful general-retail hemp in Michigan (non-intoxicating, H2-compliant) but exceeds the federal cap would face federal, not Michigan, enforcement risk. No Michigan licence (H1, H2, or a CRA marihuana licence) can authorise a product that federal law forbids, and no federal hemp status can authorise a product that Michigan classifies as marihuana. 4. USDA testing delay: The baseline delay of USDA DEA-lab testing enforcement to 31 December 2026 matters for Michigan growers ONLY in the contingent USDA-direct future (§7.3) and for Michigan's state-plan testing to the extent MDARD relies on DEA-registered labs (regulatory testing facilities are DEA-registered by definition — §7.2.4). It does not suspend Michigan's own pre-harvest sampling/testing requirements under PA 220. 5. Timing trap for applicants: A grower registering for the 2026 cycle (1 February 2026 – 31 January 2027) and a processor-handler renewing for 1 December 2026 – 30 November 2027 will both hold Michigan licences that straddle the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal dates. Neither licence's Michigan term, fee or renewal date changes on those federal dates on any law located. Applicants should therefore budget on Michigan terms (H1 $1,250; H2 $1,350) and treat federal conformity as a separate, post-December compliance question — not as a reason to delay a Michigan application, and not as a Michigan fee change.

Michigan Cannabis and Hemp — Run 2, Part 8 ONLY: Cannabis-Zoned Properties

Dossier date / date accessed for every fact below: 28 October 2026, unless a listing itself is dated otherwise. Scope: Part 8 ONLY. Parts 0–7 and 9–12 are not covered here; the parent agent compiles the dossier. No HTML was built, per task.

Federal baseline — fixed, NOT re-researched, flag contradictions only: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products to Schedule III eff. 28 Apr 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; hemp PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026, PL 119-103 §2019 limits until 11 Dec 2026, after that full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. No contradiction with that baseline was found in the property sources examined for this Part. The baseline matters here only as a warning: a listing marketed for "hemp" does not, by itself, authorise intoxicating-hemp retail in Michigan. Michigan already treats intoxicating THC as marihuana regardless of source (Run 1 Part 0 §0.4 / Part 1 §1.2.7, 2021 PA 56, eff. 11 Oct 2021), saleable only through CRA licensees. No listing in this Part was treated as creating a hemp-retail channel, and no hemp-only retail permission was inferred from a zoning label.

Run 1 cross-check — read first, and how conflicts are handled: The Run 1 reports at ~/workspace/research_notes/michigan-cannabis-hemp-run1-20261028/part0-1.md, part2-3.md, part4-5.md and part6.md were read, especially Part 3 (local rules: MRTMA opt-out vs MMFLA opt-in, MCL 333.27956; the 1,000-ft state school buffer reducible by municipal ordinance, MCL 333.27959(3)(c); the $5,000 municipal fee cap, MCL 333.27956(4)) and Part 4 (licence types: medical Class A/B/C = 500/1,000/1,500 plants; adult-use Class A/B/C = 100/500/2,000 plants; excess grower, microbusiness, retailer/provisioning centre). No Run 1 figure was silently changed. Where a listing claim sits uneasily with Run 1, the entry says so and the figure adopted is stated. The one material update is Warren (Macomb County): Run 1 Part 3 correctly recorded Warren as opted out at the 2019 snapshot and marked its current status [UNAVAILABLE]/[VERIFY]. This Part found secondary reporting of a 25 March 2025 Warren City Council amendment to Chapter 19.5 allowing unlimited adult-use businesses by zoning (1,000 ft from schools, 500 ft from residential zones, $5,000 annual city licence fee), plus a City of Warren recently-adopted-ordinances index entry for Ordinance No. 80-842 adopted 19 May 2026 amending Chapter 19.5. The ordinance text itself was not directly opened in this Part, so Warren's current open-by-zoning status is adopted as secondary-sourced, [VERIFY] against the Warren code, not as a Run 1 correction. It does, however, explain why two current Warren listings credibly claim municipal approval where Run 1's 2019 snapshot did not. See §8.1, entry A1/A13, and Research Note R-01.

Counting rule — read before using the headline count: A property is counted as qualifying only if (a) it is in Michigan, (b) it is publicly listed for sale and/or lease as real property (not a licence or business alone), (c) the listing itself markets it for cannabis and/or hemp use or states cannabis zoning/approval, and (d) county can be stated (from the listing, or from a county source cited for that town). Properties meeting (a)–(d) but identified only from a search/index extract, not from an individually opened listing page, are counted in Tier B and are flagged [VERIFY] for current status throughout. Properties that fail (b), (c) or (d), are archived, pending, out-of-state, or business-only are not counted; they are listed in §8.4 with the reason. Duplicates across sites (same street address on 420Property + BizBuySell + Crexi + LoopNet) are counted once. A licence is never inferred from zoning alone: "zoned-only", "licence-ready", "licensed", "former licence — renewal required" and "municipally approved" are kept as the listing states them.

8.7 What this Part does NOT show (limits)

  1. Not a market census. 420Property alone states 165 Michigan listings. This Part individually opened 10 listing pages (A1–A6, A8, A12, A13, B16, B17 plus the excluded 82,000 sq ft warehouse and Albion pages) and used index extracts for the rest. The 19 is a verified core + index tier, not the total number of cannabis-zoned properties for sale/lease in Michigan at 28 Oct 2026.
  2. Not a licence verification. Listing licence claims were transcribed, not checked against CRA records (except A10's 2025 renewal extract). "Licensed", "municipally approved" and "Green Zone" in a listing are marketing claims until the CRA licence list and the municipal ordinance are checked.
  3. Not a zoning verification. Zoning codes (C-2, C3, M-1, M-Heavy, M4, C-3) are as stated by listings. No zoning map, parcel record (except A10's LoopNet parcel record) or municipal code section was opened to confirm that a given code permits the stated cannabis use at that address, or that a buffer (school/park/residential/inter-store) is met.
  4. Prices are asking prices / lease asks at the listing date shown, not sale prices. No closed-sale price was found for any property in this Part. Price conflicts (A11, B14, Marshall, Genesee appendix, New Buffalo CannaMLS vs BizBuySell) are preserved, not averaged.
  5. Staleness is uneven. Tier A October 2026 listings (A1, A2, A4, A5) are the freshest; A3 (Jan 2026), A6 (Jan/Oct 2026 update), A12 (June 2025 on-market), A13 (Sept 2025 on-market), B16 (2020) and the BizBuySell appendix (June 2026 crawl) are progressively staler. The compiled dossier must date-stamp each row, not present the table as a single-day snapshot.

Federal baseline — fixed, not re-researched. State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. Nothing in Parts 9–10 contradicts this baseline; the one open application question — whether a tribal medical programme counts as "state-licensed" — is kept [VERIFY] (see §10.3.5), because no tribal medical programme was found on the record at all.
