9.1 Every state agency regulating cannabis and hemp — what each actually regulates, and what it does NOT

9.1.1 At a glance

Agency / body Parent / home Regulates Does NOT regulate (common error to avoid)
Cannabis Regulatory Agency (CRA) Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA), Type I agency Commercial medical (MMFLA) and adult-use (MRTMA) licensing, rulemaking, inspections, discipline, Metrc/statewide monitoring, MMMP patient/caregiver registry, social equity programme, hemp processor-handler licensing (since 13 Apr 2022), hemp processing/distribution/sale Home grows by patients/caregivers and personal adult-use grows (see §9.1.2); unlicensed/illicit activity as a criminal matter (referred to MSP — see §9.1.6); taxes (Treasury); hemp cultivation since 1 Jan 2025 (USDA — see §9.1.3); local zoning/opt-out decisions (municipalities)
Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD) — Hemp cultivation under the former USDA-approved state plan (to end-2024); pesticide-use guidance for cannabis; (historically) hemp processor-handler licensing before 13 Apr 2022 Marihuana licensing; hemp processing/handling/marketing since 13 Apr 2022 (CRA); hemp cultivation since 1 Jan 2025 (USDA)
Michigan Department of Treasury — 10% MRTMA retail excise, 6% sales/use tax on marihuana sales, 24% wholesale tax (2025 PA 23, from 1 Jan 2026), Marihuana Regulation Fund distribution to municipalities/counties/tribes, schools and roads; state income-tax treatment including MRTMA §12 decoupling administration Licensing, product safety/testing, Metrc, local opt-outs
Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA) Parent department of CRA Houses the CRA; administrative rulemaking machinery (MOAHR — Michigan Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules — certifies rules; JCAR — Joint Committee on Administrative Rules — reviews them); former Bureau of Marijuana Regulation (abolished 2019) Does not license marihuana establishments directly — that power sits in the CRA as a Type I agency
Michigan State Police (MSP) — Criminal enforcement against unlicensed/illicit marihuana activity (Marijuana and Tobacco Investigation Section, MTI); background-investigation cooperation for CRA applicants; forensic work in criminal cases; vehicle-search / OWI enforcement on roads Commercial licensing, civil discipline of licensees, tax collection, Metrc administration
Michigan Department of State — Bureau of Elections / Board of State Canvassers Secretary of State Statewide ballot certification, official canvass of statewide proposals, ballot-form / petition-format guidance for local initiatives Licensing, taxation, product regulation
Attorney General of Michigan — Criminal prosecution support / referrals (e.g. tax-crime charges arising from MSP MTI investigations), consumer-protection and litigation on behalf of the State in Court of Claims cases Day-to-day licensing or tax administration
Local government: city / village / township councils, clerks and county boards of canvassers — Municipal opt-in (MMFLA) / opt-out and caps (MRTMA), local licences and fees (≤$5,000/yr), zoning and buffers, local ballot questions; county canvassers certify local results State licensing, state taxes, product testing; counties are NOT "municipalities" under MRTMA and cannot opt out (Run 1, Part 3, §3.1)
Other touching agencies (narrow roles) — See §9.1.8: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) (health guidance, not licensing); Dept. of Insurance and Financial Services (DIFS) (financial institutions generally — no cannabis-banking list located, [UNAVAILABLE]); Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy / local fire authorities (environmental/fire/permitting rules of general application, not cannabis-specific licensing) None of these licenses a marihuana establishment or hemp processor

9.1.2 Cannabis Regulatory Agency (CRA) — the lead regulator

  • Website: https://www.michigan.gov/cra — opened directly in this pass (crawled copy 31 July 2026). The site's own navigation confirms the CRA's workstreams: Medical Facilities; Adult-Use Establishments; MMMP Patients & Caregivers; Social Equity Program; Hemp Processing; Enforcement Division; Applications and Forms; Licensing & Statistical Reports; Statewide Marijuana Monitoring System Information — Metrc; Consumer Connection; Laws, Rules & Regulations. Source: https://www.michigan.gov/cra — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Public address (official, from CRA enforcement documents): 2407 North Grand River Ave, Lansing, MI 48906; mailing P.O. Box 30205, Lansing, Michigan 48909. Source: CRA consent order/formal complaint letterhead, e.g. https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Disciplinary-Actions/2025/February/QPS-Michigan-Holdings-LLC-dba-High-Profile-Cannabis-Shop-AUR001103-Consent-Order.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Note: the 48906 street ZIP and 48909 P.O. Box ZIP both appear on CRA letterhead; do not "correct" one to the other.
  • Official public contacts (agency mailboxes / phone, from CRA's own complaint portal and programme pages — no individual contacts):
  • General / complaint inquiries: CRA-Info@michigan.gov (complaint-form inquiries).
  • Hemp processing licensing/regulation: CRA-Hemp@michigan.gov; telephone 517-284-8599 (also the MMMP and general CRA number as published on the complaint portal).
  • Patient/caregiver registration (MMMP): CRA-MMMPINFO@Michigan.gov; 517-284-8599.
  • Legal hearings: CRA-LegalHearings@michigan.gov; legal section 517-284-8599 (as printed on formal complaints).
  • Social equity: CRA-SocialEquity@michigan.gov (workgroup applications); CRA-SEGrants@michigan.gov (Social Equity Grant Program questions).
  • Administrative rules: CRA-AdminRules@michigan.gov.
  • Unlicensed / residential / general illegal activity not involving a CRA licensee, and caregiver issues: MSP-MTI@michigan.gov (MSP, not CRA — see §9.1.6).
  • Source for the portal contacts: Accela Citizen Access complaint disclaimer, http://aca-prod.accela.com/MIMM/Cap/CapApplyDisclaimer.aspx?FilterName=ENTER+A+COMPLAINT&amp;TabName=Enforcement&amp;module=Enforcement — accessed 2026-10-28. Caveat: portal text is a CRA-published disclaimer page; the underlying CRA "Contact Us" page itself was not separately opened in this pass, so treat these mailboxes as CRA-published [VERIFY] only to the extent of re-checking them against michigan.gov/cra before publication if a contact is to be printed in a consumer-facing document.
  • Legal home / authority: Created as the Marijuana Regulatory Agency by Executive Reorganization Order 2019-2 (MCL 333.27001), a Type I agency within LARA; renamed the Cannabis Regulatory Agency by ERO 2022-1 (MCL 333.27002), effective 13 April 2022 (see timeline §9.2). It administers: MMMA 2008 IL 1 (MCL 333.26421–333.26430) for the registry; MMFLA 2016 PA 281 (MCL 333.27101–333.27801); Marihuana Tracking Act 2016 PA 282 (MCL 333.27901–333.27904); MRTMA 2018 IL 1 (MCL 333.27951–333.27967); and, for hemp processing, the Industrial Hemp Research and Development Act 2014 PA 547 (MCL 286.841–286.859). Sources: MCL 333.27001 via https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/michigan/mi-laws/michigan_laws_333-27001 — accessed 2026-10-28; ERO 2022-1 renaming/transfer summaries via https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/agency-name-change-meet-the-michigan-cannabis-regulatory-agency/ and https://www.michigan.gov/lara/news-releases/2025/11/05/cra-is-now-accepting-applications-for-the-state-of-michigans-one-million-dollar-social-equity (CRA release describing CRA as housed within LARA and established 13 Apr 2022) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What the CRA does, in its own terms: licenses adult-use establishments and medical facilities (two-step prequalification + establishment/facility licence); runs the Michigan Medical Marihuana Program (MMMP) registry for patients and caregivers; operates the Social Equity Program (fee reductions, education, grants — see §9.1.9); licenses hemp processor-handlers; administers the statewide monitoring system (Metrc); inspects, investigates and disciplines licensees (Enforcement Division; formal complaints, consent orders, fines, suspensions, revocations — e.g. the 1 Oct 2026 Muha Meds revocation in Run 1, Part 0); publishes monthly statistical reports and weekly licensing reports; holds public meetings and rulemaking hearings.
  • What the CRA does NOT do — stated on its own complaint portal, and important to quote correctly: "The CRA does not regulate marijuana or marijuana products grown or produced by registered qualifying patients or registered primary caregivers under the MMMA, or individuals over 21 for personal use under the MRTMA." Source: Accela complaint disclaimer above — accessed 2026-10-28. In other words, home/patient/caregiver grows and personal possession are outside CRA licensing/enforcement; they are governed by the MMMA/MRTMA possession and criminal provisions and enforced, where criminal, by police/prosecutors, not by CRA discipline.
  • Public-meeting duty: The (then) MRA was required to hold at least four public meetings each calendar year to hear complaints and receive public views on administration of the MMMA, MMFLA, Tracking Act and MRTMA. Source: MRA first-public-meeting summary, https://www.chamberofcannabiz.com/marijuana-regulatory-agency-holds-first-public-meeting/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summary of the statutory duty; current meeting calendar is on michigan.gov/cra — [VERIFY] the current year's meeting dates before listing any specific meeting].
  • Leadership as of the sources reviewed: Executive Director Brian Hanna (appointed acting executive director in 2022 after serving as CRA/MRA manager of field operations, inspections and investigations; previously MSP criminal intelligence manager/analyst and Kalamazoo County deputy sheriff). Source: Governor's appointment release via https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIEOG/bulletins/32d2f1d — accessed 2026-10-28. Whether Hanna remained executive director on 28 Oct 2026 was not re-confirmed on a 2026 CRA page in this pass — [VERIFY] before naming a current director in the compiled dossier. Former executive director Andrew Brisbo led the MRA into the CRA renaming (2022) and is named in the Racial Equity Advisory Workgroup final report (2021) — do not present Brisbo as the current director.
  • Divisions/functions evidenced in CRA documents (not a published org chart): Licensing (prequalification + Step 2), Enforcement (inspections, investigations, formal complaints, hearings), Legal (hearings/compliance conferences), Social Equity, Hemp Processing, MMMP (patient/caregiver registry), and statistical reporting. A formal CRA organisation chart with division heads was NOT located in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE]; do not invent division names beyond those evidenced on michigan.gov/cra navigation and CRA documents above.

9.1.3 Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (MDARD) — hemp cultivation (current) and pesticides

  • Website: https://www.michigan.gov/mdard (MDARD home; hemp pages under MDARD's plant/agriculture programmes). The CRA site itself cross-links "MDARD: Cannabis and Pesticide Use" as a resource — see §9.1.2.
  • What MDARD regulated: Under the Industrial Hemp Growers Act 2020 PA 220 (MCL 333.29101 et seq.) and Michigan's USDA-approved state hemp plan (first plan effective 1 Dec 2020; revised plan approved 21 Oct 2021 — see §9.2), MDARD registered hemp growers, ran pre-harvest official sampling/testing oversight, and administered the state hemp programme. Under the 2014 PA 547 pilot/processor regime before 2022, MDARD also handled hemp processor-handler matters until the transfer below.
  • What MDARD does NOT regulate now:
  • Hemp processing/handling/marketing: transferred from MDARD to the CRA (then MRA) by ERO 2022-1, effective 13 April 2022. Sources: https://www.cannabis-law-blog.com/agency-name-change-meet-the-michigan-cannabis-regulatory-agency/ ; https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/legislation-and-regulation/news/15692097/cannabis-regulatory-agency-replaces-marijuana-regulatory-agency-as-michigan-cannabis-regulator — both accessed 2026-10-28. LARA's 4 Mar 2022 bulletin confirmed existing processor-handler licences remained valid and fees (set in 2014 PA 547) did not change at transfer. Source: https://www.rhoadesmckee.com/new-lara-bulletin-offers-additional-information-regarding-the-newly-formed-cannabis-regulatory-agency/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Hemp cultivation from 1 January 2025: Michigan ended its MDARD state cultivation programme at the close of 2024; growers operate directly under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program (see §9.2 and Run 1, Parts 0/6). MDARD's stated reasons (via MJBizDaily/Morning Ag Clips republication): financial unsustainability as growers fell from 631 (2020) to 34 (2024), plus investigation costs for marihuana grown under the guise of hemp. Sources: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/usda-assumes-oversight-of-michigan-hemp-farmers/398521/ ; https://mitechnews.com/featured/michigan-shuts-down-industrial-hemp-program-that-now-reverts-to-usda-control/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Marihuana licensing, testing or retail: never MDARD's (except the pre-2022 hemp-processing overlap above).
  • Remaining MDARD touchpoint: pesticide use on cannabis/hemp. The CRA site links MDARD cannabis-and-pesticide guidance; MDARD remains the state pesticide regulator of general application. Specific approved-pesticide lists for marihuana/hemp are MDARD/CRA guidance, not a separate cannabis licence — [VERIFY] the current MDARD pesticide list before citing any product as approved.
  • Formal status of 2020 PA 220 after the USDA move — [VERIFY / Run 1 internal conflict, see §9.4]: Run 1, Part 1 (§1.2.6) says whether the Growers Act "has been formally repealed or merely left dormant [VERIFY]"; Run 1, Part 1 (§1.9, HB 5977 row) calls HB 5977 "ENACTED (2024)"; Run 1, Part 6 (§6.7) says the final enacted status of HB 5977 / PA 220 repeal "was not confirmed on legislature.mi.gov in this Part 6 run — [VERIFY]". This Part 9 adopts the operational fact (state programme ended; USDA direct from 1 Jan 2025) and does NOT assert a repeal PA number. The parent must check legislature.mi.gov for HB 5977 (2024 session) and for any 2025–2026 repeal/amendment before stating that 2020 PA 220 is repealed.

9.1.4 Michigan Department of Treasury — taxes and distribution

  • Website: https://www.michigan.gov/treasury ; wholesale marihuana tax pages: https://www.michigan.gov/taxes/business-taxes/wholesale-marihuana-tax/faq (FAQ, opened via search in this pass) and Revenue Administrative Bulletin 2026-3, https://www.michigan.gov/taxes/rep-legal/rab/2026-revenue-administrative-bulletins/revenue-administrative-bulletin-2026-3 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What Treasury administers (all per Run 1, Parts 2–3, reconciled — no change in this Part):
  • MRTMA 10% retail excise (MCL 333.27963), administered under the Revenue Act 1941 PA 122.
  • 6% general sales tax (1933 PA 167, MCL 205.52) and use tax on marihuana sales, including the rule that the sales-tax base includes the 10% excise (Mich. Admin. Code R 205.141).
  • 24% wholesale tax under the Comprehensive Road Funding Tax Act 2025 PA 23 (MCL 205.901 et seq.), from 1 Jan 2026 — including quarterly Average Wholesale Price (AWP) publication for affiliated/self-supply transactions. Treasury RAB 2026-3 confirms the wholesaler (the marihuana establishment making the first sale/transfer to a retail licensee) is legally liable and must remit even if the receivable proves uncollectible; passing the tax through does not shift liability. Source: RAB 2026-3 above — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Marihuana Regulation Fund distribution (MCL 333.27964): after implementation/administration/enforcement costs (and, in the early years, the time-limited $20m veterans-research tranche — see Run 1, Part 2, §2.6), 15% municipalities / 15% counties / 35% School Aid Fund / 35% Michigan Transportation Fund, allocated by retailer/microbusiness count (tribes on Indian lands take the municipal + county shares for stores on their lands, per the 2023 PA 166 amendment). FY2024 release opened directly in Run 1 (Treasury, 21 Feb 2025): >$331m available, nearly $100m local, >$58,200 per store, 302 entities including 4 tribes. FY2025 figures ($93.7m local; $54,017.10 per store; 313 entities) are secondary-reported from the 3 Mar 2026 release and remain [VERIFY] against the primary release (Run 1, Part 2, Research Note 19).
  • State income-tax computation, including MRTMA §12 (MCL 333.27962) decoupling for marihuana establishments — ordinary-and-necessary expenses deductible for Michigan purposes notwithstanding federal §280E (scope contested for medical-only licensees and for depreciation/credits — Run 1, Part 2, §2.7; [VERIFY] RAB 2022-26 and CannArbor before advising).
  • What Treasury does NOT do: license, inspect, test or discipline marihuana businesses; set product rules; decide municipal opt-outs; run Metrc. Treasury guidance that "the wholesale tax applies independently of Metrc, with no Metrc data-entry change" (CRA Jan 2026 advisory bulletin, as reported in Run 1) is the clearest statement of that boundary.
  • Public contact (official, general Treasury): The Treasury FAQ pages are the public route for wholesale-tax questions; a general Treasury phone published on a Treasury FAQ page in this pass was 517-636-4486 for individual-income-tax "Reminder of Tax Due" queries — that number is NOT a marihuana-tax helpline and is not reproduced here as one. No dedicated public marihuana-tax phone number was confirmed on a Treasury marihuana page opened in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE]; use the Treasury wholesale-tax FAQ/guidance pages and Michigan Treasury Online (MTO) as the published routes, and do not invent a helpline number.

9.1.5 Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA) — parent department and rulemaking machinery

  • Website: https://www.michigan.gov/lara .
  • Role: LARA is the parent department within which the CRA sits as a Type I agency (ERO 2019-2, MCL 333.27001; ERO 2022-1, MCL 333.27002). LARA's former Bureau of Marijuana Regulation and the Medical Marihuana Licensing Board and Marihuana Advisory Panel were abolished and their powers transferred to the (then) MRA by ERO 2019-2 (see §9.2).
  • Rulemaking: CRA rules (Mich. Admin. Code R 420.1 et seq.) proceed through the Michigan Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules (MOAHR) within LARA (legal certification), then to the Joint Committee on Administrative Rules (JCAR — five Senate + five House members, bipartisan) before promulgation. The CRA's July 2026 public-hearing page states that sequence expressly. Source: https://www.michigan.gov/cra/public-hearing/public-hearing--administrative-rules-july-2026 — accessed 2026-10-28. The 2023-25 LR rule revision (draft approved by MOAHR 11 May 2026; second public hearing 23 July 2026, Lansing + Zoom/email) is PROPOSED, NOT final, per Run 1, Part 0, §0.3 — do not quote draft text as operative.
  • What LARA does NOT do: LARA does not itself issue marihuana establishment/facility licences, run MMMP, or collect marihuana taxes; those functions are the CRA's (licensing/registry) and Treasury's (taxes).

9.1.6 Michigan State Police (MSP) — criminal enforcement, background checks, forensics

  • Website: https://www.michigan.gov/msp . Public referral mailbox for unlicensed/residential/general illegal activity (from CRA portal): MSP-MTI@michigan.gov.
  • Unit: Marijuana and Tobacco Investigation Section (MTI) — also styled Marihuana and Tobacco Investigation Section — within MSP's Special Investigation Division. MSP's own position description states the Special Investigation Division provides statewide investigative resources and that the MMFLA, MRTMA and related laws "created new responsibilities for the Michigan State Police with regards to statewide investigation and enforcement of licensed and illicit marijuana operations," and that an MTI investigator investigates violations of the Tobacco Products Tax Act, MMFLA, MRTMA, MMMA and related laws. Source: MSP position description, https://mcsc.state.mi.us/AgencyPDFs/Detective%20Trooper%20Specialist%20PD_MTI_West.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • CRA partnership (official CRA release, 23 Apr 2024): "A person not licensed under the MRTMA or MMFLA who sells marijuana or possesses marijuana in quantities greater than allowed by statute is in violation of state law and the CRA will refer potential criminal complaints to the Michigan State Police." "The Marijuana and Tobacco Investigation Section of the Michigan State Police is a key strategic partner of the CRA, and we are committed to investigating retailers who would offer for sale marijuana products and derivatives in violation of state law" (D/F/Lt. Thomas Kish, MTI commander, as quoted). "If law enforcement identifies an unlicensed business selling cannabis in any form with a concentration of THC (including THCA) greater than 0.3%, they can seize the product and the offenders may be subject to criminal charges." Source: https://www.michigan.gov/lara/news-releases/2024/04/23/cra-issues-reminder-regarding-illegal-sales-of-marijuana-in-michigan — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Background checks: Under MMFLA §303 as amended (MCL 333.27303(2), history to 2020 PA 207), the CRA "may seek and shall receive the cooperation and assistance of the department of state police in conducting background investigations of applicants." Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/2020/chapter-333/statute-act-281-of-2016/division-281-2016-part-3-medical-marihuana-licensing-board/section-333-27303/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [mirror; official text [VERIFY] on legislature.mi.gov].
  • What MSP does NOT do: MSP does not license marihuana businesses, does not run safety-compliance testing for the licensed market (that is licensed safety compliance facilities under CRA rules), does not administer Metrc, and does not collect marihuana taxes. MSP forensic laboratories support criminal cases; they are not the CRA's product-release testing route.
  • Command note (dated, do not present as current without re-check): Lt. Chris Hawkins headed MTI in 2019 reporting; First Lieutenant Tom Kish commanded MTI in 2024–2025 reporting (CRA release 2024; 9&10 News Sept 2025 tax-crime case). Current MTI commander on 28 Oct 2026 [VERIFY] on michigan.gov/msp before naming one.

9.1.7 Department of State — Bureau of Elections and Board of State Canvassers; Attorney General; courts

  • Bureau of Elections (Department of State): Address as printed on Bureau publications: Richard H. Austin Building, 1st Floor, 430 W. Allegan, Lansing, Michigan 48918; https://www.michigan.gov/sos/elections (Michigan.gov/Elections); telephone 517-335-3234 as printed on Bureau audit publications. Role for Part 9: certifies initiative petitions to the Legislature, issues ballot-form/petition-format guidance used by local petitioners (e.g. the Menominee 9→13 petition format, held compliant by Menominee County Circuit Judge Mary Barglind 21 Sept 2026 — see §9.3.3), and administers the statewide canvass through the Board of State Canvassers. The Bureau's own 2008/2018 official canvass PDFs were NOT directly opened in this pass — statewide proposal counts in §9.3 are therefore sourced to the MCL compiler's notes (which reproduce the canvass result) and to secondary republications, and are marked accordingly. Do not cite a Bureau PDF URL that was not opened.
  • Attorney General: Prosecutes/assists criminal cases arising from MSP MTI investigations (e.g. Traverse City, Grand Traverse County, felony tax charges announced Sept 2025, arising from an MSP MTI investigation of an alleged multi-building unlicensed grow/distribution operation — 134 plants, >230 lb processed marihuana, >$100,000 cash recovered Jan 2023). Source: https://www.9and10news.com/2025/09/04/traverse-city-man-charged-with-felony-tax-crimes-in-black-market-marijuana-operation/ — accessed 2026-10-28. The AG also represents the State in Court of Claims litigation (including the wholesale-tax cases, where the Department of Treasury is a defendant). The AG does not license or tax.
  • Courts (for Part 9 timeline purposes only; full case analysis is not Part 9's job): Michigan Court of Claims (wholesale-tax and other state challenges), Michigan Court of Appeals (Brightmoore Gardens; Yellow Tail; Kejbou illicit-market penalty case — see §9.2), Michigan Supreme Court (Armstrong; Wilkins; Hess). Federal courts appear only for Detroit's ordinance litigation (Lowe v. City of Detroit, E.D. Mich. No. 2:21-cv-10709) and the Lima Township federal lawsuit (filed then dropped, per MLive reporting in §9.3.3) — neither is a state-agency function.

9.1.8 Other bodies that touch cannabis/hemp — narrow roles only

  • Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS): Health guidance, syringe-service / overdose-prevention resources, and (historically) the MMMP's predecessor home in the Department of Community Health. MDHHS does NOT license marihuana establishments, hemp processors, or MMMP cards (those are CRA). No MDHHS cannabis-licensing function was located — do not list MDHHS as a cannabis regulator.
  • Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services (DIFS): Regulates state-chartered banks/credit unions and insurers of general application. No DIFS-published list of cannabis-serving financial institutions was located (Run 1, Part 6, §6.8, [UNAVAILABLE]) — DIFS is therefore listed here only to prevent the error of presenting a secondary bank list as an official DIFS list.
  • Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) and local fire/building authorities: Rules of general application (wastewater, waste disposal, fire code, building permits) apply to cannabis facilities as they do to other industrial/commercial premises. No EGLE cannabis-specific licence was located. Secure-transporter waste-disposal protection (HB 6163, introduced 3 July 2026, pending — CannBus Q3 2026) is a pending bill, not a current EGLE programme.
  • Municipalities and county canvassers: See §9.1.1 and §9.3.3. Municipalities are regulators for local purposes (opt-in/opt-out, caps, local licences, zoning, buffers) but not for state licensing or taxation.
  • Federally recognised tribes: Tribal marihuana businesses are recognised in MRTMA §§13–14 as amended by 2023 PA 166 (excise exemption for transfers from a tribal marihuana business; tribal share of the Regulation Fund). Tribal programmes/compacts are Run 2, Part 10 territory and are NOT detailed here, per scope. No tribal regulator is listed as a state agency in this Part.

9.1.9 CRA advisory boards and workgroups — what exists, what is defunct, what is current

Defunct (do NOT present as current): - Medical Marihuana Licensing Board (MMLB): Created by MMFLA 2016 PA 281, Part 3 (MCL 333.27301 et seq.) — a board that approved/denied medical facility licences (first licences 12 July 2018, see §9.2). Abolished by ERO 2019-2 (MCL 333.27001(1)(b)); its powers transferred by Type I transfer to the Marijuana Regulatory Agency. Source: https://www.lawserver.com/law/state/michigan/mi-laws/michigan_laws_333-27001 — accessed 2026-10-28. Contemporary reporting (AP via Legal News, 4 Mar 2019) confirms the Board was criticised for slow review and that ERO 2019-2 would take effect 30 Apr 2019 unless rejected by the Legislature. Source: https://legalnews.com/Home/Articles?DataId=1471235 — accessed 2026-10-28. - Marihuana Advisory Panel: Also created by MMFLA 2016 PA 281; abolished by ERO 2019-2 (MCL 333.27001(1)(c)). Same sources. The 17-member panel referenced in April 2017 reporting (appointments delayed) is the same body — do not confuse it with the later Racial Equity Advisory Workgroup or the Medical Marihuana Review Panel. - Bureau of Marijuana Regulation (BMR, within LARA): Abolished by ERO 2019-2 (MCL 333.27001(1)(e)). Same sources.

Statutory review mechanism (current in law, membership [VERIFY]): - Medical Marihuana Review Panel (MMMP petition panel): MMMA §6 (MCL 333.26426, as amended by 2020 PA 400) provides the petition process by which a person may petition to add a debilitating medical condition, with review-panel consideration. The CRA site's "I Need To" list includes "File a petition for the medical marijuana review panel" (michigan.gov/cra, opened §9.1.2). Current panel membership, meeting schedule and pending petitions were NOT located on a CRA page opened in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE] for this Part; do not name panel members. Run 1, Part 1, §1.4.1 notes the petition process detail as [VERIFY] on the current MCL page — that flag stands.

Advisory workgroups (the only CRA workgroups evidenced in this pass): - Racial Equity Advisory Workgroup (MRA, ad hoc, 2020–2021) — COMPLETED, not standing. Established by the MRA (authority cited in its final report as ERO 2019-2, MCL 333.27001(2)(h) — [VERIFY] that subsection citation on the ERO text) after December 2020 MRA ownership data showed only 3.8% Black or African American and 1.5% Hispanic/Latino ownership interest among adult-use licensees. Composition: representatives of the Michigan Legislature; municipalities with significant minority populations; minority-focused marijuana industry groups; minority-focused business groups; attorneys experienced in racial disparities/equity and marijuana; individuals experienced in common barriers (banking, finance, real estate). It met first in July 2020 and monthly through December 2020, with five subcommittees (Social Justice; Business Development; Local Equity; Process and Pathways; Resource Deployment and Strategic Partnerships). Final recommendations issued January 2021 (MRA Executive Director Andrew Brisbo). Its own recommendation was that the MRA establish a standing Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Workgroup to continue the work. Sources: final report via https://cannabislaw.report/michigan-marijuana-regulatory-agency-racial-equity-advisory-workgroup-final-recommendationspdf/ and https://four20post.com/2021/01/marijuana-regulatory-agency-issues-final-recommendations-of-the-racial-equity-advisory-workgroup/ — accessed 2026-10-28. Committee chairs named in the report excerpt: Business Development — Cimone Casson (Chair); Local Equity — Barton Morris (Chair), with Rep. Sarah Anthony among members. Full membership list was truncated in the excerpt available — [VERIFY] against the full final-report PDF before naming the complete roster. - Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) Workgroup (CRA, standing) — CURRENT as of 2025. The successor standing workgroup recommended by the Racial Equity Advisory Workgroup. In May 2025 the CRA sought additional members: monthly meetings, 18-month staggered terms, selections announced by 4 June 2025, applications by email to CRA-SocialEquity@michigan.gov with "WORKGROUP" in the subject line by 21 May 2025, 5:00 p.m. (name, mailing address, email, phone, occupation, job title, employer/organisation, ≤250-word perspective statement; no attachments; telephone/other-contact applications not accepted). Source: https://cannabislaw.report/dont-let-trump-know-michigan-cannabis-regulatory-agency-cra-adding-members-to-its-standing-diversity-equity-and-inclusion-workgroup/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary republication of a CRA notice; the CRA notice itself was not directly opened — [VERIFY] against michigan.gov/cra]. An October 2025 CRA document, "CRA — DEI Workgroup Social Equity Proposals," records workgroup proposals on education/training/technical assistance, vendor-partnership incentives and accountability, with CRA decisions noted (e.g. CRA already conducts regular educational programming and hosts a video library; exploring college partnerships; not supporting mandated training, statewide standardised education, or preferential marketing of social-equity businesses at that time). Source: https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcoronado.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/consumer-connection/CRA-DEI-Workgroup-Social-Equity-Proposals-October-2025.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 [CRA-hosted PDF via mirror host; treat as CRA document, [VERIFY] by re-pulling from michigan.gov/cra]. Current (Oct 2026) DEI Workgroup roster and meeting minutes were NOT located — [UNAVAILABLE]; do not name 2026 members. - Social Equity Program (CRA programme, not a board): Established under MRTMA §8(1)(j) (MCL 333.27958(1)(j)) — the CRA must develop a plan to promote/encourage participation by people from communities disproportionately impacted by marihuana prohibition/enforcement. It provides fee reductions (25% residency / 25% misdemeanour / 40% felony / 10% caregiver 2008–2017, stacking to 75% max; full-term if operating inside a disproportionately impacted community, first two years only if outside), education/outreach, and the $1m/year Social Equity Grant Program (one grant per qualifying entity; equal shares; Social Equity All-Star Program participation required before a complete SEGP application is considered; questions to CRA-SEGrants@michigan.gov). 184 disproportionately impacted communities identified by CRA (method: marihuana convictions above state median + ≥20% below federal poverty level, threshold lowered from 30% 1 June 2020). Sources: Senate Fiscal Agency OneFAB 23 June 2025, https://sfa.senate.michigan.gov/Publications/OneFAB/2025/OneFAB06-23-2025jm.pdf ; CRA SEGP notice, https://www.michigan.gov/lara/news-releases/2025/11/05/cra-is-now-accepting-applications-for-the-state-of-michigans-one-million-dollar-social-equity — both accessed 2026-10-28. Note on that SEGP notice date: the release is dated 5 Nov 2025 in its URL/metadata but describes an application cycle; do not use it to date a 2026 grant cycle without checking the current SEGP page. Probable cause of a mere civil infraction (e.g. under-21 possession of ≤2.5 oz, MCL 333.27965(3)) does NOT support a warrantless automobile-exception search; police need probable cause of a criminal amount or another crime. 9.3.1 Statewide proposals

2008 Proposal 1 — Michigan Medical Marihuana Act (Initiated Law 1 of 2008)

  • Election date: 4 November 2008 (general election). Effective: 4 December 2008. Adopted figure in this Part: Yes 3,006,820 (62.67%) / No 1,790,889 (37.33%) / Total votes on the proposal 4,797,709. Sources: Wikipedia table for 2008 Michigan Proposal 1 (sourcing the result to the official canvass via its citations) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Michigan_Proposal_1 — accessed 2026-10-28; corroborated in text by Michigan Auto Law (vote "3,006,820 to 1,790,889," effective 4 Dec 2008, quoting MCL 333.26422(a)) — https://www.michiganautolaw.com/blog/2015/06/18/medical-marijuana-nofault-benefits/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Conflicts flagged (see §9.4):
  • Date: one secondary summary on the same Wikipedia page describes approval "on November 6, 2008" and another describes "63 percent to 37 percent" in rounded form. Adopted: 4 Nov 2008 (the 2008 general-election date; consistent with Run 1 and with the MCL effective date 4 Dec 2008, ten days after a 4 Nov vote under the initiative effective-date rule, allowing for canvass). The 6 Nov date is NOT adopted; it appears to conflate the 2008 election with the 6 Nov 2018 election date.
  • Counts: a contemporaneous NORML post gives 3,008,980 to 1,792,870 (difference: +2,160 Yes / +1,981 No vs adopted figures). Source: https://norml.org/blog/2008/11/11/support-for-medical-cannabis-is-broad-and-the-numbers-from-michigan-make-it-clear/ — accessed 2026-10-28. Adopted figures are 3,006,820 / 1,790,889 because they match the tabulated result (62.67%/37.33% on 4,797,709) and the Michigan Auto Law text; the NORML figures are treated as election-night/unofficial totals. The Bureau of Elections official canvass PDF was NOT directly opened — the adopted counts are therefore "official-canvass-consistent secondary" and must be re-verified against the Bureau's 2008 Official Michigan General Election Results before the compiled dossier calls them "Bureau of Elections official canvass" without qualification.
  • County sweep claim: NORML's claim that medical marihuana "won in every single county — all 83 counties" is secondary and was NOT verified county-by-county in this pass — do not repeat it as an official county result without the county canvass table.
  • Turnout (context, NOT the proposal total): Total ballots cast in Michigan in 2008 was about 5,039,080 (U.S. Election Atlas, citing Michigan Department of State, Bureau of Elections, 2008 Official Michigan General Election Results) — http://uselectionatlas.org/RESULTS/state.php?year=2008&amp;fips=26&amp;f=0&amp;off=0&amp;elect=0 — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary republication of Bureau data; voting-age-population turnout ~66.9% per Wikipedia's presidential-election page]. The proposal total (4,797,709) is lower than ballots cast because not every voter votes on every proposal (undervotes). Do not present 4,797,709 as "turnout." Voting-eligible-population turnout for 2008 is given as 68.9% in one secondary table (http://www.p2016.org/states/mi.htm) — different denominator (VEP vs VAP); do not mix the two.

9.3.2 Local ballot questions on allowing businesses — mechanism

  • MRTMA §6(1) (MCL 333.27956(1)) petition mechanism (verbatim substance, Run 1, Part 3, §3.1): electors may petition (signatures >5% of votes cast for governor in the municipality at the last gubernatorial election) to put an ordinance providing for the number of marihuana establishments allowed, or complete prohibition, on the ballot at the next regular election. A petition is subject to MCL 168.488 (Michigan Election Law §488). The same mechanism works in both directions: to prohibit/cap where officials allowed, and to allow (provide for a number) where officials opted out.
  • MMFLA has no parallel voter-initiative override in the same terms (Run 1, Part 3, §3.1) — a medical opt-in requires a municipal ordinance adopted by the governing body. [VERIFY] whether any MMFLA municipality adopted medical authorisation by initiative — none was located.
  • Certification: Local results are certified by the county board of canvassers (and, for city/village/township questions, reported through the county clerk). "Unofficial" election-night totals (e.g. Menominee, below) must be labelled unofficial until the county canvass is cited.

10.1.3 Tribe-by-tribe profiles

Conventions for profiles: "Regulator" means the tribal body named in the tribe's own code/rules. "Who may buy" is stated only where the cited source states it; for tribally regulated adult-use sales the default in the codes opened is "individuals 21 years of age or older" with government photo ID — tribal membership is NOT a purchase condition in any code opened, except for tribal-member tax/discount arrangements (Pokagon, see below), which are price benefits, not eligibility gates. "Product source" is stated only where the source states it; where a store was state-licensed before any compact, its product necessarily came through the state system (CRA licensees), because a state licensee may only obtain product from state licensees — that inference is labelled as such and is not presented as a tribal-code quotation.

1. Bay Mills Indian Community — Brimley, Chippewa County — YES, adult-use, tribally owned and regulated; cultivation, processing, retail

  • Operation: Northern Light Cannabis Company ("Northern Light Cannabis Co."), a wholly owned tribal enterprise operating a vertically integrated facility in Chippewa County. CRA/MiTechNews reporting (secondary, 1 Aug 2025) states Bay Mills "grows and produces organically cultivated cannabis at a vertically integrated facility in Chippewa County" and that the company was launched in 2021; Tribal Business News (secondary, 2021) dates the Northern Light operation's opening to November 2020. The November 2020 vs 2021 discrepancy is a brand-launch vs store-opening distinction in secondary sources and is flagged, not resolved — the tribal rules themselves do not give an opening date. Sources: https://mitechnews.com/news/tribal-cannabis-compact-signed-between-cra-and-bay-mills-indian-community/ ; https://tribalbusinessnews.com/economic-development/michigan-considering-legislation-to-finally-open-state-cannabis-markets-to-tribes/ — accessed 2026-10-28 (both secondary).
  • Personal-use legalisation first: Bay Mills adopted an ordinance on 8 Apr 2019 allowing individuals to cultivate, possess and use marijuana, mirroring state law — the first Michigan tribe to do so (tribal action reported by Sault Tribe official site, 18 Apr 2019, and by secondary reporting; the 2019 ordinance itself was not opened in this pass). Personal limits in that ordinance as secondarily reported mirror MRTMA: 2.5 oz, ≤15 g concentrate, 10 oz at home, 12 plants. Commercial activity by non-tribal businesses was NOT authorised by the 2019 ordinance; only wholly owned tribal enterprises were reserved the right to cultivate/manufacture/distribute/sell pending further legislation (secondary summary of the ordinance). Source: https://www.saulttribe.com/newsroom/6260-sault-tribe-legalizes-recreational-marijuana — accessed 2026-10-28 (official tribal site, for the 8 Apr 2019 date and the Sault comparison).
  • Regulator: Bay Mills Indian Community Cannabis Regulatory Commission, created as a regulatory subdivision of the Tribe by the Cannabis Regulatory Commission Ordinance. Verbatim (tribal source, Cannabis Regulatory Commission enactment, opened via baymills.org): "It is the purpose of this enactment to create a Tribal regulatory authority, termed the 'Cannabis Regulatory Commission' to establish and implement Tribal regulation and control of cannabis activity within the jurisdiction of Bay Mills Indian Community." Source: https://www.baymills.org/_files/ugd/869f65_7b5497641ae242739f8e1ffdacf19f4e.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Rules (tribal source, opened directly): Bay Mills Cannabis Rules & Regulations (baymills.org PDF, accessed 2026-10-28). Operative provisions verified in the opened text:
  • §101 PURPOSE: "Tribal oversight and regulation is essential to protect public health and welfare, and to protect the interests of the Tribe and of residents and visitors to the Bay Mills Indian Community lands. Bay Mills Indian Community has the legal authority to license and regulate any cannabis activity within the jurisdiction of the Tribe."
  • §102: the Cannabis Regulatory Commission "shall promulgate these rules and regulations to effectuate the safety of cannabis on Bay Mills Indian Community lands."
  • Definitions: "Cannabis Customer" means "an adult 21 years of age or older"; "Cannabis Retailer" means "a person licensed to obtain cannabis from cannabis establishments and to sell or otherwise transfer cannabis to cannabis establishments and to individuals who are 21 years of age or older"; "Cannabis" excludes "industrial hemp".
  • §104 LICENSE PERMISSIONS: the Commission "has the authority to grant, subject to further annual review and approval by the Cannabis Regulatory Commission, cannabis grower licenses, processor licenses, retailer licenses, and secure transporter licenses to wholly owned enterprises of the Bay Mills Indian Community that meet the requirements in these rules and regulations." — i.e. tribal licences under these rules are for wholly owned tribal enterprises only.
  • §105 GROWER LICENSE: "A cannabis grower license authorizes the cannabis grower to grow not more than Class A – 10,000 cannabis plants." (Only Class A is stated in the opened extract; whether further classes exist in the full rules [VERIFY] — the opened text runs to 1,763 lines and the grower-class table was not fully extracted in this pass.)
  • §107 RETAILER LICENSE: "A cannabis retailer license authorizes the purchase or transfer of cannabis or cannabis-infused products from only a licensed cannabis establishment and sale or transfer to only a licensed cannabis establishment or an individual 21 years of age or older." Retailer duties include selling only after testing and labelling, verifying age "by means of government-issued photographic identification containing a date of birth", that the sale "will not exceed the single transaction limit in these rules and regulations", entering transactions in the tribal monitoring system, video-recording security covering the entire retail establishment, and product "secured by lock and key, or other security device".
  • Tribal-State Agreement definition (§103.Y): "'Tribal-State Agreement' means the Agreement Among the Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, the Michigan Department of Treasury, and Bay Mills Indian Community dated July 24, 2025, including as may be amended." — This is the agreement date adopted here; CRA's announcement says "finalized on July 25, 2025" (see §10.2.1). The one-day difference (dated 24 July vs finalised/announced 25 July / 1 Aug) is flagged, not harmonised away.
  • "Tribal Monitoring System" is defined as an internet-based database maintained by the Commission for tracking transfers (transferee, date, quantity, price) and verifying limits. Before the compact, Bay Mills operated on this tribal system, not Metrc; under the compact it integrates into Metrc for state-market transactions (see §10.2.2).
  • Source: https://www.baymills.org/_files/ugd/869f65_b496c69515e34f0bb7ca0f298eabdb97.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Who may buy: any adult 21+ (not tribal members only) — per the "Cannabis Customer"/"Cannabis Retailer" definitions above. No tribal-member-only restriction appears in the opened rules.
  • Product source: tribally grown/processed at the Chippewa County vertically integrated facility (secondary, above) for tribal-market sales; after the July 2025 compact, Northern Light may also buy from and sell to state licensees (see §10.2.2). Whether any particular retail unit on a given date is tribal-grown vs state-sourced is [UNAVAILABLE] from the sources opened — the compact permits both channels; it does not publish a sourcing ledger.
  • Tax: under MRTMA §3(y)(iii) (see §10.3.2), a qualifying tribe must impose a tax or fee on sales from a tribal marihuana business to a non-tribal/non-establishment person, at a rate equal to or greater than the §13 rate (10%). Bay Mills is a qualifying tribe by virtue of its agreement (see §10.2.1); the rate and collection mechanics in Bay Mills' own tax law were NOT located in the sources opened — [VERIFY] against the Tribal-State Agreement text and Bay Mills tax ordinance. Do NOT state a Bay Mills retail tax rate on this pass.
  • Medical / CBD / hemp: no Bay Mills medical programme, CBD-specific operation, or hemp plan was located. Bay Mills' cannabis definition excludes industrial hemp, and no Bay Mills tribal hemp plan appears on the USDA list (see §10.4.1). Medical: none found [UNAVAILABLE to close out, but no evidence of one].

2. Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians — Peshawbestown, Leelanau County (HQ); Beach Fire Cannabis, Acme Township, Grand Traverse County — YES, adult-use, tribally owned and regulated

  • Operation: Beach Fire Cannabis, a tribal-enterprise dispensary adjacent to Turtle Creek Casino & Hotel in Acme Township, Grand Traverse County. Opening reported in secondary sources as 30 Mar 2023 (GGB Magazine; PlayMichigan). A 500 Nations casino-news summary dates the announcement to 18 Apr 2023. The 30 Mar 2023 store-opening date is adopted as the secondary-reported opening; the tribal ordinance/code does not give a store opening date. Sources (secondary): https://ggbmagazine.com/articles/michigan-tribes-find-new-cash-crop/ ; https://www.playmichigan.com/news/michigan-tribal-casinos-legal-cannabis-marijuana/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Ordinance history (tribal code via ecode360, opened in part): The Grand Traverse Band Marijuana Ordinance was enacted by Tribal Council Resolution #21-29.3368 on 9 Sept 2021, amended by Res. #23-41.3523 (15 Feb 2023) and #23-41.3534 (15 Mar 2023), and again by Res. #25-43.3841 (17 Dec 2025). Secondary reporting dates the ordinance's effectiveness to 29 Aug 2021 (Record-Eagle via MJBizDaily, 30 Aug 2021: "a tribal ordinance approved in 2019 by members went into effect on Aug. 29" — the 2019 member approval vs 2021 council enactment discrepancy is flagged; the ecode360 history line (2021 enactment) is adopted for the ordinance text, and the 2019 date is treated as the member-referendum date reported secondarily). Sources: https://ecode360.com/42419719 ; https://mjbizdaily.com/another-tribe-entering-michigans-recreational-cannabis-market/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Regulator: Grand Traverse Band Marijuana Regulatory Commission ("Commission" in the ordinance). Licence requirement (ecode360, Part 6, Marijuana License): "Every Tribal entity, employee, vendor, or consultant seeking to engage in, or assist with the cultivation, production, processing or sale of marijuana within the Band's jurisdiction must obtain and maintain a marijuana license from the Commission." Separate applications per activity type. Source: https://ecode360.com/42419935 — accessed 2026-10-28 (search-extract; full Part 6 text not line-opened in this pass — [VERIFY] against the GTB code PDF).
  • Operative definitions (ecode360 Part 2, opened directly, accessed 2026-10-28):
  • "Adult" means "a person over the age of 21 years."
  • "Marijuana retailer" means "a person or Tribal entity licensed to obtain marijuana from marijuana establishments and to sell or otherwise transfer marijuana to marijuana establishments and to individuals who are 21 years of age or older."
  • "Marijuana grower" / "Marijuana processor" definitions expressly contemplate sales "within 'Indian Country' … or specifically licensed to sell outside Indian Country to a State of Michigan licensed marijuana establishment" — i.e. the ordinance was drafted to accommodate state-market sales under a licence/compact, not only intra-tribal sales.
  • "Compact" means "the existing, or successor, Agreement between the Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, the Michigan Department of Treasury, and Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians, as authorized by MCL 333.27953(y)(ii), that establishes a framework for cooperation amongst said entities governing the transactions between Tribal and state licensed marijuana establishments". This definition alone does NOT prove a signed compact exists. It appears in the 17 Dec 2025 amendment history; no CRA announcement of a GTB cannabis compact, and no GTB compact text, was located. Status: [VERIFY] — see §10.2.1.
  • "Applicant" is limited to "the EDC acting in its Section 17 capacity … or a limited liability company established by a Tribal entity" — consistent with secondary reporting that the GTB operation is "solely for the tribe to own and operate" (Tribal Business News, 2021, quoting Chairman David Arroyo). That secondary statement is consistent with, but is not a substitute for, the ordinance text.
  • Who may buy: individuals 21+ (ordinance definition above); no tribal-member-only restriction in the opened definitions. Tribal lands limitation: secondary reporting (Record-Eagle via MJBizDaily) states businesses "must be on tribal lands such as reservation property in or near Peshawbestown" and trust lands in Acme and Whitewater Townships (Grand Traverse County). Acme Township and Whitewater Township do not allow adult-use licensing locally (secondary, PlayMichigan) — the tribal store operates there by sovereignty, not by local licence.
  • Product source / cultivation: the ordinance authorises tribal cultivation, processing and sale as a vertically integrated tribal enterprise (secondary, Tribal Business News 2021: tribe planned "control over the seed-to-sale marijuana operations and will not outsource"). Whether Beach Fire product in 2026 is tribal-grown, state-sourced, or both is [UNAVAILABLE] — no compact (which would authorise state sourcing) is confirmed, and no GTB grow-facility inventory was located.
  • Medical / hemp / CBD: no GTB medical programme, hemp plan (not on USDA tribal list), or CBD-specific operation located.

7. Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians — Harbor Springs / Petoskey area, Emmet County (HQ area); trust-land stores at Bear Creek Township near Petoskey, Emmet County and Mackinaw City, Cheboygan County — YES, adult-use retail on trust land (state-licensed operator model) + YES, hemp (USDA-approved tribal plan)

  • Cannabis operation (model matters — this is NOT a tribally owned store on the evidence): In July 2021, Troy-based Lume Cannabis Co. opened retail stores on trust lands for the Little Traverse Bay Bands at Bear Creek Township near Petoskey (1345 US-31, Petoskey, Emmet County in directory listings) and in Mackinaw City (1020 S Nicolet St, Mackinaw City, Cheboygan County), and received state licensing for a further store on Sault Tribe trust land in Sault Ste. Marie (see tribe 12). Secondary reporting (Tribal Business News, July 2021; Native News Online via NUNA clips, July 2020/2021) consistently describes the model as: Lume holds the STATE licence; the tribe is effectively landlord/licensor of trust land; the stores sit in municipalities that opted out (Bear Creek Township / Petoskey area and Mackinaw City), and local ordinances do not apply to trust land. A tribal resolution located on ltbbodawa-nsn.gov (19 June 2020, "Limited Waiver of Sovereign Immunity for Green Sunrise Products LLC — Petoskey Marijuana Retail License") waives the tribe's right to exclude MRA/Treasury/law-enforcement/building-fire officials from the premises "for the purpose of administering and enforcing the State of Michigan's marijuana laws" for that state-licensed retailer — confirming the state-licence-on-trust-land model for at least one Petoskey-area store. Whether the current Lume Petoskey/Mackinaw City stores operate under tribal licences, state licences, or both in 2026 is [VERIFY] against the CRA licence list and any LTBB code — the 2021 secondary model is not assumed to persist unchanged.
  • Tribal cannabis ordinance / regulator for commercial cannabis: no LTBB commercial-cannabis ordinance or cannabis commission was located in this pass, distinct from the hemp statute below. [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Hemp — YES, official: USDA approved a hemp production plan for the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians on 17 June 2020 (USDA announcement, via Cannabis Law Report/Morning Ag Clips republication of the USDA release, accessed 2026-10-28), and the USDA approved-plan list updated 17 Feb 2026 (opened directly) STILL lists "Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Waganakising Odawak — Approved Plan (pdf)". The tribal hemp statute is the Waganakising Odawak Statute, Hemp Authorization and Regulatory Commission Statute (WOS 2020-015, 30 May 2020), creating a Hemp Regulatory Commission of 3–5 members (secondary legal analysis, Harris Sliwoski, and tribal statute PDF on ltbbodawa-nsn.gov). The statute authorises "Production and Handling of Hemp within locations within the Territory of the Tribe" (§7.1903 in the tribal code extract). Whether any hemp is currently grown under the LTBB plan, and by whom, is [UNAVAILABLE] — a plan on the USDA list is not a production report. Hemp grown under the tribal plan is subject to the federal hemp framework in §10.4.1, not to MRTMA marihuana licensing, while it remains hemp (≤0.3% THC on the applicable federal definition at the time; post-11 Dec 2026 total-THC definition per baseline — see §10.4.1).
  • Who may buy / product source (cannabis stores): Lume stores are described secondarily as adult-use (21+) retail open to the public; product is Lume-cultivated/sourced through the state system (Lume's Evart, Osceola County cultivation facility is named secondarily for the Sault partnership; the same state-system sourcing applies in principle to state-licensed stores). Tribal-member-only purchase: NO evidence; not claimed.
  • Compact: no CRA cannabis compact for LTBB located. The 2020 Green Sunrise waiver is not a §7 compact.
  • Sources: USDA list https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 2026-10-28 (opened directly); LTBB hemp plan PDF https://www.ams.usda.gov/sites/default/files/media/LittleTraverseBayBandsofOdawaIndiansHempPlan.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 (search-extract); LTBB waiver https://ltbbodawa-nsn.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/061920-01-Limited-Waiver-of-Sovereign-Immunity-for-Green-Sunrise-Products-LLC-Petoskey-Marijuana-Retail-License-and-Related-Matters.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 (search-extract); secondary model reporting https://www.cannabisexaminers.com/michigan-native-american-tribe-announces-retail-partnership-with-cannabis-company/ — accessed 2026-10-28.

Gift cards excluded from discount offer." — i.e. tribal members 21+ get sales-tax removal + 25% discount; non-members are not excluded from purchase by that page. The sales-tax removal for members is stated as covered by "a combination of the State of Michigan through the 2004 Tax Agreement and … Pokagon Band Government expense" on the same page (tribal site, secondary-to-law but official tribal source for the benefit). The interaction of that member benefit with the post-compact tribal excise-tax sharing (see §10.2.1) is [VERIFY] — the compact text was not opened.
  • Product source: before the Dec 2025 compact, Rolling Embers "did not have access to Michigan's licensed adult-use cannabis market, including the ability to transact business with state licensees" (CRA release) — i.e. pre-compact product was tribal-market product, not state-system product. After the compact, it may buy from and sell to state licensees (see §10.2.2). Current (2026, post-compact) sourcing mix is [UNAVAILABLE].

11. Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan — Mount Pleasant, Isabella County — YES, commercial retail framework (dual state + tribal licence); operating store/brand [UNAVAILABLE]

  • Ordinance (tribal source, opened directly): Ordinance No. 36, Commercial Marijuana Ordinance, Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, as amended 29 Apr 2026 (14-page PDF on sagchip.org, accessed 2026-10-28). An earlier version (amended by Res. 24-006, 4 Oct 2023, 8 pages) was also located; the 29 Apr 2026 version is adopted as current for this dossier. Operative provisions verified in the opened text:
  • §1 PURPOSE: "to establish the legal framework for the authorization and regulation of Commercial Marijuana Activities and Designated Consumption on Saginaw Chippewa Tribal Lands."
  • §3 AUTHORITY: enacted under Art. VI, §§1(e), (i), (j), (k), (n), (o) of the Tribal Constitution (4 Nov 1986).
  • §4 DEFINITIONS: "Commercial Marijuana Activities" means "the retail sale of any portion of a marijuana plant that has a THC concentration of 0.3% or more on a dry weight basis." "Commercial Marijuana License" means "a license issued by the Tribe … to conduct Commercial Marijuana Activities". "Marijuana Retailer License" means "the license issued by the State Cannabis Regulatory Agency pursuant to the MRTMA". "Designated Consumption" means consumption of marijuana (≥0.3% THC dry weight) "at a commercial space by adults twenty-one (21) years of age and older." "Tribal Designated Consumption Establishment" means "a commercial space, owned and operated by the Tribe or a wholly owned subsidiary of the Tribe, that is licensed by the Tribe … and that is authorized to permit Designated Consumption". "Tribal Lands" includes reservation lands (including as defined in Saginaw Chippewa v. Granholm, E.D. Mich. No. 05-10296-BC), trust lands, and unextinguished-allotment lands over which the Tribe has jurisdiction.
  • §5 ADMINISTRATION: the Director of Tribal Licensing, Regulations, and Tribal Employment Rights Ordinance ("Director") administers the Ordinance, develops Commercial Marijuana Regulations (effective on Tribal Council approval), and maintains a central file of applications/renewals/correspondence/suspensions/revocations for not less than 5 years. Applications go to: Director, Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, 7500 Soaring Eagle Boulevard, Mount Pleasant, MI 48858 (Isabella County) — official public tribal office address from the ordinance itself.
  • §6 AUTHORISED ACTIVITIES — the dual-licence rule (verbatim in substance): "Only those Commercial Marijuana Activities that are authorized under an existing, current Marijuana Retailer License may be authorized under this Ordinance. All such Commercial Marijuana Activities must be conducted in compliance with the applicable Marijuana Retailer License and any Commercial Marijuana License issued pursuant to this Ordinance." And: "Licensed Marijuana Establishments must maintain a Marijuana Retailer License for the authorized Commercial Marijuana Activities for the duration of the Commercial Marijuana License." A state Retailer Licence is therefore a precondition, not an alternative, under Ordinance 36. "Designated Consumption is strictly prohibited at any Licensed Marijuana Establishment" (§6.g) — consumption is only at a separately licensed Tribal Designated Consumption Establishment.
  • §6 PROHIBITED PERSONS: Tribal Council members; employees of the licensing office or supervising departments; law-enforcement employees, judges/magistrates; gaming-enterprise executives/directors/managers (including Soaring Eagle Gaming); Gaming Commission members/employees and Key Employees — may not receive funds from or hold a financial/ownership interest in a Licensed Marijuana Establishment or Tribal Designated Consumption Establishment. Funds received by the Tribe under the Ordinance must be kept separate from gaming revenues.
  • §7 APPLICATION: applicant must attach a copy of its current Marijuana Retailer License AND State documentation issued within 30 days stating the applicant is in full compliance with that licence; must list activities, premises address, HQ address, and all employees subject to MRTMA background checks with CRA written confirmation; must submit supplemental employee lists within 30 days of hiring. Licence term 1 year; renewal application 30–60 days before expiry. Director issues only if the application is "in full compliance with this Ordinance, the Commercial Marijuana Regulations, and the MRTMA as verified by the State."
  • §8 BUFFER: no Licensed Marijuana Establishment or Tribal Designated Consumption Establishment within 750 feet of a K–12 school (shortest straight line, main entrance to main entrance); none on land/structure where gaming is permitted/performed/conducted/operated, or managed/operated by Soaring Eagle Gaming. (750 ft is below MRTMA's 1,000-ft state default — a tribal choice, not a state-law statement.)
  • §9 ENFORCEMENT: Director may conduct premises checks during regular business hours, not less than 4 times per calendar year; may enter/inspect records and all areas on not less than 24 hours' written notice; licensees must immediately notify the Director in writing of any state/federal enforcement/regulatory/administrative/judicial action; licensees consent to Tribal Court jurisdiction; licences are conditioned on compliance with Tribal Law and MRTMA.
  • §10 REVOCATION/SUSPENSION: Director SHALL revoke/suspend if the state Retailer Licence is revoked, suspended, lapsed, or otherwise no longer in effect; may suspend (7–30 days) for Ordinance/Regulations/MRTMA violations, misrepresentation, diversion, sale to under-21s, transfer/distribution in violation of MRTMA, attempted transfer of the tribal licence, harm to safety/health, or refusal of access/cooperation; SHALL revoke after a third suspension followed by a further §10.c violation, for safety/health conduct within 1 year of a prior suspension for such conduct, for conduct causing serious injury/death, or on felony/controlled-substance-crime conviction of an owner/partner/fiduciary. Appeal exclusively to Tribal Court (no jury; limited waiver of immunity for prospective injunctive/declaratory relief only, no monetary damages; Director's decision upheld absent clear-and-convincing showing it was arbitrary/capricious or contrary to law).
  • §11 APPLICABILITY OF MICHIGAN STATE LICENSE: "A Licensed Marijuana Establishment shall comply with MRTMA and any applicable Marijuana Retailer License as a condition of receiving and maintaining a Commercial Marijuana License."
  • §12 DESIGNATED CONSUMPTION ESTABLISHMENTS: tribe-owned/subsidiary only (see definition above); must have a smoke-free employee monitoring area, ventilation directing air outside through filtration "sufficient to remove visible smoke … and adequate to eliminate odor at the property line" if inhalation is permitted, and physical separation from non-smoking areas. Licence applications to the Director (same Mount Pleasant address); 1-year term; renewal 30–60 days before expiry.
  • Source: https://www.sagchip.org/tribalcourt/ordinance/Ordinance%2036%20Commercial%20Marijuana%20Ordinance%20042926.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Operating store: a tribal economic-development RFP (Migizi EDC, Mar 2021, tribal-adjacent source) sought proposals "to operate a retail cannabis dispensary within select facilities and Tribal Trust Land" on the Isabella Reservation (Isabella County and Arenac County trust lands), naming Suites 2–3 of Arnold J. Sowmick Sr. Plaza, the retail store within Soaring Eagle Casino, and a vacant parcel, with tribal cannabis regulations "to become effective sometime during the first quarter of 2021". Whether any store opened under that RFP, and whether any store operates under Ordinance 36 in 2026 (and under what brand/address), was NOT verified in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE]. The Ordinance 36 framework is therefore reported as law in force, not as proof of a currently trading store. Do NOT name a Saginaw Chippewa dispensary brand on this evidence.

The ordinance itself does not state a tribal-member-only purchase rule; none is claimed. Cultivation/processing under Ordinance 36: the ordinance as opened authorises RETAIL sale ("Commercial Marijuana Activities" = retail sale) and designated consumption; it does not by its definitions authorise tribal cultivation or processing as a standalone tribal licence type. Whether Saginaw Chippewa cultivation/processing exists under a separate instrument is [UNAVAILABLE].

MRTMA §3(y)(iii) tax/fee requirement (≥10% of sales price) applies only if the tribe seeks "qualifying Indian tribe" status under a §7 agreement (see §10.3.2); no Saginaw Chippewa §7 agreement was located, so no tribal-tax statement is made here. 12. Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians — Sault Ste. Marie, Chippewa County — YES, adult-use, dual model (tribal ordinance + state-licensed stores on trust land)

  • Personal-use legalisation: Board of Directors resolution at its 16 Apr 2019 meeting legalised marijuana on the Sault Tribe reservation, effective 15 May 2019 (tribal official site, accessed 2026-10-28). The law mirrors state law: only 21+ may possess/use/grow small amounts within their residence; public use/display prohibited; driving under the influence prohibited; past marijuana offences may be vacated via Tribal Court; "Permitted manufacture, process and sale of marijuana is limited to authorized tribal enterprises." Implemented via Tribal Code Chapter 71, Criminal Offenses, Subchapter XVI (Controlled Substances). Source: https://www.saulttribe.com/newsroom/6260-sault-tribe-legalizes-recreational-marijuana — accessed 2026-10-28 (official tribal site).
  • Commercial ordinance (tribal source, opened directly): Tribal Code Chapter 47, Commercial Marijuana Ordinance, Resolution No. 2020-47, adopted 14 Apr 2020, effective immediately (PDF on saulttribe.com/dev.saulttribe.com, accessed 2026-10-28). Operative provisions verified:
  • §47.102 PURPOSE/AUTHORITY: "to establish a legal framework for the authorization and regulation of commercial marijuana activities in the Tribe's Indian country. Authorizing such businesses will create revenue for the Tribe to support Tribal governance; remove commercial production and distribution of marijuana from the illicit market; and promote the health, safety, and wellbeing of the Tribe, its members, and the citizens of the State of Michigan." Adopted under Art. VII, §§1(g) and (n) of the Tribal Constitution.
  • §47.103 DEFINITIONS: "Indian Country" means all lands as defined by 18 U.S.C. §1151 within the Tribe's Reservation plus trust/restricted-fee lands for the Tribe/members. "Licensed Marijuana Establishment" means an entity "who currently possesses or wishes to apply for a State Marihuana Establishment License and a Tribal License to operate a Marijuana Establishment in the Tribe's Indian Country." "Marijuana" has the same meaning as "marihuana" in MCL 333.27953; "Marijuana Establishment" the same as "marihuana establishment" in MCL 333.27953. "Tribal Enterprise" means a business enterprise owned by the Tribe. "Tribal License" means a licence issued by the Tribe to operate a Licensed Marijuana Establishment in Indian Country.
  • §47.104 AUTHORISED ACTIVITIES (verbatim): "(1) Wholly owned Tribal Enterprises and Licensed Marijuana Establishments are the only persons or entities that may engage in commercial marijuana activities within Indian Country. (2) Tribal Enterprises do not need to apply for a Tribal License. (3) An Applicant wishing to become a Licensed Marijuana Establishment shall submit a Tribal License Application in accordance with the provisions of the Tribe's Commercial Marijuana Policy. At a minimum, the Tribal License Application must include a copy of the Applicant's background check performed in accordance with the terms of MRTMA; a designation indicating whether the Applicant is a member of the Tribe; and an application fee in the amount of no less than two thousand dollars ($2,000.00)." Applications to: Secretary of Board of Directors, Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, 523 Ashmun Street, Sault Ste. Marie, MI 49783 (Chippewa County), with copy to the Chief Law Enforcement Officer at the same address (official public tribal office addresses from the ordinance itself). "(4) All newly issued Tribal Licenses shall be for the remainder of the calendar year plus one year … Renewed Tribal Licenses shall be for one calendar year, from January 1 to December 31." "(5) Tribal Licenses are nonassignable and nontransferable."
  • §47.105 RENEWAL: renewal application at least 30 days before expiry; renewal fee "not less than one thousand dollars ($1,000.00)".
  • §47.106 BUFFER: no Licensed Marijuana Establishment within 1,000 feet (shortest straight line, property line to property line) of a K–12 school or playground, whether inside or outside Indian Country. (Matches MRTMA's 1,000-ft school default and adds playgrounds.)
  • §47.107 ENFORCEMENT: "The Tribal Police may conduct premises checks of any Licensed Marijuana Establishment to observe compliance with this Chapter and the Tribe's Commercial Marijuana Policy". Other civil regulatory penalties under the Policy or any other tribal ordinance are preserved.
  • §47.108 REVOCATION: a Tribal License "shall be automatically revoked if the Tribe learns that the license holder's State License has been revoked." The Board of Directors may revoke (after hearing, written grounds at least 15 days prior) for: violation of Chapter/MRTMA; material misrepresentation; conduct implicating Federal Enforcement Priorities (defined in §47.103(3) as the eight Cole/Wilkinson priorities — distribution to minors; revenue to criminal enterprises/gangs/cartels; diversion from legal states to other states; state-authorized activity as cover for other illegal drugs/activity; violence/firearms; drugged driving/adverse public health; growing on public lands; possession/use on federal property); transfer/distribution in violation of MRTMA; attempted transfer of a Tribal License; or conduct jeopardising/threatening safety/health of members, patrons or employees.
  • §47.109 APPLICABILITY OF STATE LAW (verbatim): "(1) MRTMA applies to all Licensed Marijuana Establishments. (2) The Tribe unequivocally and irrevocably waives its right to exclude LARA inspectors, regulators, and/or staff from the Tribe's Indian Country, but only to the extent such LARA inspectors, regulators, and/or staff are seeking access to a Licensed Marijuana Establishment." — i.e. the Sault model is expressly dual: tribal licence + state licence + state-inspector access, NOT a standalone tribal-only licence for non-tribal enterprises. (Wholly owned Tribal Enterprises do not need a Tribal License under §47.104(2); whether they need a state licence is not stated in Chapter 47 as opened — [VERIFY] against the Commercial Marijuana Policy, which was NOT located in this pass.)
  • §47.112: "Tribal Sovereign Immunity and Jurisdiction Preserved" (section title; full text in the opened PDF after §47.111 severability — the opened extract ends at §47.111; §47.112–§47.114 texts were not fully extracted and are [VERIFY] if quoted).
