10.2 Compacts, agreements, trading, Metrc, and distribution

10.2.1 Confirmed compacts — exactly two, by CRA's own counting

Enabling legislation (confirmed, with date note): - 2023 PA 165 (SB 179, amends MRTMA §14, MCL 333.27964) and 2023 PA 166 (SB 180, amends MRTMA §§3, 7, 8, 10, 13) were signed by Governor Whitmer on 19 Oct 2023 and assigned PA numbers on 24 Oct 2023 with immediate effect (LegiScan/legislature search index, accessed 2026-10-28). Run 1 Parts 2–3 cite "2023 PA 166 eff. 19 Oct 2023" for the package; the split (165 = distribution, 166 = definitions/qualifying-tribe/tax) is added here, and the signed-vs-assigned one-day variance is flagged — the operative date adopted is 19 Oct 2023 (signing/immediate effect), with 24 Oct 2023 noted as the PA-assignment date. No Run 1 figure is changed by this note. Sources (index): https://legiscan.com/MI/bill/SB0179/2023 ; https://legiscan.com/MI/bill/SB0180/2023 — accessed 2026-10-28 (search-index; legislature.mi.gov bill pages were not line-opened in this pass — [VERIFY] if a PA-date quotation is needed).

Compact 1 — Bay Mills Indian Community (first). - Agreement date: 24 July 2025 per Bay Mills' own Cannabis Rules & Regulations definition ("Agreement Among the Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency, the Michigan Department of Treasury, and Bay Mills Indian Community dated July 24, 2025, including as may be amended"). CRA/MiTechNews announcement (1 Aug 2025, secondary republication of CRA material) says the agreement was "finalized on July 25, 2025". ADOPTED: agreement dated 24 July 2025 (tribal source); finalised/announced 25 July / 1 Aug 2025. The one-day variance is flagged (Research Note R-02). - Effects (CRA announcement, secondary republication, accessed 2026-10-28): Northern Light Cannabis Co. "enters Michigan's statewide wholesale and distribution channels"; the agreement "allows Northern Light to sell its products through Michigan's regulated adult-use cannabis market, making it available to licensed businesses and consumers statewide"; Northern Light "must comply with the same state licensing requirements, testing, and safety standards as other adult-use cannabis businesses" and "will participate in Michigan's Metrc seed-to-sale tracking system" (MJBizDaily, 1 Aug 2025, secondary: https://mjbizdaily.com/news/tribal-cannabis-operator-enters-mainstream-michigan-marijuana-market/406190/ — accessed 2026-10-28). Bay Mills' tribal site/CRA summary adds: Bay Mills "will receive a percentage of the excise tax generated by sales of its products" (CRA summary, secondary) — the percentage is [UNAVAILABLE] (not stated in the sources opened). - Compact text: NOT located in full. No clause beyond the CRA summary and the Bay Mills rules definition is quoted here. Do NOT cite compact clauses (transport routes, inspection protocols, tax-share percentages) as if the text had been read.

Compact 2 — Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians (second). - Official source, opened directly: CRA/LARA news release, 18 Dec 2025, "The Pokagon Band and State of Michigan Sign Historic Cannabis Compact" (https://www.michigan.gov/lara/news-releases/2025/12/18/the-pokagon-band-and-state-of-michigan-sign-historic-cannabis-compact — accessed 2026-10-28). Operative statements, in the release's own terms: - "This is the state's second tribal-state cannabis compact, granting the Pokagon Band access to Michigan's licensed adult-use cannabis market." - "The agreement allows the Pokagon Band's cannabis businesses to purchase from and sell to state licensees, transport products outside of Indian lands for transactions with state licensees, and integrate into Michigan's seed-to-sale tracking system (Metrc)." - "The compact also establishes a framework for collaboration between the Pokagon Band and the CRA on inspections and enforcement." - "The Pokagon Band will share a percentage of its Cannabis Excise Tax with the state to reimburse the state for costs associated with compact administration. The remaining excise tax revenues will fund Pokagon Band government programs and projects." — the percentage is [UNAVAILABLE] (not stated in the release). - Context in the release: the Pokagon Band "legalized adult-use cannabis on its tribal land in April 2023 and launched its Rolling Embers retail store and outdoor consumption lounge under tribal law in New Buffalo, Berrien County"; "prior to this agreement, Rolling Embers did not have access to Michigan's licensed adult-use cannabis market, including the ability to transact business with state licensees"; the release describes the compact as "a government-to-government agreement" and quotes CRA Executive Director Brian Hanna that the agreement "will strengthen Michigan's regulated cannabis market, enhance consumer safety, and provide a clear, lawful pathway for tribal businesses to participate in Michigan's adult-use market." - The release does NOT state that Pokagon becomes a CRA licensee. Under MRTMA definitions (see §10.3.2), a "tribal marihuana business" is by definition NOT a marihuana establishment, and a "licensee" holds a state licence — the compact grants market ACCESS (buy/sell/transport/Metrc), not conversion into a CRA licensee. That distinction is stated as a statutory reading, not as a compact quotation. - Compact text: NOT located in full (the release is a summary). No clause beyond the release is quoted. The excise-share percentage, transport restrictions, inspection protocol, and any wholesale-tax treatment are [UNAVAILABLE].

No other CRA cannabis compact was located. In particular: - Grand Traverse Band: ordinance defines "Compact" (see §10.1.3, tribe 2) but no CRA announcement and no GTB compact text was located. Status [VERIFY] — the definition proves the code anticipates a compact; it does not prove one is signed and in effect. Do NOT list GTB as compacted. - Lac Vieux Desert Band: secondary law blog (Turtle Talk) says LVD "entered a Tribal-State cannabis compact" in 2025. That CONFLICTS with CRA's 18 Dec 2025 "second compact" counting (Bay Mills first, Pokagon second) IF the blog means a MRTMA §7 CRA compact signed before 18 Dec 2025. ADOPTED: LVD compact = [VERIFY], NOT counted as a confirmed third compact. Possible reconciliations (none adopted): loose use of "compact" for a non-§7 agreement; a post-18 Dec 2025 agreement described as "2025" in drafting; or blog error. Follow-up: CRA press-release index + LVD tribal government confirmation (Research Note R-03). - Sault Tribe, Saginaw Chippewa, Little Traverse Bay Bands, Keweenaw Bay, Hannahville, Little River Band, Gun Lake Tribe, Nottawaseppi Huron Band: no CRA cannabis compact announcement located. Their state-market access, where it exists, runs through state licences (dual model), not through a §7 compact. - Tax agreements distinct from cannabis compacts: Pokagon's 2004 Tax Agreement (referenced on the tribe's member-benefits page for the member sales-tax removal) is a general tribal-state tax agreement, NOT a cannabis compact, and is not treated as one here. Other tribes' general tax agreements (if any) were not researched for Part 10 and are not asserted.

10.2.2 Trading with CRA licensees, Metrc, and transport — the three models

Model A — Tribal-only (pre-compact) tribal marihuana business. - A tribal marihuana business operating under tribal law alone (Bay Mills pre-July 2025; Pokagon pre-Dec 2025; GTB, KBIC, LVD on current evidence) could lawfully sell within its own tribal market under tribal law, but could NOT lawfully buy from or sell to CRA licensees, could NOT enter Metrc, and could NOT lawfully transport product outside Indian lands into the state market — because CRA licensees may only obtain/transfer product through the state system, and the tribal business was not in that system. Bay Mills' pre-compact isolation is stated explicitly in secondary reporting of the tribe's 2023 legislative testimony (Tribal Business News: the tribe "was unable to sell its products to state-licensed businesses" and sought legislation to "open state cannabis markets to tribes"). The statutory basis for the post-compact opening is MRTMA §7(2)(b) (CRA agreement with a qualifying tribe) — see §10.3.2. - Model A, post-compact (Bay Mills, Pokagon): buy from / sell to state licensees; transport outside Indian lands for transactions with state licensees (Pokagon release, verbatim above); integrate into Metrc for those transactions; collaborate with CRA on inspections/enforcement. Exact transport conditions (routes, secure-transporter licensing, manifesting, delivery windows) are in the compact texts, which were NOT opened — [UNAVAILABLE]. Do NOT invent transport conditions.

Model B — Dual-licensed (tribal licence + CRA state licence). - Sault Tribe Licensed Marijuana Establishments and Saginaw Chippewa Commercial Marijuana Licensees MUST hold a CRA state licence (Sault §47.103(6)/§47.108; Saginaw §6(d)/(e)/§10). They trade through the state system already: they buy from / sell to state licensees, use Metrc, and transport under CRA rules, because their state licence requires it. The tribal licence is an additional, location-specific layer (permission to operate that state-licensed activity in Indian Country + tribal premises checks + tribal fees), not a substitute for the state licence. Loss of the state licence automatically kills the tribal licence (Sault §47.108 automatic revocation; Saginaw §10 mandatory revocation/suspension). Lume/LTBB trust-land stores (and the Green Sunrise Petoskey waiver) are the same model in practice: state licence + tribal land/waiver layer. - Metrc for Model B: state-licensed activity is in Metrc by virtue of the state licence (CRA rules, Run 1 Part 2). Tribal-only activity that is not state-licensed is not in Metrc (Bay Mills pre-compact tribal monitoring system, above).

Model C — State-licensed operator on trust land, no tribal cannabis licence evidenced. - LTBB Lume stores (2021 model) and the Hannahville-area store: state licence + trust-land location (or tribal-member discount) without a located tribal cannabis licence. Trading/Metrc/transport follow the state licence. Whether LTBB now also issues a tribal licence for those stores is [VERIFY].

What a compact does NOT do: it does not make a tribal marihuana business a "marihuana establishment" or a CRA "licensee" (MRTMA §3(g)/(z)/(bb), see §10.3.2); it does not authorise interstate marihuana commerce (see §10.4.3); it does not authorise sales to persons under 21; and it does not, on the summaries opened, authorise tribal product to bypass state testing — Bay Mills' compact summary expressly states the same testing/safety standards apply.

Wholesale tax (2025 PA 23) interaction: Run 1 Part 2 records a 24% wholesale tax from 1 Jan 2026, under live litigation. Whether that tax applies to tribal-to-state wholesale transfers under the Bay Mills/Pokagon compacts, and whether any compact provision addresses it, is [UNAVAILABLE] — neither compact text nor CRA summary opened here mentions the wholesale tax. Do NOT state that tribal wholesale transfers are exempt from or subject to the wholesale tax.

10.2.3 MRTMA §13/§14 as amended (2023 PA 165/166) — verbatim operative text

Source for the reflowed text: MRTMA as reflowed at https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/laws/mrtma/latest/ — accessed 2026-10-28. Caution: this is a mirror/reflow of the statute, NOT legislature.mi.gov. The quotations below are from that reflow and must be re-verified against legislature.mi.gov (MCL 333.27953, 333.27963, 333.27964) before publication as official-text quotations. The substance matches Run 1 Parts 2–3.

§13 (MCL 333.27963) — Marihuana excise tax, operative provisions: - §13(1): "In addition to all other taxes, a tax is imposed on marihuana sold or otherwise transferred to anyone other than a marihuana establishment or tribal marihuana business at a rate of 10% of the sales price." - §13(4)(a) (exemption, in substance): marihuana sold or otherwise transferred FROM a tribal marihuana business is exempt from the §13 tax — i.e. the exemption runs with the seller being a tribal marihuana business, not with the buyer. (Reflow text: "Marihuana sold or otherwise transferred from a tribal marihuana business is exempt from the tax imposed under this section." — re-verify wording on legislature.mi.gov.) - §13(4)(b) (in substance): the exemption does not apply to marihuana sold or transferred by a tribal marihuana business to a person other than a tribal marihuana business or marihuana establishment UNLESS the tribe imposes the §3(y)(iii) tax/fee (see §10.3.2) — i.e. the qualifying-tribe tax/fee is the condition for the exemption on retail sales to the public. (Reflow wording to be re-verified; the §3(y)(iii) condition is stated verbatim in §10.3.2 below.) - §13(5) (in substance): a tribal marihuana business that is a qualifying tribe's business and that sells to a non-tribal/non-establishment person must collect the tribal tax/fee and remit/retain it as the agreement provides. (Reflow wording to be re-verified.)

§14 (MCL 333.27964) — Distribution of Marihuana Regulation Fund, operative provisions: - §14(1)–(3) (in substance, Run 1 Part 2): after administration costs, the Fund is distributed: 15% to municipalities with a marihuana retailer or microbusiness; 15% to counties with a retailer/microbusiness; 35% to the School Aid Fund; 35% to the Michigan Transportation Fund. (Run 1 Part 2 gives the same percentages; re-verify section numbering on legislature.mi.gov.) - §14(5) (tribal redirection, in substance, Run 1 Part 2/Part 3): "If a marihuana retailer or marihuana microbusiness is located in Indian lands, the amounts that would otherwise be distributed to the municipality under subsection (4)(a) and to the county under subsection (4)(b) must instead be distributed to the Indian tribe in whose Indian lands the retailer or microbusiness is located." — i.e. the tribe receives BOTH the municipal share and the county share for a retailer/microbusiness on its Indian lands, in place of the municipality and county that would otherwise receive them. (Reflow wording to be re-verified; the substance is the Run 1 anchor and is not changed here.) - §14(4) allocation method (Run 1 Part 2): municipal/county shares are allocated in proportion to the number of retailers/microbusinesses in each municipality/county. The per-store figure is therefore Fund-local-share ÷ total statewide retailer/microbusiness count, not a fixed statutory dollar amount — which is why FY2024 ($58,200+) and FY2025 ($54,017.10, secondary) per-store figures differ year to year.

How the tribal share works in practice — what is known and what is not: - Known (Treasury release, §10.2.4): tribes received Fund money for the first time in FY2024; the release states the tribal total (over $931,000 among 4 tribes) but does not name tribes or give by-tribe amounts. - Known (statutory mechanism): a tribe's share = (municipal per-store amount + county per-store amount) × (number of qualifying retailers/microbusinesses on its Indian lands), where "qualifying" means the retailer/microbusiness that triggers the §14(4) allocation. Whether a tribally licensed-only business (Model A, pre-compact) counts as a "marihuana retailer" for §14(4) purposes, or whether only CRA-licensed retailers/microbusinesses on Indian lands trigger the share, is NOT stated in the Treasury release and was not resolved from the statute reflow in this pass — [VERIFY] against Treasury's Revenue Sharing breakdown methodology and the §14 text on legislature.mi.gov. This matters: if only CRA-licensed stores count, a pre-compact tribal-only store would not itself generate a §14 share (the tribe's FY2024 payment would then reflect CRA-licensed stores on its lands, e.g. Lume/Sault-trust-land stores), whereas if tribal businesses count, the payment reflects tribal stores. Do NOT assert either reading as settled. - Not known (official): which 4 tribes, by-tribe amounts, store counts per tribe, FY2025 by-tribe amounts. See §10.2.4.

10.3 Legal framework

10.3.1 Tribal sovereignty / federal Indian law basis — only as official sources state it

  • Federal recognition and self-government: BIA's Midwest Region page (opened directly, accessed 2026-10-28) states that the Midwest Region serves "36 federally recognized Tribes in the States of Iowa, Michigan, Minnesota, and Wisconsin" and that BIA's mission includes "enhancing the quality of life, promoting economic opportunity, and carrying out the responsibility to protect and improve the trust assets of American Indians, Indian Tribes and Alaska Natives." The MRTMA definition of "Indian tribe" (§3(e), see §10.3.2) requires recognition by the US Secretary of the Interior as eligible for BIA services AND recognition as possessing powers of self-government. No broader federal-Indian-law proposition (e.g. inherent sovereignty, trust doctrine, Public Law 280 status for Michigan) is asserted in Part 10, because no official source stating it for Michigan cannabis was opened and Public Law 280 was NOT researched in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE] for a PL 280 conclusion. Do NOT import a law-firm summary of Indian law as law.
  • What sovereignty means operationally in Part 10, on the evidence: (a) a tribe may enact its own commercial-cannabis ordinance governing activity in its Indian Country (Sault Chapter 47 §47.102; Saginaw Ordinance 36 §1/§3; Bay Mills rules §101; GTB ordinance); (b) state law does not by itself authorise or prohibit that activity on Indian lands — state law enters only where the tribe adopts it (Sault §47.109(1) "MRTMA applies to all Licensed Marijuana Establishments"; Saginaw §11), where the business holds a state licence (dual model), or where the tribe agrees by compact/waiver (Bay Mills/Pokagon compacts; LTBB Green Sunrise waiver; Sault §47.109(2) LARA-access waiver); (c) a tribe's sovereign immunity is preserved except where the tribe expressly waives it for a stated purpose (Sault Chapter 47 §47.112 title; Saginaw §10 appeal waiver limited to prospective injunctive/declaratory relief, no monetary damages; LTBB Green Sunrise waiver limited to state-law administration/enforcement access for that retailer). No wider immunity proposition is stated.
  • Local (municipal/county) law: tribal stores on Indian lands are not subject to municipal/county opt-outs or caps (e.g. Bear Creek Township / Petoskey area and Mackinaw City opt-outs do not block trust-land stores, per secondary reporting in §10.1.3 tribe 7; Acme/Whitewater Township non-licensing does not block the GTB store, per secondary reporting in §10.1.3 tribe 2). That is a sovereignty consequence stated secondarily for those stores, not a general legal rule quoted from a statute — it is labelled secondary where it appears. Michigan's MRTMA local-opt-out (§6) and local caps (e.g. Menominee City cap 9, see §10.4.5) apply to state-licensed establishments in municipal/county jurisdiction, not to tribal businesses on Indian lands operating under tribal law — that distinction follows from the ordinance/compact structure above, not from a separate local-law source opened here.

10.3.2 MRTMA definitions — "tribal marihuana business", "qualifying Indian tribe", "Indian lands", "Indian tribe", "licensee" (verbatim from reflow, re-verify on legislature.mi.gov)

Source: MRTMA reflow, https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/laws/mrtma/latest/ — accessed 2026-10-28 (mirror; re-verify on legislature.mi.gov, MCL 333.27953, before publication as official text).

  • §3(d) "Indian lands" means "all lands within the limits of an Indian reservation; and any lands title to which is either held in trust by the United States for the benefit of an Indian tribe or individual or held by an Indian tribe or individual subject to a restriction by the United States against alienation and over which an Indian tribe exercises governmental power."
  • §3(e) "Indian tribe" means "an Indian tribe, band, nation, or other organized group or community of Indians that is recognized as eligible for the special programs and services provided by the United States to Indians because of their status as Indians and is recognized as possessing powers of self-government."
  • §3(y) "Qualifying Indian tribe" means an Indian tribe that meets ALL of the following: "(i) The Indian tribe has entered into an agreement with the [CRA] under section 7(2)(b) that is in effect. (ii) The Indian tribe has entered into an agreement with the department of treasury that is in effect and that provides that revenue from a tax or fee imposed by the Indian tribe under subdivision (iii) is not money of this state and is retained and used only by the Indian tribe if the marihuana was grown and processed only on the Indian lands of the Indian tribe, and that states whether and how revenue from a tax or fee imposed by the Indian tribe under subdivision (iii) on marihuana that was not grown and processed only on the Indian lands of the Indian tribe is shared with this state. (iii) The Indian tribe imposes a tax or fee on each sale or transfer of marihuana from a tribal marihuana business on the Indian lands of the Indian tribe to a person other than a tribal marihuana business or marihuana establishment. The tax or fee must be based on the sales price of the marihuana and must be at a rate that is equal to or greater than the rate imposed under section 13."
  • §3(bb) "Tribal marihuana business" means a person that meets ALL of the following: "(i) The person engages in an activity for which a license is required under this act. (ii) The person is not a marihuana establishment. (iii) The person is wholly owned by a qualifying Indian tribe, an enrolled member of a qualifying Indian tribe, or a combination of a qualifying Indian tribe and enrolled members of a qualifying Indian tribe. (iv) The person is located in this state and in the Indian lands of the qualifying Indian tribe. (v) The person is subject to a tax or fee imposed by the qualifying Indian tribe under subdivision (y)(iii)."
  • §3(g) "Licensee" means "a person holding a state license." §3(z) "State license" means "a license issued by the [CRA] under this act."
  • §7(2)(b) (in substance, reflow): the CRA "may enter into an agreement with a federally recognized Indian tribe" (re-verify exact wording and subsection lettering on legislature.mi.gov — the GTB ordinance cites "MCL 333.27953(y)(ii)" for the compact authorisation, which appears to conflate §3(y)(ii) (Treasury agreement condition) with §7(2)(b) (CRA agreement power); the GTB citation is quoted as it appears in the GTB code and is NOT adopted as a correct MRTMA citation without legislature verification — Research Note R-05).

Consequences of the definitions (statutory reading, not compact quotation): 1. A "tribal marihuana business" is by definition NOT a marihuana establishment. A compact therefore does not convert it into one. 2. A "licensee" holds a STATE licence. A purely tribal licence is not a state licence under MRTMA, even if a compact grants market access. 3. "Qualifying" status requires BOTH a CRA agreement AND a Treasury agreement AND a tribal tax/fee ≥10% of sales price. A tribe with a CRA compact announcement but no located Treasury agreement or tax/fee law is not proven to be "qualifying" on the sources opened — for Bay Mills and Pokagon, the CRA agreement is evidenced (announcement/release); the Treasury agreement and tribal tax/fee law are [UNAVAILABLE] in the sources opened. Do NOT label either tribe "qualifying" without those two additional evidences, even though the compacts are described as granting market access. (The CRA release's "share a percentage of its Cannabis Excise Tax" for Pokagon suggests a tribal excise-tax mechanism exists, but the release does not cite a tribal tax law or a Treasury agreement, and the percentage is unstated — insufficient to prove §3(y)(ii)/(iii) satisfaction on this pass.) 4. The §3(y)(ii) Treasury-agreement condition distinguishes marihuana "grown and processed only on the Indian lands of the Indian tribe" (revenue retained solely by the tribe, not state money) from other marihuana (revenue sharing as the agreement states). That distinction is the statutory reason a compact's tax-share percentage matters, and why the Pokagon percentage being [UNAVAILABLE] is a material gap, not a detail.

10.3.3 Whether tribal retailers are CRA-licensed or tribally licensed — answer: both, by model

  • Tribally licensed only (Model A): Bay Mills (pre-compact; post-compact, tribal licence + compact market access, not a CRA licence on the evidence), Pokagon (pre-compact; post-compact, tribal licence + compact market access), GTB, KBIC, LVD — tribal licence (or tribal-enterprise authorisation) under tribal law; NOT a CRA licence on the evidence opened. For GTB/KBIC/LVD the tribal licence instrument itself was located only for GTB (ordinance + Commission); KBIC/LVD tribal licence instruments were NOT located (see profiles) — their "tribally licensed" character is inferred from tribal ownership + tribal-law operation as secondarily reported, and is flagged accordingly.
  • Both (Model B): Sault Licensed Marijuana Establishments and Saginaw Commercial Marijuana Licensees — CRA state licence (mandatory precondition) + tribal licence. LTBB trust-land Lume stores (2021 model) — CRA state licence + tribal land/waiver layer; tribal licence not evidenced.
  • State licence only (Model C): Hannahville-area store — state licence; tribal licence not evidenced and tribal ownership not evidenced.
  • No tribe was found operating a CRA-licensed-only store that is also described as "tribal" without a tribal-law layer, except Model C stores, which are not described as tribal operations in this dossier.
  • Practical consequence for a consumer/regulator: a store's licence type determines which regulator inspects it (CRA, tribal commission, or both), which tracking system it uses (Metrc, tribal system, or both post-compact), and which tax/fee applies (§13 excise vs tribal tax/fee vs member-benefit removal). A consumer cannot tell licence type from a storefront alone on the evidence in this dossier — no public tribal licence roster exists (Run 1 Part 5, confirmed §10.0).

10.3.4 Federal enforcement discretion — historical, NOT law, NOT a safe harbour (secondary summaries + tribal-code definition)

  • What the tribal codes themselves say: Sault Chapter 47 §47.103(3) defines "Federal Enforcement Priorities" as the eight priorities from the DOJ's 2013 Cole Memorandum as extended to Indian Country by the 2014 Wilkinson Memorandum: (1) preventing distribution to minors; (2) preventing revenue from going to criminal enterprises, gangs, and cartels; (3) preventing diversion from states where legal to other states; (4) preventing state-authorized activity from being used as cover for trafficking other illegal drugs or illegal activity; (5) preventing violence and use of firearms in cultivation/distribution; (6) preventing drugged driving and exacerbation of other adverse public health consequences; (7) preventing growing on public lands; (8) preventing possession/use on federal property. That tribal-code definition is the official tribal source for the list in this dossier; the DOJ originals were NOT directly opened in this pass.
  • Status (secondary summaries, marked secondary): the Cole Memorandum (Aug 2013) and Wilkinson Memorandum (Dec 2014, extending Cole to Indian Country with government-to-government consultation) were rescinded by Attorney General Sessions in Jan 2018 (Sessions Memorandum, 4 Jan 2018), per secondary legal summaries (e.g. Harris Sliwoski, National Law Review summaries, accessed 2026-10-28). The rescission itself is [VERIFY] against the DOJ originals if a legal citation is needed. Rescinded guidance creates no defence, no safe harbour, and no immunity. No post-2018 DOJ Indian-Country cannabis enforcement policy was located in this pass — [UNAVAILABLE]. Do NOT present the Wilkinson priorities as current federal law or as protection for any tribal operation.
  • Why the priorities still appear in tribal codes: tribes adopted them as their own regulatory priorities (Sault §47.108 makes conduct implicating them a revocation ground; Saginaw §10 has analogous conduct grounds). That is a tribal-law choice, not a federal-law requirement on current evidence.

10.3.5 The Schedule III "state-licensed" question — verdict: KEEP [VERIFY], NOT resolved, with reasoning

Question (Run 1 Part 1, reserved to Run 2): Does a tribal marihuana business, or a tribal medical programme, count as "state-licensed" for federal Schedule III purposes (91 FR 22714, eff. 28 Apr 2026, moving state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products to Schedule III, adult-use remaining Schedule I)?

Answer on the evidence in this pass: NOT resolved. Keep [VERIFY]. Do NOT describe any tribal product as Schedule III.

Reasoning, in order: 1. No tribal medical programme exists on the record. No tribal medical registry, tribal medical licence type, tribal medical dispensary, or tribal medical compact was located for any of the 12 tribes. Every identified tribal operation is adult-use (and/or hemp for LTBB). Schedule III attaches (on the task baseline) to state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products. There is therefore no tribal medical activity to which Schedule III could attach, even before the textual question is reached. If a tribe later creates a medical programme, the question would need to be revisited — but on the 28 Oct 2026 record, it is moot in practice and unresolved in law. 2. Textual question — "state" vs "tribal" licence. The task baseline and a secondary summary of 91 FR 22714 agree the order covers marijuana "subject to a state medical marijuana license" (secondary quotation, Ayar Law summary, accessed 2026-10-28: "Any form of marijuana other than in an FDA-approved drug product or marijuana subject to a state medical marijuana license remains a schedule I controlled substance"). The Federal Register text itself was NOT directly opened in this pass (Research Note R-01) — the secondary quotation is NOT adopted as a verbatim Federal Register quotation. No DEA, IRS, or Treasury guidance equating a tribal licence with a state licence for Schedule III / §280E purposes was located. A secondary South Dakota Attorney General summary (accessed 2026-10-28) mentions a DEA registration pathway at 21 CFR §1301.13(k)(1) for an existing manufacturer/distributor/dispensary "operating under a valid state license" — secondary, not opened, and it says "state license", not "tribal license". It does not resolve the tribal question. 3. MRTMA's own definitions cut against tribal = state. Under MRTMA §3(g)/(z)/(bb) (see §10.3.2), a "licensee" holds a state licence and a "tribal marihuana business" is by definition NOT a marihuana establishment. A compact grants market access; it does not deem a tribal licence a state licence. That is a Michigan-statute reading, not a federal Schedule III ruling — it is evidence about what "state licence" means in Michigan law, not proof of the federal meaning. Do NOT over-claim it as a federal answer. 4. Dual-licensed businesses are a different question. A business that ALSO holds a CRA state licence (Sault/Saginaw Model B) IS state-licensed in that capacity. If such a business held an MMFLA provisioning-centre (medical) licence and sold medical product under it, that medical product's Schedule III status would follow the state medical licence, not the tribal licence. No such tribal medical operation was identified, so this branch is hypothetical on this record and is NOT asserted as a current fact. 5. Hemp is not Schedule III by this route. Hemp (as defined federally, subject to the baseline's PL 119-37/119-103 changes) is excluded from the CSA definition of marihuana; the Schedule III question does not arise for hemp. LTBB's hemp plan is therefore irrelevant to Schedule III. 6. §280E consequence, stated only as the baseline states it: §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical, adult-use fully subject (task baseline). Because no tribal medical Schedule III product is identified, no tribal §280E benefit is claimed in this dossier. A tribal adult-use business remains fully subject to §280E on the baseline (adult-use = Schedule I), compact or not — the compact does not change federal scheduling. That last sentence is a baseline application, not a new IRS ruling, and is labelled as such.

Follow-up sources for resolution: DEA final order text (91 FR 22714) directly; DEA/IRS guidance on tribal licences (if any); any future tribal medical ordinance/compact. See Research Note R-01.

  • Public Law 280 status for Michigan tribes (not researched) — [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Whether tribal cannabis activity is subject to federal prosecution, forfeiture, or banking restrictions beyond the fixed baseline (no federal banking law; adult-use Schedule I) — no new federal-law conclusion is drawn.
  • Tribal tax rates, compact tax-share percentages, and wholesale-tax treatment for tribal transfers — [UNAVAILABLE] (see §10.2.2).

10.4 Interstate issues

10.4.1 Hemp shipments into/out of Michigan — federal protection, Michigan plan conflict, documentation

Federal transport protection (official text, from Federal Register/eCFR via search, accessed 2026-10-28): - 7 CFR §990.63 (USDA hemp regulations, final rule eff. 22 Mar 2021): "No State or Indian Tribe may prohibit the transportation or shipment of hemp or hemp products lawfully produced under a State or Tribal plan approved under subpart B of this part, under a license issued under subpart C of this part, or under 7 U.S.C. 5940 through the State or territory of the Indian Tribe, as applicable." — i.e. a state or tribe may not bar transit of lawfully produced hemp/hemp products through its territory. The protection covers ONLY lawfully produced hemp; material over the applicable THC threshold, or produced without a plan/licence, gets no shield from §990.63. (eCFR text to be re-verified on ecfr.gov if quoted in publication — the text above is from the Federal Register/eCFR extract returned in search, accessed 2026-10-28.) - Michigan overlay (Run 1 Part 4, preserved): Michigan has treated intoxicating THC as marihuana since 11 Oct 2021 (2021 PA 56, amending MRTMA/MMFLA definitions to capture THC from any source above the hemp threshold). A product that is hemp federally but intoxicating under Michigan's definition is marihuana in Michigan — §990.63 does not override Michigan's marihuana licensing for in-state sale; it bars prohibition of TRANSPORT through the state. The distinction (transit vs in-state sale) is stated as a reading of §990.63 + 2021 PA 56, not as a Michigan court ruling. - Federal hemp dates (fixed baseline, NOT re-researched): PL 119-37 §781 eff. 12 Nov 2026; PL 119-103 §2019 limits until 11 Dec 2026, after that full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg/container cap; USDA DEA-lab delay to 31 Dec 2026. No Michigan official response to PL 119-37/119-103 or to the post-11 Dec 2026 total-THC/0.4 mg cap was located in Part 10, consistent with Run 1. Michigan hemp products that exceed the post-11 Dec 2026 federal definition will be marihuana federally as well as in Michigan (2021 PA 56) — that is a baseline application, not a Michigan conformity statement. Do NOT state that Michigan has conformed (or refused to conform) to the federal dates.

USDA approved-plan list — Michigan and tribal plans (opened directly, updated 17 Feb 2026): - Source: https://www.ams.usda.gov/rules-regulations/hemp/state-and-tribal-plan-review — accessed 2026-10-28. - Michigan: "MI Approved Plan (pdf) *" — asterisk = "Approved under the final rule, effective March 22, 2021" (USDA list legend). The plan PDF is linked from the list (MI Approved Plan PDF). - Tribal plans on the same list (relevant to Michigan): "Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians Waganakising Odawak — Approved Plan (pdf)" (no asterisk — i.e. approved under the interim final rule period, per USDA legend, or as listed without the final-rule marker; the legend distinction is noted, not interpreted as a substantive difference). NO other Michigan tribe appears on the USDA tribal-plan list in the opened table. - Neighbouring states on the same list (for §10.4.3 context): Ohio — "USDA Hemp Producer License" (i.e. no state plan; producers licensed directly by USDA under subpart C); Wisconsin — "USDA Hemp Producer License" (same); Indiana — "IN Approved Plan (pdf)" (state plan). Illinois (not a Michigan border state for Part 10's Indiana/Ohio/Wisconsin focus, but listed for completeness in the opened table) — state plan (see Illinois Run 1 in standing memory; not re-verified here). - CONFLICT with Run 1 (see §10.0): Run 1 Parts 0/6 (secondary reporting of MDARD statements) say the MDARD industrial hemp programme ended at close of 2024, cultivation moved to USDA direct from 1 Jan 2025, and HB 5977 abolished the industrial hemp fund; growers fell 631 (2020) → 34 (2024). Run 1 Parts 4/5 AND this pass's direct opening of the USDA list (17 Feb 2026) show Michigan STILL listed with an approved plan. A secondary 2026 fee sheet (Michigan Hemp Industries Association / MDARD fee schedule extract, accessed 2026-10-28) also describes an MDARD grower registration cycle 1 Feb 2026–31 Jan 2027 ($1,250 grower registration) — consistent with a continuing MDARD programme, inconsistent with a clean 1 Jan 2025 termination. ADOPTED: USDA list status (plan still listed as of 17 Feb 2026). The Run 1 termination claim is NOT adopted as settled without (a) a USDA plan-withdrawal notice, or (b) an MDARD programme-end page, or (c) HB 5977's enacted text on legislature.mi.gov — none of which was located in this pass. Operational route for a Michigan hemp grower in 2026 (MDARD registration vs USDA licence) is therefore [VERIFY] — do NOT advise a grower which licence to obtain on this dossier. Follow-up: MDARD industrial hemp page + legislature.mi.gov HB 5977 (Research Note R-06). - LTBB hemp plan — approved, production [UNAVAILABLE]: USDA approved LTBB's plan 17 June 2020; the plan remains on the USDA list (17 Feb 2026). Whether hemp is currently grown/handled under it, and by whom, is not stated on the USDA list and was not located — [UNAVAILABLE]. A plan is not a production report.

Transport documentation — practice, NOT a Michigan statutory requirement found in Part 10: - Secondary practical advice (hemp-industry and USDA guidance summaries, accessed 2026-10-28) recommends carrying: producer/processor licence or plan authorisation, lot identification, laboratory test results / certificate of analysis (COA) showing THC compliance, and a bill of lading/manifest identifying the hemp lot and destination. No Michigan statute or MDARD rule stating a documentation checklist for hemp transport was located in this pass — the checklist is marked as secondary practical advice, NOT Michigan law. Do NOT cite it as a Michigan legal requirement. Law-enforcement verification practice (e.g. field THC testing, detention pending lab results) was not researched — [UNAVAILABLE]. - Interstate hemp shipments INTO Michigan: hemp lawfully produced under another state's approved plan, a tribal plan, or a USDA licence may be transported THROUGH Michigan under §990.63, and may be sold IN Michigan only if it complies with Michigan law (including 2021 PA 56's intoxicating-THC-as-marihuana rule and any applicable Michigan hemp/cannabis licensing for the intended sale). Hemp that is lawful in the origin state but intoxicating under Michigan's definition is NOT lawfully sellable in Michigan as hemp — that is a Run 1 Part 4 reading, preserved, not a new ruling. - Interstate hemp shipments OUT of Michigan: same §990.63 transit protection applies in destination states, subject to the destination state's own law for in-state sale and to the federal definition at the time of shipment (pre- vs post-11 Dec 2026 baseline dates). No Michigan export licence or export permit for hemp was located — [UNAVAILABLE] whether Michigan requires one for commercial hemp export (as distinct from transport).

10.4.2 Residents of Indiana, Ohio, and Wisconsin buying in Michigan — what Michigan law allows in-state

Michigan in-state purchase rules (Run 1 Part 1, preserved — not re-derived here): - MRTMA §5 allows any person 21 years of age or older to purchase adult-use marihuana in Michigan. There is NO residency requirement in §5. A resident of Indiana, Ohio, or Wisconsin who is 21+ may therefore lawfully BUY adult-use marihuana at a Michigan licensed retailer (or at a tribal retailer open to 21+ adults, see §10.1 profiles) while in Michigan, subject to the same rules as a Michigan resident. - Purchase limit per transaction: 2.5 oz of marihuana, of which not more than 15 g may be marihuana concentrate (R 420.506, Run 1 Part 1). Possession limits (Run 1 Part 1): 2.5 oz on the person, 10 oz + home-grown product at residence, 12 plants per premises (with the MRTMA §5 provisos). These are Michigan in-state limits; they do NOT authorise possession in the buyer's home state (see §10.4.3). - Age/ID: government photo ID proving 21+ is required at retail (tribal codes mirror this: Bay Mills retailer verification by government-issued photographic ID with date of birth; Sault revocation for sales to under-21s; Saginaw state-licence compliance). A tribal ID, state driver's licence, or passport that proves age 21+ satisfies the age check in principle; whether a particular retailer accepts a particular out-of-state ID format is a retailer policy matter, not stated in the statutes opened — [VERIFY] for any specific store. - Tribal stores: the same 21+ rule applies at tribal retailers open to the public (Bay Mills, GTB, Pokagon, LVD, KBIC, Sault/Saginaw dual stores, LTBB trust-land stores). No tribal store profiled here limits purchase to tribal members; Pokagon's member benefit is a price/tax benefit, not an eligibility gate (see §10.1.3 tribe 10). A non-resident (including a non-Michigan resident) 21+ may buy at those stores on the same terms as a Michigan resident, while in Michigan. - Medical access for visitors — DIFFERENT and contested (Run 1 Part 1, preserved): MMMA §3 defines a "visiting qualifying patient" and MMFLA §102(y) cross-references visiting patients, but Run 1 Part 1 states the retail-acceptance question is contested — i.e. whether a Michigan provisioning centre may/does accept an out-of-state medical card (or an out-of-state registry identification) for a medical sale is NOT settled on Run 1 evidence. Part 10 did NOT resolve it and does NOT claim that out-of-state medical cards are accepted at Michigan retail. Keep [VERIFY]. An out-of-state visitor who is 21+ may buy adult-use regardless of medical status; medical-specific purchase (higher limits, tax treatment, medical-only products) for a visitor is the contested part. - What Michigan law does NOT allow a visitor to do: Michigan law does not authorise a visitor to take purchased marihuana out of Michigan (see §10.4.3), does not authorise a visitor to use marihuana in Michigan in a place where MRTMA prohibits use (public places, vehicles — Run 1 Part 1), and does not authorise a person under 21 to buy even with a medical card from another state (medical age rules are MMMA/MMFLA matters, not MRTMA §5 adult-use rules, and were not re-researched here).

10.4.3 What can legally be taken across state lines — stated clearly, no evasion advice

Short answer: marihuana (adult-use, and medical except as narrowly provided by federal law for FDA-approved products) may NOT lawfully be taken across a state line from Michigan to Indiana, Ohio, or Wisconsin, or vice versa, on the authorities in this dossier. Hemp that is lawfully produced and remains hemp under the applicable federal definition may be transported across state lines under §990.63 (see §10.4.1); marihuana may not.

  • Michigan law: MRTMA authorises possession/use/sale WITHIN Michigan; it does not authorise export, interstate transport, or interstate commerce in marihuana, except for the compact/Metrc framework for tribal-state transactions WITHIN Michigan's regulated system (see §10.2.2) — and even that framework is intrastate (tribal lands ↔ state licensees within Michigan), not interstate commerce with another state. No Michigan statute authorising interstate marihuana commerce with Ohio, Indiana, Wisconsin, or any other state was located. Michigan has entered NO interstate marihuana commerce agreement (see §10.4.4).
  • Federal law: adult-use marihuana remains Schedule I (task baseline). Interstate transport of a Schedule I controlled substance is prohibited by federal law (21 U.S.C. §841/§844 framework; no interstate-commerce authorisation for adult-use marihuana was located). Schedule III for state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana (eff. 28 Apr 2026, baseline) does NOT authorise interstate commerce in medical marihuana — the rescheduling order, as summarised secondarily, moves scheduling, not commerce authorisation; no federal interstate medical-commerce authorisation was located. FDA-approved products (e.g. Epidiolex) are a separate, prescription-drug matter and are not "Michigan marihuana" for Part 10 purposes.
  • Destination-state notes — strictly limited, each flagged:
  • Ohio: adult-use is legal IN Ohio under SB 56 (signed 19 Dec 2025, eff. 20 Mar 2026, per Ohio Run 1 in standing memory — Ohio Run 1 is a separate dossier and its findings are carried here only as a cross-reference, not re-verified in Part 10). A secondary tourist guide (accessed 2026-10-28) claims that since 20 Mar 2026 it has been illegal in Ohio to possess cannabis not bought at an Ohio store — that claim is SECONDARY and [VERIFY] against Ohio law (ORC Chapter 3796 as amended by SB 56); it is NOT presented as settled Ohio law. Even if Ohio in-state possession is legal, that does NOT make Michigan→Ohio transport legal (see federal prohibition above).
  • Wisconsin: no state-licensed medical programme; marijuana remains Schedule I in Wisconsin under split scheduling (Wisconsin Run 1 in standing memory — carried as cross-reference, not re-verified here). Border application (e.g. whether Wisconsin's local decriminalisation ordinances in Madison/Milwaukee County/La Crosse County affect a Michigan purchase brought into Wisconsin) is [VERIFY] and is NOT stated as a defence to transport.
  • Indiana: destination-state law was NOT researched in Part 10 — [UNAVAILABLE]. Do NOT assert Indiana's possession law, penalties, or any Indiana medical programme in this dossier.
  • No evasion advice is given. Part 10 states the law as found; it does not advise how to conceal, repackage, or mislabel marihuana for transport, how to evade border or law-enforcement checks, or how to exploit a medical-card or hemp-labelling route to transport marihuana. Any such advice would be outside the task and is expressly not provided.
  • Hemp vs marihuana at a state line — the practical line: the line is the applicable THC definition at the time of transport (federal hemp definition pre- vs post-11 Dec 2026 baseline; Michigan's 2021 PA 56 intoxicating-THC rule for in-state sale). A product that tests as hemp in the origin state but exceeds the destination/federal threshold at transport is marihuana for transport purposes and gets no §990.63 shield. Laboratory testing, chain of custody, and enforcement practice at state lines were not researched — [UNAVAILABLE].

10.4.4 Canada (Ontario) border — CBSA/Canada law (official, opened directly) and US federal border rules (secondary, [VERIFY])

Canada — official CBSA source, opened directly (accessed 2026-10-28): - Source: Canada Border Services Agency, "Travellers: Cannabis at the border" — https://www.cbsa-asfc.gc.ca/travel-voyage/cannabis-eng.html — accessed 2026-10-28. Page last modified 26 Mar 2021 (as shown on the page; the page was not updated in the opened copy to reflect any post-2021 change — [VERIFY] if a post-2021 CBSA update is needed, but the prohibition stated has not been superseded in any source opened). - Verbatim operative statements from the CBSA page: - "Transporting cannabis across the border in any form – including any oils containing THC or cannabidiol (CBD) – without a permit or exemption authorized by Health Canada remains a serious criminal offence subject to arrest and prosecution, despite the legalization of cannabis in Canada." - "Don't bring it in. Don't take it out." - "Persons entering Canada with cannabis must declare it" (non-declaration can also lead to arrest/prosecution, per the page's "What happens if you don't declare" framing). - "Only Health Canada may issue permits or exemptions, under very limited circumstances, for medical, scientific, or industrial hemp purposes" (paraphrase of the page's permit/exemption section — re-verify exact wording on the CBSA page if quoted in publication). - Consequences stated plainly: the prohibition applies REGARDLESS of amount, regardless of whether the traveller holds a medical document, and regardless of whether the cannabis was lawfully purchased in Michigan (or in Ontario). Ontario's domestic legalisation (Cannabis Act, federal; Ontario Cannabis Control Act for in-Ontario sale/possession) does NOT authorise cross-border transport — the border rule is federal Canadian law, not Ontario domestic possession law. Ontario domestic possession limits (e.g. 30 g public possession under the federal Cannabis Act) were NOT separately researched and are NOT presented as the border rule — do NOT confuse the two. - Hemp/CBD at the Canada border: the CBSA page expressly includes "any oils containing THC or cannabidiol (CBD)" in the prohibition. Industrial hemp for a Health Canada permit/exemption is the only stated exception category, and it is "very limited". A Michigan hemp product (including CBD) taken across the Canada border without a Health Canada permit/exemption is therefore within the CBSA prohibition as stated — do NOT present Michigan hemp as border-exempt. - Michigan–Ontario crossings in scope: Detroit–Windsor (Ambassador Bridge / Detroit-Windsor Tunnel), Port Huron–Sarnia (Blue Water Bridge), Sault Ste. Marie (International Bridge, Chippewa County) — all are federal border crossings subject to the CBSA rule above (Canada-bound) and to US CBP rules (US-bound, below). No crossing-specific cannabis rule was located; the federal rule applies at all crossings.

United States — CBP position (secondary summaries only, [VERIFY] against a CBP source): - The CBP page itself was NOT directly opened in this pass. Secondary summaries (CBP news releases / legal summaries, accessed 2026-10-28) state CBP's position as: importation of cannabis into the United States remains illegal under federal law even if the cannabis is medical or state-authorised; CBP may seize cannabis at ports of entry, and importation may result in fines, arrest, and, for non-citizens, immigration consequences (inadmissibility / removal proceedings). Those consequences are SECONDARY summaries and are marked [VERIFY] against a CBP source (cbp.gov) before publication as CBP law. No CBP seizure statistics for Michigan crossings were located — [UNAVAILABLE]. - US-bound direction, stated on the baseline: adult-use marihuana is Schedule I federally; bringing it into the United States from Canada (even from Ontario, where it is legal domestically) is federal importation of a controlled substance. No Michigan law authorises it. The same "don't take it out / don't bring it in" logic applies in both directions, under different sovereigns' laws.

10.4.5 Interstate agreements Michigan has (or has not) entered, and cross-border market context

Interstate agreements — none for marihuana located: - No Michigan interstate marihuana commerce agreement (with Ohio, Indiana, Wisconsin, or any other state), no interstate compact for marihuana, and no Canada–Michigan cannabis agreement was located in this pass. The ONLY interstate-style agreements in Part 10 are the tribal-state agreements in §10.2.1 (Bay Mills, Pokagon), which are intrastate (tribe ↔ Michigan) government-to-government agreements, not interstate commerce agreements. - No Michigan agreement to recognise another state's cannabis licences, to allow cross-state delivery, or to share Metrc data with another state was located. Michigan's Metrc system is a Michigan system (plus tribal compact integration, see §10.2.2); no interstate Metrc sharing agreement was located. - Hemp interstate framework: the federal §990.63 transit protection (see §10.4.1) is a federal rule, not a Michigan interstate agreement. Michigan's USDA-approved plan (see §10.4.1) and LTBB's tribal plan are federal-plan instruments, not interstate agreements. - No ranked cluster/concentration list is created in Part 10, per task. Cross-border market context below is limited to officially sourced or clearly marked secondary facts, without a ranking.

Cross-border market context — officially sourced or clearly marked secondary (Run 1 Part 3, preserved): - Niles Charter Township, Berrien County (Indiana border corridor): Nov 2024 referendum allowed marihuana commerce in the township; the township board then allowed unlimited retailers on South 11th Street (the Indiana border corridor); on 4 Nov 2025 voters approved (nearly 6 in 10, secondary reporting) a ballot measure prohibiting any cannabis stores in the township, reversing the allowance. The City of Niles is a DIFFERENT municipality from Niles Charter Township — do NOT merge them. Source: Run 1 Part 3 (secondary reporting); no new Niles fact is asserted in Part 10. - Menominee City, Menominee County (Wisconsin border): on 4 Nov 2025 voters approved a cap of 9 marihuana retailers (unofficial 1,429 for, 402 against, ~78%, secondary reporting); 8 shops already existed at the time. On 21 Sep 2026, Menominee County Circuit Judge Mary Barglind rejected a challenge to the FORMAT of the petition to raise the cap 9 → 13 on the 3 Nov 2026 ballot — the vote could proceed; the merits of the cap increase were NOT decided by that ruling. The 3 Nov 2026 vote post-dates the 28 Oct 2026 dossier date and its outcome is NOT reported as decided in this dossier. Source: Run 1 Part 3 (secondary reporting); no new Menominee fact is asserted in Part 10. - Berrien County / border-county concentration (secondary, NOT adopted as official): Run 1 Part 3 §3.6 cites a secondary Indiana Lawyer calculation that Berrien County had 27 shops and that border counties had "two or three times" the dispensaries per capita of interior counties. That is a secondary calculation, NOT an official source, and is NOT adopted as an official concentration finding in Part 10. No per-capita, per-county, or border-vs-interior ranking is created here. - Tribal stores as border-market participants (secondary context, not a ranking): Pokagon's Rolling Embers (New Buffalo, Berrien County, near the Indiana border and I-94) and LTBB's Mackinaw City store (Cheboygan County, near the Mackinac Bridge corridor) are tribal/trust-land stores in border/corridor locations, but Part 10 does NOT rank them against state-licensed border stores, does NOT estimate their market share, and does NOT attribute cross-border customer flows to them on the evidence opened. Any such flow claim would require customer-origin data, which was not located — [UNAVAILABLE].

Federal baseline — fixed, not re-researched

State-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); all adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. IRS 280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to 280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered lab testing for hemp is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. Anything in Parts 11–12 contradicting this baseline is flagged, not adopted.

Run 1 locked figures — adopted unchanged in Parts 11–12

Adult-use possession 2.5 oz (≤15 g concentrate) in public, 10 oz at residence plus home-grown product in locked storage, 12 plants per premises, gifting up to 2.5 oz without remuneration; public consumption not authorised. Purchase limits: adult-use 2.5 oz/transaction; medical 2.5 oz/day, 10 oz/30 days (Part 11 notes the rule text wording "per month" in R. 420.506(2) — wording only, see Combined Notes). Equivalencies 16 oz solid / 36 fl oz liquid = 1 oz (retained as a Run 1 locked figure; Part 11 could not locate the ratios in the R. 420.506 text read — rule home [VERIFY]). Edible caps: adult-use 10 mg/serving, 200 mg/container; medical 50 mg/serving, 200 mg/container (CRA bulletin 24 April 2025). Caregiver: 5 patients / 12 plants each / 60 max (the "72" figure is rejected in both runs). Plant limits: medical 500/1,000/1,500; adult-use 100/500/2,000; microbusiness 150; Class A microbusiness 300; excess grower in 2,000-plant increments. Fees: R. 420.7 — $3,000 prequalification plus Table 1 fees (retailer $15,000, Class C $24,000, microbusiness $8,300, Class A microbusiness $18,600, designated consumption $1,000, event organiser $1,000, temporary event per R. 420.26). Tax stack: 24% wholesale tax (2025 PA 23, eff. 1 Jan 2026) / 10% MRTMA excise / 6% sales tax on the excise-inclusive price. CRA draft rules set 2023-25 LR (second hearing 23 July 2026) are NOT final law and are never presented as current law below.
