PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

Dossier date / date accessed for every fact below: 28 October 2026. Scope: Part 11 ONLY (operations rules). Parts 0–10 and 12 are not covered here; the parent agent compiles the dossier. No HTML was built, per task.

Spelling note: Michigan statutes and rules spell the plant "marihuana." This report preserves "marihuana" in statute/rule names, citations and verbatim quotations, and uses "marijuana" only in plain-English discussion or where a secondary source uses it.

Federal baseline — fixed, NOT re-researched: state-licensed MEDICAL marijuana and FDA-approved products to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I; §280E generally lifted for Schedule III medical, adult-use fully subject; hemp PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 November 2026, PL 119-103 §2019 limits until 11 December 2026, after that the full total-THC definition and 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply; USDA DEA-lab testing delay to 31 December 2026; medical rider through 11 December 2026; no federal banking law. Nothing found in Part 11 contradicts that baseline; operations rules below are state law and do not change the federal schedule/§280E split. A dual-licensed business must still split medical vs adult-use inventory, records and Metrc activity, because the rules treat the two programmes as separate licences even at a co-located site.

Sourcing method and honesty rule used here. The operative rule text is Mich. Admin. Code R. 420.1–R. 420.1004. The rule set as reproduced in this run carries history lines "2020 AACS; 2022 AACS" (2022 MR 5, effective 7 March 2022) for most rules cited, and Justia's mirror states "Current through Volume 25-10, June 15, 2025." Key rules were cross-checked between the 420tax reflowed compilation of R. 420 (a secondary reflow, which itself warns "Cross-check against the authoritative source for legal precision"), Cornell LII, and Justia, and, where a CRA enforcement document quotes a rule, that quotation. Where the reflow and Cornell/Justia agree, the rule is treated as confirmed; where only the reflow was read, that is stated. The CRA draft rule set 2023-25 LR (second public hearing 23 July 2026, Lansing, Ingham County) is NOT final law and is never quoted below as operative. Where a draft provision would move or renumber a current rule (e.g. draft R. 420.508 would become an advertising rule and trade-sample provisions would move to draft R. 420.408), that is noted only to prevent a reader from mistaking a draft renumbering for current law. Before publication the parent should re-pull the current Administrative Code PDF from the Michigan Office of Administrative Hearings and Rules (MOAHR) / ars.apps.lara.state.mi.us and confirm no rule was amended between 15 June 2025 and 28 October 2026.

How to read rule citations. The R. 420 set is organised in separately numbered "Parts" that reuse rule numbers: e.g. adult-use grower rules (R. 420.102), medical grower rules (R. 420.108), general-operations rules (R. 420.201 et seq.), sampling/testing rules (R. 420.301 et seq.), infused-product rules (R. 420.401 et seq.), sales-location rules (R. 420.501 et seq.), employee rules (R. 420.601 et seq.), hearing rules (R. 420.701 et seq.) and social-equity rules (R. 420.801 et seq.). A bare "R. 420.102(7)" without saying adult-use vs medical is therefore ambiguous — see the correction in §2.8 / Research Notes C-01. Every citation below names the programme where the rule is programme-specific.

County rule: county is given for every Michigan place named below.

11.1 Testing: required tests, sampling, failed tests and remediation, recalls and health advisories, safety compliance facilities

11.1.1 The gate: no sale before passing tests in Metrc

  • Harvest batches. R. 420.303(5): "Before the cultivator transfers or sells the marihuana product to a marihuana sales location, a sample of the harvest batch must be tested for all required safety tests by a licensed laboratory as provided in R 420.304 and R 420.305. All test results must indicate passed in the statewide monitoring system before the marihuana is packaged for sale." A package may not contain more than one harvest batch, and harvest batches may not be combined. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.303) and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-303 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Final-form products. R. 420.303a(2): a producer of a product in final form must have the sample tested under R. 420.304/R. 420.305, must quarantine product with test results pending, and "shall not transfer or sell a marihuana product to a marihuana sales location until after test results entered into the statewide monitoring system indicate a passed result for all required safety tests." The exception in the same subrule is a transfer/sale "in accordance with the remediation protocol provided by the agency and these rules" (see §11.1.4). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-303a — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Point-of-sale verification. R. 420.505(1)(e)–(f): before sale a sales location must verify the product "has been tested in accordance with R 420.305" and is labelled/packaged under R. 420.504. R. 420.505(1)(a) adds verification that the product has not been placed on administrative hold, recalled, or ordered destroyed. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.505) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • What "passed" means. R. 420.305(10): "The agency shall publish a list of action limits for the required safety tests in subrule (3) of this rule, except for potency. A marihuana sample with a value that exceeds the published action limit is a failed sample. A marihuana sample that is at or below the action limit is a passing sample." For chemical residue and target analytes, R. 420.305(11): the agency publishes quantification levels (LOQs); "Any result that exceeds the action limit is a failed sample." Potency is reported, not pass/failed against an action limit, except through the infused-product maximum-THC rules (R. 420.404 / CRA bulletin 24 April 2025 — see Run 1 §1.3.5, locked figures in §11.1.7 below). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.305) and https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-sampling-and-testing/section-r-420-305/ (current through Vol. 25-10, 15 June 2025) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Results deadline. R. 420.304(2)(j) and R. 420.305(12)–(13): the laboratory must enter test results into the statewide monitoring system (Metrc) within 3 business days of test completion; passed results must be in Metrc for a batch to be released for processing, packaging and labelling for transfer or sale. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-304 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Laboratory prohibitions. R. 420.305(16): a laboratory shall not (a) desiccate samples, (b) pre-test samples, (c) select the best or most desirable material from a batch for testing ("All sample increments must have the same chances of being selected"), or (d) manipulate samples in any way that would alter sample integrity or homogeneity. "Pre-test" is defined in R. 420.301(1)(y) as performing full compliance testing without reporting results to the agency and reporting only subsequent results. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.301, R. 420.305) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Random compliance checks. R. 420.305(17) and R. 420.206(15): the agency or its authorised agents may collect a random sample from a business (or designate another laboratory to collect it) and test it for compliance. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.2 Required tests — R. 420.305(3)(a)–(i)

A laboratory "shall conduct the required safety tests specified in subdivisions (a) to (i)" on product that is part of the harvest batch or production batch as specified in R. 420.303, except as provided in R. 420.305(4) (GMP/GACP-GMP certification allowances, below). The agency "may publish a guide indicating which of the following safety tests are required based on product type when the marihuana product has changed form." The nine tests, verbatim in substance:

Subrule Test Notes in the rule
(a) Potency analysis Total THC (including all reportable THC isomers; Total THC = ΣTHC + 0.877 × ΣTHC-A, R. 420.305(9)(c)), THC-A, total CBD (CBD + 0.877 × CBD-A), CBD-A, plus additional cannabinoids with agency approval. Flower/concentrates reported in percentages; infused products in mg total THC/CBD per gram. Sample preparation must not adulterate or manipulate total potency (e.g. by adding back trichomes removed during grinding/homogenisation); kief must not be reintroduced to a flower potency sample unless fully validated to AOAC Appendix K. No moisture-content corrective factor.
(b) Inspection for foreign matter Including powdery mildew, organic and inorganic material.
(c) Microbial screening Including an optimised incubation period for all non-molecular automated-systems methods and all plating-based methods used to report quantitative total yeast and mold results.
(d) Chemical residue testing For the list of banned chemical residues and the required LOQs published by the agency (see §11.6.2).
(e) Heavy metals testing As required in the rule (agency-published action limits; see §11.1.5 for recall examples naming cadmium, arsenic, total chromium).
(f) Residual solvents For production batches of marihuana-infused products and edible marihuana products; the agency publishes the required residual solvents and action limits. R. 420.305(7) separately requires residual-solvent testing on batches of concentrates and infused products.
(g) Water activity Required test; action limit published by the agency.
(h) Mycotoxin screening "If requested by the agency." R. 420.305(20): a sample exceeding the published acceptable level is failed; below it is passing.
(i) Target analytes "If requested by the agency. The agency shall publish a list of required target analytes to be tested for and their LOQs." Target analyte is defined (R. 420.301(1)(ee)) as "a non-marihuana inactive ingredient designated for analysis."

Sources: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.305) and https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-sampling-and-testing/section-r-420-305/ — accessed 2026-10-28.

GMP/GACP-GMP allowances (R. 420.305(4)–(5)) — not an exemption from testing. A producer certified to GMP by an ISO 17065-accredited body (ANSI-accredited or equivalent standard) and a cultivator certified to GACP-GMP by an ISO 17065-accredited body (WHO / American Herbal Products Association or equivalent) "may" be enabled "certain allowances with testing," which "The agency will publish." The allowances themselves were not located as a published CRA list in this run — [VERIFY] against CRA guidance before any operator relies on a reduced-testing claim. Do not present GMP certification as a waiver of compliance testing.

Terpenes (optional). R. 420.305(18): a laboratory may perform terpene analysis by an agency-approved method, accredited on the same frequency as required safety tests. Terpene analysis is not listed in R. 420.305(3)(a)–(i) and is not a required safety test.

Pathogen reporting. R. 420.305(21): marihuana-infused products found to contain Salmonella spp. or Shiga toxin producing E. coli (STEC) "must be reported to the agency, in a separate written communication, at the same time as the safety compliance test results are entered into the statewide monitoring system."

11.1.3 Sampling rules — R. 420.303, R. 420.304

  • Immature plant batches. R. 420.303(1): each immature plant batch gets a single batch name recorded in Metrc and consists of no more than 100 immature plants. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-303 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Individual plant tags. R. 420.303(2)–(3): a cultivator must tag each individual plant greater than 8 inches in height from the growing/cultivating medium or more than 8 inches in width with an individual plant tag recorded in Metrc, keep the tag identified with the plant throughout the growing cycle, and separate plants as they go through different growth stages. The tag is destroyed before packaging; once harvested, the plant is part of a harvest batch. Immature plant is defined (R. 420.301(1)(k), R. 420.1) as a nonflowering plant no taller than 8 inches and no wider than 8 inches. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Harvest-batch quarantine. R. 420.303(4) and R. 420.304(2)(k): a harvest batch must be separated by product type, quarantined from all other marihuana/marihuana products while test results are pending, kept easily distinguishable until broken down into packages, and may not be packaged, transferred, or sold until passing test results are entered into Metrc. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Who collects the sample. R. 420.304(2)(a): the laboratory must physically collect the sample from the other business; that business "shall not interfere or prevent" compliance. Samples must be identified in Metrc and placed in secured, sealed containers bearing required labelling; route plan and manifest entered in Metrc with a copy carried in the vehicle and presented to law enforcement on request; transported in sealed containers not accessible in transit; laboratory sample-transport vehicle must bear no marihuana markings. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-304 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Sample sizes. R. 420.304(2)(b)–(e):
  • Harvest batch: sample size sufficient to complete all required analyses and not less than 0.5% of the weight of the harvest batch (except as otherwise required by the agency); maximum harvest batch is 50 pounds; at least 50% of the sample taken must be homogenised for testing; the agency may publish sample sizes for other products.
  • Concentrates: 0.25 g increments — 12 increments for a 1–2 lb production batch; 15 for 2–3 lb; 18 for 3–4 lb; 23 for 4–10 lb; 29 for over 10 lb.
  • Infused products (units): 2 units for up to 100 units; 4 for 101–500; 6 for 501–1,000; 8 for 1,001–5,000; 10 for 5,001–10,000; 12 for over 10,001 units.
  • The laboratory must develop a statistically valid sampling method approved by the agency to collect a representative sample from each batch and must have access to the entire batch for sampling (R. 420.304(2)(f)).
  • Observation and chain of custody. R. 420.304(2)(g)–(j): an employee of the business must be physically present to observe collection and ensure increments are taken from throughout the batch, but must neither assist the laboratory employee nor touch the product or sampling equipment while sampling is underway. After selection, both employees sign and date the chain-of-custody form attesting to product name, weight, correct Metrc identification, and (for a retest) that the laboratory confirms it is not accepting a sample prohibited from being retested. The business enters the collected test sample in Metrc including date/time collected and transferred. The agency may publish chain-of-custody guidance that must be followed (R. 420.304(2)(n)).
  • Sample may not be diverted. R. 420.304(2)(l): product collected for testing may not be transferred or sold to any other business other than the licensee it was collected from, except a laboratory engaging another laboratory on a subcontracted basis. Additional sample material may be collected from the same licensee to complete required tests (R. 420.304(2)(m)).
  • Immature-plant-batch exception. R. 420.503a: immature plant batches transferred from an agency-approved cultivator to a sales location do not require a secure transporter and are not required to undergo R. 420.304/R. 420.305 testing. This is the only testing exception of that breadth in the rules read; it applies to immature plants only, not to flower, concentrates or infused products. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.503a) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Laboratory accreditation and methods. R. 420.305(1)–(2): a laboratory must become accredited for all required safety tests in at least one matrix to ISO/IEC 17025:2017 by an ILAC-recognised accreditation body or an agency-approved entity within 1 year after the laboratory licence is issued, and agree to have inspections, reports and scope documents sent to the agency. Methods must be based on published peer-reviewed methods, validated for cannabis testing by an independent third party, and internally verified under AOAC Official Methods of Analysis Appendix J or K, with guidance from published cannabis standard method performance requirements where available. The agency may monitor methodologies on an ongoing basis. Annual proficiency testing is required (R. 420.305(14)): proficiency samples from an ISO 17043-accredited vendor, externally graded, results submitted directly to the agency by the vendor; failed proficiency tests require corrective-action documentation and repetition until an acceptable result is obtained for all analytes. Validations must be submitted for agency approval with an acceptable proficiency test (R. 420.305a). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.305, R. 420.305a) and https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-305a — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Medical SCF accreditation variant. R. 420.112(2)–(3) (medical): a safety compliance facility must be accredited by an agency-approved entity by 1 year after licence issue, or have previously provided drug-testing services to the state or its court system and be a vendor in good standing; the agency may grant a variance where necessary to protect public health, safety or welfare. An unaccredited facility may not perform safety-compliance or R&D testing for a licensed facility and may not charge for testing until compliance is demonstrated. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.112) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Sample retention. R. 420.305(8): a laboratory must maintain marihuana samples for at least 30 calendar days after test completion and destroy resulting waste in accordance with R. 420.209 as reproduced in the compilation — note: the compilation's cross-reference reads "R 420.209" but the waste rule is R. 420.211; treat the "209" as a compilation/printing cross-reference error and apply R. 420.211 for destruction (see §11.5). [VERIFY] the cross-reference against the official Administrative Code PDF.
  • Research and development testing. R. 420.307: R&D testing is optional testing before final compliance testing; except for R. 420.304(2)(b) (the 0.5% harvest-batch sample-size rule), the laboratory must comply with the rules; no punitive action may be taken for R&D testing when permitted; all R&D testing must be entered in Metrc; R&D testing performed after compliance testing shall not replace safety-compliance test results. The agency may publish R&D guidance that must be followed. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.307) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.4 Failed tests, retesting and remediation — R. 420.305(6), R. 420.306

  • Default consequence of failure. R. 420.305(6), verbatim in substance: "Except as otherwise provided in R 420.306, if a sample collected pursuant to R 420.304 or provided to a laboratory pursuant to these rules does not pass the required safety tests, the marihuana business that provided the sample shall destroy the entire batch from which the sample was taken and document the destruction of the sample using the statewide monitoring system pursuant to the acts and these rules within 90 calendar days." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.305) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Retest path. R. 420.306(1)–(2): "A laboratory may test marihuana product that has failed initial safety testing." "A failed marihuana product must pass 2 separate tests with new samples consecutively to be eligible to proceed to sale or transfer." The business that provided the sample bears all retest costs (R. 420.306(5)). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.306) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Remediation — narrow, protocol-dependent. R. 420.306(3)–(4): products that failed testing for Aspergillus may be remediated after subsequent testing for mycotoxins under R. 420.305(3)(h); "The agency may publish a remediation protocol including, but not limited to, the sale or transfer of marihuana product after a failed safety test as provided in these rules." No general right to remediate any failed test appears in R. 420.306 itself. Secondary guidance routinely summarised in compliance literature (CRA Compliance Best Practice Guide, July 2025, and CRA Disciplinary Guidelines, July 2025, as summarised in secondary sources) states remediation is permitted in limited cases — most often microbial or residual-solvent failures — and not for heavy-metals or pesticide failures, that retesting must occur at the original safety compliance facility only with CRA authorisation, that unauthorised retesting may draw discipline, and that the entire compliance panel must be retested. Those secondary propositions were not verified against the CRA guides themselves in this run and are marked [VERIFY] here; the rule text alone supports only: destroy within 90 days, unless the R. 420.306 retest/remediation route is followed (two consecutive passing tests on new samples; Aspergillus remediation after mycotoxin testing; agency-published remediation protocol). Do not publish a blanket "microbial failures are remediable, metals/pesticides are not" rule as rule text — it is guidance-level at best in the sources read. Source for the guide summaries: https://weedbizwiz.substack.com/p/what-to-do-when-a-product-fails-safety (secondary summary of CRA July 2025 guides) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA guides].
  • Destruction clock for failed batches vs other destruction. The 90-day clock in R. 420.305(6) (destroy the entire failed batch and document in Metrc within 90 calendar days) sits alongside the general destruction clock in R. 420.502(6) (destroy all product required to be destroyed for any reason within 90 calendar days of when the business became aware it must be destroyed) and R. 420.214c(2)(b) for returned product (see §11.1.5). They are consistent (90 days), but they run from different triggers — failed-test documentation vs awareness — so a business should diary the earliest applicable date.
  • Falsification. R. 420.305(15): "The agency shall take immediate disciplinary action against any laboratory that falsifies records or does not comply with the provisions of this rule, including sanctions or fines, or both." The Viridis Laboratories / Viridis North settlement (August 2025) is the largest recent illustration: CRA settlement revoking the Lansing, Ingham County licences, requiring closure of the Bay City, Bay County facility, and permanently excluding three majority owners, after admitted violations across six complaints for failure to follow approved testing procedures producing inaccurate/unreliable results. Source: https://www.newswire.com/news/doj-called-state-marijuana-systems-robust-the-states-own-records-say-otherwise (secondary report of the CRA settlement, August 2025) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA settlement/final order before quoting its terms as CRA-confirmed].

11.1.5 Recalls, administrative holds and health advisories

  • Agency powers. R. 420.502(2): "The agency may place an administrative hold on marihuana products, recall marihuana products, issue safety warnings, and require a marihuana business to provide informational material or notifications to a marihuana customer at the point of sale." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.502) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Sale ban. R. 420.502(3): "A marihuana business shall not sell or transfer a marihuana product that has been placed on administrative hold, recalled, or ordered or otherwise required to be destroyed." R. 420.502(5) requires pre-sale Metrc verification that the product has not been held, recalled or ordered destroyed. R. 420.502(4): a business shall not sell/transfer product after its printed expiration date; expired product must be destroyed except as provided in R. 420.214c(2)(f) (retailer return of expired product to its processor for destruction). Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Investigation holds. R. 420.16(4): "The agency may place an administrative hold on a marihuana product and order that no sales or transfers occur during an investigation for an alleged violation or violation of the acts or these rules." Products on administrative hold require agency approval before destruction (CRA Compliance Best Practice Guide, July 2025, as reproduced in secondary compilation — [VERIFY] against the guide; the rule text itself does not state the hold-removal procedure). Source for the guide point: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/authoritative-documents/CRA_Compliance-Best-Practices-(2025-07).pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Recall duties for infused products. R. 420.403(4): marihuana-infused products that are part of a product recall must be (a) immediately pulled from production by the producer, (b) immediately removed from the sales area of a sales location, and (c) not sold or transferred. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.403) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Returns. R. 420.214c: a sales location may accept return of product reported to have caused an adverse reaction or determined to be defective; it must have a written return policy providing at minimum that (a) returned product is tracked in Metrc as waste under R. 420.211, (b) it is destroyed under R. 420.211 within 90 calendar days of when the business became aware it must be destroyed, (c) it cannot be resold, repackaged or otherwise transferred to a customer or another business, (d) it is prohibited from being returned by way of a delivery driver, and (f) a retailer may instead return expired product to the processor who produced it for destruction. Non-compliance may draw discipline. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.214c) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Adverse reactions. Secondary CRA recall-bulletin practice (see Run 1 §5.6) requires licensees that become aware of adverse reactions to notify the CRA and enter the information in Metrc within one business day, and recall bulletins direct consumers to return product to the retailer for disposal and to report reactions to their healthcare provider and to the CRA. The one-business-day Metrc entry proposition is secondary-sourced in this run — [VERIFY] against the current CRA bulletin template / adverse-reaction form instructions. No CRA bulletin PDF was opened in this run, so no batch/tag numbers are quoted here.
  • Recent recall examples (secondary-reported, for scale and failure modes only — bulletin PDFs not opened, do not quote tag numbers from these summaries):
  • Flight Live Resin Disposable vape cartridges (processor Sky Labs, Mount Morris, Genesee County; batches Grease Monkey / Space Ether / Bubblegum; July 2023 CRA recall): possible banned chemical residue exceeding action limits; residues named in reporting as bifenthrin, bifenazate, permethrins, myclobutanil and paclobutrazol; over 13,000 cartridges sold, about 2,200 still for sale at 59 dispensaries at recall. Source: https://www.cannabisequipmentnews.com/news/news/22868433/michigan-recalls-vape-cartridges-over-banned-chemical-residue — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Fawn River Cultivation Hash Melts Green Crack 1G Live Rosin Dab (licence AU-P-000460; produced 16 June 2026; CRA public health and safety advisory 18 September 2026): 786 units recalled after testing indicated a banned chemical (substance not named in the advisory as reported). Source: https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/09/michigan-recalls-786-marijuana-concentrates-after-testing-finds-banned-chemical/ (via Run 1 §5.6) and https://www.cannabisnews.org/united-states-cannabis-news/michigan-recalls-786-hash-melts-concentrates-after-testing-finds-banned-chemical/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Viridis-related recall bulletins (2021–2022, Marijuana Regulatory Agency era): retailers that sold recalled product had to display the recall notice on the sales floor, visible to all customers, for 30 days; licensees with remaining recalled inventory could destroy with proof to the agency, have the product retested for the microbials panel, or send it back to the source licensee for destruction/retesting as a larger batch, creating new Metrc packages with new IDs before transfer/testing. Source: https://kirkhuthlaw.com/marijuana-regulatory-agency-issues-notice-of-product-recall-as-retailers-work-to-navigate-next-steps/ (secondary report of MRA guidance) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the bulletin itself; the 30-day display instruction is bulletin-specific guidance, not a rule-text requirement located in R. 420].
  • Where recalls are published — route, not a list. Run 1 §5.6 found no consolidated recall dataset and no directly opened CRA bulletins hub URL in that run; the same finding stands in this run. The route is: michigan.gov/cra bulletins (searchable by Metrc tag number per secondary reporting) plus individual bulletin PDFs. No CRA bulletins hub URL is invented here — [VERIFY] the exact hub URL on michigan.gov/cra before publication.

11.1.6 Safety compliance facilities — no public roster; counts and verification route

  • Finding, stated plainly as the task requires: No official CRA-published roster/list of licensed safety compliance facilities was retrievable as a bulk list in this run, and no individual holders are listed here beyond what official sources publish in aggregate counts. A secondary directory states the same in terms: "Although Michigan does not provide a list of licensed safety compliance facilities, there are over 20 cannabis testing labs with active licenses in the state. The Cannabis Regulatory Agency provides a tool on its website for users to verify licensed marijuana businesses in the state." Source: https://michigancannabis.org/testing-lab — accessed 2026-10-28 (secondary; the "over 20" figure is not adopted as a count — see below).
  • Verification route (from Run 1 §5.3–§5.4, still the route): (1) CRA weekly licensing reports (PDF, weekly; e.g. week of 26 October–1 November 2025 at https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Agency-Reports/Licensing-Reports/AU-Licensing-Reports/2025/October/Licensing-Report-10262025---11012025.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 in Run 1; a single week's report is NOT a roster, reconstructing one requires collecting every weekly PDF and de-duplicating); (2) LARA MiCLEAR license verification search (record-by-record by name or licence number; general entry www.michigan.gov/miclear — [VERIFY] the exact CRA verification URL on michigan.gov/cra, per Run 1); (3) CRA monthly statistical reports for aggregate counts by type. No CSV/XLSX roster download was found in either run.
  • Aggregate counts (licences, not distinct laboratories — a co-located medical + adult-use pair counts as two licences):
  • 30 September 2025, directly opened CRA September 2025 monthly report (Run 1 §5.2): medical safety compliance facilities 17; adult-use safety compliance facilities 20.
  • December 2025, secondary-routed via CannBus citing CRA: medical 17 (same as September). Source: https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mi_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA December 2025 PDF].
  • August 2026, secondary-routed via CannBus citing CRA via Marijuana Herald: adult-use 19. Source: same CannBus page — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA August 2026 PDF].
  • Conflicting secondary counts — rejected, not adopted: (a) "over 20 cannabis testing labs" (MichiganCannabis.org, undated) is consistent in direction with 17 + 20 licences but is not a count and does not distinguish licences from distinct labs; (b) "Currently, Michigan has six accredited independent marijuana safety compliance facilities" operating under a "Michigan Coalition of Independent Cannabis Testing Laboratories" (https://michigancannabis.org/licensing/testing — accessed 2026-10-28) is stale and rejected as a current count — it conflicts with the CRA-derived 17/20 licence counts and appears to describe a coalition subset or an older snapshot, not all licensed facilities. Do not publish "six labs" as the Michigan total. (c) Individual lab marketing claims (e.g. named Ann Arbor, Washtenaw County, or Warren, Macomb County, labs in directories) are not an official roster and are not reproduced here.
  • Independence (why the count stays small). Medical: R. 420.112(4) — "To be eligible for a safety compliance facility license, the applicant, and each investor with any interest in the safety compliance facility must not have an interest in a grower, secure transporter, processor, or provisioning center." Mirror restrictions: medical grower R. 420.108(7), processor R. 420.109(3), provisioning centre R. 420.111(3) and secure transporter R. 420.110(2) (which also bars the transporter investor from being a registered patient/caregiver). Adult-use SCF independence clause location: not verified in the adult-use Part 1 rules text read in this run — [VERIFY] before stating an adult-use equivalent; do not cite medical R. 420.112(4) for an adult-use licence. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.108–R. 420.112) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Laboratory manager. R. 420.112(5)(g) (medical) and the adult-use SCF rule as reproduced in Run 1: the facility must retain and employ at least one laboratory manager with a relevant advanced degree in a medical or laboratory science, responsible for ensuring tests follow R. 420.305, results are accurate and valid, overseeing day-to-day operations, and validating Metrc reporting. Notice of a laboratory manager's departure: written notice to the agency within 7 days, interim manager designated within 7 days, permanent manager hired within 60 calendar days unless a written waiver (plus up to 60 more days with a detailed oversight plan) is granted — R. 420.206(8). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.206, R. 420.112) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Hemp testing by SCFs. R. 420.112(6): "A safety compliance facility is not prohibited from taking or receiving industrial hemp for testing purposes and testing the industrial hemp pursuant to the industrial hemp research and development act." Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.1.7 Potency caps carried forward (locked Run 1 figures — not re-derived here)

Adult-use infused edibles 10 mg THC/serving, 200 mg/container; medical infused edibles 50 mg/serving, 200 mg/container; beverages 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/container for both programmes — per the CRA technical bulletin under R. 420.404 dated 24 April 2025, as reproduced in secondary sources in Run 1 §1.3.5. The bulletin PDF itself was not opened in Run 1 or in this run; the figures are carried forward as locked Run 1 figures and remain [VERIFY] against the CRA bulletin PDF. The competing secondary figure of 500 mg medical per package (Cova) is not adopted, for the reasons in Run 1. No statutory THC percentage cap on flower or concentrates was located in Run 1 and none was located in this run; caps operate at the infused-product serving/container level and at purchase/possession weight (§11.3, §11.7).

11.2 Licence rules: transfers and sales, ownership changes, renewal, stacking and ownership caps, relocation, surrender/revocation, insurance and bonding

11.2.1 Licences are not transferable; sales are asset purchases with a new Step 2

  • The rule in one sentence: a Michigan marihuana licence cannot be sold, assigned or conveyed from one entity to another; what is sold is the business's assets, and the purchaser must itself be approved and licensed. CRA Amendment Application Instructions, "Supporting Documentation — Asset Purchase," verbatim in substance: "Any attempted transfer, sale, or conveyance of an interest in a marijuana license. The direct purchase and/or transfer of a license from one entity to another will not be permitted. The purchase of all assets of a marijuana facility and/or establishment in order to operate the location under a new entity requires a proposed amendment application to be submitted to the agency." Required documents include the amendment application, purchaser governing documents, organisational structure and purchase agreement, and: "Please note a Step 2 license application will be required to be submitted by the purchaser." Source: https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Amendments/728407---Amendment-Application-Instructions.pdf (CRA form CRA 5389, via the state CDN mirror host as returned by search) — accessed 2026-10-28. The CRA amendment form itself lists the amendment types as Change of Ownership (Adding/Removing/Change of Equity), Change of Entity Name, Conversion, and Asset Purchase. Source: https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Amendments/728392---Amendment-Application.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Both URLs are the CDN-mirror host returned by search; the canonical michigan.gov/cra equivalents were not separately verified — [VERIFY] before republication.
  • Report-before-you-change rule. R. 420.14(3): "Applicants shall report to the agency any proposed material changes to the marihuana business before making a material change." Material changes include, at minimum: (a) change in owners, officers, members or managers; (b) change of processing machinery or equipment; (c) addition or removal of persons named in the application or disclosed; (d) change in entity name; (e) any attempted transfer, sale or conveyance of an interest in a marihuana licence; (f) any change/modification not preinspected/inspected or part of the business location plan or final inspection (operational/method changes requiring inspection, equipment/process additions or reductions, size/capacity increases or decreases, ingress/egress alterations, changes impacting security, fire safety or building safety). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.14) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Post-licensure changes need prior approval. R. 420.18(1): "Any change or modification to the marihuana business after licensure is governed by the standards and procedures set forth in these rules… Any material change or modification to the marihuana business must be approved by the agency before the change or modification is made." Source: same (R. 420.18) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Management / licensing agreements need prior approval. R. 420.112a(2): a licensee must submit a complete, unredacted, signed copy of any licensing, management or other agreement to the agency for review and approval prior to performance under the agreement. Agency approval indicates only that it does not appear, on the information provided, that the other party meets the definition of "applicant." Acting under an unapproved agreement, or holding oneself out as a licensee/partner before filing the ownership amendment, has drawn discipline (see the DNVK / Consume Cannabis matters, Lapeer County and Ionia County, November 2024 consent orders, cited in Run 1 research — secondary summaries of CRA orders, [VERIFY] against the orders). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.112a) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Who counts as an "applicant" for ownership purposes. R. 420.1(1)(c): "applicant" includes a managerial employee, a person holding a direct or indirect ownership interest of more than 10% in the applicant, and — by entity type — proprietors/spouses, all partners (with a ≤10% non-controlling limited-partner carve-out), LLC members/managers (≤10% non-controlling carve-out), corporate officers/directors/stockholders above 10%, multilevel-enterprise profit recipients above 10%, nonprofit members/shareholders, and trust trustees/controllers/beneficiaries above 10%. It excludes bona fide financiers at a reasonable rate who do not control/manage, franchisors without marihuana-sale royalties, fixed-rent landlords who do not control/manage, approved IP licensors, profit-sharing employees at ≤10% who are not managerial, and capped employee bonuses. This 10% threshold is why "change of ownership" for CRA purposes reaches well beyond a majority sale. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.1) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Other notification clocks that attach to ownership/standing changes. R. 420.14(4): notify the agency within 3 business days of becoming aware (or when the applicant should have been aware) of criminal convictions, charges or civil judgments against an applicant in any jurisdiction, and of disciplinary action (including pending action) in any jurisdiction. R. 420.14(5): notify within 10 calendar days of initiation or conclusion of any new judgments, lawsuits, legal proceedings, charges or government investigations involving the applicant. R. 420.14(6): notify within 10 calendar days of notification of an alleged violation of a municipal ordinance or zoning regulation under MMFLA §205 / MRTMA §6 relating to licensed activities. R. 420.14(8): notify within 10 business days of appointment of a court-appointed personal representative, guardian, conservator, receiver or trustee. Failure to notify may result in sanctions or fines. Source: same (R. 420.14) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Social-equity caution on ownership changes. The CRA amendment form warns applicants to "be mindful of any social equity eligibility requirements prior to a change of ownership" (majority-ownership test, Run 1 §4.11). A change that drops the qualifying majority below 50% can end fee-reduction eligibility; the form does not state a clawback, and whether any fee-reduction repayment applies on an equity sale is [UNAVAILABLE] in the sources read — do not assert a clawback.

11.2.2 Renewal — annual term, what must be shown, the MMFLA 60-day grace, nonrenewal hearings

  • Term. All medical and adult-use licences are annual. R. 420.21: designated consumption establishment, excess grower, event organiser, Class A microbusiness and marihuana educational research licences are each "valid for 1 year"; a temporary marihuana event licence is valid for a minimum of 1 day and ends on the date specified. The CRA Municipal Guide (revised March 2026) states the same one-year renewal for medical facility and adult-use establishment licences generally (Run 1 §4.0). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-21 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Renewal rule (R. 420.13, as reproduced in the compilation — rule number confirmed from the compilation's sequence; the heading was not separately opened on Cornell in this run, [VERIFY] the number against the official PDF). In substance: the renewal applicant files an annual renewal form with municipal confirmation (municipality has not adopted a prohibiting ordinance; applicant complies with municipal ordinances including zoning; applicant will report ordinance/zoning changes, approval changes and violations), attests the form provides all information/documentation required to establish eligibility, qualification and suitability and readiness to continue operating in compliance throughout the new one-year period, and supplies any other information the agency requires. The agency "shall not renew a marihuana license unless the agency determines, as part of the license renewal, that each person required… to meet licensing standards is eligible, qualified, and suitable." Failure to comply with the acts/rules may result in nonrenewal. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.13) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Grounds for refusal / notice of nonrenewal. The agency may refuse to renew and issue a notice of nonrenewal if (a) the licensee fails to apply for renewal under MMFLA §402, MCL 333.27402, and the renewal rule; (b) the annual renewal form does not provide the information/documentation required to determine eligibility, qualification, suitability and readiness; or (c) the licensee failed to submit a required annual financial statement for the licence being renewed or for a previously held licence. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • MMFLA 60-day grace — and its limit. R. 420.13(6): "If a license renewal application for a license under the MMFLA is not submitted by the license expiration date, the license may be renewed within 60 days after its expiration date upon submission of the required application, payment of the required fees, and satisfaction of any renewal requirements. The licensee may continue to operate during the 60 calendar days after the license expiration date if the licensee submits the renewal application to the agency and complies with the other requirements for renewal." That grace is stated for MMFLA licences only in the text read. Whether an equivalent grace applies to MRTMA licences is not stated in the text read — [VERIFY] before advising an adult-use licensee it may operate past expiry. Do not generalise the 60 days to adult-use.
  • Nonrenewal hearing. R. 420.13(8)–(9): a licensee served with a notice of nonrenewal may request a hearing under the hearing rules; if no written hearing request is made within 21 calendar days after service, the notice of nonrenewal becomes the final order of the agency. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Cease-and-desist for unrenewed licences. R. 420.13(10): "A person who has not applied for marihuana license renewal for any and all licenses that are due for renewal shall cease and desist operation and is subject to any sanctions or fines, or both." Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Renewal notice. R. 420.13(7): the agency sends a renewal notice to the last known address on file; failure to notify the agency of an address change does not extend the expiration date and may result in discipline. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Fees on renewal. Adult-use renewal fees equal initial licensure fees in R. 420.7 Table 1 (retailer $15,000; Class C $24,000; microbusiness $8,300; Class A microbusiness $18,600; excess grower $24,000 per 2,000-plant increment — see §11.2.4; plus the $3,000 prequalification application fee at Step 1, subject to the excess-grower exception in §11.2.4). Medical renewal is by regulatory assessment under MCL 333.27603 (Run 1 §4.10; FY2026 per-licence assessments remain [VERIFY] against the CRA FY2026 notice). Social-equity fee reductions (25%/25%/40%/10%, stacking to 75%) apply to adult-use application and licensure/renewal fees on the Run 1 terms (Run 1 §4.11, secondary-sourced, [VERIFY] against the CRA programme page).
  • Application-fee timing (adult-use). R. 420.6(1) / R. 420.7(7): an MRTMA applicant must pay initial licensure fees within 10 calendar days of approval of the licence or within 90 calendar days of submitting a complete application, whichever date is first; failure to pay may be grounds for denial. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-6 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Prequalification validity. Step 1 prequalification status is valid for 2 years after the CRA issues the notice of prequalification; if no Step 2 application is submitted within that period it expires (CRA Step 1 instructions, Run 1 §4.0). Step 2 should not be submitted more than 60 days before the establishment is ready to pass inspection; MRTMA requires a licence determination within 90 days of a complete application (Run 1 §4.0, secondary summary of the CRA instructions — [VERIFY] the 90-day determination period against MRTMA §9, MCL 333.27959).

11.2.3 Stacking and ownership caps

  • Grower stacking — unlimited in number, per-licence plant counts. R. 420.17(1): a licensee holding a grower licence under MMFLA or MRTMA, or both, "may apply to stack class C licenses at a marihuana business specified in the marihuana license application" and "shall pay a separate initial licensure fee or regulatory assessment, as applicable, for each marihuana license issued and stacked." R. 420.1 defines "stacked license" as more than one licence issued to a single licensee to operate as a Class C grower under either act or both. Plant counts are per licence (see §11.3). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.17, R. 420.1) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No statewide numerical cap on most types. Michigan imposes no statewide cap on most adult-use or medical licence types in statute or rule (Run 1 §4.0); the gates are municipal authorisation (MMFLA opt-in ordinance; MRTMA opt-out/limit ordinance), the excess-grower eligibility threshold (§11.2.4), microbusiness single-location/stand-alone limits (§11.3.4), and the independence restrictions (§11.1.6, §11.2.5).
  • Ownership caps — what exists and what does not:
  • No general "one person may hold no more than X licences" cap was located in the rules read, other than the type-specific limits below. Do not invent one.
  • Dispensary/retailer ownership cap from the former Issue 2 text is gone: Run 1 records that SB 56 (Ohio) is a different state's law and must not be confused with Michigan; for Michigan, the often-quoted "8 dispensaries / 1 cultivator / 1 processor" cap belongs to Ohio (Run 1 Ohio file), not Michigan. No equivalent Michigan cap was located in this run. [VERIFY] if the parent dossier's Michigan chapter contains any such cap — it would be an Ohio import error.
  • Microbusinesses do not stack with other licences: a microbusiness (either class) is a single-location, stand-alone licence; Run 1 §4.7 cites MRTMA §9, MCL 333.27959, via secondary summary, for the proposition that holding another licence alongside a microbusiness violates §9. That proposition remains [VERIFY] against the statute text in this run as in Run 1; the rule text that is confirmed is R. 420.105(3) / R. 420.105a(3) (shall not operate at multiple locations) and the no-wholesale limits in §11.3.4.
  • Secure transporter / SCF independence: see §11.1.6. A secure transporter investor may not hold an interest in a grower, processor, provisioning centre/retailer or SCF (medical R. 420.110(2); adult-use equivalent [VERIFY] location), and an SCF investor may not hold an interest in a grower, transporter, processor or provisioning centre (medical R. 420.112(4)).
  • Grower/processor/provisioning-centre independence (medical): R. 420.108(7), R. 420.109(3), R. 420.111(3) — applicant and each investor must not have an interest in a secure transporter or safety compliance facility. Correction to Run 1 citation (see Research Notes C-01): Run 1 §4.2/§4.6 cited this as "R. 420.102(7)." In the current rule set, adult-use R. 420.102(7) is the Metrc-entry duty, not an independence rule; the independence sentence sits in medical R. 420.108(7). The substance (medical grower investors barred from transporter/SCF interests) is confirmed; the citation is corrected here. Whether adult-use growers/processors/retailers carry the same transporter/SCF bar in a differently numbered adult-use rule was not verified in the adult-use Part 1 text read — [VERIFY] before stating it for adult-use.
  • Equivalent licences across programmes are permitted, not capped: R. 420.1 "equivalent licenses" — a person may hold the medical and adult-use equivalents at the same premises (grower+grower, processor+processor, retailer+provisioning centre, transporter+transporter, SCF+SCF). They remain separate licences, separately fee'd, separately counted, and product must not move between medical and adult-use inventories except as the rules and Metrc allow. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-1 (Run 1 §4.5) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Co-location without a transporter: transfers between businesses occupying the same location without using a secure transporter are permitted only if the transfer uses only private real property without accessing public roadways and is entered in Metrc (grower R. 420.102(4) / medical R. 420.108(4); processor R. 420.103(2) / R. 420.109(2); retailer R. 420.104(1) / provisioning centre R. 420.111(1)). Same-location microbusiness internal transfers follow R. 420.105(2) / R. 420.105a(2) on the same Metrc-entry condition.

11.2.4 Excess grower — eligibility and per-increment fee (locked, re-confirmed)

R. 420.23(2)–(3), (7)–(8), (11), re-read in this run: an excess grower licence authorises sale of marihuana (other than seeds, seedlings, tissue cultures, immature plants and cuttings) to a processor or retailer; it "may be issued only to a person who holds 5 stacked class C marihuana grower licenses issued by the agency under the MRTMA and at least 2 grower class C licenses issued by the agency under the MMFLA"; the agency sets the plant count "in increments of 2,000 marihuana plants not in excess of the total marihuana plants permitted under grower class C licenses held under the MMFLA"; the Class C initial licensure fee ($24,000) "is assessed on the excess marihuana grower license at every 2,000 marihuana plant increment authorized." Worked example (Run 1 §4.3, unchanged): two medical Class C licences = 3,000 medical plants, supporting one 2,000-plant excess increment; three medical Class C licences support up to 4,000 excess plants (two increments, $48,000). Correction to Run 1 §4.3: R. 420.23(11) states "An applicant for an excess grower license is not required to pay the application fee under these rules." Run 1 §4.3 said "plus the $3,000 prequalification application fee." The rule text is adopted here: no application fee for the excess-grower application itself (the holder will already have been prequalified through its stacked licences); the per-increment $24,000 initial licensure fee, payable within 10 calendar days of approval or 90 calendar days of a complete application, whichever is first (R. 420.23(10)), stands. See Research Notes C-02. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.23) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.5 Relocation — a new licence application, not an amendment

R. 420.18(2), verbatim in substance: "Any change of a location of a marihuana business after licensure requires notification to the agency prior to the change of location, must be approved by the agency, requires a new marihuana license application under these rules, and may include, but is not limited to, all of the following: (a) Additional application fees. (b) Additional inspections by the agency or BFS. (c) Initial licensure fees or regulatory assessment, as applicable, or both." A relocation therefore re-opens municipal authorisation (MMFLA §205 ordinance / MRTMA §6 non-prohibition and zoning), the 1,000-foot school buffer question (MRTMA §9, Run 1 §1.6.4, [VERIFY] exact text), building/fire inspection (R. 420.208) and security-plan review (R. 420.209). A licence cannot simply be carried to a new address, and a transporter may not use relocation as a way to operate from an unapproved site: a secure transporter must have its primary place of business in a municipality that has not prohibited establishments (adult-use, R. 420.206(5)) or has adopted an authorising ordinance (medical, R. 420.206(6)). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.18, R. 420.206) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.2.6 Surrender and revocation

  • No standalone "voluntary surrender" rule was located in R. 420. The word "surrender" does not appear in the R. 420 compilation text searched in this run. Surrender in Michigan practice therefore takes two forms, both documented in enforcement records rather than in a surrender rule: 1. Negotiated surrender in a consent order / stipulation. Examples: Cherry Industries LLC (Detroit, Wayne County) — consent order and stipulation under which the grower "agreed to permanently voluntarily surrender the license (effective 10 days after the effective date of the order)" and agreed it "shall not be renewed, reinstated, reissued or reactivated, limited or otherwise, at any future date," following findings including mixing harvests, transferring product that failed testing for a banned pesticide, selling contaminated pre-rolls, improper batch sampling, denial of full batch access to the laboratory, and incomplete surveillance footage. Source: https://www.cannabisbusinesstimes.com/us-states/michigan/news/15768259/detroit-cannabis-grower-surrenders-license-in-resolution-with-cra (30 September 2025, secondary report of the CRA announcement) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA consent order]. July 2026 CRA actions (secondary, Run 1 §5.5) included 3 surrenders among 75 enforcement actions dated in July 2026. 2. Surrender as a sanction outcome alongside revocation. The October 2026 orders illustrate the severe end: Budbridge LLC d/b/a Muha Meds Ypsilanti (19 N. Hamilton St., Ypsilanti, Washtenaw County) — adult-use retailer licence revoked 1 October 2026 plus $251,250 fine (Run 1 §0.2); GP Holdings LLC (Millie Montana Industries, Clare, Clare County) — 20 medical Class C licences revoked plus $2 million fine (secondary, Run 1 §5.5); Michigan Investment 10 LLC — adult-use + medical processor licences shut down effective 24 September 2026 plus $2 million fine (secondary, Run 1 §5.5). All three are secondary-reported in Run 1; underlying CRA final orders should be opened before quoting them as CRA-confirmed.
  • Hearing rights on adverse action. R. 420.704(2) (cited in CRA complaints): a party aggrieved by suspension, revocation, restriction, refusal to renew, or a fine is given a hearing on written request within 21 days after service of the complaint; certified-mail service is complete on the business day following mailing. A compliance conference under R. 420.704(1) (and R. 420.808(4) for social-equity matters) may also be requested in writing. Source: CRA formal complaints quoting R. 420.704, e.g. https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Disciplinary-Actions/2025/April/XYZ-Ventures-LLC-dba-JARS-Cannabis-Ann-Arbor-PC000622-Consent-Order-and-Stipulation-and-Formal-Compl.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Effect of surrender/revocation on product and records — [VERIFY]. No rule text located in this run states a post-surrender wind-down period for inventory destruction, a records-retention period after surrender, or whether a surrendered licence's Metrc inventory must be destroyed before the surrender takes effect. Do not state a wind-down period. The general destruction clock (90 days, R. 420.502(6)) and the prohibition on selling held/recalled/destroy-ordered product (R. 420.502(3)) are the only destruction rules located; how the CRA applies them to a surrendering licensee is a follow-up for the CRA (see Research Notes).
  • Licence as property. Run 1 §4.9 notes the MMFLA principle that a licence is not a property right and cannot be pledged as collateral, with the MRTMA equivalent marked [VERIFY] against current R. 420.6 in Run 1. That [VERIFY] stands: no collateral/property-right clause was located in the R. 420 text read in this run. Do not state it as a current rule citation until located.

11.2.7 Insurance and bonding — the $100,000 figures CONFIRMED as current law (Run 1 [VERIFY] resolved)

  • R. 420.10 — Proof of financial responsibility; insurance (history: 2020 AACS; 2022 AACS — i.e. current rule, not draft). Verbatim in substance:
  • (1) "Before a marihuana license is issued or renewed, the licensee or renewal applicant shall file a proof of financial responsibility for liability for bodily injury to lawful users resulting from the manufacture, distribution, transportation, or sale of adulterated marihuana or adulterated marihuana-infused products on the form prescribed by the agency, for an amount not less than $100,000.00. If the proof required in this subrule is a bond, the bond must be in a format acceptable to the agency."
  • (2) In addition, a marihuana transporter must show proof of auto insurance, vehicle registration, and registration as a commercial motor vehicle, as applicable, for any vehicles used to transport marihuana product as required by the acts and rules.
  • (3) Event-organiser exception: proof of financial responsibility for bodily injury is not required for an event-organiser licence itself, but the organiser must file it when applying for a temporary marihuana event licence, or prove each participating microbusiness, Class A microbusiness and retailer has bodily-injury coverage when applying for the temporary event licence.
  • (4) "In addition to the proof of financial responsibility requirements contained in subrule (1) of this rule, a renewal applicant or licensee holding a license under the MMFLA shall also carry commercial general liability insurance covering premises liability for an amount not less than $100,000.00. An applicant shall provide proof of commercial general liability insurance covering the premises liability to the agency no later than 60 days after a state operating license is issued or renewed." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.10) — accessed 2026-10-28. Conclusion: both Run 1 $100,000 figures are current-rule figures, not draft-only. Run 1 §4.12's [VERIFY] on R. 420.10 is resolved in favour of the figures.
  • Statutory home (medical). MCL 333.27408 (MMFLA §408), as amended by 2021 PA 55 / SB 461 (effective 30 March 2022 per secondary summary): before the agency grants or renews any licence, the licensee/applicant must file proof of financial responsibility for bodily injury to lawful users from adulterated product "in an amount not less than $100,000.00 for each license," in the form of a liability insurance policy issued by a licensed insurer or licensed captive insurer in Michigan, without any condition/provision/stipulation/limitation or endorsement relieving the insurer from liability for a claim the insured may be held liable for under the act, and covering bodily injuries to a qualifying patient including injuries caused by intentional conduct of the licensee/employee/agent (but not required to cover injuries where the licensee/employee/agent acted with intent to harm). An insured licensee may not cancel the required insurance without (a) 30 days' prior written notice to the department and (b) procuring new proof and delivering it within 30 days after giving notice. Failure to maintain proof may result in suspension (per the 2025 Justia section title). Source: https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/chapter-333/statute-act-281-of-2016/division-281-2016-part-4-licensing/section-333-27408/ (2025) — accessed 2026-10-28. Nuance: the rule text (R. 420.10(1)) as reproduced does not include the words "for each license"; the statute does. Adopt "per licence" on the statute's authority, and note the rule/statute wording difference.
  • What the $100,000 does NOT cover. It is narrow: bodily injury to lawful users from adulterated product (defined in MCL 333.27408(1) as product sold as marihuana containing an unintended substance or chemical/biological matter other than marihuana that causes adverse reaction after ingestion/consumption; "bodily injury" excludes the expected/intended effect or long-term adverse effect of smoking/ingesting/consuming marihuana). It is not general liability, not cargo insurance, not vehicle-accident cover, and not theft cover. Transporters additionally need auto insurance/vehicle registration/commercial-motor-vehicle registration (R. 420.10(2)); delivery vehicles need proof of vehicle insurance recorded under R. 420.207(6)(d)(vii). No other bonding minimum (e.g. a surety bond for tax, or a waste bond) was located in R. 420 in this run — no general "bonding minimum" beyond the R. 420.10(1) bond-as-proof option should be stated. Whether Treasury requires any separate tax bond for the 24% wholesale tax or 10% excise is [UNAVAILABLE] in this run.
  • MMFLA capitalisation (separate from insurance, Run 1 §4.12, unchanged). R. 420.11 (medical only): CPA-attested proof of total capitalisation, ≥25% in liquid assets — Grower Class A $150,000; Class B $300,000; Class C $500,000; Processor $300,000; Provisioning Center $300,000; Secure Transporter $200,000; Safety Compliance Facility $200,000. There is no equivalent MRTMA capitalisation schedule. Source: https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-licenses/section-r-420-11/ (Run 1) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY the current R. 420.11 text in the official PDF; it was not re-opened in this run].
  • MMFLA §402 insurance-adequacy ground. MCL 333.27402(2)(e) (as reproduced in secondary sources, Run 1): an applicant is ineligible if it "fails to demonstrate the applicant's ability to maintain adequate premises liability and casualty insurance for its proposed marihuana facility." That is a qualification ground in addition to the $100,000 floors above. Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27402/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against legislature.mi.gov].

11.2.8 Discipline, inspection and theft/loss reporting (operations context for §11.2)

  • Inspections without warrant/notice during business hours. R. 420.16(3): "a licensee may not refuse the agency access to the marihuana business during the hours of operation. The agency may access the marihuana business without a warrant and without notice to the licensee during the marihuana business's hours of operation." The agency may inspect/examine/audit records and, on non-cooperation, impound/seize/assume physical control of/summarily remove records (R. 420.16(5)). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.16) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Theft/loss/criminal activity. R. 420.15(1): applicants must notify the agency and local law enforcement within 24 hours of becoming aware (or when they should have been aware) of theft or loss of any marihuana product or criminal activity at the business. Delivery-specific theft/loss/diversion/accident reporting is in R. 420.207(14) (notify agency, state police or local law enforcement). Source: same (R. 420.15, R. 420.207) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Unwanted fire. R. 420.14(7): notify the agency and the Bureau of Fire Services (BFS) within 1 business day following an unwanted fire. Source: same (R. 420.14) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Standard operating procedures. R. 420.206a: a business must have up-to-date written SOPs on site at all times, available to the agency on request, detailing operations/activities necessary to comply with the acts/rules/safe food management guidelines as applicable; if the agency finds an SOP inaccurate or non-compliant, the licensee may be required to correct the practice immediately and update the SOPs within 1 business day. Source: same (R. 420.206a) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.3 Cultivation rules: plant counts by class, canopy, indoor/outdoor/greenhouse, caregiver and home grow

11.3.1 Licensed cultivation — plant counts (locked Run 1 figures, re-confirmed in rule text)

Programme Class A Class B Class C Source rule
Adult-use (MRTMA) 100 mature plants per licence 500 per licence 2,000 per licence R. 420.102(1)–(2): "only mature marihuana plants are included in the plant count"
Medical (MMFLA) 500 per licence 1,000 per licence 1,500 per licence R. 420.108(1)–(2): a plant meeting the MMFLA definition of "plant" is included in the count

Microbusiness (adult-use only): 150 mature plants (R. 420.105(1)(a)); Class A microbusiness: 300 mature plants (R. 420.105a(1)(a)). Excess grower: 2,000-plant increments capped by medical Class C allowance (§11.2.4). All counts are per licence, so stacking multiplies the count (R. 420.17; R. 420.102(1) "for each marihuana grower license the marihuana grower holds in that class"). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.102, R. 420.105, R. 420.105a, R. 420.108) — accessed 2026-10-28. These match Run 1 §4.2 exactly; the conflated secondary table ("A ≤500, B ≤1,000, C ≤2,000" as a single row, CannBus) is again rejected for the reasons in Run 1.

11.3.2 Canopy — no canopy (square-footage) cap was located

No canopy limit, plant-count-only system. The rules read impose plant counts, not canopy area, for licensed growers and microbusinesses. No rule in R. 420.102, R. 420.105, R. 420.105a, R. 420.108 or R. 420.206 states a maximum canopy square footage, a maximum number of grow rooms, or a lighting wattage cap. Do not state a Michigan canopy cap. If a canopy figure appears in a municipal ordinance (e.g. a local zoning cap on grow area) or a building/fire approval, it is local, not state rule, and must be cited as such. The only size-related state constraints located are: immature plant batches ≤100 plants (R. 420.303(1)); harvest batches ≤50 lb (R. 420.304(2)(c)); and the plant-tag size threshold (8 inches, §11.1.3).

11.3.3 Indoor / outdoor / greenhouse

  • Default: inside a building. R. 420.206(1)(a): a cultivator may not operate unless its operations are within a building that meets the security requirements, passes inspections, and has a building permit under R. 420.208. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.206) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Outdoor cultivation — permitted only as a contiguous, enclosed adjunct to a building. R. 420.206(1)(b): cultivation may occur in an outdoor area only if (i) the outdoor area is contiguous with the building, fully enclosed by fences/barriers ensuring plants are not visible from a public place without binoculars, aircraft or other optical aids, with fences secured and compliant with security measures including locked entries accessible only to authorised persons or emergency personnel; (ii) after harvest, all drying, trimming, curing and packaging occurs inside the building meeting all requirements; and (iii) the building meets security requirements, passes inspections, and has a building permit under R. 420.208. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Greenhouse — no separate greenhouse rule was located. A greenhouse is treated in practice as either a "building" (if it meets building/fire/security/inspection requirements) or as an outdoor area (if it does not), but no rule text in R. 420 uses the word "greenhouse" as a distinct cultivation category in the sections read — [VERIFY] by a full-text search of the official PDF before stating any greenhouse-specific rule. Do not import another state's greenhouse provisions. Local zoning may treat greenhouses distinctly; that would be a municipal rule, not R. 420.
  • Zoning for growers. Adult-use R. 420.102(8): a grower licence "does not authorize the marihuana grower to operate in an area unless the area is zoned for industrial or agricultural uses or otherwise meets the requirements established in section 9(3)(c) of the MRTMA, MCL 333.27959(c)." Medical R. 420.108(9) (numbered "(89)" in the reflow, a printing artefact): the area must be zoned industrial or agricultural, or unzoned and otherwise meeting MMFLA §205(1), MCL 333.27205. Microbusinesses are expressly excepted from adult-use R. 420.102(8) (R. 420.105(7): microbusiness subject to grower/retailer/processor provisions "except for R 420.102(8)"). Source: same (R. 420.102, R. 420.105, R. 420.108) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Building and fire safety. R. 420.208: the proposed/licensed business is subject to inspection by a state building code official, state fire official or code-enforcement official to confirm no health/safety concerns; prelicensure and post-licensure inspections may be conducted; NFPA 1 (2021 edition, Fire Code) is adopted by reference (R. 420.402(1)(a)). Grower operations need a building permit under R. 420.208 (R. 420.206(1)). Egress locks must meet NFPA 1, local fire codes and the Michigan building code, R. 408.30401–R. 408.30499 (R. 420.209(3)). Source: same (R. 420.208, R. 420.209, R. 420.402) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Grower sales channels (licensed). Adult-use R. 420.102(3)–(6): sale to another grower only by secure transporter, except seeds/seedlings/tissue cultures/immature plants, which may go grower-to-grower without a transporter; transfer to a processor/retailer without a transporter only if the recipient occupies the same location and the transfer uses only private real property without accessing public roadways, with each transfer entered in Metrc; otherwise transfer only by secure transporter; sale (other than seeds/seedlings/tissue cultures/immature plants/cuttings) to a processor or retailer. A grower may purchase/accept seeds, tissue cultures and clones not meeting the "marihuana plant" definition at any time from another licensed grower (R. 420.102(9)); a Class A grower may accept plants only once on licensure from a registered primary caregiver who was an applicant for that Class A licence (R. 420.102(10)); a grower may not purchase/accept a mature plant from an individual, patient or caregiver (R. 420.102(12)). Medical equivalents: R. 420.108(3)–(6), (10)–(11), including the bar on accepting product back from a processor/provisioning centre once received into its Metrc inventory without written agency approval (R. 420.108(11); processor equivalent R. 420.109(5)). Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.

Adult-use home grow (MRTMA §5, MCL 333.27955(1)(b)) Medical patient (MMMA §4, MCL 333.26424(a)) Medical caregiver (MMMA §4, MCL 333.26424(b))

Patient cap — 1 (own) Maximum 5 patients → maximum 60 plants (5 × 12)
Possession alongside grow 10 oz at residence + any marihuana produced by plants on the premises 2.5 oz usable marihuana (plus incidental seeds/stalks/unusable roots) 2.5 oz usable per connected patient
