Sources: Run 1 §§1.3.1, 1.3.3, 1.4.4 (statute text via Justia mirrors, accessed 2026-10-28 in Run 1) — carried forward unchanged. Conflicts re-affirmed, not re-opened: (a) the "72-plant caregiver" figure (patient-as-caregiver stacking) is not adopted; 5 × 12 = 60 is the arithmetic and the adopted figure. A secondary article in this run repeating a "72-plant limit for a medical marijuana caregiver's residential grow" (Electrical Contractor Magazine, on home-grow energy demand) is the same conflation and is rejected for the same reason. Source for that article: https://www.ecmag.com/magazine/articles/article-detail/in-the-weeds-of-energy-use-home-marijuana-growers-in-michigan-must-follow-proper-guidelines — accessed 2026-10-28. (b) Caregiver eligibility: ≥21, agreed to assist, never convicted of a felony involving illegal drugs (MMMA §3 definition as summarised in Run 1); the "no felony of any type within 10 years" formulation conflates MMFLA licence ineligibility (MCL 333.27402) with the MMMA caregiver definition — see Run 1 §1.4.4. (c) Caregiver compensation for costs is not a sale (MMMA §4(e)/(f)); caregiver-to-provisioning-centre commercial sales and patient-to-patient/dispensary sales are not protected (People v McQueen, 493 Mich 135 (2013), Run 1 §1.2.1). (d) Caregiver hired as a grower/processor/secure-transporter employee under MMFLA must withdraw their caregiver registration in the manner established by the agency (R. 420.602(2)(i)). - Home-grow energy/safety note (guidance, not a plant rule). The CRA has published home-grow electrical-safety guidance with utilities/licensed electrical contractors (a 12-plant home grow can increase a home's energy demand by 2.75 times, per the agency as reported in the Electrical Contractor Magazine piece above). That is safety guidance, not a plant-count or energy-cap rule, and no state energy-efficiency mandate for home grows was located. See §11.6.3.

11.4 Security requirements: cameras, alarms, storage, transport (Metrc manifests, secure transporter rules)

11.4.1 Premises security — R. 420.209 (verbatim thresholds)

  • Security plan. R. 420.209(1): an applicant must submit a security plan demonstrating, at minimum, the ability to meet the rule. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.209) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Escort. R. 420.209(2): any person at the business other than employees must be escorted at all times by the licensee or an employee when in limited-access and restricted-access areas.
  • Locks. R. 420.209(3): securely lock the business, including interior rooms as required by the agency, windows, and points of entry/exits, with commercial-grade, nonresidential door locks or other electronic or keypad access. Egress locks must meet NFPA 1, local fire codes and the Michigan building code (R. 408.30401–R. 408.30499).
  • Alarm. R. 420.209(4): maintain an alarm system; on request, make all alarm-system, monitoring and alarm-activity information available to the agency. (No rule-text requirement for 24/7 third-party monitoring was located in R. 420.209 itself; a "monitored 24/7" alarm appears in some municipal ordinances — local, not state rule — and must not be cited as R. 420.209.)
  • Video system components. R. 420.209(5): at minimum, digital or network video recorders, cameras capable of meeting the recording requirements, video monitors, digital archiving devices, and a colour printer capable of delivering still photos.
  • Areas that must be recorded. R. 420.209(6)(a): (i) areas where product is weighed, packed, stored, loaded/unloaded for transportation, prepared or moved within the business; (ii) limited-access areas and security rooms, including transfers between rooms; (iii) areas storing a surveillance-system storage device, with not less than one camera recording access points to the secured surveillance-recording area; (iv) entrances/exits to the building, recorded from both indoor and outdoor vantage points; (v) areas of entrance/exit between marihuana businesses at the same location, including transfers between them; (vi) point-of-sale areas where product is sold and displayed for sale; (vii) areas where marihuana/product is destroyed.
  • Resolution, placement, lighting, time/date. R. 420.209(6)(b): minimum 720p resolution. R. 420.209(7): each camera permanently mounted in a fixed location, placed to clearly record activity within 20 feet of all points of entry/exit and to allow clear and certain identification of any person (including facial features) and activities (including sales/transfers) in all required areas. R. 420.209(8): sufficient lighting to meet the requirements. R. 420.209(9): cameras record when motion is detected and record images clearly and accurately displaying time and date.
  • Retention — 30 days (confirmed; 45-day claim rejected). R. 420.209(11), verbatim: "A licensee shall keep surveillance recordings for a minimum of 30 calendar days, except in instances of investigation or inspection by the agency in which case the licensee shall retain the recordings until the time as the agency notifies the licensee that the recordings may be destroyed." This is confirmed by multiple CRA formal complaints quoting R. 420.209(11) in those terms (e.g. ENF 24-00507, ENF 23-00940, ENF 24-01399, ENF 22-00066). Conflict resolved: a secondary security-industry page claiming "a minimum of 45 days per Michigan Administrative Code R 420.209" (https://www.security101.com/blog/michigan-security-camera-laws-for-2025-what-you-need-to-know-now — accessed 2026-10-28) is wrong as a statement of the state rule and is not adopted; 45 days appears in some municipal ordinances and in other states' rules, not in Michigan R. 420.209(11). Likewise, a vendor guide's "60-day footage retention (some inspectors expect 90 days)" (https://greenthumbdepot.com/blogs/grow-guides/how-one-detroit-grow-went-live-3-weeks-early-and-saved-over-40k-doing-it — accessed 2026-10-28) describes inspection practice/expectation, not the rule, and is not adopted as a retention rule. Operators should retain longer than 30 days where an investigation/inspection is pending, because the rule then requires retention until the agency authorises destruction.
  • Access and copies. R. 420.209(12): recordings are subject to agency inspection and must be kept so the agency can view and obtain copies at the business immediately on request; the licensee must also send/provide copies on request within the time specified by the agency.
  • Failure notification and log. R. 420.209(13): maintain a video-surveillance system equipped with a failure-notification system alerting the licensee to any interruption/failure of the system or storage device. R. 420.209(14): maintain a log including (a) identity of employees responsible for monitoring the system, (b) identity of the employee who removed any recording and the time/date removed, (c) identity of the employee who destroyed any recording.
  • Exempt licence types. R. 420.209(15): the rule does not apply to (a) designated consumption establishment applicants/licensees, (b) event-organiser applicants/licensees, or (c) temporary marihuana event applicants/licensees under MRTMA. (Temporary events have their own security-personnel rule, R. 420.25(9): licensed security personnel ≥21, present at all times product is for sale or consumption is allowed, who must not consume product before/during the event.)
  • Storage. R. 420.212: all product must be stored at the business in a secured limited-access or restricted-access area and identified/tracked in Metrc; containers for transfer/sale between businesses must be clearly marked/labelled/tagged, enclosed on all sides in secured containers latched or locked to keep contents secured, each identified/tracked; chemicals/solvents stored separately from product in closed containers in locked storage; infused/edible products and direct-contact materials stored separately from toxic/flammable materials; unpackaged product stored separately by product type; a sales location must store product for transfer/sale behind a counter or other barrier separated from stock rooms; stock/storage rooms must meet the security requirements. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.212) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Point-of-sale area. R. 420.206(9): a sales location must have a separate room dedicated as the point-of-sale area; product kept behind a counter or other barrier so customers have no direct access; a designated area for contactless/limited-contact transactions (curbside, drive-through window) is permitted unless prohibited by municipal ordinance (R. 420.207a), must be identified in the business location plan, have a written SOP, anti-theft policy/procedure/capability, comply with R. 420.209, R. 420.505 and R. 420.506, operate during normal business hours, and product transferred in an opaque bag with contents not visible to the general public on pick-up. Source: same (R. 420.206, R. 420.207a) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.4.2 Transport — secure transporters, manifests, and the same-location exception

  • Who must use a secure transporter. As a default, transfers between separate licensed businesses must be by secure transporter (grower R. 420.102(6)/R. 420.108(6); processor R. 420.103(2)/R. 420.109(2); retailer R. 420.104(1); provisioning centre R. 420.111(1)). Exceptions: (a) seeds/seedlings/tissue cultures/immature plants/clones grower-to-grower without a transporter; (b) same-location transfers using only private real property without accessing public roadways, with each transfer entered in Metrc; (c) laboratory sample collection/transport under R. 420.304 (see §11.1.3); (d) SCF take/test/return without a transporter under R. 420.112(1) (medical); (e) trade samples below the thresholds in §11.7.2; (f) delivery to consumers by the sales location's own employees under R. 420.207 (§11.4.3) — not by a secure transporter (a secure transporter licence "does not authorize transport to a registered qualifying patient or registered primary caregiver," R. 420.106(1)/R. 420.110(1)).
  • Secure transporter licence scope. R. 420.106(1) (adult-use) / R. 420.110(1) (medical): authorises storing and transporting marihuana and money associated with purchase/sale between establishments/facilities for a fee on request of a person with legal custody of the product/money. Legal custody remains with the transferor/transferee; the transporter takes only physical custody (R. 420.206(7)(a)). A transporter "shall not sell or purchase marihuana products" (R. 420.206(7)(b)) and must hold a separate licence for every transporter location (R. 420.206(7)).
  • Crew, driver, vehicle. R. 420.106(3) / R. 420.110(4): (a) each driver must hold a chauffeur's licence issued by Michigan; (b) each vehicle operated with a 2-person crew, with at least 1 individual remaining with the vehicle at all times during transportation; (c) route plan and manifest entered in Metrc, copy carried in the vehicle and presented to a law-enforcement officer on request; (d) product in sealed containers, not accessible in transit; (e) vehicle must bear no markings or other indication it is carrying marihuana/infused product; (f) vehicle stored other than at the primary place of business only if it contains no product and the storage address is reported to the agency. Medical transporter-employee bar: R. 420.110(4)(b) — each employee with custody of product/money must not have been convicted of or released from incarceration for a felony within the past 5 years, nor convicted of a controlled-substance misdemeanour within the past 5 years. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.106, R. 420.110) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Manifest and route-plan duties (general transporter rule). R. 420.206(7)(e)–(k): have a route plan and manifest available for agency inspection; carry a copy during transport; present to law enforcement on request; subject to administrative inspection by a law-enforcement officer at any point during transport; shall not possess product not on a manifest; shall follow the manifest; store vehicles at the primary place of business (empty-vehicle off-site storage must be in the business plan); remain on site until product is weighed and accepted or rejected before leaving the receiving business; shall not maintain custody for more than 96 hours unless agency permission is sought and granted on a case-by-case basis; identify/record all vehicles with the agency, with Secretary of State registration as required by state law; vehicles subject to agency inspection at any time. Money transported must be locked in a sealed container kept separate from product and accessible only to the licensee/employees, with all money handling logged/tracked and records available to the agency (R. 420.206(7)(c)–(d)). Product from separate businesses must not be commingled; each business's product labelled and kept in separate compartments/containers within the main locked, secured, sealed container (R. 420.206(7)(c)).
  • Manifest contents — [VERIFY] the field list. R. 420.208 in the compilation is "Building and fire safety," not the manifest rule; the manifest-creation rule cited in secondary guidance is R. 420.208(2) in an older numbering ("A licensee shall create a transport manifest through the statewide monitoring system before transporting marihuana products," as quoted at https://weedbizwiz.substack.com/p/how-to-use-the-transport-manifest — accessed 2026-10-28). That numbering does not match the current compilation's R. 420.208 and is not adopted as a current citation. The current rules that are confirmed require a Metrc route plan and manifest, a copy in the vehicle, and Metrc entry of all transactions/inventory (R. 420.106(2), R. 420.206(7)(e), R. 420.201c principles in Run 1 §1.7), but the exhaustive manifest field list (origin/destination licence numbers, departure/arrival times, product/tag/weight/unit list, driver/employee ID, vehicle make/model/plate/registration) is secondary guidance — [VERIFY] against the current Metrc manifest specification / CRA transporter instructions before publishing a field list. What is confirmed is that a manifest is required for every inter-business transfer, including transfers between commonly owned facilities, and that transporter-to-transporter handoffs are permitted only at a licensed transporter location, on the Metrc manifest, and at the sending establishment's request (R. 420.106(5) / R. 420.110(6)).
  • Metrc (statewide monitoring system) duties generally. Tracking Act, MCL 333.27903, and R. 420.201c principles (Run 1 §1.7): licensees must enter every plant, product, package, batch, test, transfer, conversion, sale, recall, waste/destruction and return, linked to a unique Metrc tag where practicable; lot/batch chain of custody; transfers including transferee, date, quantity and price; safety-compliance results received electronically before sale; patient/caregiver purchase totals and limit-flagging; inventory adjustments with reason codes. Employee Metrc access: enter employee information and access level within 10 days after hiring (general operations rule as summarised in Run 1 §1.7; R. 420.602(2)(b) states 7 business days for the employee rule — see §11.8.1 for the discrepancy, [VERIFY] which period governs Metrc access vs general employee records). System information is confidential and FOIA-exempt (Tracking Act §4, MCL 333.27904), with law-enforcement/authorised-agency access. Metrc does not determine wholesale-tax liability (CRA January 2026 bulletin, Run 1 §1.7) and does not replace the registry card.

11.4.3 Delivery to consumers — R. 420.207 (caps CONFIRMED, citation corrected)

  • No standalone delivery licence; CRA-approved procedures required. R. 420.207(1): "A marihuana sales location licensee may engage in the delivery of a marihuana product for sale or transfer to marihuana customers upon approval by the agency of the licensee's delivery procedures." Medical delivery is to a patient at the patient's residential address (or to the patient's caregiver if the patient is a minor); adult-use delivery is to an individual 21+ at a residential address or at a designated consumption establishment address provided at order time (R. 420.207(2)–(3)). Deliveries only during the sales location's business hours (R. 420.207(11)). Delivery authorisation may be denied, suspended or withdrawn (R. 420.207(5)(g)).
  • Vehicle caps — CONFIRMED, Run 1 [VERIFY] on the $3,000 sub-cap resolved. R. 420.207(9)(d), verbatim in substance: "A marihuana delivery employee shall not carry marihuana product in the delivery vehicle with a value in excess of $5,000.00 at any time. The value of marihuana products carried in the delivery vehicle for which a delivery order was not received and processed by the licensed retailer prior to the delivery employee departing from the marihuana sales location may not exceed $3,000.00. For the purposes of this subrule, the value of marihuana products must be determined using the current retail price of all marihuana products carried by, or within the delivery vehicle of, the marihuana delivery employee." Adopted: $5,000 total vehicle cap + $3,000 unordered-inventory sub-cap, both at current retail price. Run 1 §1.6.3 flagged the $3,000 figure as [VERIFY]; it is confirmed here.
  • Weight caps — CONFIRMED. R. 420.207(10), verbatim: "A marihuana retailer licensed under the MRTMA, in making deliveries, shall not transport more than 15 ounces of marihuana or more than 60 grams of marihuana concentrate at 1 time pursuant to section 11 of the MRTMA, MCL 333.27961." Adopted: 15 oz / 60 g per delivery run for adult-use retailers. Run 1 §1.6.3 attributed these caps to "R 420.506/507 summaries"; the correct operative citation is R. 420.207(9)(d) and (10). That is a citation correction, not a figure change (see Research Notes C-03). The delivery amount is also limited to the customer's daily/monthly (medical) or single-transaction (adult-use) purchase limits (R. 420.207(5)(c)).
  • Other delivery duties. Delivery employees must meet R. 420.602 and be employees of the sales location (R. 420.207(4)(c)); a delivery employee may work for only one sales location (R. 420.207(9)(e)); must not leave without at least one order already received and processed (R. 420.207(9)(f)); must carry a physical/electronic copy of employee ID number, sales-location licence number/address/contact, and the delivery log (R. 420.207(7)); must have a secure communication device (e.g. cell phone) at all times (R. 420.207(8)); must carry each delivery request and make it available to the agency (R. 420.207(9)(a)); must not leave product in an unattended vehicle unless locked with an active alarm (R. 420.207(9)(b)); vehicle must contain a GPS device, permanently or temporarily affixed while in operation, active and in the delivery employee's possession at all times, with the sales location able to identify the geographic location of all delivery vehicles/employees and provide it to the agency on request (R. 420.207(9)(c)); must maintain a delivery inventory ledger (type, brand, retail value, Metrc tag, weight/volume/measure) updated after each delivery (R. 420.207(9)(g)–(i)); must maintain a log of all stops with reasons, turned in on return and kept by the sales location for at least 1 year from delivery (R. 420.207(9)(j)); if no delivery request is to be performed for a 30-minute period, must make no additional deliveries and return, with undelivered product returned to inventory and Metrc updated (R. 420.207(9)(l)); delivery product stored in a secured compartment clearly marked and latched/locked (R. 420.207(11)); delivery begins when the employee leaves with product and ends on return (R. 420.207(12)); delivery log per delivery (begin/end date/time, employee name, amount allowed for delivery, tag number and strain, recipient signature) (R. 420.207(13)); theft/loss/criminal activity, accidents and diversion during delivery reported to agency and law enforcement as provided (R. 420.207(14)). Vehicle records kept and available: make, model, colour, VIN, plate, registration, proof of insurance (R. 420.207(6)(d)). Recipient verification: the person taking delivery must be the patient (or caregiver for a minor patient) or the 21+ individual who placed the order, verified by photo ID and (medical) registry card (R. 420.207(5)(e)–(f), (6)(a)–(b)); delivery address must be validated as the patient's residence or the 21+ customer's residence/designated-consumption-establishment address given at order time (R. 420.207(6)(c)); customer consent including acknowledgement for release of information necessary to fulfil delivery (R. 420.207(6)(e)). Returned product may not come back by delivery driver (R. 420.214c(2)(d)).
  • Delivery counts (context, Run 1 §5.2): 30 September 2025 — adult-use retailers approved for home delivery 350; medical provisioning centres approved 58 (CRA September 2025 monthly report, directly opened in Run 1). August 2026 delivery sales: adult-use ~$3.43m; medical $11,061.87 (CRA August 2026 report via Marijuana Herald, Run 1 §1.6.3).

11.5 Waste disposal rules

  • Render unusable and unrecognisable — 50% rule. R. 420.211(1): product to be destroyed or considered waste "must be rendered into an unusable and unrecognizable form through grinding or another method as determined by the agency that incorporates the marihuana product waste with 1 or more of the following types of non-consumable solid waste so that the resulting mixture is not less than 50% non-marihuana product waste": paper waste; plastic waste; cardboard waste; food waste; grease or other compostable oil waste; fermented organic matter or other compost activators; soil; other waste approved in writing by the agency. R. 420.211(2) (plant waste — roots, stalks, leaves, stems not processed with a solvent): same grinding/other agency-determined method, mixed with compostable waste (food waste; yard waste; vegetable-based grease/oils; other agency-approved compostable wastes) so the mixture is not less than 50% non-marihuana plant waste. "Unrecognizable" means "marihuana product rendered indistinguishable from any other plant material" (R. 420.211(9)). Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.211) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Hazardous waste. R. 420.211(3): manage all hazardous waste under Part 111 of the Natural Resources and Environmental Protection Act (NREPA), 1994 PA 451, MCL 324.11101–324.11153. R. 420.211(13): a grower may, with agency approval, dispose of plant waste as compost feedstock or by another organic-waste method at its business in compliance with Part 111. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Record in Metrc; never sell waste. R. 420.211(4): rendered waste and plant waste "must be recorded in the statewide monitoring system." R. 420.211(5): a licensee "shall not sell marihuana waste, marihuana plant waste, or marihuana products that are to be destroyed, or that the agency orders destroyed." R. 420.211(8): maintain accurate and comprehensive waste records accounting for, reconciling and evidencing all waste disposal activity; the agency may publish waste-management guidance. CRA Compliance Best Practice Guide practice (secondary compilation, [VERIFY] against the guide): destruction documentation including full Metrc tag number, reason, method, photos/video of destroyed product and tags, with packages adjusted to 0 in Metrc using reason code "waste" and a note of reason/date; evidence available to the CRA on request, not routinely sent; product on administrative hold requires agency approval before destruction. Source for the guide practice: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/authoritative-documents/CRA_Compliance-Best-Practices-(2025-07).pdf — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Permitted disposal routes (secured receptacle, compliant with state/local law). R. 420.211(6): (a) a licensed municipal solid waste landfill; (b) a registered composting facility with specific approval under NREPA Part 115, MCL 324.11501–324.11554, to accept the material; (c) an anaerobic digester with specific Part 115 approval to accept the material; (d) an in-state municipal solid waste or hazardous waste incinerator permitted under NREPA Part 55, MCL 324.5501–324.5542. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.211) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Wastewater. R. 420.211(7): "A licensee shall dispose of wastewater generated during the cultivation of marihuana and the processing of marihuana products in a manner that complies with applicable state and local laws and regulations." No cannabis-specific wastewater standard is stated in R. 420.211 itself; discharge permitting is under EGLE/NREPA and local sewer authority (see §11.6.1).
  • Destruction clocks. General: R. 420.502(6) — destroy all product required to be destroyed for any reason within 90 calendar days of when the business became aware it must be destroyed. Failed batches: R. 420.305(6) — destroy the entire batch and document in Metrc within 90 calendar days (see §11.1.4). Returned product: R. 420.214c(2)(b) — destroy within 90 calendar days of awareness (see §11.1.5). Destruction areas must be camera-recorded (R. 420.209(6)(a)(vii)) and waste disposed of in a secured waste receptacle (R. 420.211(6); enforced as R. 420.211(6) in CRA complaints, e.g. DKB2 LLC, July 2024).
  • Event and consumption-establishment waste. R. 420.211(10)–(12): a microbusiness/Class A microbusiness/retailer participating in a temporary event destroys its own event waste under the rule; otherwise the event organiser is responsible for destroying/disposing of all event waste under the rule and applicable state/local law; a designated consumption establishment destroys/disposes of product left at the establishment and plant waste under the rule and maintains a waste log (description, amount, manner of disposal) available to the agency on request. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No "waste hauler licence" was located. No R. 420 rule creates a licensed marihuana-waste hauler category; disposal is by the licensee through the permitted routes above. Whether a third-party waste contractor needs any EGLE registration for the route it operates is an EGLE question, [VERIFY] with EGLE before engaging a contractor.

11.6 Environmental rules: water, pesticide limits, energy

11.6.1 Water

  • State rule anchor is general, not cannabis-specific. R. 420.211(7) (wastewater disposed of in compliance with applicable state/local law, §11.5) is the only water provision in the R. 420 operations rules read. There is no R. 420 water-use limit, irrigation standard, or runoff standard located in this run.
  • Water withdrawals (EGLE, general law). Under Michigan's water-withdrawal framework (NREPA Part 327, MCL 324.32701 et seq., as summarised in the Michigan Bar Journal article on cannabis water issues), new or increased large-quantity withdrawals — greater than a daily average of 100,000 gallons per day in any consecutive 30-day period supplying a common distribution system — must be registered with the Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE) using the Water Withdrawal Assessment Tool (WWAT), which evaluates location, amount/rate and source. Source: http://www.michbar.org/file/barjournal/article/documents/pdf4article4185.pdf (Michigan Bar Journal, June 2021, "water supply and groundwater discharge concerns") — accessed 2026-10-28. The 100,000-gallon threshold is a general Michigan threshold, not a cannabis rule; a cannabis grower below it is not thereby exempt from local water/sewer rules, and a grower above it must complete the EGLE process. Whether any Michigan cannabis facility has registered a large-quantity withdrawal, and whether EGLE has issued any cannabis-specific water guidance, is [UNAVAILABLE] in this run.
  • Discharge permits. Direct discharge of pollutants to surface waters requires a permit (NPDES/state discharge permit via EGLE); secondary reporting (Great Lakes Echo, June 2019, citing the former DEQ marijuana working group) stated EGLE had not issued discharge permits to growers at that date and that nutrient/chemical runoff into wetlands/waterways was the principal concern, with an estimate of up to six gallons per plant per day for water use. Source: http://greatlakesecho.org/2019/06/21/growing-green-michigan-marijuana-presents-water-air-and-energy-challenges/ — accessed 2026-10-28. The "no discharge permits" statement is a 2019 snapshot and must not be presented as current without an EGLE re-check — [VERIFY].
  • Sewer discharge. Cultivation/processing wastewater discharged to a municipal sewer is governed by the local sewer authority's ordinance/pretreatment rules and by R. 420.211(7); no statewide cannabis sewer standard was located. Do not state a statewide sewer limit.

11.6.2 Pesticides — approved list, banned list, testing consequence

  • Two CRA lists, required by rule. R. 420.206(3): "The agency shall publish a list of approved chemical residue active ingredients for cultivators to use in the cultivation and production of marihuana plants and marihuana products to be sold or transferred in accordance with the acts or these rules." R. 420.206(4): "The agency shall publish a list of banned chemical residue active ingredients that are prohibited from use in the cultivation and production of marihuana plants and marihuana products to be sold or transferred in accordance with the acts or these rules." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.206) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • The lists themselves — [VERIFY] current editions. The current CRA approved/banned lists were not opened as PDFs in this run; the only banned-list document returned was a 2018-era LARA/BMMR technical bulletin (representative, expressly "not intended to be exhaustive," warning that non-listing does not authorise use). Source: https://komornlaw.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Department_Banned_Pesticide_Active_Ingredient_List_620039_7.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Do not reproduce the 2018 list as current. Examples of banned residues that have actually failed Michigan tests and triggered recalls, as reported (not as a list): bifenthrin, bifenazate, permethrin/permethrins, myclobutanil, paclobutrazol (Flight vapes, §11.1.5); bifenazate (RSO syringe recall, secondary report); cadmium/arsenic/total chromium are heavy metals, not pesticides, and are listed here only to prevent conflation. Source: https://cannabislaw.report/michigan-marijuana-regulatory-agency-issues-recall-after-testing-finds-banned-pesticides-heavy-metals-in-medical-cannabis-products/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • MDARD pesticide lists (hemp and marijuana). MDARD's Pesticide and Plant Pest Management Division states it "has developed lists of pesticides approved for use on hemp and marijuana," updated periodically, with a new product added by evaluation request form plus label review (label language appropriateness and toxicological assessment). Source: https://www.michigan.gov/mdard/licensing/pesticide/pestregistration — accessed 2026-10-28. The MDARD "Michigan Marijuana Pesticide List" and "Michigan Hemp Pesticide List" PDFs themselves were not opened in this run — [VERIFY] the current lists on the MDARD page before quoting any product as approved.
  • Federal overlay (why the lists are narrow). Because cannabis has no established food/feed tolerances under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, most EPA-registered pesticides are not labelled for cannabis; in practice cultivators are generally limited to FIFRA §25(b) minimum-risk exempt products (e.g. rosemary oil, peppermint oil, citric acid as active ingredients meeting EPA tolerance exemptions) unless the CRA/MDARD list specifically permits another product. That framing is secondary (https://legalclarity.org/michigan-outdoor-cannabis-cultivation-rules-compliance-guide/ — accessed 2026-10-28) and is stated as practice, not as a Michigan rule. A failed chemical-residue test fails the batch (R. 420.305(10)–(11)) and, by default, requires destruction within 90 days unless the R. 420.306 route is followed (§11.1.4).
  • No numeric pesticide "limit" table is reproduced here. Action limits and LOQs are agency-published lists (R. 420.305(10)–(11)); the current numeric table was not opened in this run — [VERIFY] against the CRA action-limit/LOQ publications before quoting any ppm/ppb figure. Any secondary table of Michigan pesticide action limits found in a later pass must be checked against the CRA publication, not adopted from a vendor summary.

11.6.3 Energy — no statewide cannabis energy mandate was located

  • No R. 420 energy rule. No provision in the R. 420 operations, cultivation or building rules read imposes an energy-efficiency standard, a lighting-efficiency standard, a renewable-energy percentage, or an energy-reporting duty on licensed cannabis businesses. Building/fire rules (R. 420.208; NFPA 1 adopted by reference) and the Michigan building/electrical codes govern safety of electrical installations, not energy efficiency of cultivation.
  • Local energy rules exist in at least one city — local, not state. Secondary reporting states Ann Arbor, Washtenaw County, requires cannabis cultivators to generate at least 10% of power from on-site solar panels (in a list of local energy responses alongside Boulder, Colorado, and Arcata/Riverside, California). Source: https://gemstatepatriot.com/blog/the-real-costs-of-marijuana-legalization-vote-no/ (advocacy secondary source, undated in extract) — accessed 2026-10-28. That Ann Arbor claim is [VERIFY] against the City of Ann Arbor ordinance before publication; it is included here only to show that energy rules, where they exist, are municipal. Do not present any statewide renewable percentage.
  • Utility / safety practice. The CRA has worked with major utilities and state agencies on home-grow electrical safety (sizing service, licensed electrical contractor — §11.3.4), and commercial operators commonly use LED lighting and solar offsets as business practice (e.g. a Dimondale, Ingham County, operator's LED + Lansing Board of Water & Light solar partnership, as reported in 2019). Source: http://greatlakesecho.org/2019/06/21/growing-green-michigan-marijuana-presents-water-air-and-energy-challenges/ — accessed 2026-10-28. Practice is not a mandate.
  • Air emissions. No R. 420 air-emission standard (e.g. odour, VOC from extraction) was located in the rules read. Extraction equipment may need an EGLE air permit depending on emissions, and municipalities commonly impose odour controls by ordinance (Run 1 local-rules research); both are [VERIFY] facility-by-facility. Do not state a statewide odour or VOC limit.

11.7 Sampling, giveaways, discounts and promotions

11.7.1 Consumer purchase limits that bound every giveaway/discount (locked Run 1 figures, re-confirmed in rule text)

R. 420.506, re-read in this run, verbatim in substance: - Medical, per day (R. 420.506(1)): patient — "an amount of marihuana product that does not, in total, exceed 2.5 ounces of marihuana or marihuana equivalent per day"; caregiver — 2.5 oz or equivalent per day for each connected patient. - Medical, per month (R. 420.506(2)): "the monthly purchasing limit of 10 ounces of marihuana product per month to a qualifying patient, either directly or through the qualifying patient's registered primary caregiver," verified in Metrc before sale. - Adult-use, per single transaction (R. 420.506(3)): a retailer "is prohibited from making a sale or transferring marihuana to an adult 21 years of age or older in a single transaction that exceeds 2.5 ounces. Not more than 15 grams of marihuana may be in the form of marihuana concentrate." - Immature plants (R. 420.506(4)): a sales location may sell no more than 3 immature plants to a customer per transaction. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.506) — accessed 2026-10-28. Wording note (not a figure change): R. 420.506(2) says "per month"; Run 1 states the medical limit as "10 oz per 30 days." Adopt the rule wording ("per month") for the compiled dossier and treat "30 days" as Run 1's paraphrase of the monthly limit (see Research Notes C-04). Equivalency note: the R. 420.506 text read does not itself state the 16 oz solid / 36 fl oz liquid = 1 oz ratios; those ratios are carried forward from Run 1 §1.3.2 (MMMA equivalency as reproduced in bill/rule summaries) and remain [VERIFY] as to their current rule/guidance home — the per-transaction equivalents they imply (2.5 oz × 16 = 40 oz solid; 2.5 oz × 36 = 90 fl oz liquid) are arithmetically consistent with secondary per-transaction tables (e.g. Cova: solid edibles 40 oz, liquid edibles/beverages 90 fl oz per transaction), which is corroboration, not a rule citation. Source for the secondary table: https://www.covasoftware.com/us-dispensary-laws/Michigan — accessed 2026-10-28. No daily adult-use cap in R. 420.506 as read: the adult-use limit is per single transaction, not per day. Possession limits (2.5 oz outside the residence; 10 oz + home-grown product inside, MRTMA §5) still apply at any one time, and a retailer that knowingly facilitates evasion by splitting transactions risks discipline — the Muha Meds Ypsilanti revocation (1 October 2026, §11.2.6) turned in part on splitting transactions to bypass oversale warnings. Splitting a sale to evade a limit is therefore a discipline risk even though the rule states a per-transaction limit.

11.7.2 Trade samples — R. 420.508 (current rule; draft renumbering is NOT law)

  • Who may give trade samples, and to whom. R. 420.508(1): (a) a cultivator may transfer trade samples to a producer or a sales location; (b) a producer may transfer trade samples to a producer or sales location. Trade samples may not go to consumers/patients (see (3) below). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-508 (history: 2020 AACS; 2022 MR 5, eff. 3/7/2022) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No transporter needed below a threshold. R. 420.508(2): transfer does not require a secure transporter under MMFLA/MRTMA if the amount does not exceed 15 ounces of marihuana or 60 grams of marihuana concentrate (either threshold; the rule states them as alternatives).
  • No onward sale/transfer by the recipient. R. 420.508(3): trade samples "must not be sold or transferred by the receiving producer or marihuana sales location to another producer or marihuana sales location or to a consumer."
  • Metrc + testing + labelling. R. 420.508(4)–(5), (7): every trade-sample transfer/receipt recorded in Metrc; samples must be tested under the rules before transfer to a producer/sales location; label must bear, in addition to R. 420.403 information, the statement "TRADE SAMPLE NOT FOR RESALE" in bold, capital letters.
  • 30-day aggregate caps on giving. R. 420.508(6): a cultivator and producer are limited to transferring, in aggregate to a producer or sales location in a 30-day period: (a) 2.5 ounces of marihuana; (b) 15 grams of marihuana concentrate. (Note the distinction: 15 oz/60 g is the per-transfer transporter threshold; 2.5 oz/15 g is the 30-day aggregate giving cap. Do not conflate them.)
  • Onward distribution to the recipient's employees. R. 420.508(8): a receiving producer/sales location may distribute the trade sample to its employees to determine whether to purchase the product, limited to 1 ounce of marihuana, 6 grams of concentrate, and infused products with total THC of 2,000 mg to each employee in a 30-day period. (That employee-distribution cap is the same as the internal-sample cap in §11.7.3, but the two rules are distinct: R. 420.508(8) is distribution of a received trade sample; R. 420.509 is the licensee's own internal samples.)
  • Draft-rule warning. The CRA draft rules guide states current R. 420.508 trade-sample provisions would move to draft R. 420.408 and draft R. 420.508 would become an advertising rule (marihuana not treated with radiation/gas/radio-frequency/chemical/thermal processing). Source: https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Laws-Rules-Other-Resources/Draft-Marihuana-Rules_Guide-to-Changes.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. That guide describes proposed changes only; current law is R. 420.508 as above.

11.7.3 Internal product samples — R. 420.509

  • Who and why. R. 420.509(1): a cultivator, producer, sales location, microbusiness or Class A microbusiness may transfer internal product samples directly to its employees for ensuring product quality and making determinations about whether to sell the product. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.509) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • No onward transfer/sale. R. 420.509(2): internal samples may not be transferred or sold to another licensee or consumer.
  • Metrc + testing. R. 420.509(3), (7): record the transfer in Metrc; have internal samples tested under R. 420.304/R. 420.305 before transfer to employees.
  • 30-day per-employee caps. Cultivator (R. 420.509(4)): 1 ounce per employee per 30 days. Producer (R. 420.509(5)): 6 grams of concentrate and infused products with total THC of 2,000 mg per employee per 30 days. Sales location / microbusiness / Class A microbusiness (R. 420.509(6)): 1 ounce of marihuana, 6 grams of concentrate, and infused products with total THC of 2,000 mg per employee per 30 days.
  • Product development. R. 420.510: only a cultivator or producer may engage in product development; designated plants count toward the cultivator's authorised plant total and must be tracked in Metrc; designated concentrate must be tracked; product-development inventory may be submitted for R&D testing (no discipline for failed R&D results on that inventory); it may be transferred to employees for consumption only after R. 420.304/R. 420.305 testing, counts toward the R. 420.509 caps, must be recorded in Metrc, may not be consumed/used on the licensee's premises, and may not be transferred/sold to a sales location or customer until it passes full compliance testing and is labelled under R. 420.504. A cultivator/producer may also engage in a research study with a DEA-authorised entity, with agency approval, tracking all product in Metrc (R. 420.510(11)) — see §11.9. Source: same (R. 420.510) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.7.4 Consumer giveaways, donations and discounts — what the rules do and do not say

  • Giveaways to consumers are not prohibited by a price rule, but they are capped transactions. CRA Compliance Best Practice Guide (July 2025), as reproduced in secondary compilation: "The administrative rules do not require specific pricing for marijuana products. If a sales location or microbusiness chooses to provide marijuana product to customers at no cost, the transaction must be recorded in Metrc and cannot exceed the purchasing limits." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/authoritative-documents/CRA_Compliance-Best-Practices-(2025-07).pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA guide itself; the guide is CRA guidance, not rule text]. Consequences: a "$0" giveaway is still a Metrc sale/transfer subject to R. 420.505 verification (ID, hold/recall check, testing, labelling, purchase limit) and to R. 420.506 limits. A giveaway recorded under a fictitious customer account, or split across fictitious accounts to evade limits, is a violation — the Muha Meds Ypsilanti matter (October 2026 final order, §11.2.6) included fictitious "Chris Peterson" accounts used to process promotional giveaways, product samples and other transfers so transactions were not accurately associated with actual recipients in Metrc, plus 887 vape cartridges given to social-media influencers and failures to verify ID and report criminal activity. Source: https://themarijuanaherald.com/2026/10/michigan-marijuana-social-media-influencers/ — accessed 2026-10-28 (secondary report of the CRA final order; [VERIFY] against the order).
  • Donations (business-to-business-to-consumer). Same guide, as reproduced: "All cultivators, producers, and microbusiness license types may designate marijuana or marijuana products that they hold in their inventory for donation to retailers, who in turn can donate to consumers. To use this functionality in Metrc, please follow the instructions found here." Source: same guide compilation — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the CRA guide / Metrc donation instructions]. Donated product is still tested product, still Metrc-tracked, and still subject to the consumer purchase limit at the point of donation to the consumer. No rule text creating a "donation licence" or a donation tax exemption was located.
  • Discounts and promotions — no R. 420 price floor, cap, or "no discount" rule was located. No rule in R. 420.501–R. 420.511 as read prohibits discounts, loyalty pricing, bundle pricing, or promotional pricing as such. Three adjacent constraints do apply and must not be confused with a discount ban: 1. Tax bundling: MRTMA §13(2), MCL 333.27963(2) — a product subject to the 10% excise "may not be bundled in a single transaction with a product or service that is not subject to the tax" except as a Treasury rule allows (Run 1 §2.2). A "buy marihuana, get a free non-marihuana item" bundle in one transaction therefore needs Treasury-rule cover, not just a marketing decision. 2. Wholesale-price integrity: for the 24% wholesale tax, the wholesale price for unaffiliated transactions is the actual price paid including any tax/fee/charge on the invoice and "may not be reduced by rebates, discounts or trade allowances" (2025 PA 23, Run 1 §§0.1, 2.4). A retail discount does not reduce the wholesale tax base; a wholesale discount does not either, on the enrolled summary. 3. Advertising: discounts/promotions advertised must comply with R. 420.507 (see §11.7.5) — 30% audience test, warnings, no youth appeal, no deceptive/false/misleading claims, no unapproved health claims. A promotion that advertises potency, pricing or promotional offers in a way that violates R. 420.507, or that targets under-21 / under-17 audiences, is an advertising violation even if the price itself is lawful. (A secondary advertising summary's statement "You cannot advertise pricing, promotional offers, or potency" (https://www.mediajel.com/cannabis-advertising-laws/michigan — accessed 2026-10-28) is not a rule-text proposition located in R. 420.507 as read and is not adopted; R. 420.507 as read prohibits deceptive/false/misleading advertising and unapproved health claims, and imposes audience/warning conditions — it does not impose a blanket ban on advertising price or potency. [VERIFY] whether any CRA bulletin imposes a narrower pricing/potency advertising restriction before publishing either version.)
  • Gifting between adults (non-commercial). MRTMA §5(1)(d), MCL 333.27955(1)(d): an adult 21+ may "giv[e] away or otherwise transfer[] without remuneration up to 2.5 ounces of marihuana, except that not more than 15 grams of marihuana may be in the form of marihuana concentrate, to a person 21 years of age or older, as long as the transfer is not advertised or promoted to the public." That is a personal-use gifting right, not a licensee promotion right; a licensee "giveaway" advertised to the public is a commercial transfer under R. 420.505/R. 420.506, not a §5(1)(d) gift. Source: Run 1 §1.3.1 — carried forward unchanged.
  • Influencer transfers. Transfers to social-media influencers are transfers to consumers (or, if the influencer is not a licensee, unlicensed distribution) unless they fit a lawful category (a Metrc-recorded consumer transaction within purchase limits, or an employee-sample transfer to an actual employee). The Muha Meds matter (hundreds of cartridges to influencers, June–July 2025, as found in the October 2026 final order) is the enforcement illustration that influencer product is not a free category. Do not describe influencer seeding as permitted "marketing samples" — trade samples go only to producers/sales locations (§11.7.2), internal samples only to the licensee's own employees (§11.7.3).

11.7.5 Advertising and promotions — R. 420.507 (current rule)

  • R. 420.507(1): advertising/marketing only in compliance with applicable municipal sign/advertising ordinances, state law and the rules.
  • R. 420.507(2): no deceptive, false or misleading advertising, assertions or statements on any product, sign or document.
  • R. 420.507(3): no health or health-benefits claim unless a qualified health claim complies with an FDA Letter of Enforcement Discretion or has been approved under the FDA significant-scientific-agreement standard.
  • R. 420.507(4): marketing/advertising only where the advertiser has reliable evidence that no more than 30% of the audience/readership for the TV programme, radio programme, website or print publication is reasonably expected to be under the age in subrules (7)–(8); advertised/marketed product must include the warnings in R. 420.504(1)(j).
  • R. 420.507(5): a person receiving reasonable payment under an agency-approved IP licensing agreement is responsible for marketing/advertising undertaken by either party to the agreement.
  • R. 420.507(6)–(9): MMFLA product marketed as "medical marihuana" for registered patients/caregivers only; must not be marketed/advertised to minors aged 17 years or younger (sponsorships targeting ≤17 prohibited); MRTMA product marketed as "marihuana" for individuals 21+ only; must not be marketed/advertised to individuals under 21 (sponsorships targeting under-21 prohibited). Version note (Run 1 §1.6.2, unchanged): a 2025 draft version uses "less than 18 years" for medical advertising; the current rule text read says "17 years or younger." Adopt the current text; the draft is not law.
  • R. 420.507(10) (as reproduced in Run 1 §1.6.2 from draft/secondary sources): advertising/marketing must include the warnings listed in R. 420.405(2)(m) in the draft numbering — the current-text equivalent located in this run is R. 420.507(4)'s reference to R. 420.504(1)(j) warnings. Cite R. 420.504(1)(j) for warnings in the compiled dossier, not R. 420.405(2)(m), unless the official PDF shows otherwise [VERIFY]. Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.507) — accessed 2026-10-28.

11.8 Drug testing and background checks for licence holders and employees

11.8.1 Licence holders and applicants — fingerprint-based background checks (Step 1)

  • Applicants/supplemental applicants. CRA Step 1 prequalification instructions (Run 1 §4.0, §4.12): background checks are completed on the main applicant and all supplemental applicants; fingerprints are taken only after CRA notification — pre-notification fingerprint records are not accepted. The $3,000 application fee is for the main applicant only and is nonrefundable. Source: https://www.michigan.gov/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Adult-Use-Establishment-Licensing/Adult-Use-Paper-Application-Forms-and-Resources/Paper-Application-Instructions/Step-1---Supplemental-Individual-Prequalification-Application-Instructions.pdf (Run 1, accessed 2026-10-28) — carried forward; the instruction sheet was not re-opened in this run, so any 2026 change to fingerprint procedure is [VERIFY].
  • Applicant ineligibility — MRTMA (R. 420.6). An applicant is ineligible for a state licence under MRTMA if: (a) prior conviction involving distribution of a controlled substance to a minor; (b) knowingly submitted an application containing false information; (c) is an employee, advisor or consultant of the agency involved in MRTMA implementation/administration/enforcement (MRTMA §7, MCL 333.27957); (d) holds elective office / is a member of or employed by a regulatory body / is employed by a governmental unit in Michigan, another state or the federal government — subject to exceptions for (i) elected officers/employees of federally recognised Indian tribes, (ii) elected precinct delegates, (iii) spouses unless the spouse's position creates a conflict or is within the Marijuana Regulatory Agency (and further listed bodies, text truncated in the source read — [VERIFY] the full spouse exception on Cornell/Justia). Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-6 — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Applicant ineligibility — MMFLA (MCL 333.27402(2)). An applicant is ineligible if: (a) convicted of or released from incarceration for a felony (any jurisdiction) within the past 10 years, or convicted of a controlled-substance-related felony within the past 10 years — except a felony for manufacture/processing/distribution of marihuana or possession with intent, unless it involved distribution to a minor; (b) within the past 5 years convicted of a misdemeanour involving a controlled substance, theft, dishonesty or fraud, or found responsible for a corresponding local-ordinance violation — except a misdemeanour/ordinance violation for possession or use of marihuana; (c) knowingly submitted false information; (d) is an employee of the Marijuana Regulatory Agency; (e) fails to demonstrate ability to maintain adequate premises liability and casualty insurance. Source: https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27402/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against legislature.mi.gov].
  • Medical employee 10-year rule (statute, distinct from applicant rule). MMFLA §405, MCL 333.27405 (as summarised in Run 1 §1.8 and in secondary employment guidance): a business may not employ a person with a pending charge or conviction for a controlled-substance felony within 10 years without CRA written permission. Source: https://legalclarity.org/michigan-dispensary-jobs-rules-for-felons/ (secondary summary citing MCL 333.27405) — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY against the statute text].
  • No "licence-holder drug test" was located. No R. 420 rule requires applicants, owners or supplemental applicants to pass a drug test (as opposed to a criminal-history/fingerprint background check) as a condition of licensure. Do not state one.

11.8.2 Employees — criminal-history background check, excluded list, age, training (R. 420.602)

  • Pre-hire background check. R. 420.602(1): "A licensee shall conduct a criminal history background check on any prospective employee before hiring that individual. A licensee shall keep records of the results of the criminal history background checks for the duration of the employee's employment with the licensee. A licensee shall record confirmation of criminal history background checks and make the confirmation available for inspection upon request by the agency." Source: https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ (R. 420.602) — accessed 2026-10-28. Fingerprinting for ordinary employees: R. 420.602 as read says "criminal history background check" and does not specify fingerprinting for employees (fingerprinting is the Step 1 applicant process, §11.8.1). Whether the CRA in practice requires fingerprint-based checks for employees in any category is [VERIFY] against CRA employee instructions; do not state employee fingerprinting as a rule requirement on the basis of R. 420.602 alone.
  • Reporting and excluded list. R. 420.602(2)(a): the licensee must have a policy requiring employees to report new/pending criminal charges or convictions; if an employee is charged with or convicted of a controlled-substance-related felony or any other felony, the licensee must immediately report it to the agency; if an MRTMA employee is convicted of distribution of a controlled substance to a minor, the licensee must immediately report it; "The agency shall maintain a list of excluded employees." R. 420.602(2)(g): screen prospective employees against the excluded-employees list maintained under R. 420.808a(6). Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Permanent employment bar (adult-use). R. 420.602(2)(k) (as reproduced in the compilation's employee rule): "A licensee under the MRMTA shall not employ any individual who has been convicted of an offense involving distribution of a controlled substance to a minor." No time limit and no exception mechanism appears in the rule text read — consistent with Run 1 §1.8. If a licensee learns of such a conviction after hiring, it must immediately notify the CRA (R. 420.602(2)(a)). Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Age bars. R. 420.602(2)(j): an MRTMA licensee "shall not allow a person under 21 years of age to volunteer or work for the marihuana establishment pursuant to section 11 of the MRTMA, MCL 333.27961." (Medical employee age is governed by MMFLA provisions and the general 21+ rule for adult-use establishments; no separate medical employee age was located in R. 420.602 as read — [VERIFY] if the compiled dossier needs a medical employee age statement.)
  • Metrc access timing — discrepancy to resolve. R. 420.602(2)(b): enter employee information and Metrc access level within 7 business days of hiring for the system to assign an employee ID; update information/status/access changes within 7 business days. R. 420.602(2)(c): remove employee access/permissions to the business and Metrc within 7 business days after termination. Run 1 §1.7 summarised a general-operations rule as "within 10 days after hiring / 10 days after a change / 10 days after employment ends" (R. 420.201c as reproduced in draft materials). The 7-business-day figures in current R. 420.602 are adopted here for employee Metrc records; the 10-day summary is treated as either a different rule (R. 420.201c) or a draft/older version — [VERIFY] R. 420.201c against the official PDF and reconcile before publication (see Research Notes C-05).
  • Training manual and responsible operations plan. R. 420.602(2)(d)–(f): train employees under an employee training manual (kept and available to the agency) covering employee safety procedures, employee guidelines, security protocol, and educational training (product information; dosage and purchasing limits if applicable; educational materials). An MRTMA business selling/transfers to 21+ individuals must include a responsible operations plan explaining how employees will monitor/prevent over-intoxication, underage access, illegal sale/distribution within the establishment, and potential criminal activity on the premises. Point-of-sale/transfer procedures for sales-location employees must cover dosage training, product information, health/educational materials, point-of-sale training, purchasing limits, CBD/THC information, serving size, and consumption information including warnings. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Other employee rules. R. 420.602(2)(h): employees must handle product in compliance with Current Good Manufacturing Practice, Hazard Analysis and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food, 21 CFR part 1107, as specified in the rules (note: the compilation prints "part 1107"; the food CGMP/HARPC rule is 21 CFR part 117 — treat "1107" as a compilation/printing error and cite part 117 only after verifying against the official PDF [VERIFY]). R. 420.602(2)(i): a registered primary caregiver hired as a grower/processor/secure-transporter employee under MMFLA must withdraw their caregiver registration as established by the agency. R. 420.602(5): no food/beverage consumption by employees/visitors where product is stored/processed/packaged or hazardous materials are used/handled/stored, except in a designated area separated by floor-to-ceiling walls and a door. R. 420.602(6)–(7): trade/professional service providers not normally engaged in operating the business, and visitors generally, must be reasonably monitored, logged in as visitors, and escorted through limited-access areas; visitors are prohibited where hazardous materials are used/handled/stored. R. 420.602(3): a person present at the business or in a transporter vehicle who is not identified as a licensee/employee in Metrc, or who violates the acts/rules, may be subject to agency action (authorised escorted visitors excepted). R. 420.602(4): employee records are subject to agency inspection/examination. Source: same — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Employee drug testing (general employment) — no protection, no mandate located. Run 1 §1.8, unchanged: Michigan has no statute prohibiting a private employer from pre-employment, random, post-accident or reasonable-suspicion drug testing for marihuana, and no statute requiring accommodation of off-duty use. MRTMA §4(3), MCL 333.27954(3), expressly preserves employer discipline/refusal to hire/discharge for violation of a workplace drug policy or working under the influence. MMMA §7(c)(2), MCL 333.26427(c)(2), expressly does not require an employer to accommodate ingestion in the workplace or an employee working under the influence; Michigan courts have not read MMMA §4(a) as creating a right to at-will employment or barring termination for a positive test. No R. 420 rule was located requiring licensees to drug-test their employees (as opposed to background-checking them). A licensee may therefore drug-test under its own workplace policy within general Michigan employment law, but must not be described as CRA-required to do so. Federal safety-sensitive / DOT testing is unaffected by state law; whether DOT drug testing applies to any particular transporter driver (chauffeur-licence holders, §11.4.2) depends on vehicle size/weight and interstate/intrastate commercial-vehicle status and is [VERIFY] with the Michigan State Police Commercial Vehicle Enforcement / FMCSA rules — do not assert DOT testing applies to all Michigan cannabis drivers.
  • No employee licence/registration card was located. Michigan does not issue a separate "budtender licence" or employee registration card in the rules read; employees are Metrc-identified (employee ID assigned by the system, R. 420.602(2)(b)) and background-checked/screened by the licensee. Do not describe a Michigan employee licence. (Delivery employees carry an employee identification number under R. 420.207(7)(a) — that is a Metrc/employment identifier, not a separate state licence.)

11.9 Research and university cannabis and hemp licences

11.9.1 MRTMA marihuana educational research licence (the state licence)

  • Licence type and term. R. 420.21(1)(e): "Marihuana educational research license. A marihuana educational research license is valid for 1 year." It is a "special license" under MRTMA §8, MCL 333.27958, issued under MRTMA §9, MCL 333.27959 (R. 420.21(1)). An applicant must meet MRTMA and rule requirements to be eligible (R. 420.21(2)). Fee: N/A in R. 420.7 Table 1 (no fee listed); no $3,000 application fee is shown for this type in Table 1. Source: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-21 and https://regulations.justia.com/states/michigan/licensing-and-regulatory-affairs/marijuana-regulatoty-agency/marihuana-licenses/section-r-420-7/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Count — 1 active licence (locked Run 1 figure, stable across two snapshots). CRA September 2025 monthly report (directly opened in Run 1): 1 adult-use educational research licence active at 30 September 2025. August 2026 secondary-routed count (CannBus citing CRA via Herald): 1. Source: Run 1 §5.2; https://www.cannbus.org/cannmir/mi_cannmir.html — accessed 2026-10-28 [VERIFY the holder against CRA weekly reports / MiCLEAR — the monthly reports give counts, not names, and the holder's identity is not stated here because no official source publishing it was opened in this run].
  • Eligibility and application details — [VERIFY]. No CRA educational-research instruction sheet was opened in Run 1 or in this run. Whether the licence is open to any educational institution, requires accreditation, limits plant counts, or authorises sale/transfer (vs research possession only) is not stated in the rule text read and must not be assumed. In particular, do not assume the single active licence is held by Michigan State University or the University of Michigan — that identification was not verified (see §§11.9.2–11.9.3). Follow-up: CRA educational-research instruction sheet / application form (see Research Notes).

11.9.2 University research — Michigan State University (East Lansing, Ingham County) and University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Washtenaw County)

  • What was verified: both universities are recipients of Veteran Marijuana Research Grant Program funding (see §11.9.3) and both conduct cannabinoid research under federal/state constraints, but neither university's holding of a CRA marihuana educational research licence, nor any university-specific cannabis licence, was verified in this run. University cannabis research in Michigan operates at the intersection of (a) the state MRTMA educational research licence (above, holder unverified), (b) federal DEA Schedule I researcher registration for marihuana research (required for delta-9-THC compounds, as described by Michigan State University pharmacology/toxicology researchers in secondary reporting — see below), and (c) FDA-approved clinical-trial sponsorship for VMR-funded trials. Those three tracks must not be conflated: a VMR grant does not itself confer a CRA licence, and a CRA licence does not itself confer DEA registration or FDA trial approval.
  • Michigan State University. Secondary reporting (The State News, Michigan State University student newspaper, April 2022) describes MSU pharmacology/toxicology laboratory work with cannabis compounds, notes that obtaining delta-9-THC for research requires a Schedule I DEA licence with protocols, funding disclosure and substantial paperwork, and describes a state inspection expectation for research-compound storage (a 700-pound refrigerated safe required to be bolted/chained to floor or wall, with photographs of securing). The same reporting notes few dedicated cannabis classes in the pharmacology/toxicology department and no identified faculty move to create cannabis-focused degree programmes at that date. Source: https://statenews.com/article/2022/04/few-options-at-msu-for-prospective-cannabis-students?ct=content_open&amp;cv=cbox_latest — accessed 2026-10-28 (secondary, 2022 — stale for current programme claims; do not present its programme description as current). No MSU CRA licence, MSU hemp licence, or MSU cannabis research facility licence was located — [UNAVAILABLE] in this run; follow up with MSU's research office / CRA licence verification before naming MSU as a licence holder.
  • University of Michigan. The University of Michigan has a Center for Cannabis Research (secondary summary, undated, via StateRegstoday) described as expanding knowledge on medical cannabis through studies and educational events for healthcare professionals and the public. Source: https://www.stateregstoday.com/health/marijuana-legalization/research-and-development-in-michigan — accessed 2026-10-28 (secondary, undated — [VERIFY] against the University of Michigan's own centre page). Separately, University of Michigan researchers are VMR grant recipients for CBD-in-chronic-pain / veteran-suicide-risk research (§11.9.3). No University of Michigan CRA educational research licence was verified — [UNAVAILABLE] in this run on the same basis as MSU. Note also the federal-property overlay: University of Michigan facilities receiving federal funding remain subject to federal prohibition, and campus policy prohibits marihuana use/possession on campus notwithstanding state legalisation (secondary legal summary, https://easthopelaw.com/practice-areas/possession-of-marijuana-cannabis/ — accessed 2026-10-28) — that is a campus/federal-compliance point, not a CRA licensing point, and must be cited as such if used.
  • Other research routes in the rules (not university-specific). R. 420.510(11): a cultivator/producer may participate in a research study with an entity duly authorised by the DEA to handle marihuana, with agency approval, tracking all product in Metrc. R. 420.307: R&D testing (see §11.1.3). R. 420.112(6): SCFs may test industrial hemp. None of these creates a university licence.

11.9.3 Veteran Marijuana Research Grant Program (MRTMA §14, MCL 333.27964)

  • Statutory basis and sunset. MRTMA §14 (MCL 333.27964), as reproduced in Run 1 §2.6: the department must expend Marihuana Regulation Fund money first for implementation/administration/enforcement, and second, "until 2022 or for at least two years, to provide $20 million annually to one or more clinical trials that are approved by the United States food and drug administration and sponsored by a nonprofit organization or researcher within an academic institution researching the efficacy of marihuana in treating the medical conditions of United States armed services veterans and preventing veteran suicide." The $20 million is therefore a time-limited, front-loaded obligation ("until 2022 or for at least two years"), NOT a permanent annual deduction — secondary summaries presenting "$20M yearly for veterans" as a current, ongoing deduction misread §14(3) (Run 1 §2.6, note 1). Whether any veterans-research appropriation continued after the two-year window is [VERIFY] against Treasury/CRA appropriations; do not assert a current $20M annual grant round.
  • Awards (2021 and 2022 rounds, $40 million total across the two years). Secondary reporting, consistent across outlets:
  • 2021 round ($20 million): $13 million to MAPS (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, California-based nonprofit) for an FDA-approved Phase 2 trial of smoked/vaporised cannabis for PTSD in veterans (FDA approval reported November 2024 for the smoked-cannabis protocol, with vaporisation on hold pending device safety evaluation; participants required to have prior inhalation experience); $7 million to Wayne State University (Detroit, Wayne County) Bureau of Community Action and Economic Opportunity, partnered research on cannabis for PTSD, anxiety, sleep disorders, depression and suicidality. Sources: https://themarijuanaherald.com/2024/11/fda-approves-landmark-study-on-smoked-marijuana-for-treating-ptsd-in-veterans/ and https://peaceloveandgas.com/uncategorized/treating-ptsd-with-cannabis-long-awaited-study-gets-fda-green-light/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • 2022 round ($20 million, recommended 21 July 2022 by the then-Marijuana Regulatory Agency after five applications totalling over $37 million, assessed by a Joint Evaluation Committee on experience/financial stability, work plan, management summary and budget/budget narrative): Wayne State University ~$12.5 million across two proposals (~$9 million + ~$3.5 million) — one described as the first randomised, controlled, large-scale trial of cannabinoids for veterans with PTSD undergoing prolonged-exposure therapy, another on neuroinflammation/neurobiology of suicide ideation in veterans with PTSD; University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, Washtenaw County) ~$7.5 million (of $12 million requested) for CBD-based capsules for chronic pain in veterans, towards reducing suicide risk. Sources: https://www.mjlink.com/crypto-and-blockchain-news/michigan-announces-20m-in-veteran-marijuana-research-grants-to-two-state-universities/amp and https://moderncannabislifestyle.com/michigan-awards-20-million-in-marijuana-tax-funded-grants-to-fund-veterans-focused-research/ — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • Combined total: "about $40 million" across the two rounds (Wayne State University, University of Michigan, MAPS) — source: https://www.cannabisevidence.org/the-state-of-michigan-supplied-40m-for-marijuana-research-in-veterans-heres-what-its-funding/ (secondary summary of Detroit News reporting) — accessed 2026-10-28. All VMR award figures above are secondary-reported; the CRA award announcements themselves were not opened in this run — [VERIFY] against CRA announcements before quoting dollar splits as CRA-confirmed. The $13M/$7M (2021) vs $12.5M/$7.5M (2022) splits are consistent across the outlets cited, but the 2022 Wayne State split ($9M + $3.5M = $12.5M) vs the rounded $12.5M total should be cited as approximate ("about") unless the CRA announcement is opened.
  • Federal Schedule III interaction (analysis, not a VMR rule change). On the fixed baseline, state-licensed medical activity moves to Schedule III, but VMR trials are FDA-approved clinical trials sponsored by nonprofits/academic institutions — a federal trial pathway that predates and is independent of the Schedule III move for state-licensed medical sales. Whether Schedule III changes DEA researcher-registration burdens for VMR-type trials is [VERIFY] against DEA/FDA guidance; do not state that Schedule III eliminates DEA registration for university marihuana research.

11.9.4 Hemp research

  • No separate "university hemp licence" was located. Hemp cultivation in Michigan is now under the USDA Domestic Hemp Production Program directly (from 1 January 2025; Run 1 §§0.4, 6.7), and hemp processing/handling/marketing remains under the CRA processor-handler regime (2014 PA 547, MCL 286.847) until/unless pending SB 599–602 passes (Run 1 §§1.5.4, 1.9). University hemp research would therefore proceed, as applicable, as a USDA-licensed producer (cultivation), a CRA processor-handler (processing/handling), and/or under the university's federal research authorisations — not under a distinct Michigan university hemp licence located in this run. MDARD's former state hemp programme reports (2021–2024) do not identify university research plots separately, and no university hemp research licence list was found — [UNAVAILABLE].
  • Hemp research under the 2014 Act. The Industrial Hemp Research and Development Act (2014 PA 547) is a research-and-development act in name, but its operative licensing in current practice is the processor-handler licence, not a research-only licence (Run 1 §1.2.5). Do not describe PA 547 as conferring a university research licence without a primary source.
  • Pending consumable-hemp package (SB 599–602). If enacted, SB 599 would create the Industrial Hemp Processing Act under the CRA and repeal PA 547 (Run 1 §§0.4, 1.9). Whether that package contains a research exemption or a university provision is [VERIFY] against the enrolled/pending bill text; it is not stated here. Status at 28 October 2026 per Run 1: passed the Senate 16 December 2025, referred to the House Committee on Regulatory Reform 17 December 2025, no later action located — not law.

12.1 Paraphernalia and smoke shop rules

12.1.1 Two different words: "marihuana accessories" (MRTMA) vs "drug paraphernalia" (Public Health Code)

Michigan law uses both terms, and they do not mean the same thing in every context: - MRTMA "marihuana accessories" is the consumer-facing term. MRTMA §4, MCL 333.27954(1)(b), provides the Act "does not authorize" transfer of marihuana or marihuana accessories to a person under 21; §4(1)(h) provides it does not authorize "possessing marihuana accessories or possessing or consuming marihuana on the grounds of a public or private school where children attend classes in preschool programs, kindergarten programs, or grades 1 through 12, in a school bus, or on the grounds of any correctional facility." A municipality may regulate "the time, place, and manner of operation … and of the production, manufacture, sale, or display of marihuana accessories" under MRTMA §6(2)(b), MCL 333.27956(2)(b), and a property owner may prohibit or regulate accessories on their property under §4(4) (see §12.6). Source: MCL 333.27954 via https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27954/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [FindLaw reproduction; official text at legislature.mi.gov to be re-checked before publication]. - Public Health Code "drug paraphernalia," MCL 333.7451, is the older, broader controlled-substance term: "any equipment, product, material, or combination of equipment, products, or materials, which is specifically designed for use in planting, propagating, cultivating, growing, harvesting, manufacturing, compounding, converting, producing, processing, preparing, testing, analyzing, packaging, repackaging, storing, containing, concealing, injecting, ingesting, inhaling, or otherwise introducing into the human body a controlled substance," with a non-exhaustive list including an object specifically designed for ingesting/inhaling marihuana, cocaine, hashish or hashish oil. Source: MCL 333.7451 as quoted in Brang Inc v. Liquor Control Commission, 910 N.W.2d 309 (2017), Court of Appeals opinion — https://www.courts.michigan.gov/siteassets/case-documents/uploads/opinions/final/coa/20170810_c333007(40)_rptr_89o-333007-final-i.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. - Sale prohibition, MCL 333.7453(1): "a person shall not sell or offer for sale drug paraphernalia, knowing that the drug paraphernalia will be used to plant, propagate, cultivate, grow, harvest, manufacture, compound, convert, produce, process, prepare, test, analyze, pack, repack, store, contain, conceal, inject, ingest, inhale, or otherwise introduce into the human body a controlled substance." Source: same Brang opinion, quoting §7453(1) — accessed 2026-10-28. The operative word is knowing — the offence turns on the seller's knowledge of the intended unlawful use, not on the object alone. How that knowledge test applies to a pipe sold for lawful adult-use marihuana, as opposed to an unlawful controlled substance, is the central tension below and is not settled by a single clean statutory carve-out located in this pass [VERIFY].

12.1.2 What is lawful for a consumer 21+ to possess and buy

  • A person 21+ lawfully possessing marihuana may possess the accessories used with it as part of that lawful use; licensed retailers and microbusinesses sell accessories as part of the licensed sales location, and MRTMA §6(2)(b) expressly contemplates municipal regulation of accessory sale/display, which presupposes lawful accessory commerce. No Michigan statute located in this pass makes mere possession of a pipe, grinder, rolling papers or vape device by a person 21+ a standalone offence when the marihuana use itself is lawful. That negative finding is limited to the sources reviewed; the paraphernalia statutes in §12.1.1 remain on the books and are the reason smoke shops operate in the grey area described in §12.1.3.
  • Under 21: transfer of accessories to a person under 21 is not authorised (MCL 333.27954(1)(b)), and a person under 21 is not authorised to possess, consume, purchase or otherwise obtain marihuana (MCL 333.27954(1)(c)). Possession of marihuana paraphernalia by a person under 21 remains the subject of local paraphernalia ordinances that track MCL 333.7451 (see §12.1.3).
  • Medical: Under MMMA §4(g) as discussed in People v. Mazur, 497 Mich. 302 (2015), an individual could claim immunity for providing a registered qualifying patient or registered primary caregiver with marijuana paraphernalia for the patient's medical use. Source: Mazur discussion as reproduced at https://arklegal.ai/state_statute/2350681/download.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary reproduction of the opinion discussion; opinion itself to be re-checked before publication]. Medical paraphernalia immunity is therefore clearer in the MMMA context than the general adult-use paraphernalia position in §12.1.1.

12.1.3 Smoke shops — no state "smoke shop licence" located; the operating model and its risks

  • No standalone state smoke-shop licence was located in this pass. A shop that sells only accessories (no marihuana, no marihuana-infused product) is not a marihuana establishment under MRTMA and not a marihuana facility under MMFLA, and therefore does not hold a CRA licence for that accessory-only trade.
