Whether any local licence (general business licence, tobacco retailer licence, zoning approval, or a municipal paraphernalia ordinance permit) is required depends on the municipality — [UNAVAILABLE] as a statewide rule; do not publish a statewide smoke-shop licensing requirement on this pass.
  • What a smoke shop may not do without a CRA licence: sell marihuana or marihuana-infused product, including intoxicating hemp-derived cannabinoids treated as marihuana since 11 Oct 2021 (2021 PA 56; Run 1 Part 1, §1.5.2). Unlicensed sale of delta-8, THCA flower and similar products from a smoke shop or gas station is unlawful in Michigan even if labelled "hemp" — see Run 1 Part 0, §0.4.
  • Paraphernalia penalties (secondary-sourced, [VERIFY] against MCL 333.7455 before publication): a secondary criminal-law summary states possession of drug paraphernalia under MCL 333.7451/333.7455(1) is a misdemeanour punishable by up to 90 days' imprisonment and/or a fine up to $5,000, and sale by a person 18+ to a person under 18 under MCL 333.7455(2) is a misdemeanour punishable by up to 1 year and/or a fine up to $7,500. Source: https://www.michigancriminalattorneysblog.com/drug-paraphernalia_ae154/ — accessed 2026-10-28. Do not publish those penalty figures as confirmed until MCL 333.7455 is read directly — the blog is the only source for the figures in this pass, and its "MCL 333.74511" citation for the sale offence is a typographical error on its face.
  • Local paraphernalia ordinances: Many Michigan municipalities have their own paraphernalia ordinances tracking MCL 333.7451, commonly with an express carve-out that the ordinance "shall not apply to the lawful use of marihuana, but shall apply to possession of marihuana paraphernalia by persons less than 21 years of age" (example: Plymouth Township ordinance as reproduced at https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/plymouthtwpmi/latest/plymouthtwp_mi/0-0-0-3939 — accessed 2026-10-28; Independence Township, Oakland County, ordinance to the same effect — https://thecitizenonline.com/articles/archives/independence-township-752/ — accessed 2026-10-28). Those are local examples, not a statewide ordinance; a consumer or shop must check the municipality's own ordinance. County is given for each example above.
  • Practical consequence, stated without legal advice: A smoke shop's lawful trade in Michigan is accessories for lawful use (and non-marihuana goods); the moment it sells marihuana product, or sells paraphernalia knowing it will be used for an unlawful controlled substance, it leaves that trade and enters CRA-licensing or paraphernalia-offence territory. The "for tobacco use only" labelling practice is a marketing claim, not a statutory safe harbour located in this pass [VERIFY].

12.1.4 Consumer penalty tiers that frame §§12.1–12.5 (MRTMA §15, MCL 333.27965)

These tiers are included here because they are the consumer-facing penalties for the conduct in this Part, and because Run 1 Part 1, §1.3.4 expressly left exact fine amounts [VERIFY]. The figures below are now sourced to the statute text as reproduced, and supersede that Run 1 caution for the tiers stated: - §27965(1) — except for a person who engaged in conduct described in §4(1)(a), (b), (c), (d), (g) or (h), a person who possesses, cultivates, delivers without remuneration, or possesses with intent to deliver not more than the §5 amount is responsible for a civil infraction, fine up to $100 and forfeiture of the marihuana. Public consumption (§4(1)(e)) and unsecured residence excess (§4(1)(i)) are not in that exclusion list, so a §4(1)(e)/(i) violation within the §5 amount falls in this $100 civil-infraction tier on the text as reproduced. Source: MCL 333.27965 as reproduced at https://www.casemine.com/act/us/644a0d2976d4ee6f6825f47b and https://law.justia.com/cases/michigan/court-of-appeals-published/2024/370138.html — accessed 2026-10-28. - §27965(2) — not more than twice the §5 amount (≤5 oz in public / ≤20 oz at residence / ≤24 plants, on the Run 1 summary): first violation civil infraction, fine up to $500 + forfeiture; second, civil infraction, fine up to $1,000 + forfeiture; third or subsequent, misdemeanour, fine up to $2,000 + forfeiture. Same sources. - §27965(4) — more than twice the §5 amount: misdemeanour, but no imprisonment unless the violation was habitual, wilful, and for a commercial purpose or involved violence. Same sources. - §27965(3) — under 21, ≤2.5 oz or ≤12 plants (except §4(1)(a), (d), (g) conduct): first violation civil infraction — under 18: fine up to $100 or community service, forfeiture, 4 hours drug education/counselling; 18–20: fine up to $100, forfeiture. Second violation — under 18: fine up to $500 or community service, forfeiture, 8 hours drug education/counselling; 18–20: fine up to $500, forfeiture. Same sources. - What these tiers do NOT cover: unlicensed sale for remuneration, sale to a minor, impaired driving, and Public Health Code felonies (MCL 333.7401/7403/7404) for over-double amounts or §4 violations excluded above are charged outside the MRTMA civil-infraction tiers. Do not present the $100 tier as the penalty for selling without a licence.

12.2 THC driving limits and impairment testing

12.2.1 Answer in one paragraph: no per se THC concentration limit — but that does NOT mean "presence is irrelevant"

Michigan has no per se THC blood-concentration limit (no ng/mL figure at or above which a driver is automatically "under the influence"), unlike its 0.08 g/100 mL blood-alcohol per se rule in MCL 257.625(1)(b). Secondary law summaries are unanimous on that negative point. Source: https://www.michiganautolaw.com/blog/2026/04/16/thc-limit-driving/ — accessed 2026-10-28 ("No. Michigan does not have a legal THC limit"). That negative point must not be read alone, because Michigan law has two separate driving tracks, and the second track is a presence offence with no impairment proof: 1. Impairment track — MCL 257.625(1)(a) (OWI): operating a vehicle while "under the influence" of marihuana (and, under MRTMA §4(1)(a), MCL 333.27954(1)(a), operating/navigating/being in physical control of a motor vehicle, aircraft, snowmobile, off-road recreational vehicle or motorboat while under the influence of marihuana is not authorised). "Under the influence" requires an effect on the person — it is not satisfied by mere presence in the body. See People v. Koon, 494 Mich. 1 (2013), §12.2.2. 2. Presence track — MCL 257.625(8) (OWPCS, "operating with presence of a controlled substance"): a person, whether licensed or not, shall not operate a vehicle upon a highway or other place open to the general public or generally accessible to motor vehicles if the person has in their body any amount of a controlled substance listed in Schedule 1 under MCL 333.7212 (Public Health Code) or a controlled substance described in MCL 333.7214(a)(iv). Source: MCL 257.625(8) as quoted at https://www.michiganlawgrad.com/operating-presence-of-controlled-substance.html and https://legalclarity.org/michigan-bac-limits-and-penalties-for-violations/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary quotations; official text at legislature.mi.gov to be re-checked before publication]. For a non-patient driver, that is a zero-tolerance presence rule: no minimum threshold and no proof of impairment is required on the statute's face. So the accurate sentence is: no THC concentration limit, but a Schedule 1 presence offence for non-patients. Any summary that says only "Michigan has no THC limit" without the §625(8) track, or only "Michigan is zero-tolerance" without the Koon patient exception and the no-concentration-limit point, is incomplete.

12.2.2 The Koon exception — registered medical patients are judged on impairment, not presence

People v. Koon, 494 Mich. 1 (2013) (unanimous, per curiam), held:

"The Michigan Vehicle Code's zero-tolerance provision, MCL 257.625(8), which is inconsistent with the MMMA, does not apply to the medical use of marijuana." "If defendant is shown to have been under the influence of marijuana, then the MMMA's protections will not apply, and the prosecution may seek to convict defendant under any statute of which he was in violation, including MCL 257.625(8)." Source: Koon as summarised at https://law.justia.com/cases/michigan/supreme-court/2013/145259.html and https://static.case.law/mich/494/case-pdfs/0001-01.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Reasoning, in brief: MMMA "medical use" includes internal possession; MMMA §7 (MCL 333.26427(b)) lists driving while under the influence as unprotected, which "clearly contemplates something more than having any amount of marijuana in one's system and requires some effect on the person"; and MMMA §10 (all other acts inconsistent with the MMMA do not apply to medical use) therefore displaces §625(8) for a compliant registered patient who is not under the influence. A registered patient who is under the influence loses that protection and may be prosecuted under §625(1) and, on the Court's words, §625(8). Limits of Koon (do not overstate): - Koon is an MMMA case. It does not by its terms extend the impairment-only standard to adult-use (MRTMA) consumers, who have no MMMA registration and no §10 displacement argument. Whether any post-2018 case extends Koon reasoning to MRTMA consumers was not located in this pass [VERIFY] — do not state that adult-use users enjoy the Koon protection. - Koon does not protect driving while under the influence for anyone, patient or not. - Metabolite nuance [VERIFY]: secondary sources state Michigan courts have held that the inactive metabolite 11-carboxy-THC is not a Schedule 1 controlled substance under MCL 333.7212, so a §625(8) prosecution cannot rest on 11-carboxy-THC alone. Source: https://www.michiganlawgrad.com/operating-presence-of-controlled-substance.html — accessed 2026-10-28. That proposition is secondary-sourced here; the Derror line of cases should be read directly before publication, and no ng/mL metabolite threshold should be quoted from it.

12.2.3 Effect of the federal Schedule III move (28 Apr 2026) on Michigan driving law — unsettled, do not overstate

  • What the federal move does not do by itself: MCL 257.625(8) points to Michigan scheduling (MCL 333.7212 / 333.7214(a)(iv)), not to the federal schedules. The federal Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana therefore does not amend the text of §625(8), and no Michigan statute or court decision located in this pass reclassifies marihuana under MCL 333.7212 in response to 91 FR 22714. Whether a court would treat federally Schedule III medical marihuana as no longer a "Schedule 1" substance for §625(8) purposes, or whether the Legislature will conform MCL 333.7212, is [VERIFY] / unsettled as of 28 Oct 2026.
  • Practical interaction: For a compliant registered patient, the question is largely academic under current law because Koon already requires impairment proof — the patient is not convicted on presence alone whether marihuana is Schedule I or III in Michigan. For an adult-use user, the federal move does not change anything: adult-use remains Schedule I federally and remains within Michigan Schedule 1 on the sources reviewed, so §625(8) presence liability on the statute's face is unchanged. No safe harbour for any driver is asserted here.
  • Implied-consent / chemical testing: Michigan's implied-consent and chemical-test provisions (MCL 257.625c–625d, blood/urine testing after arrest for OWI) are the enforcement mechanism for both tracks, but the specific test-refusal sanctions and warrant requirements for blood draws were not re-verified in this pass [VERIFY] and are not stated as figures here. Do not import another state's implied-consent penalties.

12.2.4 Roadside testing — preliminary oral fluid analysis (MSP programme), DREs, and what a roadside result is not

  • Statutory home: 2016 PA 242–243, MCL 257.625r and 257.625t, and the definition of "preliminary oral fluid analysis" in MCL 257.43b: "the on-site taking of a preliminary oral fluid test, performed by a certified drug recognition expert … from the oral fluid of [a driver] for the purpose of detecting the presence of a controlled substance." Source: https://www.michiganautolaw.com/blog/2017/11/08/roadside-drug-testing-drugged-drivers/ — accessed 2026-10-28 (quoting the statutes).
  • How it works, on the sources reviewed: Only a certified Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) participating in the programme may request a preliminary oral fluid analysis, and only where the DRE has reasonable cause to believe consumption of a controlled substance may have affected the driver's ability to operate, or that the driver had in their body any amount of a controlled substance (MCL 257.625r(1)). The test is a mouth-swab screen, administered alongside the DRE 12-step evaluation and field sobriety testing; it screens for presence, it does not prove impairment and it is not a blood THC concentration. Refusal to submit to a preliminary oral fluid analysis upon lawful request is a civil infraction (MCL 257.625r(5)). Same source.
  • Pilot history and current scope [VERIFY for current statewide status]: The pilot began 8 Nov 2017 in five counties — Berrien, Delta, Kent, St. Clair and Washtenaw — chosen on impaired-driving crashes, arrests and DRE availability. Source: https://wbch.com/news/331892 — accessed 2026-10-28; MSP announcement via https://www.michiganautolaw.com/blog/2017/11/08/roadside-drug-testing-drugged-drivers/ — accessed 2026-10-28. A later secondary source (Northern Michigan University, undated) states the programme "recently expanded to all counties and is administered by the Michigan State Police" using the Abbott SoToxa handheld device with preliminary results in about five minutes. Source: http://news.nmu.edu/swift-honored-efforts-curb-drugged-driving — accessed 2026-10-28. The expansion to all counties and the current device are secondary-sourced and marked [VERIFY] against a current MSP page before publication; the five pilot counties are the only MSP-announced geography confirmed in this pass.
  • Device thresholds are NOT legal limits: A secondary summary of the pilot device lists manufacturer threshold limits including marihuana/cannabis (THC) 25 ng/mL in oral fluid (alongside amphetamine 50, benzodiazepines 20, cocaine 30, methamphetamine 50). Source: https://www.nemannlawoffices.com/blog/roadside-drug-tests-to-check-for-marihuana-cocaine-opiates-and-more.cfm — accessed 2026-10-28. That 25 ng/mL figure is a device screening cut-off, not a Michigan per se driving limit, not a blood limit, and not a finding of impairment. Do not quote it as "the THC limit."
  • What roadside evidence is used for in court: Officer observations (driving behaviour, speech, balance), field sobriety performance, DRE evaluation, admissions, and a confirmatory blood test showing active delta-9 THC (as opposed to inactive metabolite) are the evidence prosecutors typically rely on for an impairment prosecution; presence alone, without impairment, is the §625(8) track for non-patients (§12.2.1), not an impairment finding. Sources: https://www.1866hirejoe.com/blog/drugged-driving-in-detroit-michigan-area-what-you-need-to-know-to-save-lives/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary].

12.2.5 Vehicle searches — People v. Armstrong (2025) and People v. Wilkins, No. 167737 (22 July 2026), reconciled and verified

Both holdings were verified in this pass; neither is overstated below. - People v. Armstrong, ___ Mich. ___ (2 Apr 2025) (Docket No. 165233): Because marihuana possession and use is generally legal for adults in Michigan, the odour of marihuana alone does not supply probable cause for a warrantless vehicle search. The Court overruled People v. Kazmierczak, 461 Mich. 411 (2000), to that extent. Odour remains a factor in the totality of the circumstances; it is not irrelevant, and it is not a per se basis. Sources: Armstrong as quoted in Wilkins (dissent, citing Armstrong, slip op at 1–2, 8, 12–13) and in Court of Appeals, People v. Villarreal, unpublished 17 Apr 2026 (No. 373353): "because 'marijuana possession and use is generally legal, the odor of marijuana does not on its own supply a substantial basis for inferring a fair probability that contraband or evidence of illegal activity will be found in a particular place' … However, post-MRTMA the smell of marijuana may still be a factor in determining if probable cause exists, under the totality of the circumstances, to conduct a warrantless search of a vehicle." Villarreal PDF: https://cases.justia.com/michigan/court-of-appeals-unpublished/2026-373353.pdf?ts=1776524405 — accessed 2026-10-28. The Armstrong slip opinion itself was not directly opened in this pass; the holding is verified through its quotation in Wilkins and Villarreal, and the parent should open Armstrong directly before publication [VERIFY]. - People v. Wilkins, No. 167737 (Mich. 22 July 2026) — directly opened and read in this pass. Opinion by Justice Thomas, joined by Chief Justice Cavanagh and Justices Welch, Bolden and Hood (5–2; Justice Welch concurring on state-constitutional grounds; Justices Zahra and Bernstein dissenting). Facts: a Michigan State Police trooper stopped Freddie Wilkins, III, for speeding (Kent County; 63rd District Court / Kent Circuit Court); smelled marihuana from the open passenger window but saw no marihuana in plain view and neither occupant appeared intoxicated or was smoking; both occupants were under 21; the passenger later admitted she had some "shake" (a small amount). The trooper searched the vehicle and found a loaded semiautomatic pistol in a backpack; no marihuana was recovered. Wilkins was charged with carrying a concealed weapon in a vehicle, MCL 750.227. Source: Wilkins slip opinion, syllabus and opinion, directly opened — https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4a4f15/siteassets/case-documents/uploads/opinions/final/sct/167737_60_01.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. - Holding, verbatim in substance (syllabus, which states it "constitutes no part of the opinion" but accurately summarises it):

"The warrantless search of defendant's car was unlawful under the automobile exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement because the trooper did not have probable cause to believe there was a criminal amount of marijuana in the vehicle." "Probable cause to believe only that a defendant is responsible for a civil infraction does not establish probable cause to conduct a warrantless search under the automobile exception. Instead, a police officer performing a warrantless search under the automobile exception must have probable cause to believe that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place. Because the amount of marijuana present defines the distinction between a civil infraction and a crime, the officer must have probable cause to believe that a criminal amount of marijuana is present; substances prohibited only by civil law are not 'contraband' for purposes of supporting a warrantless search of an automobile based on probable cause under the Fourth Amendment." "Moreover, the smell of marijuana does not per se provide probable cause regarding possession of a criminal amount." "In this case, where the trooper had probable cause to believe that the vehicle contained a small amount of marijuana — i.e., that a civil infraction had occurred, but not that the vehicle contained evidence of a crime — this probable cause was insufficient to support a warrantless search under the automobile exception." Same Wilkins opinion, syllabus — accessed 2026-10-28. The Court reversed the Court of Appeals and remanded to the circuit court; the majority expressly did not resolve the state-constitutional (Const. 1963, art. 1, §11) ground, which Justice Welch would have reached. - Reconciliation — what the two cases together do and do not do: - Armstrong answers the odour question: odour alone ≠ probable cause (but odour + other facts can contribute to totality). - Wilkins answers the civil-infraction question Armstrong left open: probable cause of only a civil infraction (here, under-21 possession of ≤2.5 oz, MCL 333.27965(3)) ≠ probable cause for a warrantless automobile-exception search, because the automobile exception requires probable cause of contraband or evidence of a crime, and quantity is what separates civil from criminal marihuana possession. - Neither case legalises driving under the influence, blocks a consent search, blocks a search on another lawful basis (warrant, search incident to arrest, inventory, plain view of a crime, probable cause of a criminal amount or of another crime), or makes odour irrelevant. Signs of impairment, active smoking, smoke in the vehicle, marihuana in plain view suggesting a criminal amount, or evidence of unlicensed sale remain facts that can support further investigation and, if they establish probable cause of a crime, a search. Secondary MSP guidance reported after Wilkins states the holding reaches beyond cannabis: police may not search a vehicle based solely on evidence of any civil infraction — that MSP-guidance claim is secondary-sourced [VERIFY] against the MSP Legal Update itself (reported as MSP Legal Update No. 171). - Run 1 consistency: Run 1 Part 0, §0.5 stated both holdings in exactly this form ("odour alone does not supply probable cause"; "probable cause of a mere civil infraction does not support a warrantless automobile-exception search; police need probable cause of a criminal amount or another crime. Odour remains a factor in the totality"). Part 12 confirms Run 1 on both points and adds the verified Wilkins vote (5–2), author (Thomas, J.), and remand disposition. No conflict.

12.3 Expungement and sealing, including Clean Slate automatic expungement

12.3.1 Two routes that must not be conflated: application (petition) vs automatic

Michigan has both an application-based set-aside system (1965 PA 213, MCL 780.621 et seq.) and an automatic set-aside system (MCL 780.621g, "Clean Slate" automatic expungement). "Expungement" in Michigan practice means setting aside a conviction: the conviction is removed from the public record and a nonpublic record is retained for authorised law-enforcement/court use (MCL 780.623). It is not a federal expungement and does not clear a federal record. - Application route: the person files in the convicting court (forms MC 227 for general convictions, MC 227a for misdemeanour marihuana convictions). The court decides eligibility, waiting periods and, for general convictions, whether the circumstances warrant set-aside. - Automatic route: the Michigan State Police (MSP) searches the state's Criminal History Record database daily for newly eligible convictions and sets them aside without any application. The programme launched 11 Apr 2023 under the Clean Slate legislation enacted in 2020. Source: Michigan Attorney General release, 11 Apr 2023 — https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIAG/bulletins/3541e65?reqfrom=share — accessed 2026-10-28 ("the Michigan State Police are launching a new automatic expungement program, which will search the state's Criminal Historical Record database system daily for eligible convictions to automatically expunge").

12.3.2 Automatic expungement — eligibility, numbers and waiting periods (MCL 780.621g)

On the Attorney General's launch statement and consistent secondary summaries of §780.621g: - Misdemeanours punishable by less than 93 days: automatically expunged after 7 years from the date of sentence imposition; no limit on the number. - Misdemeanours punishable by 93 days or more: automatically expunged after 7 years from sentence imposition; up to 4 convictions. - Felonies: automatically expunged after 10 years from whichever is later — the date of sentence imposition or completion of any term of imprisonment with the Department of Corrections; up to 2 convictions. Source: AG release, 11 Apr 2023 (same URL) — accessed 2026-10-28; corroborated at https://www.wsgw.com/automatic-expungement-program-can-benefit-those-with-criminal-records/ — accessed 2026-10-28. - Launch scale (anticipation, not a confirmed outcome count): the AG anticipated "over 1 million residents will receive automatic expungements on this, the first day of the program's rollout, and 400,000 residents are expected to end the day completely conviction free." Same AG release. Do not present "1 million expunged" as a confirmed cleared count — it is the launch-day anticipation in the release; a confirmed cumulative automatic-expungement count as of 28 Oct 2026 was not located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE]. - Exclusions from automatic expungement (summary; full §780.621 list [VERIFY] before publication): assaultive crimes (beyond the limited assaultive allowance in the application route), serious misdemeanours, crimes of dishonesty, offences punishable by 10 or more years' imprisonment, offences involving minors or vulnerable adults, crimes causing injury or death, human trafficking offences, operating while intoxicated (OWI) convictions, and certain commercial-vehicle violations. Sources: https://legalclarity.org/michigan-background-check-laws-criteria-process-and-compliance/ and https://legalclarity.org/how-to-clear-your-driving-record-in-michigan/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summaries of the AG/MSP lists; the MSP Clean Slate page itself was not directly opened in this pass — [VERIFY] against michigan.gov/msp Clean Slate page]. - Effect: an automatically set-aside conviction no longer appears in employer background checks (public record). If a person believes an eligible conviction was missed, the remedy described in secondary sources is to check the public record via Michigan's ICHAT system and contact the court or file a standard application. Source: https://legalclarity.org/michigan-expungement-guide-statute-eligibility-and-process/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary].

12.3.3 Marihuana-specific set-aside — MCL 780.621e (application route, with a presumption in the applicant's favour)

This is the marihuana-specific provision, and it is application-based, not automatic — a distinction secondary summaries sometimes blur. The statute itself says a person "may apply." - Text, MCL 780.621e(1): "Beginning on January 1, 2020, a person convicted of 1 or more misdemeanor marihuana offenses may apply to set aside the conviction or convictions under this subsection." Source: MCL 780.621e as reproduced at https://law.justia.com/codes/michigan/chapter-780/statute-act-213-of-1965/section-780-621e/ — accessed 2026-10-28 (2020 PA 192, HB 4982, approved 12 Oct 2020, effective 11 Apr 2021; the §621e(1) application window is stated as beginning 1 Jan 2020 in the enrolled text). - Rebuttable presumption, §780.621e(4), verbatim in substance: "A rebuttable presumption that a conviction for a misdemeanor marihuana offense sought to be set aside by an applicant was based on activity that would not have been a crime if committed on or after December 6, 2018 arises upon the filing of an application under subsection (1). The presumption … may be rebutted by the presentation of evidence by the prosecuting agency … that demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence that the conduct … would constitute a criminal violation of the laws of this state or a political subdivision of this state if it had been committed on or after December 6, 2018. An answer … must be filed no later than 60 days from the date of service of the application." Same Justia source. 6 Dec 2018 is the MRTMA effective date — the presumption therefore asks whether the old conduct would be lawful under the post-legalisation regime. - What counts as a "misdemeanor marihuana offense" for §621e — narrow list on the official form: Form MC 227a (Michigan courts, rev. 7/24) lists eligible convictions as violations of MCL 333.7403(2)(d) (possession), MCL 333.7404(2)(d) (use), MCL 333.7453 (selling marihuana paraphernalia), or a local ordinance substantially corresponding to one of those. Source: https://courts.michigan.gov/49bf50/siteassets/forms/scao-approved/mc227a.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. Felony marihuana convictions are not §621e convictions; they must proceed, if at all, under the general §780.621 application route or the §780.621g automatic route, subject to their own eligibility and waiting periods. - No waiting period stated in §621e, and no number cap stated in §621e(1): secondary summaries state there is no minimum waiting period to apply under §621e and no requirement of a conviction-free interval after the marihuana conviction itself. Source: http://www.ericsheppardlaw.com/expungement-of-record.html — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; the §621e text as reproduced imposes no waiting period, which is consistent with that summary, but the parent should confirm no waiting period is imposed by another subsection or court rule before publication — [VERIFY]]. - Procedure: application must contain the applicant's full name and current address and a certified record of each conviction to be set aside (§621e(2)); a copy must be served on the prosecuting agency (§621e(3)); the applicant files in the court where the conviction occurred, on a separate application per court (MC 227a instructions, same form source). - What set-aside under §621e does NOT do (MCL 780.621f): if granted, the arresting agency and MSP maintain the nonpublic record under §780.623 for authorised use (§621f(1)); the applicant may not thereafter seek resentencing in another criminal case in which the set-aside conviction was used in sentencing, whether or not set-aside would have changed guidelines scoring (§621f(2)); set-aside does not entitle the applicant to return of any fines, costs or fees or of any money/property forfeited as a result of the conduct or conviction (§621f(4)). Source: MCL 780.621f via https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-780-criminal-procedure/mi-comp-laws-780-621f/ — accessed 2026-10-28. - General application-route caps and waiting periods (for context; [VERIFY] exact waiting periods against MCL 780.621 before publication): a person may apply to set aside not more than 3 felony offences in total, not more than 2 assaultive-crime convictions in a lifetime, and not more than 1 felony for the same offence punishable by more than 10 years (MCL 780.621(1) as reproduced at https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-780-criminal-procedure/mi-comp-laws-780-621/ — accessed 2026-10-28). The general-route waiting periods described on form MC 227 (7 years for multiple felonies, 5 years for a single felony or a serious misdemeanour, 3 years for other misdemeanours, each from sentence/discharge, whichever is later, with no intervening conviction) are form instructions, not verified here against the current §780.621 text, and are therefore stated as form-sourced [VERIFY]. - OWI carve-out — do not conflate with marihuana possession: OWI convictions are excluded from automatic expungement (§12.3.2). Whether a first-offence OWI may be set aside by application (and after what waiting period) under MCL 780.621c was described inconsistently in secondary sources in this pass and is marked [VERIFY] — do not state a first-OWI application rule in the compiled dossier until §780.621c is read directly. A marihuana-possession set-aside does not set aside an OWI conviction arising from the same stop. - Estimated population: secondary sources estimate about 240,000–250,000 Michigan residents with marihuana-related convictions could benefit from the marihuana set-aside provisions. Sources: https://georgelaw.com/blog/michigan-clean-slate-law/ and https://us3.campaign-archive.com/?u=7c883e98d9456d19b452e9857&amp;id=176c6fce4b — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary estimates; treat as estimates, not an official count].

12.3.4 What "set aside" means in practice, and what it does not do

  • Public-record removal: a set-aside conviction is removed from the person's public criminal history and no longer appears in employer/landlord background checks that use the public record.
  • Nonpublic retention: law enforcement and courts retain a nonpublic record under MCL 780.623 for authorised uses (e.g. subsequent sentencing, licensing, law-enforcement checks as the statute allows).
  • No federal effect: Michigan set-aside does not expunge a federal conviction or a federal agency record, and does not by itself restore federal firearms rights (see §12.7 — federal restoration is a separate federal question [VERIFY]).
  • No refund: fines, costs, fees and forfeited money/property are not returned on a §621e set-aside (§12.3.3, §621f(4)).

12.4 Consumption lounges and events

12.4.1 The baseline rule: public consumption is prohibited, with two licensed exceptions

MRTMA §4(1)(e), MCL 333.27954(1)(e), provides the Act does not authorise "consuming marihuana in a public place or smoking marihuana where prohibited by the person who owns, occupies, or manages the property, except … a public place does not include an area designated for consumption within a municipality that has authorized consumption in designated areas that are not accessible to persons under 21 years of age." Source: MCL 333.27954 via https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27954/ — accessed 2026-10-28. MRTMA §6(2)(c), MCL 333.27956(2)(c), separately allows a municipality to adopt an ordinance authorising "sale for consumption in designated areas not accessible to persons under 21, or at special events in limited areas/times" (Run 1 Part 2, §3.1). Those two provisions are the statutory home for both lounges and events below. Parks, sidewalks, streets, restaurants, bars and public transit are public places for this purpose; a private residence with the owner's permission is not a public place, and is the default lawful consumption location for adults 21+.

12.4.2 Designated consumption establishments (DCEs / lounges) — licence, fees, counts, operating rules

  • Licence type and fees (Run 1-locked, not contradicted): Designated Consumption Establishment is an MRTMA adult-use licence type. $3,000 nonrefundable prequalification application fee + $1,000 initial licensure fee + $1,000 renewal (R 420.7 Table 1; Run 1 Part 4, §§4.1, 4.8). Source for the $1,000 figure: R 420.7 via https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-7 — accessed 2026-10-28 (Run 1). A DCE licence does not by itself authorise retail sale; a DCE licensee may sell only if it also holds a retailer or microbusiness licence, typically in an adjoining, physically separated suite. Sources: https://cannacon.org/michigan-designated-consumption-establishments/ and https://www.covasoftware.com/us-dispensary-laws/Michigan — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summaries of the rule structure; the current R 420.21/420.203 text for DCEs should be re-checked before publication — [VERIFY] rule number].
  • Count (Run 1-locked): 5–6 statewide per Run 1 (5 at Dec 2025, 6 in the 2026 secondary count; Run 1 Part 6, §6.4). No newer CRA lounge count was located in this pass; do not publish a higher count without a CRA licence-list check [VERIFY]. The small count reflects municipal authorisation as the real gate, not the $1,000 state fee.
  • Municipal gate: A DCE requires local municipality approval before state licensing, and the municipality must have authorised consumption in designated areas not accessible to persons under 21 (MCL 333.27954(1)(e); 333.27956(2)(c)). A municipality that has opted out of marihuana establishments, or has not authorised designated consumption, cannot host a DCE. No statewide list of DCE-authorising municipalities was located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE]; the dossier must not present a lounge directory without a CRA/municipal check.
  • Operating requirements (secondary-sourced, [VERIFY] against current R 420.203 / DCE rule text): 21+ only, with age verification; a designated consumption area physically separated by barriers/walls from non-smoking space so smoke does not infiltrate it; a smoke-free space for employees to monitor the consumption area; a ventilation/filtration system that exhausts consumption-area air outside the building through filtration removing visual smoke and odour; security monitoring of consumption areas; staff supervision and a responsible operations plan covering over-intoxication, underage access, illegal sale/distribution and other criminal activity on the premises; no alcohol sale or consumption on the premises and no holding of an alcohol licence alongside a DCE licence on the secondary summaries. Sources: https://michigancannabis.org/licensing/designated-consumption-establishment and https://catalyst-bc.com/michigan-consumption-lounge-licenses-what-you-need-to-know/ — accessed 2026-10-28. The ventilation, barrier and alcohol points are secondary summaries of rule text; the exact rule citations are [VERIFY].
  • What is prohibited everywhere except a DCE or temporary event: Under Mich. Admin. Code R 420.203(2)(b), a marihuana business shall not allow on site: (i) sale, consumption or serving of food except as provided in the rules unless the business is a DCE or temporary event with required authorisations from other agencies; (ii) consumption, use or inhalation of a marihuana product unless the licensee holds a DCE or temporary event licence. Source: R 420.203(2)(b) as quoted in CRA formal complaint ENF-24-01311 — https://sup1rpr1lh5l3porl3qi.vcsolaris.top/cra/-/media/Project/Websites/cra/Disciplinary-Actions/2025/April/Anna-Sloan-LLC-dba-URB-AUR000596-Consent-Order-and-Stipulation-and-Formal-Complaint.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28. A retailer sales floor is therefore not a consumption lounge by default, and employee consumption on a sales floor is a rule violation on that complaint's theory.
  • Bring-your-own vs purchase on site: A DCE without a retailer/microbusiness licence operates on a bring-your-own model (customers consume product lawfully purchased elsewhere); a DCE co-located with a retailer allows purchase in the retail suite and consumption in the separated consumption suite. Delivery to a customer at a DCE by a licensed retailer is described in secondary sources as permitted — [VERIFY] against the current delivery rule before publication.
  • Private "cannabis clubs": Secondary summaries state a person/entity that permits consumption on nonresidential premises and charges an entry fee or requires membership must hold a DCE licence. Source: https://michigancannabis.org/licensing/designated-consumption-establishment — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; rule cite given there as former R 240.21(3) — [VERIFY] current rule number]. Operating a pay-to-enter consumption space without a DCE licence is not a lawful workaround for the public-consumption ban.

12.4.3 Temporary marijuana events — organiser licence, per-event licence, fees, conditions

  • Two licences, not one (Run 1-locked): (a) Marihuana Event Organizer — annual licence, $1,000 initial + $1,000 renewal + $3,000 prequalification (R 420.7 Table 1; Run 1 Part 4, §4.8); (b) Temporary Marihuana Event — per-event licence, no application fee (R 420.26(3)), initial licensure fee $500 per day for events without sale, and for events with sale $500 per selling licensee + $500 per day (R 420.26(1)). If a scheduled selling licensee withdraws before day 1, the organiser may request a refund of that licensee's portion. Source: R 420.26 via https://law.cornell.edu/regulations/michigan/Mich-Admin-Code-R-420-26 — accessed 2026-10-28 (Run 1). Because a temporary event is per-event, a CRA "active licences" count for this type (5 in Sept 2025 per Run 1 Part 4, §4.8) is a point-in-time snapshot, not a stock of permanent businesses.
  • Organiser count (Run 1 context): 31 event organisers in the 2026 secondary count (Run 1 Part 6, §6.4) — secondary/modelled [VERIFY] against the CRA licence list.
  • Conditions (MRA/CRA bulletin and rule summaries; [VERIFY] current R 420.25 text for any renumbering):
  • A person must hold an event organiser licence to hold a temporary event.
  • The temporary-event application must be received by the agency at least 90 days before the first day of the event to allow processing (MRA bulletin as republished at https://four20post.com/2020/01/mra-requirements-for-temporary-marijuana-events/ — accessed 2026-10-28). Draft-rule note (not law): the 2023-25 LR draft would change this to 120 days and would provide a temporary-event licence is only required if marihuana will be sold, not if it is only consumed. Source: draft summary at https://www.jdsupra.com/post/contentViewerEmbed.aspx?fid=90ffc776-f47d-4f32-b24f-bef8190225db — accessed 2026-10-28. Do not apply the 120-day or sale-only draft changes as current law.
  • Access restricted to persons 21+; a clearly legible sign not less than 7 × 11 inches reading "No Persons Under 21 Allowed," lettering not less than 1 inch, at or near each public entrance to any sale/consumption area; sales/consumption not visible from any public place or non-age-restricted area; event only at a venue expressly approved by the municipality for temporary events; event licence for a single day or up to seven consecutive days (MRA bulletin, same source).
  • Only a marihuana retailer, microbusiness or Class A microbusiness may sell at a temporary event; sales only within the assigned area and during event dates/times, with ID/age verification (Run 1 Part 4, §4.8).
  • Organiser must hire/contract licensed security personnel, 21+, present at all times marihuana is for sale or consumption is allowed, who shall not consume marihuana before or during the event; organiser is responsible for ensuring all on-site consumption rules are followed and all marihuana waste is collected/disposed of under the rules; organiser and participants must comply with MRTMA, the rules and municipal ordinances; the agency may require the event to cease immediately to protect public health/safety. Source: rule compilation at https://420tax.github.io/michigan-cannabis-compliance/rules/latest/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [rules compilation, not the official Administrative Code PDF — [VERIFY] against current R 420.25].
  • No on-site sale, consumption or serving of food or alcohol unless the establishment has the appropriate authorisations from other federal, state or local agencies (MRA bulletin, same source; R 420.203(2)(b) in §12.4.2).
  • Municipal special-event authorisation vs temporary-event licence: MRTMA §6(2)(c) allows a municipality to authorise consumption "at special events in limited areas/times" by ordinance. That municipal authorisation is in addition to, not a substitute for, the state temporary-event licence where sale is involved. A municipality-only "special event" permission does not authorise unlicensed retail sale.

12.5 Cannabis tourism and visitor purchase rules

12.5.1 Adult-use: no residency requirement — visitors 21+ buy on the same terms as residents

  • MRTMA §5, MCL 333.27955(1), says "a person 21 years of age or older" with no residency qualifier. Run 1 Part 1, §1.1 reached the same conclusion. Visitors 21+ may therefore purchase adult-use marihuana from a licensed retailer on the same transaction and possession terms as Michigan residents.
  • ID: A valid, unexpired government-issued photo ID showing the buyer is 21+ is required at the door and at the point of sale; a driver's licence, state ID card or passport from any U.S. state or another country is accepted in practice as described in secondary retailer/visitor guides. Sources: https://cannabismichigan.org/visitor-guide/overview and https://legalclarity.org/can-anyone-buy-from-a-dispensary-in-michigan/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; the ID-verification duty itself is R 420.505 (Run 1 Part 1, §1.7), but the "any-state / passport" acceptance detail is secondary-sourced and should be confirmed against a CRA retailer checklist before publication — [VERIFY]]. A retailer that cannot verify age must not complete the sale (R 420.505).
  • Same limits for visitors: 2.5 oz/transaction (≤15 g concentrate), 2.5 oz public possession, 10 oz at a Michigan residence (a visitor's temporary residence/hotel room is not automatically a "residence" for the 10 oz rule on any source located — [VERIFY]; visitors should assume the 2.5 oz public limit governs what they carry outside a private home), gifting up to 2.5 oz without remuneration to another person 21+, public consumption prohibited (§12.4.1), vehicle-passenger smoking prohibited, driving under the influence prohibited (§12.2). A visitor's home-state purchase limits do not travel with them; Michigan limits apply in Michigan.
  • No visitor permit, no reciprocity needed for adult-use: No special visitor permit, medical card or reciprocity agreement is required for an adult-use purchase. Sources: same visitor guides.

12.5.2 Medical visitors — unresolved, preserved from Run 1 (do not resolve here)

Run 1 Part 1, §1.4.6 found directly conflicting secondary sources on whether Michigan provisioning centres recognise out-of-state medical cards: (a) full reciprocity claimed; (b) discretionary/dispensary-choice claimed; (c) no reciprocity claimed. The MMMA §3 "visiting qualifying patient" definition and MMFLA §102(y) ("registered qualifying patient … or a visiting qualifying patient") prove Michigan law contemplates a visiting-patient category, but no operative MMMA §3 visiting-patient text or CRA rule stating which credentials, if any, must/may be accepted, whether the medical tax exemption applies to visitors, or whether visitors may cultivate, was located in Run 1, and none was located in this Part 12 pass either. Status therefore remains [VERIFY] / unresolved. What is not in dispute: a visitor 21+ may buy adult-use without any medical card, at adult-use prices and taxes (10% excise + 6% sales tax; Run 1 Part 2). A visitor should confirm with a specific provisioning centre before travelling for medical access, and should not assume a home-state card guarantees medical pricing or medical inventory access in Michigan.

12.5.3 What visitors may NOT do — interstate transport, and the limits of "legal at both ends"

  • Interstate transport remains unlawful under federal law even if marihuana is legal in both the origin and destination states. Marihuana is a federally controlled substance; transporting it across a state line is a federal offence, and the fact that Michigan and, for example, Ohio or Illinois each have legal adult-use markets does not make Michigan-to-that-state (or that-state-to-Michigan) transport lawful. This is stated as a statement of federal law, not legal advice for any traveller.
  • Neighbouring states' laws do not create a Michigan export right: Indiana and Wisconsin prohibit adult-use marihuana, and Ohio and Illinois regulate it under their own laws; carrying Michigan-purchased marihuana into any neighbouring state exposes the carrier to that state's possession/transport law and to federal law. Specific neighbouring-state possession penalties were not researched in this Part and are not stated here — the point for this dossier is only that Michigan legality ends at the Michigan border.
  • Air travel and federal property: Airports, aircraft and federal property (national parks, federal buildings, and federally funded facilities that enforce federal prohibition) are federal jurisdiction; Michigan legality provides no protection there. TSA does not specifically search for marihuana but must refer marihuana discovered during screening to law enforcement (secondary summary at https://legalclarity.org/where-can-you-legally-smoke-weed-in-michigan/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; TSA policy itself [VERIFY] before publication]).
  • Hotels, short-term rentals and private property: A hotel, Airbnb host or other property owner/manager may prohibit consumption on their property (MCL 333.27954(1)(e), (4); §12.6). A visitor has no right to consume in a hotel room that prohibits it, and a "private residence" consumption right does not override a host's house rules.
  • Driving home with product: Lawful transport within Michigan is possession/transport of ≤2.5 oz under MCL 333.27955(1)(a); smoking in the passenger area on a public way and driving under the influence are prohibited (MCL 333.27954(1)(a), (g); §12.2). MRTMA states no closed-container/trunk rule in the text quoted in Run 1, §1.3.4 — do not invent one. Once the vehicle crosses a state line, §12.5.3's federal/neighbouring-state point applies.

12.5.4 Cannabis tourism — what is actually on offer, without overstating it

Michigan's visitor-facing cannabis offer, on the sources reviewed, is: licensed adult-use retail statewide (subject to municipal opt-outs; Run 1 Part 3), a small number of licensed consumption lounges (§12.4.2), and licensed temporary events (§12.4.3). There is no Michigan "cannabis tourism licence," no visitor consumption permit, and no state-run cannabis-tourism programme located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE as a programme]. Border-town retail (e.g. communities near the Ohio, Indiana and Wisconsin borders) is a market fact described in secondary visitor guides, not a distinct legal regime — the same MRTMA limits, taxes and consumption bans apply there. Secondary commercial rankings (e.g. "second-largest adult-use market behind California," Run 1 Part 6, §6.5) are market context, not tourism law, and are not repeated as a tourism claim here.

12.6 Landlord and tenant rules, including home grow and smoking in rentals

12.6.1 The MRTMA landlord rule — what a lease may and may not prohibit (verbatim)

MRTMA §4(4), MCL 333.27954(4):

"This act allows a person to prohibit or otherwise regulate the consumption, cultivation, distribution, processing, sale, or display of marihuana and marihuana accessories on property the person owns, occupies, or manages, except that a lease agreement may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marihuana by means other than smoking." Source: MCL 333.27954(4) via https://www.casemine.com/act/us/6433f3a090d8824f645b7021/amp and the Michigan courts' MRTMA scope summary at https://www.courts.michigan.gov/4a8168/siteassets/publications/benchbooks/csbb/csbbresponsivehtml5.zip/CSBB/Ch_8_Marijuana/Scope_of_Michigan_Regulation_and_Taxation_of_Marihuana_Act_(MRTMA).htm — accessed 2026-10-28. Consequences, in the statute's own terms: - A landlord/owner/occupier/manager may prohibit or regulate smoking, cultivation, processing, sale and display on their property, including by a lease term. - A lease may not prohibit a tenant from lawfully possessing and consuming marihuana by means other than smoking — i.e. edibles, tinctures, capsules and other non-smoked lawful consumption, and mere possession, cannot be lease-banned for a tenant. Secondary summaries phrase the same point as "a landlord can ban growing and can ban smoking, but cannot ban you from possessing edibles or using other non-smoked forms." Source: https://legalclarity.org/how-many-marijuana-plants-can-you-grow-in-michigan/ — accessed 2026-10-28. - Vaping: whether "smoking" in §27954(4) includes vaping/aerosol inhalation was not settled by a statutory definition located in this pass [VERIFY] — secondary summaries variously treat vaping as within a smoking ban and as a non-smoked form. A lease that bans "smoking" should not be assumed to ban or to permit vaping without reading the lease's own definitions. Do not state a vaping rule as settled law. - The lease-ban limit protects tenants; it does not create a right to grow or to smoke: a tenant with a lease banning cultivation who grows anyway, or with a lease banning smoking who smokes anyway, is in breach of the lease on the statute's face, and eviction/termination remedies are governed by the lease and Michigan landlord-tenant law (including, for drug activity, the demand/termination procedures in MCL 600.5718 et seq. as described in secondary summaries — [VERIFY] the specific form/procedure before advising on any eviction).

12.6.2 Home grow in a rental — the landlord's ban is enforceable, and the grow rules still apply

  • If the lease prohibits cultivation, the tenant may not cultivate on the premises even though MRTMA §5 would otherwise allow 12 plants per premises for an owner-occupier. The landlord's §27954(4) right to prohibit cultivation is the operative rule for renters.
  • If the lease is silent on cultivation, the tenant's MRTMA grow rights still depend on the property owner's §27954(4) right to "prohibit or otherwise regulate" — silence is not a permanent waiver, and a later lease amendment or house-rule change can restrict growing. Secondary guidance to "confirm with your landlord before setting up a grow space" even where the lease is silent is practical advice, not a statute, but it reflects the §27954(4) allocation of control to the owner.
  • Where growing is permitted (owner-occupier, or tenant with permission), all MRTMA grow conditions still apply: ≤12 plants per premises, enclosed area with locks/functioning security devices, not visible from a public place without binoculars/aircraft/optical aids (MCL 333.27954(1)(f)); excess over 2.5 oz at residence only in locked storage (MCL 333.27954(1)(i)); no butane/flashpoint-below-100°F extraction in a public place, vehicle or residential curtilage (MCL 333.27954(1)(d)).
  • Damage / nuisance / insurance: No Michigan statute located in this pass creates a specific "grow damage" or "smoke nuisance" cause of action beyond general lease, nuisance, property-damage and insurance law. Claims that a grow caused mould, electrical or odour damage, or that smoke migrated between units, are fact-specific lease/nuisance matters, not MRTMA penalty matters — [UNAVAILABLE] as a Michigan cannabis-specific rule; do not invent a statutory damages figure.

12.6.3 Medical tenants — the MMMA lease rule is narrower than the MRTMA rule

MMMA §7, MCL 333.26427(c)(3), provides the MMMA does not require "a private property owner to lease residential property to any person who smokes or cultivates marihuana on the premises, if the prohibition against smoking or cultivating marihuana is in the written lease." Source: MMMA §7 as quoted in the Pontiac tenant toolkit at https://cms3.revize.com/revize/pontiacminew/tenantstoolkit.pdf — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary reproduction of the statute; official text to be re-checked]. In other words, a medical patient has no MMMA right to smoke or cultivate in a rental against an express written-lease prohibition. The MRTMA non-smoking possession/consumption protection in §12.6.1 is the broader tenant protection for adult-use tenants; whether it also protects a medical tenant's non-smoked consumption in a rental that bans all marihuana is a question of reading MRTMA §4(4) together with MMMA §7, and was not resolved by a case located in this pass [VERIFY].

12.6.4 Public housing and federally subsidised housing — federal law overrides Michigan tenant protections

This is the sharpest landlord/tenant conflict in Part 12, and Michigan law does not resolve it in the tenant's favour: - Federal rule: Public housing agencies (PHAs) must deny admission to a household with a member currently using a controlled substance illegally under federal law, and owners of federally assisted properties may (and under HUD guidance must have policies allowing them to) terminate tenancy for drug-related activity, including marihuana use. HUD has stated that "the use of 'medical marijuana' is illegal under federal law even if it is permitted under state law" and that PHAs may not make a reasonable accommodation for medical marijuana. Sources: HUD "Use of Marijuana in Multifamily Assisted Properties" memorandum (2014) as summarised at https://legalclarity.org/section-8-drug-policy-marijuana-rules-and-eviction/ and https://legalclarity.org/can-i-get-evicted-for-smoking-weed-in-my-apartment/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summaries of HUD guidance; HUD memorandum itself [VERIFY] before publication]. Whether HUD has updated that guidance in response to the 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III move was not confirmed in this pass — secondary sources as of mid-2026 state it had not been updated [VERIFY against a current HUD page; do not assume a post-Apr 2026 HUD update]. - Michigan case: Forest City Residential Management, Inc. v. Beasley, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 167532 (E.D. Mich. 3 Dec 2014) — a tenant in a project-based Section 8 complex (Plymouth Square Village; county not stated in the summary — do not assign one) with multiple sclerosis and a Michigan medical card sought a Fair Housing Act / Section 504 reasonable accommodation to use medical marihuana in her unit; the court held federal law preempts the MMMA on this point and the FHA/Section 504 do not require the accommodation. Sources: https://www.bairdholm.com/blog/michigan-federal-court-holds-housing-providers-are-not-required-to-accommodate-use-of-medical-marijuana/ and https://www.studicata.com/summaries/united-states-district-court-eastern-district-of-michigan/forest-city-residential-management-inc-v-beasley-2014-t6zhbm/ — accessed 2026-10-28. - Admission vs existing tenancy — discretion, not a safe harbour: Secondary HUD summaries distinguish mandatory denial of admission for new applicants currently using a controlled substance from discretionary termination for existing tenants, where a PHA/owner weighs the circumstances. That discretion does not create a right to use marihuana in federally assisted housing, and a tenant who cultivates in a federally assisted unit creates a documented, ongoing violation. Source: https://www.thehabitatgroup.com/fair-housing-at-50-emerging-trends-that-could-affect-your-community/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary]. - Interaction with §12.6.1: The MRTMA lease protection (a private lease may not ban non-smoked possession/consumption) does not override federal assisted-housing law. A tenant in public housing, Section 8 / Housing Choice Voucher housing, or other federally assisted housing cannot rely on MRTMA §4(4) against a federal drug-related-activity termination. State-law-only rentals (no federal assistance) are governed by §12.6.1–§12.6.3. - No Michigan state-law public-housing marihuana protection was located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE]. Do not state that Michigan housing authorities have adopted a marihuana-tolerant admission policy without a PHA-specific source.

12.6.5 Employer/property-owner rights — cross-reference (not duplicated)

MRTMA §4(3), MCL 333.27954(3), provides the Act does not require an employer to permit or accommodate MRTMA conduct in any workplace or on employer property, and does not prohibit discipline for a workplace drug-policy violation or for working while under the influence, or adverse action for those reasons (Run 1 Part 1, §1.8, verbatim). That employer rule is distinct from the landlord rule in §12.6.1: an employer may ban all on-site use including non-smoked forms at work, while a landlord may not lease-ban a tenant's non-smoked possession/consumption at home. Do not conflate the two.

12.7 Gun ownership conflicts

12.7.1 Federal prohibition — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3), ATF Form 4473, and the 2011 ATF open letter (pre-Schedule III baseline)

  • Statute: 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) makes it unlawful for any person "who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance" to ship, transport, possess or receive firearms or ammunition. The statute covers controlled substances in every schedule — it is not limited to Schedule I. That scheduling point matters for §12.7.3: moving medical marihuana from Schedule I to Schedule III does not by the statute's text remove it from §922(g)(3).
  • ATF Form 4473: A purchase from a federally licensed firearms dealer requires ATF Form 4473 (Firearms Transaction Record). The form's drug-use question (Question 21e in the version described in secondary sources) asks whether the buyer is an unlawful user of a controlled substance, with a warning that marihuana use is unlawful under federal law regardless of state legalisation. Answering "no" while being a prohibited user is itself a federal false-statement offence. Sources: https://www.njmedicalmarijuana.us/blog/medical-marijuana-and-gun-ownership-nj.html and https://legalclarity.org/can-you-have-a-cpl-and-med-card-in-michigan/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary descriptions of the form; the current Form 4473 itself [VERIFY] before publication, especially after the draft revision in §12.7.3].
  • 2011 ATF open letter: ATF's 2011 open letter to federal firearms licensees stated a dealer may not sell to a person the dealer knows or has reasonable cause to believe is a medical marihuana cardholder, because such a person is by definition an unlawful user under federal law. Source: same NJ summary — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summary of the 2011 letter; letter itself [VERIFY]]. That letter predates the 2026 Schedule III move and the draft Form 4473 revision below, and its current status after those developments is unsettled [VERIFY].

12.7.2 Michigan state law — no medical-card CPL bar located, but no state safe harbour either

  • No Michigan statute located in this pass lists medical-patient status, or adult-use use, as a standalone disqualifier for a Concealed Pistol License (CPL) under MCL 28.425b. Secondary Michigan CPL summaries list felony convictions, mental-health adjudications, dishonourable discharge, domestic-assault and recent DUI convictions, personal protection orders and similar grounds, and state that a medical card is not a question on the CPL application and county clerks do not have access to the MMMP patient list for that purpose. Sources: https://michigancriminalattorney.com/medical-marijuana-and-concealed-carry/ and https://legalclarity.org/michigan-cpl-eligibility-and-disqualification-criteria/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; MCL 28.425b itself [VERIFY] before publication].
  • That state-law negative does not create a federal safe harbour: A person who holds a valid Michigan CPL but is a federal prohibited person under §922(g)(3) still faces federal possession liability on the federal theory described in §12.7.1. Secondary summaries phrase it as "a valid state license but a federal offense every time they possess a firearm" for a regular user — that is a secondary characterisation of the federal risk, not a Michigan holding, and it is stated here only to show the direction of the conflict.
  • Possession while under the influence: Secondary Michigan sources state Michigan law prohibits a person under the influence of marihuana from possessing a firearm. No statute number for that state prohibition was verified in this pass [VERIFY] — do not cite a section number for it in the compiled dossier until it is located. It is listed here only as a secondary claim to check, not as a confirmed Michigan rule.

12.7.3 What changed in 2026, and what did NOT settle — Hemani, the ATF "unlawful user" rule, and the draft Form 4473 (all [VERIFY] against primary federal sources)

No safe harbour is asserted in this section. Each 2026 development below is narrow, pending, or both. - United States v. Hemani, No. 24-1234 (decided 18 June 2026, Gorsuch, J.): The Supreme Court held, as applied and narrowly, that a status-only §922(g)(3) prosecution of a regular marijuana user for in-home possession, with no danger showing, was inconsistent with the Second Amendment. The statute itself remains in effect; Hemani does not strike down §922(g)(3) on its face, does not authorise purchase from a dealer, does not address carrying outside the home, and does not address a user shown to be dangerous. Sources: secondary summaries at https://www.cannamd.com/can-i-own-a-gun-in-florida-if-i-get-my-medical-marijuana-card/ and https://www.njmedicalmarijuana.us/blog/nj-medical-marijuana-laws-patient-guide.html — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; the Hemani opinion itself [VERIFY] before publication]. Do not cite Hemani as "medical users may now own guns." - ATF interim final rule eff. 22 Jan 2026 (27 CFR 478.11): Secondary federal summaries state ATF rewrote the "unlawful user" definition to require regular use continuing into the present (regular and recent use over an extended period), so isolated or sporadic use no longer automatically triggers the prohibition — but the rule did not create an exception for state-legal use. Source: https://legalclarity.org/michigan-cpl-eligibility-and-disqualification-criteria/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary summary of the Federal Register rule "Revising Definition of Unlawful User of or Addicted to Controlled Substance"; rule text [VERIFY]]. A regular medical or adult-use user therefore remains within the narrowed definition on that summary's reading; an isolated past user may not be. - ATF draft Form 4473 revision (reported 8 May 2026, comments closed 6 Aug 2026, not final as of Sept 2026): Secondary summaries state ATF published a draft revision of Form 4473 that would exclude medical cannabis used in accordance with state law from the drug-use question, focusing the warning on recreational use. As of September 2026 the draft had not been finalised and the older form remained in force. Sources: https://leafwell.com/medical-card/minnesota?knowledgebase_id=cost-information and https://legalclarity.org/legalisation-of-weed-federal-and-state-laws-today/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [both secondary; the draft form and its Federal Register notice [VERIFY] before publication]. Until a final form is published, no medical user should treat the draft as the operative form. - Schedule III effect — the argument, and why it is not a conclusion: Because state-licensed medical marihuana is now Schedule III, a medical user acting in compliance with Michigan's programme is arguably no longer an "unlawful user" of a controlled substance (the use is lawful under state law and the substance is no longer Schedule I). Secondary summaries make that argument expressly for medical users. Sources: same LegalClarity summary — accessed 2026-10-28. Counter-points that keep this [VERIFY] / unsettled: (1) §922(g)(3) covers all schedules, so Schedule III status alone does not remove the substance from the statute; (2) "unlawful" in §922(g)(3) has been read by ATF to mean unlawful under federal law, and medical marihuana remains federally controlled (Schedule III, not descheduled); (3) no ATF guidance or case law after 28 Apr 2026 settling the medical Schedule III question for Michigan users was located in this pass — the draft Form 4473, if finalised as described, would be the first such settlement, and it is not final; (4) adult-use users are not within the argument at all — adult-use remains Schedule I federally, and secondary summaries are unanimous that recreational users remain federally prohibited on the current form. Adopted position for this dossier: medical Schedule III gun status is UNSETTLED; adult-use gun prohibition under current federal form/guidance is the stated federal position; no safe harbour for either track is asserted. - Circuit background (context, not Michigan law): The Fifth Circuit (Jan 2025) and Eleventh Circuit (Aug 2025) found constitutional issues with §922(g)(3) as applied to cannabis users at preliminary stages. Those are not Sixth Circuit (Michigan) holdings and do not bind a Michigan federal court. Source: NJ summary — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary]. Any Sixth Circuit post-Hemani §922(g)(3) decision for a Michigan user was not located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE].

12.7.4 Practical summary for a Michigan consumer (law stated, not advice)

  • Michigan CPL law, on secondary sources, does not itself bar a medical patient from holding a CPL; federal law, on the current (pre-final-draft) Form 4473 and ATF guidance, treats regular marihuana users — medical and adult-use — as prohibited persons for dealer purchase and possession.
  • Hemani narrows status-only in-home possession prosecutions without a danger showing; it does not create a purchase right.
  • The draft Form 4473 medical exclusion, if finalised, would change the dealer-purchase form position for state-law-compliant medical users; it would not by itself decide possession prosecutions, CPL revocation, or employment/housing consequences.
  • A person in this position needs advice on their specific facts (regularity/recency of use, medical vs adult-use track, home possession vs carrying, dealer purchase vs existing possession) — this dossier does not give it.

12.8 Pet and veterinary products (CBD/THC for animals)

12.8.1 Veterinarians may consult — HB 5085 (2020), signed Dec 2020

  • Law: House Bill 5085 (Rep. Greg Markkanen, Hancock), passed by both chambers in Dec 2020 (Senate unanimously, per secondary reporting) and signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer in Dec 2020, "would update state law to make it clear that a veterinarian can consult with animal owners on the use of marihuana or CBD oil for the pet." Before HB 5085, veterinarians described advice on CBD/THC for pets as a legal grey area: clients asked, but offering advice was not expressly permitted. Sources: https://gophouse.org/posts/markkanens-plan-clearing-way-for-cbd-thc-treatments-for-pets-heads-to-governor and https://rss.investorbrandnetwork.com/cnw-full/420-with-cnw-michigan-governor-approves-bill-that-allows-veterinarians-to-discuss-marijuana-cbd-treatments-for-pets/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary/legislative summaries; the Public Act number and MCL citation for HB 5085 were not verified in this pass [VERIFY] — do not cite a PA/MCL number for it until legislature.mi.gov is checked].
  • What HB 5085 does and does not do: It permits consultation/discussion (including recommending for or against a product, on secondary summaries). It does not create a Michigan veterinary cannabis licence, does not authorise a veterinarian to dispense marihuana product from a clinic as a retailer, does not make a veterinary cannabis product FDA-approved, and does not set a dose. A veterinarian's consultation is not a substitute for a licensed retail purchase by the owner, and a THC product for a pet must still come through a lawful channel for the owner (adult-use retailer for an adult owner, or medical channel for a registered patient owner — a pet is not itself a registered patient).
  • No Michigan veterinary cannabis prescribing/dispensing regime was located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE as a regime]. Do not describe Michigan as having "veterinary medical marijuana cards" or a pet registry — none was found.

12.8.2 What may be sold for animals — feed ban, supplement discretion, no approved drug

  • Commercial animal feed (including pet food/treats): NO. MDARD's hemp-in-feed guidance states: "hemp and hemp-derived products are not approved feed ingredients. This includes feeds intended for livestock, pets (including pet treats), or any other animal." A person therefore may not sell or distribute commercial feed products containing hemp or hemp-derived products, including CBD. Source: MDARD bulletin via https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/MIDARD/bulletins/29be2d7 — accessed 2026-10-28 (GovDelivery reproduction of MDARD guidance).
  • Supplements (not commercial feed) — regulatory discretion, case-by-case: The same MDARD guidance states supplements (not commercial feed) such as CBD oil and other hemp/hemp-derived products can be sold, that "regulatory discretion is used to regulate these types of products at this time," and that enforcement varies by label claims and marketing, "including no enforcement at all" in some cases. Hemp products making drug claims are not permitted and are subject to regulatory action. Same MDARD bulletin.
  • Owner supplementing their own pet: MDARD states "a person can choose to supplement their own pet's food with hemp or hemp-derived products like CBD oil, but safe levels for animal consumption have not been established." Same bulletin. That "safe levels not established" point is the operative consumer warning in this section; no dose is stated in this dossier.
  • Livestock fed hemp: MDARD states it does not regulate commodities that have undergone normal harvesting practices, are not intermixed/chemically changed or are unadulterated, but meat, eggs, milk and other food products obtained from livestock fed hemp cannot enter commerce. Same bulletin.
  • FDA approval — none for animals in the U.S.: A peer-reviewed veterinary review states: "as of this writing, there are no hemp- or marijuana-derived foods, drugs, or supplements approved for use in animals in the US." Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8003882/ — accessed 2026-10-28. That review also notes Michigan's HB 5085 consultation law as the most recent state veterinary-consultation legislation at its writing. No FDA-approved veterinary CBD/THC drug was located in this pass; any product marketed as a veterinary drug without FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine approval is making an unapproved-drug claim on the MDARD framework above.
  • THC risk to pets (general, no dose): Secondary veterinary summaries warn that marihuana-derived oil can intoxicate a pet (difficulty walking/eating, need for veterinary support) if overused, while hemp-derived CBD carries a much lower intoxication risk — but that risk comparison is secondary and dose-free here. Source: https://furryfootsteps.com/new-medicine-cabinet-cbd-oil-pets/ — accessed 2026-10-28 [secondary; veterinary toxicology guidance [VERIFY] before any clinical statement]. Pet owners should discuss any CBD/THC product with their veterinarian (now expressly permitted under §12.8.1) rather than relying on product marketing or internet dosing charts, which this dossier does not reproduce.

12.8.3 Licensed products for animals — none identified as a Michigan licence category

No Michigan CRA licence category for "pet cannabis products," no MDARD pet-product registration, and no Michigan-approved pet CBD/THC product list was located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE]. Products sold for pets in Michigan are therefore either (a) general-retail hemp supplements sold under MDARD's discretionary framework (§12.8.2), (b) adult-use marihuana products lawfully purchased by an adult owner and then given to a pet on veterinary advice (a use the product was not licensed/tested for as a veterinary drug — flagged, not endorsed), or (c) unlawful commercial feed/treats (§12.8.2). The dossier does not endorse (b) as a veterinary use; it records that no veterinary-licensed product category exists to endorse.

12.9 Medical cannabis in schools

12.9.1 Current law: no school administration, and possession/consumption on school grounds is not authorised

  • MRTMA bar: MCL 333.27954(1)(h) provides MRTMA does not authorise "possessing marihuana accessories or possessing or consuming marihuana on the grounds of a public or private school where children attend classes in preschool programs, kindergarten programs, or grades 1 through 12, in a school bus, or on the grounds of any correctional facility." Source: MCL 333.27954 via https://codes.findlaw.com/mi/chapter-333-health/mi-comp-laws-333-27954/ — accessed 2026-10-28. That bar covers accessories as well as marihuana itself, and covers school buses as well as grounds.
  • MMMA bar, by the same logic: The MMMA does not require a school to permit medical use on campus, and no MMMA provision located in this pass creates a school-administration right. MMMA §7 (MCL 333.26427) lists activities the Act does not authorise/require accommodation for, including operating a vehicle while under the influence and (by the §7(c) structure) workplace/school accommodation questions — but the specific MMMA school-administration text was not re-verified in this pass [VERIFY]; the firm ground in this section is the MRTMA §4(1)(h) bar plus the absence of an enacted school-administration law in §12.9.2.
  • Paediatric patients exist, but school access does not follow from registration: Since 2008, minors may be registered paediatric patients (with two-physician certification and a custodial parent/guardian as registered caregiver; Run 1 Part 1, §1.4.2). Registration entitles the patient/caregiver to MMMA protections outside school grounds; it does not entitle the student to possess or consume on school grounds or on a school bus under current law as sourced here.
  • Current reported practice (secondary, not a statute): Secondary reporting on "Jayden's Law" (below) describes the current workaround as: a registered paediatric patient who needs a dose during the school day must be checked out of school and moved off school grounds by a parent/guardian before receiving the product, then signed back in — with resulting missed instruction time, stigma and parental burden. Source: https://four20post.com/2023/10/dems-introduce-jaydens-law-for-school-administered-medical-marijuana/ — accessed 2026-10-28. The "1,000 feet away" detail in that reporting is a reported practice description, not a statutory distance rule located in this pass [VERIFY] — do not present "1,000 feet" as the school-administration statute. The 1,000-foot figure that is statutory in Michigan cannabis law is the MRTMA §9 establishment-to-school buffer (Run 1 Part 1, §1.6.4), a different rule.
  • School discipline / district policy: No officially sourced Michigan school-district policy on medical marihuana (possession, discipline, or accommodation) was located in this pass [UNAVAILABLE]. District student codes of conduct, which commonly prohibit drugs on campus, and Michigan school-discipline law were not reviewed district-by-district. Do not cite any district as an example on this pass. A district policy cannot override the MRTMA §4(1)(h) state bar, and a district policy purporting to permit on-campus possession/consumption would conflict with that bar on the text as quoted.

12.9.2 Pending, not law: "Jayden's Law" — reintroduced, not enacted (status after 2023 [VERIFY])

  • What it would do (as introduced): A bill package reintroduced 28 Sept 2023 by Reps. Jimmie Wilson Jr. (Ypsilanti) and Dylan Wegela (Garden City), referred to the House Regulatory Reform Committee, modelled on Illinois' "Ashley's Law" (2018), would allow registered paediatric patients to receive medical marihuana on school campuses — with schools mandated to establish administration rules, designated staff supervising administration, a written treatment plan from the parent/guardian, supervision during administration, and annual proof of the student's medical card; products described as edibles, beverages and other low-THC products, administered like other student medication (nurse's/administration office), not by smoking on campus. Sources: https://four20post.com/2023/10/dems-introduce-jaydens-law-for-school-administered-medical-marijuana/ and https://wbckfm.com/ixp/690/p/proposed-michigan-law-could-allow-kindergarteners-to-use-cannabis-in-schools/ (identifying the package as House Bill 5063 in the 2023 reporting) — accessed 2026-10-28.
  • History: The package was previously introduced in 2021 (former Rep. Alex Garza) and in 2019 (Rep. Kara Hope). Source: Four20 Post, same URL. No enactment was located in this pass, and the post-2023 status (reintroduction in the 2025–2026 session, committee action, or lapse) was not verified on legislature.mi.gov [VERIFY] — do not state Jayden's Law as current law, as pending in a specific 2026 committee, or as dead, until the bill history is checked. The compiled dossier should carry Jayden's Law only as "introduced 2023, not enacted on sources reviewed; 2025–2026 status [VERIFY]."
  • What Jayden's Law would NOT do even if enacted (on its introduced description): It would not authorise adult-use possession by students, smoking on campus, student self-administration without supervision, or possession by non-registered students. Those limits are in the introduced description itself (registered paediatric patients only, designated-staff supervision, written authorisation with timing/purpose). Secondary summaries that describe the bill as "allowing kindergarteners to smoke at school" misstate the introduced text and must not be repeated.

12.9.3 School-adjacent rules that are sometimes confused with school administration

  • Establishment buffer (not administration): A marihuana establishment may not be sited within 1,000 feet of a pre-existing K–12 school unless the municipality reduces the buffer (MRTMA §9, MCL 333.27959, as summarised in Run 1 Part 1, §1.6.4 — [VERIFY] exact text). That is a zoning/licensing rule for businesses, not a rule about students' medication.
  • Drug-free school zones / enhanced penalties: Michigan Public Health Code drug provisions (e.g. MCL 333.7410, delivery within 1,000 feet of school property — cited in secondary possession summaries) create enhanced penalties for delivery near schools. Those provisions were not re-verified in this pass [VERIFY] and are not stated as a school-administration rule here; they are listed only to prevent confusion with §12.9.1's possession/consumption bar.
  • CBD in schools: No Michigan law located in this pass separately authorises CBD administration in schools. Hemp-derived CBD that is not marihuana under the MRTMA §3 THC definition is not covered by the §4(1)(h) marihuana bar on its face, but school medication policies, the FDA status of the product, and district rules still govern whether a school will store/administer it — [UNAVAILABLE] as a statewide CBD-in-schools rule. Do not state that CBD is "allowed in Michigan schools" on the basis that it is not marihuana.
